traps.too_broad: Too broad: claims more than the text supports
traps.too_narrow: Too narrow: a detail, not the whole point
traps.not_in_text: Not in the text: brings in an idea the text never states
traps.reversed: Reversed: flips the relationship or the author's view
traps.true_irrelevant: True but irrelevant: accurate, but does not answer the question
traps.wrong_tone: Wrong tone or shade: a near-synonym that does not fit the context
traps.wrong_logic: Wrong logic: the wrong relationship between ideas
traps.misses_goal: Misses the goal: uses the notes but not for the stated purpose
traps.grammar_rule: Grammar rule broken: does not follow Standard English conventions

levels._note: Papers split each type's items by difficulty: lowest third to m2_easy, middle third to m1, highest third to m2_hard (pipeline/assemble_forms.py). validate.py checks mean difficulty m2_easy < m1 < m2_hard.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Honeybees tell their hive mates where to find food by performing a movement called the waggle ______ angle of the dance shows the direction of the food, and the length of each waggle shows how far away the food is.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: dance, the
choices.B: dance the
choices.C: dance. The
choices.D: dance and the

explanation.why: "Honeybees tell their hive mates … called the waggle dance" is a complete sentence, and "the angle of the dance shows the direction of the food …" is another complete sentence. Two independent clauses need a strong boundary, such as a period, between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.C: Correct. A period ends the first independent clause, and the second one starts as a new sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Kintsugi is a Japanese method of repairing broken pottery with lacquer dusted with powdered gold. Instead of hiding the cracks, the ______ them, treating the damage as part of the object's history.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: method highlights
choices.B: method, highlights
choices.C: method; highlights
choices.D: method: highlights

explanation.why: "The method" is the subject of the sentence and "highlights" is its verb. No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, so nothing goes between "method" and "highlights."
explanation.A: Correct. The subject "the method" flows straight into its verb "highlights" with no punctuation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A single comma can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses; here it would cut the subject off from its verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "Instead of hiding the cracks, the method" is not one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Karakoram Highway, which links Pakistan and China, climbs to more than 4,600 meters at the Khunjerab ______ it is one of the highest paved international roads in the world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Pass,
choices.B: Pass;
choices.C: Pass and
choices.D: Pass

explanation.why: The text has two complete sentences: "The Karakoram Highway … climbs to more than 4,600 meters at the Khunjerab Pass" and "it is one of the highest paved international roads in the world." Two independent clauses can be joined with a semicolon.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The axolotl, a salamander native to a few lakes and canals near Mexico ______ can regrow lost limbs, parts of its heart, and even sections of its spinal cord. Unlike most salamanders, however, it normally spends its whole life in the water, keeping its feathery external gills even as an adult.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: City
choices.B: City;
choices.C: City—
choices.D: City,

explanation.why: "A salamander native to a few lakes and canals near Mexico City" is extra information that describes the axolotl. It opens with a comma after "axolotl," so it must close with a comma too before the verb "can regrow."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The axolotl" from its verb "can regrow."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "axolotl" and completes the pair around the extra information.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Indian physicist Jagadish Chandra Bose, remembered for his pioneering experiments with radio waves, later turned his attention to plants, arguing that their responses to light, touch, and temperature could be measured as precisely as those of animals. The crescograph—an instrument he designed to magnify the minute movements of a growing plant by a factor of about ten ______ allowed him to record changes in growth rate that would otherwise have been far too small to detect.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: thousand,
choices.B: thousand—
choices.C: thousand;
choices.D: thousand

explanation.why: The words between "The crescograph" and "allowed" are extra information describing the instrument. That information opens with a dash, so it must close with a matching dash before the main verb "allowed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a dash can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Correct. The second dash closes the pair of dashes around the extra information, and the subject "The crescograph" connects to its verb "allowed."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "The crescograph" from its verb "allowed," and what comes before it is not an independent clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs into the main verb "allowed."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Although Ludwig van Beethoven had lost nearly all of his hearing by the time he completed his Ninth Symphony in ______ the work is among the most ambitious he ever attempted: its final movement adds vocal soloists and a full chorus to the orchestra, an unusual choice for a symphony at the time. Scholars generally credit the achievement to an inner ear trained by decades of composing, which let him imagine sounds he could no longer hear.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

explanation.why: The first sentence begins with "Although," so everything up to "in 1824" is a dependent clause, and "the work is among the most ambitious he ever attempted" is the main clause. A dependent clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. A comma correctly links the introductory "Although" clause to the main clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Although" clause is dependent.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave "Although Ludwig van Beethoven … in 1824" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the "Although" clause is not one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Ada Lovelace's notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, a general-purpose mechanical computer that Babbage designed but never ______ appended to her 1843 English translation of an article about the machine by the Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea. Running to roughly three times the length of the article itself, the notes include a step-by-step method for calculating Bernoulli numbers, which many historians describe as the first published computer program.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: completed; were
choices.B: completed—were
choices.C: completed, were
choices.D: completed were

explanation.why: The subject of the first sentence is "Ada Lovelace's notes," and its verb is "were appended." In between, "a general-purpose mechanical computer that Babbage designed but never completed" is extra information about the Analytical Engine. It opens with a comma after "Engine," so it must close with a comma before "were."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Ada Lovelace's notes" from its verb "were appended," and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.C: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "Engine," setting off the extra information so the subject connects to "were appended."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and the verb "were" seems to belong to "Babbage designed but never completed."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Sigiriya, a granite outcrop rising some 180 meters above the plains of central Sri Lanka, was transformed in the late fifth century CE into a royal stronghold by King Kashyapa, who ringed its base with terraced gardens, pools, and moats. Halfway up the rock, visitors today pass through the remains of a monumental ______ pair of enormous paws, built of brick and plaster, that once belonged to a lion figure through whose open mouth the final staircase climbed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: gateway; a
choices.B: gateway a
choices.C: gateway. A
choices.D: gateway: a

explanation.why: "Halfway up the rock, visitors today pass through the remains of a monumental gateway" is a complete independent clause. What follows, "a pair of enormous paws … that once belonged to a lion figure …," is a long noun phrase, not a clause: "belonged" and "climbed" sit inside relative clauses, so it has no main verb of its own. It explains what the gateway is, and a colon after an independent clause is the right mark to introduce such an explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a pair of enormous paws … that once belonged to a lion figure" has no main verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the explanation runs straight into "gateway" and the sentence can't be read clearly.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave "A pair of enormous paws … the final staircase climbed" as a sentence fragment, because it has no main verb.
explanation.D: Correct. A colon follows the independent clause and introduces the phrase that explains what the gateway is.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Tardigrades are tiny animals, usually less than a millimeter long, that live in moss, soil, and ocean ______ they begin to dry out, they pull in their legs, curl into a shape called a tun, and slow their body processes almost to a stop. In this state, some tardigrades can survive for years without water.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: sediment when
choices.B: sediment and when
choices.C: sediment, when
choices.D: sediment. When

explanation.why: "Tardigrades are tiny animals … that live in moss, soil, and ocean sediment" is a complete sentence. "When they begin to dry out, they pull in their legs … and slow their body processes" is a second complete sentence: the "When" clause introduces its main clause, "they pull in their legs." Two independent clauses need a strong boundary, such as a period, between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a period, the two independent clauses are joined only by the comma after "out," which creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.D: Correct. A period ends the first independent clause, and the second sentence begins with its introductory "When" clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Deosai Plains, a high plateau in the Gilgit-Baltistan region of northern ______ sit at an average height of about 4,000 meters above sea level. For much of the year the plains are covered in snow, but in summer they fill with wildflowers. The area is also an important home for the rare Himalayan brown bear.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Pakistan
choices.B: Pakistan—
choices.C: Pakistan,
choices.D: Pakistan;

explanation.why: "A high plateau in the Gilgit-Baltistan region of northern Pakistan" is extra information that describes the Deosai Plains. It opens with a comma after "Plains," so it must close with a comma before the verb "sit."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "sit."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.C: Correct. The closing comma matches the opening comma after "Plains" and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The Deosai Plains" from its verb "sit."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sea otters spend much of their lives floating on their backs in coastal waters. To open hard-shelled prey such as clams and sea urchins, an otter often rests a flat stone on its chest and repeatedly ______ the shell against the stone until the shell cracks.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: strikes
choices.B: strikes—
choices.C: strikes,
choices.D: strikes:

explanation.why: "Strikes" is a verb, and "the shell" is its object: the shell is the thing the otter strikes. No punctuation should come between a verb and its object.
explanation.A: Correct. The verb "strikes" leads straight into its object, "the shell," with no punctuation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A dash can't separate the verb "strikes" from its object, "the shell."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "strikes" from its object, "the shell."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and it can't come between a verb and its object.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: More than 5,000 years ago, scribes in Mesopotamia began writing by pressing the cut end of a reed into soft ______ each press left a small wedge-shaped mark. The script is now called cuneiform, from the Latin word cuneus, meaning "wedge."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: clay, and
choices.B: clay
choices.C: clay and,
choices.D: clay,

explanation.why: "Scribes in Mesopotamia began writing … into soft clay" and "each press left a small wedge-shaped mark" are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the conjunction "and" is a standard way to join two independent clauses.
explanation.A: Correct. A comma plus "and" correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, the comma goes before "and," not after it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the late 1950s, the Brazilian ______ Niemeyer designed many of the most important buildings in Brasília, the country's new capital. His National Congress building, with two tall towers rising beside a dome and a bowl-shaped structure, became a symbol of the city.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: architect, Oscar
choices.B: architect; Oscar
choices.C: architect Oscar
choices.D: architect: Oscar

explanation.why: "Oscar Niemeyer" tells which Brazilian architect the sentence means, so the name is essential information and is not set off with punctuation. The subject is "the Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer," and its verb is "designed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The name is essential, so it isn't set off with commas, and a single comma here would also wrongly separate parts of the subject.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but "In the late 1950s, the Brazilian architect" is not an independent clause.
explanation.C: Correct. No punctuation is used, because the name "Oscar Niemeyer" is essential to identify the architect.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "In the late 1950s, the Brazilian architect" is not one.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Saffron, one of the most expensive spices in the world, comes from the saffron crocus flower. Producing it is slow because almost every step is done by hand. Workers must complete three main ______ picking the flowers early in the morning, removing the thin red threads from each flower, and drying the threads with gentle heat.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: tasks;
choices.B: tasks:
choices.C: tasks.
choices.D: tasks

explanation.why: "Workers must complete three main tasks" is a complete independent clause, and what follows is a list that names those tasks. A colon placed after an independent clause is the right mark to introduce such a list.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but the list of tasks has no subject and main verb of its own.
explanation.B: Correct. A colon follows the independent clause and introduces the list of three tasks.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave the list "Picking the flowers … with gentle heat" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the list runs straight into "tasks," and the sentence can't be read clearly.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In Dhaka, Bangladesh, many cycle rickshaws are decorated with hand-painted pictures of film stars, animals, and village ______ the bright designs help each rickshaw stand out on the city's crowded streets. In 2023, UNESCO recognized Dhaka's rickshaws and rickshaw painting as an important part of the world's cultural heritage.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: scenes;
choices.B: scenes and
choices.C: scenes
choices.D: scenes,

explanation.why: "Many cycle rickshaws are decorated with … village scenes" and "the bright designs help each rickshaw stand out" are both independent clauses. A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.A: Correct. A semicolon correctly joins the two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. When "and" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Titan, which is the largest of Saturn's moons and is even bigger than the planet ______ is the only moon in the solar system known to have a thick atmosphere. Its surface holds lakes and seas, but they are filled with liquid methane and ethane rather than water.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Mercury;
choices.B: Mercury,
choices.C: Mercury
choices.D: Mercury—

explanation.why: The clause "which is the largest of Saturn's moons and is even bigger than the planet Mercury" is extra information about Titan. It opens with a comma after "Titan," so it must close with a comma before the main verb "is."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Titan" from its verb "is."
explanation.B: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "Titan" and sets off the "which" clause, so the subject "Titan" connects to its verb "is."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the "which" clause runs straight into the main verb "is," and the sentence can't be read clearly.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The "which" clause opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For many years, researchers have asked why the Nazca people of southern Peru made enormous drawings on the desert ______ lines, created about 2,000 years ago, form shapes such as a hummingbird, a monkey, and a spider. Many of the figures are easiest to see from the air or from nearby hills.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: floor, the
choices.B: floor. The
choices.C: floor the
choices.D: floor? The

explanation.why: The first sentence is a statement that reports a question (researchers "have asked why…"); it is not itself a direct question. A statement ends with a period, and the next sentence begins with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. The first sentence is a statement, so it ends with a period, and the new sentence begins with "The."
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.D: Incorrect. The sentence only reports what researchers asked; it is a statement, not a direct question, so it doesn't take a question mark.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Homing pigeons can find their way back to their lofts from hundreds of kilometers away. On sunny days, the birds appear to rely mainly on the position of the ______ pigeons also seem to sense Earth's magnetic field, which may help guide them when clouds hide the sky.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Sun, however,
choices.B: Sun however,
choices.C: Sun; however,
choices.D: Sun, however;

explanation.why: "The birds appear to rely mainly on the position of the Sun" and "pigeons also seem to sense Earth's magnetic field" are both independent clauses. "However" begins the second clause, so a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma before "however" can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation before "however," the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.C: Correct. The semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and the comma after "however" sets off the transition that begins the second clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "However" introduces the contrast in the second clause, so the semicolon must come before it, not after it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A sourdough starter—a simple mixture of flour and water that becomes home to wild yeast and ______ can be kept alive for many years if it is fed fresh flour and water regularly. Bakers add a portion of the starter to bread dough, where the yeast produces the gas that makes the bread rise.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: bacteria;
choices.B: bacteria
choices.C: bacteria—
choices.D: bacteria,

explanation.why: The words between "A sourdough starter" and "can be kept" are extra information describing the starter. That information opens with a dash, so it must close with a matching dash before the verb "can be kept."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "A sourdough starter" from its verb "can be kept."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "can be kept."
explanation.C: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the extra information, so the subject "A sourdough starter" connects to its verb "can be kept."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a dash can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Honey can stay safe to eat for a very long time when it is stored in a sealed container. The low water content and natural acidity of ______ make it very difficult for bacteria and molds to grow. Bees help create these conditions by fanning the nectar with their wings, which makes much of its water evaporate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: honey,
choices.B: honey
choices.C: honey;
choices.D: honey:

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is "The low water content and natural acidity of honey," and its verb is "make." No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, even when the subject is long.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A single comma can't separate the subject from its verb, "make."
explanation.B: Correct. The long subject flows straight into its verb, "make," with no punctuation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses; here it would cut the subject off from its verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "The low water content and natural acidity of honey" is not one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Chess is thought to have developed from chaturanga, a game played in India by around the sixth century CE. The pieces of chaturanga stood for the four divisions of an ancient army: foot soldiers, horsemen, elephants, and chariots. From India the game spread to ______ it became known as shatranj. Centuries later, it reached Europe.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Persia, where
choices.B: Persia; where
choices.C: Persia. Where
choices.D: Persia, it

explanation.why: "From India the game spread to Persia" is an independent clause. "Where it became known as shatranj" is a dependent clause that adds information about Persia, so it is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. A comma correctly attaches the dependent "where" clause to the main clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "where it became known as shatranj" is a dependent clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave "Where it became known as shatranj" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It became known as shatranj" is an independent clause, and a comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Glass frogs live in the rainforests of Central and South America. Many species have see-through skin on their ______ a feature that lets an observer watch the frog's heart beating. Researchers have also found that sleeping glass frogs hide most of their red blood cells in their livers, which makes the frogs even harder to spot.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: bellies
choices.B: bellies,
choices.C: bellies;
choices.D: bellies.

explanation.why: "Many species have see-through skin on their bellies" is a complete independent clause. "A feature that lets an observer watch the frog's heart beating" is a noun phrase that adds extra information about that skin, so it is set off with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a comma, the extra information runs straight into "bellies," and the sentence can't be read clearly.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma correctly sets off the extra information at the end of the sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a feature that lets an observer watch the frog's heart beating" has no main verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave "A feature that lets an observer watch the frog's heart beating" as a sentence fragment.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In January 1610, the Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei pointed his telescope at Jupiter and noticed several small points of light near the planet. After watching them change position over several nights, he ______ they were moons orbiting Jupiter. It was the first clear evidence that objects in the sky could orbit a body other than Earth.

choices.A: concluded: that
choices.B: concluded; that
choices.C: concluded that
choices.D: concluded, that

explanation.why: "Concluded" is a verb, and "that they were moons orbiting Jupiter" is its object: it tells what Galileo concluded. No punctuation should come between a verb and its object.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon can't separate the verb "concluded" from its object, the "that" clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but "that they were moons orbiting Jupiter" is not an independent clause.
explanation.C: Correct. The verb "concluded" leads straight into its object, "that they were moons," with no punctuation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "concluded" from its object, the "that" clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many lodgepole pines produce cones that are sealed shut with a sticky resin. These cones can stay closed on a tree for years. When the heat of a forest fire finally melts the ______ cones open and drop their seeds onto the freshly burned ground, where young trees can grow in the sunlight.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: resin. The
choices.B: resin, the
choices.C: resin: the
choices.D: resin; the

explanation.why: The third sentence begins with "When," so "When the heat of a forest fire finally melts the resin" is a dependent clause. "The cones open and drop their seeds" is the main clause. A dependent clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A period would leave "When the heat of a forest fire finally melts the resin" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma correctly links the introductory "When" clause to the main clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the "When" clause is not one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "When" clause is dependent.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The ______ a hotel in the village of Jukkasjärvi in northern Sweden, is built again every winter from blocks of ice cut from the nearby Torne River. Artists design new rooms each year, and most of the building melts back into the river in spring.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Icehotel—
choices.B: Icehotel,
choices.C: Icehotel;
choices.D: Icehotel

explanation.why: "A hotel in the village of Jukkasjärvi in northern Sweden" is extra information that describes the Icehotel. It closes with a comma after "Sweden," so it must open with a comma after "Icehotel."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The extra information closes with a comma, so it can't open with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Correct. The opening comma matches the comma after "Sweden" and completes the pair around the extra information.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but "The Icehotel" is not an independent clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without an opening comma, the extra information has only a closing comma, which wrongly separates the subject from its verb "is built."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Visitors who kayak at night in Mosquito Bay, on the Puerto Rican island of Vieques, often ask the same question: why does the water glow when a paddle moves through ______ answer is tiny organisms called dinoflagellates, which give off a blue-green light when the water around them is disturbed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it? The
choices.B: it the
choices.C: it. The
choices.D: it, the

explanation.why: The words after the colon, "why does the water glow when a paddle moves through it," form a direct question, so the sentence ends with a question mark. "The answer is tiny organisms …" is a new sentence and begins with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Correct. A direct question ends with a question mark, and the next sentence begins with a capital letter.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the question runs straight into the next independent clause (a run-on sentence).
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sentence ends with a direct question ("why does the water glow …"), so it needs a question mark, not a period.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma can't end a direct question or join it to the next independent clause; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many Sherpa people live in the high valleys of Nepal near Mount Everest, where the air holds far less oxygen than it does at sea level. Studies suggest that the bodies of many Sherpas use oxygen very ______ can often work hard in thin air that would quickly exhaust visitors from lower places.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: efficiently, they
choices.B: efficiently, so they
choices.C: efficiently so, they
choices.D: efficiently they

explanation.why: "The bodies of many Sherpas use oxygen very efficiently" and "they can often work hard in thin air" are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the conjunction "so" correctly joins them and shows cause and effect.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma plus "so" correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "so" joins two independent clauses, the comma goes before "so," not after it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Much of the Netherlands lies at or below sea level. Over many centuries, the Dutch created polders (low-lying areas of land reclaimed from the sea, lakes, or ______ by building dikes around them and pumping out the water. For hundreds of years, windmills powered many of these pumps.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: marshes)
choices.B: marshes;
choices.C: marshes
choices.D: marshes—

explanation.why: The definition of "polders" is extra information that opens with a parenthesis before "low-lying." It must close with a matching parenthesis before the sentence continues with "by building dikes."
explanation.A: Correct. The closing parenthesis matches the opening one and completes the pair around the definition.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon can't close a parenthetical element; the opening parenthesis must be matched by a closing one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing parenthesis, the definition is never closed and runs into the rest of the sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a parenthesis can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every summer, Ines helped her grandfather sort the old photographs he kept in a shoebox under his bed. He had never labeled a single one, yet he could name every face. He held up a picture of a young woman standing beside a bicycle and smiled. "This ______ he said, "is your grandmother at nineteen."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: one"
choices.B: one,"
choices.C: one",
choices.D: one."

explanation.why: The grandfather's sentence, "This is your grandmother at nineteen," is interrupted by "he said." The first part of the quotation ends with a comma, and in American English that comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma is needed to separate the quotation from the speaker tag "he said."
explanation.B: Correct. The comma before "he said" goes inside the closing quotation mark, as American English requires.
explanation.C: Incorrect. In American English, a comma always goes inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The quoted sentence continues after "he said," so the first part can't end with a period.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before the 1840s, rubber goods had a serious flaw: they turned sticky in hot weather and stiff in cold weather. In 1839, the American inventor Charles Goodyear found that heating rubber with sulfur kept it firm and flexible in both heat and cold. He patented the process in ______ he made little money from it and was deep in debt when he died in 1860.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.B: 1844 but

explanation.why: "He patented the process in 1844" and "he made little money from it" are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the conjunction "but" correctly joins them and shows the contrast.
explanation.A: Incorrect. When "but" joins two independent clauses, the comma goes before "but," not after it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. When "but" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.C: Correct. A comma plus "but" correctly joins the two independent clauses.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: African wild dogs, which live and hunt in close-knit packs in parts of southern and eastern ______ seem to decide when to set off on a hunt by sneezing. In a study of packs in Botswana, the more often the dogs sneezed during a gathering, the more likely the pack was to leave and hunt.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Africa;
choices.B: Africa:
choices.C: Africa,
choices.D: Africa

explanation.why: The clause "which live and hunt in close-knit packs in parts of southern and eastern Africa" is extra information about the dogs. It opens with a comma after "dogs," so it must close with a comma before the verb "seem."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "African wild dogs" from its verb "seem."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the words before it are not one.
explanation.C: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "dogs" and sets off the "which" clause, so the subject connects to its verb "seem."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the "which" clause runs straight into the main verb "seem."

items.subject: science
items.passage: The ginkgo tree is sometimes called a living fossil because fossil leaves almost identical to its own are tens of millions of years old. Because the tree tolerates polluted air and poor soil, it is now planted along streets in many cities, ______ New York, Tokyo, and Seoul.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: including;
choices.B: including—
choices.C: including:
choices.D: including

explanation.why: "Including" leads directly into the examples it introduces, "New York, Tokyo, and Seoul." No punctuation should come between "including" and those examples.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but "New York, Tokyo, and Seoul" is not an independent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A dash can't separate "including" from the examples it introduces.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and it can't come between "including" and the examples it introduces.
explanation.D: Correct. "Including" flows straight into the list of cities with no punctuation.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Rani ki Vav, a stepwell built in the eleventh century in Patan, in the Indian state of Gujarat, descends seven levels below the ground to reach the water table. Its walls—decorated with hundreds of carved figures of gods, goddesses, dancers, and ______ were later buried under silt from a flooding river. That layer of mud protected the carvings for centuries, until archaeologists began clearing the site in the twentieth century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: musicians
choices.B: musicians,
choices.C: musicians—
choices.D: musicians;

explanation.why: The words between "Its walls" and "were later buried" are extra information describing the walls. That information opens with a dash, so it must close with a matching dash, even though the list inside it uses commas. The subject "Its walls" then connects to its verb "were buried."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "were buried."
explanation.B: Incorrect. This comma could continue the list inside the dashes, but it can't close extra information that opens with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.C: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the extra information, so the subject "Its walls" connects to its verb "were buried."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Its walls" from its verb "were buried."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Each year, bar-tailed godwits fly from Alaska to New Zealand without stopping, a journey of more than 11,000 kilometers across the Pacific Ocean that can take over a week. Although such a flight might seem to require stops for food and ______ birds neither eat nor drink along the way. Before leaving, they build up large stores of fat and shrink some of their digestive organs, which lightens the load they must carry.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: rest: the
choices.B: rest, the
choices.C: rest; the
choices.D: rest. The

explanation.why: The second sentence begins with "Although," so "Although such a flight might seem to require stops for food and rest" is a dependent clause. "The birds neither eat nor drink along the way" is the main clause. A dependent clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the "Although" clause is not one.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma correctly links the introductory "Although" clause to the main clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Although" clause is dependent.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave "Although such a flight might seem to require stops for food and rest" as a sentence fragment.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: For centuries, Inuit communities across the Arctic have built inuksuit, figures made of carefully stacked stones. Some inuksuit are shaped roughly like people, but most are simple piles or pillars. Each one usually carries a practical message for ______ location of a good fishing spot, the direction of a safe route across the ice, or the place where food has been stored.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: travelers the
choices.B: travelers. The
choices.C: travelers: the
choices.D: travelers; the

explanation.why: "Each one usually carries a practical message for travelers" is a complete independent clause. What follows is a list of noun phrases that explains what the message might be; the list has no main verb of its own. A colon after an independent clause is the right mark to introduce such an explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the list runs straight into "travelers," and the sentence can't be read clearly.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A period would leave "The location of a good fishing spot … or the place where food has been stored" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.C: Correct. A colon follows the independent clause and introduces the list that explains the message.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "the location of a good fishing spot … or the place where food has been stored" has no main verb.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mr. Adeyemi had repaired clocks in the same narrow shop for forty years, and he claimed he could diagnose most of them by sound alone. When a customer set a brass carriage clock on the counter, he did not reach for his tools. Instead he listened—head tilted, eyes half closed, one finger raised for ______ and then announced that the mainspring was nearly worn through.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: silence—
choices.B: silence
choices.C: silence;
choices.D: silence,

explanation.why: The description "head tilted, eyes half closed, one finger raised for silence" interrupts the sentence "he listened … and then announced." It opens with a dash after "listened," so it must close with a matching dash, even though the phrases inside it are separated by commas.
explanation.A: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the description, and the sentence continues with "and then announced."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the description is never set off, and "one finger raised for silence and then announced" can't be read correctly.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "and then announced that the mainspring was nearly worn through" is not one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This comma looks like the commas inside the description, but it can't close an interruption that opens with a dash; the two marks must match.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a giant hornet enters a nest of Japanese honeybees, hundreds of bees may surround it at once, forming a tight ball around the intruder. The bees then vibrate their flight muscles, raising the temperature inside the ball to about 46°C. The hornet cannot survive this ______ bees, which can tolerate temperatures a few degrees higher, usually do.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: heat, but, the
choices.B: heat; the
choices.C: heat, the
choices.D: heat the

explanation.why: "The hornet cannot survive this heat" and "the bees, which can tolerate temperatures a few degrees higher, usually do" are both independent clauses; the "which" clause inside the second one is extra information. A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma before "but" is enough to join the two independent clauses; no comma should follow "but."
explanation.B: Correct. A semicolon correctly joins the two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In Kathakali, a classical dance-drama from Kerala in southern India, the color of a performer's makeup signals what kind of character he or she is playing. The green face paint worn by actors who portray noble heroes such as the warrior prince ______ is known as pacha. Fierce or arrogant characters, by contrast, wear designs with bold patches of red or black.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Arjuna,
choices.B: Arjuna—
choices.C: Arjuna;
choices.D: Arjuna

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is the long phrase "The green face paint worn by actors who portray noble heroes such as the warrior prince Arjuna," and its verb is "is known." Because no comma comes before "such as," there is no opening mark to pair with, so nothing should separate "Arjuna" from the verb.
explanation.A: Incorrect. No comma comes before "such as," so this single comma doesn't close a pair; it only separates the subject from its verb "is known."
explanation.B: Incorrect. No dash comes earlier in the sentence, so this single dash doesn't close a pair; it only separates the subject from its verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon joins two independent clauses; here it would cut the subject off from its verb "is known."
explanation.D: Correct. The long subject flows straight into its verb, "is known," with no punctuation.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A gecko can run up a glass window and even hang from a ceiling by a single toe. Its toes are covered with millions of microscopic hairs, and each hair splits into hundreds of even tinier tips. These tips come so close to a surface that weak attractive forces form between their molecules and the molecules of the surface ______ the gecko can cling to almost anything without using glue or suction.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: itself. As a result;
choices.B: itself, as a result,
choices.C: itself as a result,
choices.D: itself; as a result,

explanation.why: "These tips come so close … the surface itself" is an independent clause, and "the gecko can cling to almost anything …" is another. "As a result" is a transitional phrase, not a conjunction, so it can't join the clauses with only a comma. A semicolon goes before it, and a comma follows it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; it can't separate the introductory phrase "As a result" from the rest of its own sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "As a result" is not a conjunction, so a comma before it can't join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation before "as a result," the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.D: Correct. The semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and the comma after "as a result" sets off the transitional phrase.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Archaeologists working at sites of the Indus Valley Civilization, in present-day Pakistan and northwestern India, have found thousands of small square seals carved from a soft stone called steatite. The most common image on these seals, a one-horned animal that researchers often call a ______ usually appears above a short line of Indus script. Because the script has never been deciphered, scholars still debate exactly how the seals were used.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: unicorn—
choices.B: unicorn;
choices.C: unicorn
choices.D: unicorn,

explanation.why: The phrase "a one-horned animal that researchers often call a unicorn" is extra information describing "The most common image." It opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb "appears."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a comma must close with a comma; a dash doesn't match the opening mark.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The most common image" from its verb "appears."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off and runs straight into the verb "appears."
explanation.D: Correct. The comma closes the extra information, so the subject "The most common image" connects cleanly to its verb "appears."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For three evenings, Mrs. Nwosu worked on Adaeze's graduation dress at the small table by the window, letting out the seams and raising the hem by two careful centimeters. When Adaeze finally tried it on, she turned slowly in front of the mirror and could not stop smiling. Mrs. Nwosu only nodded, but later that night Adaeze heard her tell her sister on the phone ______ the dress was the finest thing she had sewn all year.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: : that
choices.B: , that
choices.C: that
choices.D: ; that

explanation.why: "That the dress was the finest thing she had sewn all year" is what Mrs. Nwosu told her sister, so it works as the object of the verb "tell." No punctuation belongs between a verb and its object, even when a short phrase such as "on the phone" comes between them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and it can't come between a verb and its object.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "tell" from its object, the clause beginning with "that."
explanation.C: Correct. No punctuation separates the verb "tell" from the "that" clause that serves as its object.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "that the dress was …" is not one; it is the object of "tell."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the 1880s, the French painter Georges Seurat developed a technique that later became known as pointillism. Instead of blending colors on a palette, he applied them to the canvas as thousands of small, separate dots. The method depended on a simple ______ when the painting is seen from a distance, the viewer's eye merges neighboring dots, so that patches of pure color seem to blend into new shades.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: principle:
choices.B: principle,
choices.C: principle
choices.D: principle that:

explanation.why: "The method depended on a simple principle" is an independent clause, and what follows is another independent clause that explains what the principle is. A colon can introduce an explanation after a complete independent clause.
explanation.A: Correct. The colon follows a complete independent clause and introduces the explanation of the principle.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but "a simple principle that" leaves the clause unfinished.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Every summer, the city of Kandy, Sri Lanka, holds the Esala Perahera, a festival that lasts about ten days and includes a series of nighttime processions. Each procession brings together three main groups of performers: drummers, who set the pace for the whole ______ dancers, whose costumes glitter with beads and silver ornaments; and elephants, many of them draped in embroidered cloth and strings of lights.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: line,
choices.B: line;
choices.C: line:
choices.D: line

explanation.why: The colon introduces a list of three items, and each item already contains a comma ("drummers, who …" and "dancers, whose …"). When list items contain commas, semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon after "ornaments" shows. The same mark is needed after the first item.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Because the list items contain their own commas, a comma here would blur where the first item ends; semicolons must separate the items.
explanation.B: Correct. The semicolon separates the first list item from the second, matching the semicolon used between the second and third items.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon can introduce a list, but it can't separate one item in a list from the next.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the first list item runs straight into the second.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: About 1,000 years ago, Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was the largest city in North America north of Mexico. Its central feature—Monks Mound, an earthen platform that covers about fourteen acres and rises roughly thirty ______ was built by hand from basketloads of soil carried by workers over many generations. Archaeologists estimate that between 10,000 and 20,000 people may have lived in the city at its height.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: meters—
choices.B: meters
choices.C: meters,
choices.D: meters;

explanation.why: The information describing the central feature opens with a dash after "Its central feature," so it must close with a matching dash, even though it contains commas of its own. After the closing dash, the subject "Its central feature" connects to its verb "was built."
explanation.A: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the extra information, so the subject connects to its verb "was built."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs into the verb "was built."
explanation.C: Incorrect. This comma could seem to continue the description, but extra information that opens with a dash must close with a dash.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Its central feature" from its verb "was built."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Before her architecture students draw a single line, Professor Amara Diallo asks them two questions about any building they plan to design. The first is practical: what will people actually do inside it? The second is harder to answer: how should those people feel while they are ______ students often say that the second question changes their designs more than the first one does.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: there. Her
choices.B: there; her
choices.C: there? Her
choices.D: there, her

explanation.why: "How should those people feel while they are there" is a direct question, like "what will people actually do inside it?" in the sentence before, so it ends with a question mark. "Her students often say …" then begins a new sentence with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "How should those people feel …" asks a direct question, so it must end with a question mark, not a period.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon can't end a direct question; the question must close with a question mark.
explanation.C: Correct. The question mark ends the direct question, and the next sentence begins with a capital letter.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma can't end a question or join it to the next independent clause; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many hoverflies have bold yellow and black stripes that make them look like wasps or bees. Although these flies have no sting and pose no danger to a predator that catches ______ birds that have learned to fear wasps often leave them alone. The disguise does not need to be perfect, since even a moment of hesitation from a bird may give a fly time to escape.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: one:
choices.B: one.
choices.C: one;
choices.D: one,

explanation.why: The second sentence begins with "Although," so everything up to "catches one" is a dependent clause. The main clause is "birds that have learned to fear wasps often leave them alone." A dependent clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the "Although" clause is not one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A period would leave "Although these flies … catches one" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Although" clause is dependent.
explanation.D: Correct. The comma correctly links the introductory "Although" clause to the main clause.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every spring, Hamza spent his afternoons in his uncle's cramped workshop in Gujranwala, watching him build kites from tissue paper and thin strips of bamboo. Uncle Tariq, who had been making kites in the same small room for nearly thirty ______ never measured anything. He simply held a sheet of paper up to the light, bent a strip of bamboo between his fingers, and knew exactly where to cut.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: years—
choices.B: years;
choices.C: years
choices.D: years,

explanation.why: The clause "who had been making kites in the same small room for nearly thirty years" adds extra information about Uncle Tariq. It opens with a comma after "Uncle Tariq," so it must close with a comma before the verb "measured."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a comma must close with a comma; a dash doesn't match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Uncle Tariq" from its verb "never measured."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the "who" clause is never set off, and it seems to continue into "never measured anything."
explanation.D: Correct. The comma closes the nonessential "who" clause, so the subject "Uncle Tariq" connects to its verb "never measured."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the late 1100s and the 1200s, Ancestral Puebloan families at Mesa Verde, in what is now southwestern Colorado, built villages of stone and mortar inside shallow alcoves in the canyon walls. The largest of these cliff dwellings contained more than a hundred ______ by about 1300 the people had left the region and moved south. Archaeologists still debate why, though long droughts and growing conflict are among the most common explanations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: rooms; yet,
choices.B: rooms: yet
choices.C: rooms, yet
choices.D: rooms yet

explanation.why: "The largest of these cliff dwellings contained more than a hundred rooms" and "by about 1300 the people had left the region" are both independent clauses. When a coordinating conjunction such as "yet" joins two independent clauses, a comma goes before the conjunction and nothing separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The comma after "yet" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces, and a semicolon isn't used before a conjunction joining these clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon introduces an explanation or a list; it isn't used before a conjunction such as "yet" that links two contrasting clauses.
explanation.C: Correct. The comma and the coordinating conjunction "yet" correctly join the two independent clauses.
explanation.D: Incorrect. When "yet" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Welwitschia mirabilis, a plant found only in the Namib Desert of Namibia and Angola, grows just two leaves in its entire life. The leaves (which can keep growing from their base for many ______ become split and frayed at their tips as the desert wind whips them against the ground. Some individual plants are thought to be more than a thousand years old.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: centuries)
choices.B: centuries;
choices.C: centuries),
choices.D: centuries,

explanation.why: The words inside the parentheses add extra information about "The leaves." An opening parenthesis needs a closing parenthesis. After it, the subject "The leaves" must connect directly to its verb "become," with no other punctuation in between.
explanation.A: Correct. The closing parenthesis ends the extra information, and the subject "The leaves" connects directly to its verb "become."
explanation.B: Incorrect. An opening parenthesis must be closed with a parenthesis, and a semicolon can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The parenthesis is closed correctly, but the comma after it separates the subject "The leaves" from its verb "become."
explanation.D: Incorrect. An opening parenthesis must be closed with a parenthesis, not a comma.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the shallow lakes of the Valley of Mexico, Aztec farmers built chinampas, narrow rectangular plots made by piling layers of mud and plants inside fences of woven reeds. Trees planted along the edges helped hold each plot in place. Because the soil stayed rich and moist, farmers could harvest several crops a year, growing foods such ______ maize, beans, squash, and chili peppers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: as
choices.B: as;
choices.C: as,
choices.D: as:

explanation.why: "Such as" introduces examples that are part of the same sentence. No punctuation goes between "such as" and the examples that follow it.
explanation.A: Correct. No punctuation is needed between "such as" and the list of examples it introduces.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and neither "growing foods such as" nor the list is one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate "such as" from the examples it introduces.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; it can't come between "such as" and the examples.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Multan, a city in the Punjab province of Pakistan, is known for kashi, a style of glazed tilework in deep cobalt blue, turquoise, and white. For centuries, artisans there have painted flowers, vines, and geometric patterns onto clay tiles and fired them in ______ creating hard, glossy surfaces that keep their color for generations. Such tiles still decorate the walls of many of the city's shrines and mosques.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: kilns; creating
choices.B: kilns, creating
choices.C: kilns. Creating
choices.D: kilns, and creating

explanation.why: "Artisans there have painted … and fired them in kilns" is a complete independent clause. "Creating hard, glossy surfaces …" is a participial phrase with no subject of its own; it describes the result of the firing. A phrase like this is attached to the clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "creating hard, glossy surfaces …" has no subject or main verb.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma attaches the participial phrase "creating hard, glossy surfaces …" to the independent clause it describes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave "Creating hard, glossy surfaces …" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "And" should join matching parts, but "creating" doesn't match the verbs "have painted" and "fired," so the sentence becomes ungrammatical.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Giant sequoias, which grow naturally only on the western slopes of California's Sierra Nevada, can live for more than 3,000 years. Fires sweep through their forests every few decades, but mature trees usually survive ______ their bark, which can be more than half a meter thick, contains very little resin and helps shield the living wood inside from the heat.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them,
choices.B: them;
choices.C: them, and,
choices.D: them

explanation.why: "Fires sweep through their forests …, but mature trees usually survive them" is an independent clause, and "their bark … helps shield the living wood …" is another. A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. The semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma and "and" could join the clauses, but the comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1976, the voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed more than 4,000 kilometers from Hawaii to Tahiti without a compass or any other modern instrument. Its navigator, Mau Piailug of Micronesia, judged the canoe's direction from the stars, the ocean swells, and the flight of seabirds. The knowledge that allowed him to find a small island in the middle of the open ______ been passed down to him by his grandfather and other master navigators.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Pacific; had
choices.B: Pacific—had
choices.C: Pacific, had
choices.D: Pacific had

explanation.why: The subject of the last sentence is long: "The knowledge that allowed him to find a small island in the middle of the open Pacific." Its verb is "had been passed down." No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb, however long the subject is.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; here it would split the subject from its verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A single dash can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the subject "The knowledge …" from its verb "had been passed down."
explanation.D: Correct. No punctuation separates the long subject from its verb "had been passed down."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Just after midnight, Noor and her younger brother carried their grandfather's old telescope up to the flat roof of their apartment building. The meteor shower had already begun, but the city's lights washed out all but the brightest ______ they waited for their eyes to adjust, Noor showed her brother how to find the constellation Perseus, the point from which the streaks seemed to fly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: streaks while
choices.B: streaks. While,
choices.C: streaks, while
choices.D: streaks. While

explanation.why: "The meteor shower had already begun, but the city's lights washed out all but the brightest streaks" is a complete sentence. "While they waited for their eyes to adjust, Noor showed her brother …" is another complete sentence: a dependent "While" clause followed by the main clause "Noor showed her brother." A period should separate them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the first sentence runs into the second, creating a run-on sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The period is correct, but the comma after "While" wrongly separates the conjunction from the rest of its clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Noor showed her brother …" is an independent clause, so joining everything before it with commas creates a comma splice.
explanation.D: Correct. The period ends the first sentence, and the second begins with its introductory "While" clause.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For more than a century, the Olympic motto consisted of three Latin words, "Citius, Altius, Fortius," which Pierre de Coubertin proposed when the International Olympic Committee was founded in 1894. Coubertin had borrowed the phrase from his friend Henri Didon, a priest who used it as a motto for the athletes at his school. In English, the motto means ______ Higher, Stronger." In 2021, the committee added a fourth word, "Communiter," which means "Together."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: "Faster,
choices.B: : "Faster,
choices.C: "Faster;
choices.D: "Faster",

explanation.why: The translation "Faster, Higher, Stronger" is the object of the verb "means," so no punctuation comes between "means" and the opening quotation mark. Inside the quotation, the three words of the motto are separated by commas, just as they are in the Latin.
explanation.A: Correct. No punctuation separates "means" from its quoted object, and a comma separates the first two words of the motto.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon can't come between the verb "means" and its object, the quoted translation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate simple words in a short list; the words of the motto are separated by commas.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The quotation does not end after "Faster"; the closing quotation mark comes after "Stronger," so this mark is misplaced.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In Bhaktapur, a historic city in the Kathmandu Valley of Nepal, one public square is known simply as Pottery Square. On sunny mornings, its paving stones disappear beneath rows of drying clay pots. The potters who work there—many of whom learned to shape clay on a spinning wheel from their parents and ______ sell their bowls, lamps, and water jars to residents and visitors alike.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: grandparents;
choices.B: grandparents—
choices.C: grandparents,
choices.D: grandparents

explanation.why: The words after the dash, "many of whom learned to shape clay … from their parents and grandparents," add extra information about the potters. Because the information opens with a dash, it must close with a dash. Then the subject "The potters who work there" connects to its verb "sell."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The potters who work there" from its verb "sell."
explanation.B: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the extra information, so the subject connects to its verb "sell."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a dash must close with a dash, not a comma.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs into the verb "sell."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Sapporo Snow Festival in northern Japan began in 1950, when local high school students built six snow statues in Odori ______ modest beginning for an event that now draws about two million visitors each winter. Today, teams spend weeks shaping enormous sculptures of castles, animals, and famous buildings from packed snow and ice. The largest can stand more than fifteen meters tall and require thousands of truckloads of snow.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Park a
choices.B: Park, a
choices.C: Park; a
choices.D: Park. A

explanation.why: "A modest beginning for an event that now draws about two million visitors" is not a clause; it is a noun phrase that sums up the statue-building just described. A phrase like this is attached to the end of the sentence with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a comma, the summarizing phrase runs straight into "Odori Park," and the sentence no longer makes sense.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma attaches the summarizing noun phrase "a modest beginning …" to the sentence it comments on.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a modest beginning for an event …" is a noun phrase.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave "A modest beginning for an event …" as a sentence fragment.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1963, a Tanzanian student named Erasto Mpemba noticed that a warm ice cream mixture seemed to freeze faster than a cool one. Since then, the claim that hot water can freeze more quickly than cold water has become known as the Mpemba effect. Scientists still disagree about whether the effect is real or simply the result of differences in how experiments are set ______ careful studies have found no effect at all.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: up? Some
choices.B: up some
choices.C: up. Some
choices.D: up, some

explanation.why: "Scientists still disagree about whether the effect is real …" is a statement that reports a question indirectly; it is not itself a question, so it ends with a period. "Some careful studies have found no effect at all" is a new independent clause and starts a new sentence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. An indirect question introduced by "whether" is part of a statement, so it ends with a period, not a question mark.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.C: Correct. The period ends the statement containing the indirect question, and the next sentence begins with "Some."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Kalash people, who number only a few thousand, live in three narrow valleys in the Chitral District of northern Pakistan. Each May, they welcome the arrival of spring with Chilam Joshi, a festival of music, dancing, and ______ the festival, women and girls wear long black dresses embroidered in bright colors, along with headdresses decorated with cowrie shells and beads. Visitors from across Pakistan and abroad often travel to the valleys to watch.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: feasting. During
choices.B: feasting, during
choices.C: feasting during
choices.D: feasting. During,

explanation.why: "Each May, they welcome the arrival of spring with Chilam Joshi, a festival of music, dancing, and feasting" is a complete sentence. "During the festival, women and girls wear …" is another complete sentence. A period should separate the two, and no comma should split "During" from its object, "the festival."
explanation.A: Correct. The period ends the first sentence, and the second begins with the introductory phrase "During the festival."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Women and girls wear …" is an independent clause, so joining it to the first sentence with only a comma creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the first sentence runs into the second, creating a run-on sentence.
