explanation.D: Incorrect. The period is correct, but a comma can't separate the preposition "During" from its object, "the festival."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When the bees swarmed out of one of her aunt's hives, Ines expected panic. Instead, Aunt Rosa calmly pulled on her veil, shook the buzzing cluster from a low branch into an empty wooden box, and carried it to the far end of the ______ the new colony would have room to settle, well away from the other hives. Ines had never seen anyone move so slowly on purpose.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: orchard; where
choices.B: orchard, where
choices.C: orchard: where
choices.D: orchard. Where

explanation.why: "Aunt Rosa calmly pulled on her veil, shook …, and carried it to the far end of the orchard" is an independent clause. "Where the new colony would have room to settle" is a dependent clause that adds information about the orchard, so it is attached to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "where" clause is dependent.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma attaches the dependent "where" clause to the independent clause it describes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon can follow an independent clause, but it can't introduce a dependent clause such as "where the new colony would have room to settle."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave "Where the new colony would have room to settle …" as a sentence fragment.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Ahmed Baba Institute in Timbuktu, Mali, holds tens of thousands of handwritten manuscripts on subjects ranging from law and medicine to astronomy and poetry. The institute takes its name from the sixteenth-century ______ Baba, who taught in Timbuktu and wrote dozens of works, many of them on Islamic law. Many of the institute's manuscripts were preserved for generations in private family libraries across the region.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: scholar, Ahmed
choices.B: scholar; Ahmed
choices.C: scholar: Ahmed
choices.D: scholar Ahmed

explanation.why: The name "Ahmed Baba" tells which sixteenth-century scholar the institute is named for; without it, "the sixteenth-century scholar" would not identify anyone. Because the name is essential, it is not set off with punctuation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma would treat the name as extra information, but the name is essential to identify the scholar, so no comma belongs here.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and neither side of this one is independent.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "The institute takes its name from the sixteenth-century scholar" is not complete without the name.
explanation.D: Correct. No punctuation is used because the name "Ahmed Baba" is essential: it identifies which scholar is meant.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most cheeses are solid all the way through. Emmental, ______ is famous for its large round holes, which cheesemakers call "eyes." The eyes form as bacteria in the ripening cheese release carbon dioxide gas, which collects in small pockets and slowly expands them. Researchers in Switzerland have also found that tiny particles of hay in the milk give the gas places to gather, which may explain why cheese made from very clean modern milk often has fewer eyes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: however;
choices.B: however,
choices.C: however:
choices.D: however

explanation.why: "However" interrupts the sentence "Emmental is famous for its large round holes" to signal a contrast with the sentence before. An interrupting word is set off by a pair of commas; the first comma is already there after "Emmental," so a second comma must follow "however."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Emmental" from its verb "is."
explanation.B: Correct. The comma after "however" completes the pair of commas that sets off the interrupting word.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; it can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The comma after "Emmental" opens a pair, so a matching comma must close it after "however."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Beginning in the sixteenth century, metalworkers in the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria, cast hundreds of rectangular brass plaques for the royal palace. The ______ which once covered the wooden pillars of the palace, show the oba, or king, along with court officials, warriors, musicians, and European traders. Many of the plaques are now held in museums in Europe and North America.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: plaques
choices.B: plaques—
choices.C: plaques;
choices.D: plaques,

explanation.why: The clause "which once covered the wooden pillars of the palace" is extra information about the plaques. It closes with a comma before the verb "show," so it must also open with a comma after "plaques."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without an opening comma, the comma before "show" would separate the subject from its verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Extra information must be set off by matching marks; a dash can't open a phrase that closes with a comma.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The plaques" from the rest of its own clause.
explanation.D: Correct. The comma opens the pair of commas around the nonessential "which" clause, matching the comma before "show."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Peas, beans, and other legumes can thrive in soil that is poor in nitrogen, a nutrient that all plants need. Their secret is a partnership with ______ that live inside small swellings, called nodules, on the plants' roots. These bacteria take nitrogen gas from the air and convert it into a form the plant can use; in return, the plant supplies them with sugars.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: bacteria
choices.B: bacteria;
choices.C: bacteria,
choices.D: bacteria—

explanation.why: The clause "that live inside small swellings … on the plants' roots" tells which bacteria the legumes partner with, so it is essential information. A "that" clause like this is never set off from the noun it describes with punctuation.
explanation.A: Correct. No punctuation is needed because the "that" clause is essential: it identifies which bacteria are meant.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "that live inside small swellings …" is not one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate a noun from the essential "that" clause that identifies it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A dash would set off the "that" clause as extra information, but it is essential and needs no punctuation.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Angkor Wat, in northwestern Cambodia, was built in the early twelfth century under the Khmer king Suryavarman II. The temple, which was first dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later became a Buddhist ______ is surrounded by a moat about 190 meters wide. Its five central towers represent the peaks of Mount Meru, the home of the gods in Hindu and Buddhist tradition.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: shrine:
choices.B: shrine,
choices.C: shrine;
choices.D: shrine

explanation.why: The clause "which was first dedicated … and later became a Buddhist shrine" is extra information about the temple. It opens with a comma after "The temple," so it must close with a comma before the verb "is surrounded."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; it can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma closes the nonessential "which" clause, so the subject "The temple" connects to its verb "is surrounded."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The temple" from its verb "is surrounded."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the "which" clause runs straight into the main verb "is surrounded."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Mariachi music developed in western Mexico, in and around the state of Jalisco. A traditional mariachi ensemble usually includes violins, trumpets, and a trio of stringed instruments that are strummed or plucked. These three instruments ______ six-string guitar, the small round-backed vihuela, and the guitarrón, a deep-voiced bass guitar so large that the player holds it against the chest. Some ensembles also add a harp.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are: the
choices.B: are; the
choices.C: are, the
choices.D: are the

explanation.why: In the last sentence, the subject is "These three instruments," the verb is "are," and the list of instruments completes the verb. No punctuation belongs between a verb and the words that complete it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "These three instruments are" is not complete.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; it can't separate a verb from its complement.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "are" from the list that completes it.
explanation.D: Correct. No punctuation separates the verb "are" from the list that completes it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Male satin bowerbirds of eastern Australia do not attract mates with their glossy feathers alone. Instead, each male builds a bower, a structure of sticks arranged in two parallel walls, and decorates the ground in front of it with a collection ______ blue objects: feathers, flowers, berries, and even bottle caps and drinking straws. Females visit several bowers before choosing a mate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: of
choices.B: of:
choices.C: of—
choices.D: of,

explanation.why: "Of blue objects" is a prepositional phrase: the preposition "of" is followed by its object, "blue objects." No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.
explanation.A: Correct. No punctuation separates the preposition "of" from its object, "blue objects."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; it can't separate a preposition from its object.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A dash can't separate the preposition "of" from its object.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the preposition "of" from its object.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Rain drummed on the roof of the bus shelter as Mr. Lindqvist checked his watch for the third time. Beside him, a small boy in a yellow raincoat had been watching the empty road with great seriousness. "Do you think the bus forgot about ______ the boy asked at last. Mr. Lindqvist considered the question carefully before admitting that he had been wondering the same thing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: us"? the
choices.B: us?" the
choices.C: us?," the
choices.D: us," the

explanation.why: The boy's words, "Do you think the bus forgot about us," are a direct question, so they end with a question mark placed inside the closing quotation mark. When a quoted question is followed by a tag such as "the boy asked," no comma is added after the question mark.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The question belongs to the boy's words, so the question mark must go inside the closing quotation mark.
explanation.B: Correct. The question mark ends the quoted question inside the quotation marks, and no extra comma is needed before "the boy asked."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A question mark already ends the quotation, so a comma after it is not used.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The boy's words are a question, so they must end with a question mark, not a comma.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The radio had warned of a hard frost, so by nine o'clock the whole family was out in the apple orchard. Ana's father moved down the rows lighting small smudge pots, whose smoky flames would keep the cold from settling on the blossoms. Ana's job was simpler but felt just as important: she ______ thermos of cocoa to each person in turn and stayed long enough to warm her hands.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: carried—a
choices.B: carried: a
choices.C: carried a
choices.D: carried, a

explanation.why: In the clause after the colon, "she" is the subject, "carried" is the verb, and "a thermos of cocoa" is the direct object. No punctuation belongs between a verb and its direct object.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A dash can't separate the verb "carried" from its direct object.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "she carried" is incomplete without its object.
explanation.C: Correct. No punctuation separates the verb "carried" from its direct object, "a thermos of cocoa."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "carried" from its direct object.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The ruins of Taxila, near present-day Islamabad, Pakistan, include the remains of cities, monasteries, and Buddhist stupas built over a span of more than a thousand years. The site owed much of its importance to its ______ it lay at a crossroads where trade routes from Central Asia, Persia, and the plains of northern India met. Today, Taxila is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: location:
choices.B: location that:
choices.C: location
choices.D: location,

explanation.why: "The site owed much of its importance to its location" is an independent clause, and "it lay at a crossroads …" is another independent clause that explains what was special about the location. A colon can introduce such an explanation after a complete independent clause.
explanation.A: Correct. The colon follows a complete independent clause and introduces the explanation of why the location mattered.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but "its location that" leaves the clause unfinished.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every Sunday that summer, Lucía walked the crooked streets of her village with her grandmother, who was drawing a map of it entirely by hand. Her ______ a retired cartographer who had once charted rivers across half the country—insisted on measuring every lane by counting her own steps. Lucía carried the notebook and wrote down the numbers, and by August she could have walked the whole village blindfolded.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: grandmother:
choices.B: grandmother,
choices.C: grandmother;
choices.D: grandmother—

explanation.why: The phrase "a retired cartographer who had once charted rivers across half the country" is extra information about Lucía's grandmother. It closes with a dash before the verb "insisted," so it must open with a matching dash after "grandmother."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "Her grandmother" is not one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Extra information must be set off by matching marks; a comma can't open a phrase that closes with a dash.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Her grandmother" from the rest of its own clause.
explanation.D: Correct. The dash opens the pair of dashes around the extra information, matching the dash before "insisted."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Rafflesia arnoldii, a plant of the rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo, has no leaves, stems, or roots of its own. It lives as a parasite inside a single genus of vines, Tetrastigma, drawing water and nutrients from its host's tissues; for most of its life, it exists only as threads of cells within the vine. The plant cannot carry out photosynthesis and spends nearly its entire existence hidden from ______ it produces the largest single flower known, a fleshy bloom that can measure nearly a meter across and smells strongly of rotting meat.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: view; nevertheless,
choices.B: view. Nevertheless;
choices.C: view, nevertheless,
choices.D: view nevertheless,

explanation.why: "The plant cannot carry out photosynthesis and spends nearly its entire existence hidden from view" is an independent clause, and "it produces the largest single flower known …" is another. "Nevertheless" is a transitional word, not a conjunction, so the clauses need a semicolon before it, with a comma after it.
explanation.A: Correct. The semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and the comma after "nevertheless" sets off the transitional word.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; it can't separate the transitional word "Nevertheless" from the rest of its own sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Nevertheless" is not a conjunction, so a comma before it can't join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation before "nevertheless," the two independent clauses run together.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1956, physicists Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang proposed that parity, a basic symmetry long assumed to hold throughout nature, might be violated in the weak interactions responsible for certain kinds of radioactive decay. Many physicists doubted the idea, and testing it required extraordinary precision. Within months, a team led by the Chinese American ______ Wu had cooled radioactive cobalt-60 to near absolute zero and shown that the decaying nuclei emitted electrons preferentially in one direction, strong evidence that parity is not conserved. Lee and Yang received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1957.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: physicist, Chien-Shiung
choices.B: physicist: Chien-Shiung
choices.C: physicist—Chien-Shiung
choices.D: physicist Chien-Shiung

explanation.why: The name "Chien-Shiung Wu" tells which Chinese American physicist led the team; "the Chinese American physicist" alone would not identify her. Because the name is essential to the meaning, it is not set off from "physicist" with any punctuation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma would treat the name as removable extra information, but the name is needed to identify the physicist, and no closing comma follows it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "Within months, a team led by the Chinese American physicist" is not one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A dash would open an interruption that is never closed, and the name is essential information that shouldn't be set off.
explanation.D: Correct. No punctuation is used because the name is essential: it identifies which physicist led the team.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Founded in 1865, the Lahore Museum in Pakistan holds one of the most important collections of art from the region. Visitors often seek out three treasures in particular: the Fasting Buddha, a Gandharan stone sculpture made around the second or third century CE; a group of Mughal miniature paintings, some of them produced for the imperial ______ and Zamzama, a huge bronze cannon that stands outside the museum and appears in the opening scene of Rudyard Kipling's 1901 novel Kim.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: court,
choices.B: court:
choices.C: court
choices.D: court;

explanation.why: The colon introduces a list of three treasures, and each item contains its own commas. In such a list, semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon after "third century CE" shows. The same mark must follow the second item, before "and Zamzama."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Because the list items contain their own commas, a comma here would blur the boundary between the second and third items; semicolons must separate them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon has already introduced the list; another colon can't separate one list item from the next.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the second list item runs straight into the third.
explanation.D: Correct. The semicolon separates the second list item from the third, matching the semicolon between the first and second items.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Scattered across the fields of New England and northern Europe are boulders that seem strangely out of place, their minerals matching no bedrock for many kilometers around. Geologists call them glacial erratics. During the last ice age, advancing sheets of ice tore such rocks from distant outcrops and dragged them slowly across the landscape. When the ice finally melted, it left the boulders stranded on ground of an entirely different ______ surfaces often still scored with long parallel scratches from the journey.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: type their
choices.B: type, their
choices.C: type; their
choices.D: type. Their

explanation.why: "When the ice finally melted, it left the boulders stranded on ground of an entirely different type" is a complete sentence. "Their surfaces often still scored with long parallel scratches" has no main verb ("scored" is a participle), so it is an absolute phrase, like "their minerals matching no bedrock" in the first sentence. An absolute phrase is attached to the clause it describes with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a comma, the absolute phrase runs into "type," and "type their surfaces" makes no sense.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma attaches the absolute phrase "their surfaces often still scored …" to the independent clause it describes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "their surfaces often still scored …" has no main verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A period would leave "Their surfaces often still scored …" as a sentence fragment.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mr. Castellanos had built violins for forty years, and he rarely explained what he was doing. Elena, his newest apprentice, had spent the afternoon watching him tap the thin spruce top of an unfinished instrument with one knuckle, pausing after each tap to listen. When he finally set it down, she asked him what he could possibly hear in a piece of wood that was not yet anything. He considered the question for so long that she began to wonder whether he had heard her at ______ he handed her the spruce and told her to tap it herself.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: all then
choices.B: all? Then
choices.C: all, then
choices.D: all. Then

explanation.why: "She began to wonder whether he had heard her at all" is a statement that reports a question indirectly, so it ends with a period, just as "she asked him what he could possibly hear …" does. "Then he handed her the spruce …" is a new independent clause and starts a new sentence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Whether he had heard her at all" is an indirect question inside a statement, so the sentence ends with a period, not a question mark.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Then" is not a conjunction, so a comma before it can't join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
explanation.D: Correct. The period ends the statement containing the indirect question, and the next sentence begins with "Then."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1769, astronomers stationed at dozens of sites around the world, from Tahiti to Hudson Bay, timed the moment when Venus passed across the face of the Sun. By comparing timings recorded at widely separated locations, they hoped to calculate the distance between Earth and the ______ goal that had eluded astronomers for centuries. The results were imperfect, partly because a blurring effect made it hard to judge the exact moment of contact, but later analyses of the data brought the estimate within a few percent of the modern value.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Sun, a
choices.B: Sun; a
choices.C: Sun. A
choices.D: Sun a

explanation.why: "A goal that had eluded astronomers for centuries" is not a clause; it is a noun phrase that renames the calculation just described. A summarizing phrase like this is attached to the end of the sentence with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma attaches the noun phrase "a goal that had eluded astronomers …" to the sentence it comments on.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a goal that had eluded astronomers for centuries" is a noun phrase; its verb belongs to the "that" clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave "A goal that had eluded astronomers for centuries" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a comma, the phrase runs into "the Sun," and the sentence seems to describe "the Sun a goal," which makes no sense.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Zellige, a form of tilework found throughout Morocco, is assembled from small pieces of glazed clay that are cut by hand into stars, crosses, and other geometric shapes. The craft demands extraordinary patience. A single panel—which may contain thousands of pieces, each chipped to shape with a sharp hammer and fitted tightly against its ______ can take a team of artisans several weeks to complete, and the finest examples, such as those in the old religious schools of Fez, have survived for centuries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: neighbors,
choices.B: neighbors
choices.C: neighbors—
choices.D: neighbors;

explanation.why: The clause "which may contain thousands of pieces, each chipped to shape … and fitted tightly against its neighbors" is extra information about "A single panel." It opens with a dash, so it must close with a dash, even though commas appear inside it. Then the subject "A single panel" connects to its verb "can take."
explanation.A: Incorrect. This comma might seem to continue the inner description, but extra information that opens with a dash must close with a dash.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs into the verb "can take."
explanation.C: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the extra information, so the subject "A single panel" connects to its verb "can take."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "A single panel" from its verb "can take."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Each spring, groups of honey collectors known as mawals enter the Sundarbans, the vast mangrove forest on the coast of Bangladesh and India, in search of wild hives. The honey they gather, which comes from the nests of giant honeybees that hang from branches high in the mangrove ______ is harvested with the help of smoke from smoldering bundles of leaves. The forest is also home to Bengal tigers, so collectors travel in teams and take turns keeping watch while others climb.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: canopy
choices.B: canopy,
choices.C: canopy—
choices.D: canopy;

explanation.why: The clause "which comes from the nests of giant honeybees that hang from branches high in the mangrove canopy" is extra information about "The honey they gather." It opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb "is harvested." The "that" clause inside it is essential and needs no commas of its own.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the "which" clause is never set off, and "is harvested" seems to belong to the canopy.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma closes the nonessential "which" clause, so the subject "The honey" connects to its verb "is harvested."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a comma must close with a comma; a dash doesn't match.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The honey they gather" from its verb "is harvested."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Around 1754 BCE, the Babylonian king Hammurabi had a collection of laws carved onto a tall pillar, or stele, of black stone. The stele, now in the Louvre in Paris, was rediscovered in 1901 at Susa, in present-day Iran, where it had been carried as war plunder centuries after it was made. A carved scene of Hammurabi standing before the sun god Shamash and nearly three hundred laws written in cuneiform beneath ______ the surface of the stone from top to bottom.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it, cover
choices.B: it: cover
choices.C: it cover
choices.D: it; cover

explanation.why: The last sentence has a long compound subject: "A carved scene of Hammurabi … and nearly three hundred laws written in cuneiform beneath it." Its verb is "cover." No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb, however long the subject is.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the compound subject from its verb "cover."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the subject alone is not one.
explanation.C: Correct. No punctuation separates the long compound subject from its verb "cover."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; here it would split the subject from its verb.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Jackdaws, small gray-naped members of the crow family, live both in quiet farmland and in busy cities. Behavioral ecologist Kirsi Mäkelä wanted to know whether city life changes how these birds respond to new things. Over two breeding seasons, her team placed unfamiliar objects, such as a brightly colored cup or a small plastic toy, beside feeding sites in both settings. The researchers ______ jackdaws approached the objects sooner than rural jackdaws did, a result the team suggests may reflect the constant novelty of city life.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: found that, urban
choices.B: found, that urban
choices.C: found that urban
choices.D: found: that urban

explanation.why: In the last sentence, "The researchers" is the subject, "found" is the verb, and the clause "that urban jackdaws approached the objects sooner than rural jackdaws did" is the verb's object. No punctuation belongs between a verb and its object, and none belongs between "that" and the rest of its clause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma can't separate "that" from the subject of its own clause, "urban jackdaws."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "found" from its object, the "that" clause.
explanation.C: Correct. No punctuation separates the verb "found" from its object, the clause beginning with "that."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "The researchers found" is incomplete without its object.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Petrarchan sonnet, named for the fourteenth-century Italian poet Francesco Petrarca, divides its fourteen lines into two unequal parts. Much of its power depends on a single structural ______ after an opening octave of eight lines raises a problem, a question, or a longing, the poem turns in its closing sestet of six lines toward a response, a resolution, or at least a change in perspective. Poets writing in English, from Thomas Wyatt to John Milton, adopted the form and often bent its rules.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: shift:
choices.B: shift,
choices.C: shift that:
choices.D: shift

explanation.why: "Much of its power depends on a single structural shift" is an independent clause. What follows, "after an opening octave … raises a problem …, the poem turns …," is another independent clause that explains the shift. A colon can introduce such an explanation after a complete independent clause.
explanation.A: Correct. The colon follows a complete independent clause and introduces the explanation of the shift.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "The poem turns …" is an independent clause, so joining it to the first clause with only a comma creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but "a single structural shift that" leaves the clause unfinished.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).

items.subject: science
items.passage: Saturn's main rings stretch more than 270,000 kilometers from edge to edge but are, in most places, only about ten meters thick. The rings, made up of countless particles of nearly pure water ice ranging in size from tiny grains to boulders several meters ______ reflect sunlight so brightly that they can be seen through a small backyard telescope. Measurements from the Cassini spacecraft suggested that the rings may be far younger than Saturn itself, though some planetary scientists continue to question that conclusion.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: across—
choices.B: across
choices.C: across;
choices.D: across,

explanation.why: The long phrase "made up of countless particles … ranging in size from tiny grains to boulders several meters across" adds extra information about "The rings." It opens with a comma after "The rings," so it must close with a comma before the verb "reflect."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a comma must close with a comma; a dash doesn't match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the phrase is never set off, and "reflect" seems to belong to the boulders.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The rings" from its verb "reflect."
explanation.D: Correct. The comma closes the nonessential phrase, so the subject "The rings" connects to its verb "reflect."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Ranikot Fort, in the Kirthar hills of Sindh, Pakistan, is enclosed by stone walls that wind for roughly thirty kilometers over ridges and valleys, earning it the nickname "the Great Wall of Sindh." Although historians generally agree that much of the present structure dates from the early nineteenth century, when the Talpur rulers of Sindh rebuilt and strengthened ______ fort's earliest origins remain uncertain, and some scholars argue that a fortification stood on the site many centuries before. Among its best-preserved features are several massive stone gateways.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it: the
choices.B: it; the
choices.C: it. The
choices.D: it, the

explanation.why: Everything from "Although historians generally agree" through "rebuilt and strengthened it" is one long dependent clause, even though it contains a comma and a "when" clause of its own. The main clause is "the fort's earliest origins remain uncertain." A dependent clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and the "Although" clause is not one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Although" clause is dependent.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A period would leave the long "Although" clause as a sentence fragment.
explanation.D: Correct. The comma correctly links the long introductory "Although" clause to the main clause.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: On Matteo's first morning in the studio, the furnace roared so loudly that he could barely hear a word. Signora Ferri, the glassblower who had agreed to train him after watching him sketch vases at her market stall for an entire ______ simply handed him a long iron pipe and pointed at the glowing opening. By noon he had ruined four gathers of molten glass, and she had not once raised her voice—which, he would later learn, was her highest form of encouragement.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: summer
choices.B: summer,
choices.C: summer—
choices.D: summer;

explanation.why: The phrase "the glassblower who had agreed to train him after watching him sketch vases … for an entire summer" renames Signora Ferri. Although the phrase contains a "who" clause, it is all one piece of extra information; it opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before the verb "handed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information never ends, and "handed" seems to belong to the "who" clause.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma closes the long phrase that renames Signora Ferri, so the subject connects to its verb "handed."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a comma must close with a comma; a dash doesn't match.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "Signora Ferri" from its verb "handed."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When the pianist Delia Moreau released her first solo album, few critics knew what to make of it. Its pieces were long and slow, built from simple melodies that returned again and again with small changes. One reviewer complained that the record "never quite arrives anywhere." Another, writing in a small jazz magazine, argued that the refusal to arrive was the point, comparing the experience of listening to the album to ______ light move across a wall." Neither critic, it turned out, had predicted how widely the album would come to be loved.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: "watching
choices.B: : "watching
choices.C: , "watching
choices.D: ; "watching

explanation.why: The quoted words "watching light move across a wall" are the object of the preposition "to." When a quotation is woven into a sentence this way, it takes no introductory punctuation; like the earlier quotation after "that," it simply continues the sentence.
explanation.A: Correct. No punctuation separates the preposition "to" from the quotation that serves as its object.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and it can't come between a preposition and its object.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the preposition "to" from its object, even when the object is a quotation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and the quotation is not one.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The sweet potato was domesticated in the Americas, yet it was being grown in Polynesia long before Europeans reached the Pacific; charred remains from the Cook Islands have been dated to around 1000 CE. Many researchers have taken this as evidence that Polynesian voyagers reached South America and returned with the plant. A 2018 genetic study proposed a different explanation, suggesting that the plant's seeds may have drifted across the ocean on their ______ many scholars still find the voyaging account more convincing, pointing to the similarity between the plant's names in Polynesian languages and in Quechua.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: own, even so,
choices.B: own, even so
choices.C: own even so,
choices.D: own. Even so,

explanation.why: "A 2018 genetic study proposed a different explanation, suggesting … on their own" is a complete sentence, and "many scholars still find the voyaging account more convincing …" is another. "Even so" is a transitional phrase, not a conjunction, so a comma can't join the clauses; a period should come before it, and a comma after it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Even so" is not a conjunction, so a comma before it can't join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Even so" can't join two independent clauses, so a comma before it still creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation before "even so," the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.D: Correct. The period ends the first sentence, and the comma after "Even so" sets off the transitional phrase that begins the next.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Near the oasis town of Dunhuang, in western China, nearly five hundred cave temples were carved into a cliff between the fourth and fourteenth centuries. In 1900, a Daoist monk named Wang Yuanlu, who had made himself caretaker of the site, discovered a small side chamber that had been sealed in the early eleventh century. The chamber (now known as the Library ______ held tens of thousands of manuscripts and paintings, among them a copy of the Diamond Sutra printed in 868 CE, the oldest known printed book that bears a date.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Cave),
choices.B: Cave);
choices.C: Cave)
choices.D: Cave,

explanation.why: The words in parentheses add extra information about "The chamber." An opening parenthesis must be closed with a parenthesis. After it, the subject "The chamber" must connect directly to its verb "held," with no other punctuation in between.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The parenthesis is closed correctly, but the comma after it separates the subject "The chamber" from its verb "held."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; it can't separate the subject "The chamber" from its verb "held."
explanation.C: Correct. The closing parenthesis ends the extra information, and the subject "The chamber" connects directly to its verb "held."
explanation.D: Incorrect. An opening parenthesis must be closed with a parenthesis, not a comma.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Bharatanatyam, a classical dance form from Tamil Nadu in southern India, combines intricate rhythmic footwork with a rich vocabulary of facial expressions and hand positions. The single-hand ______ that a student learns first, each with its own Sanskrit name, can stand for very different things depending on context: the same shape of the fingers might suggest a cloud, a forest, or a river. Because the audience reads these gestures alongside the dancer's eyes and face, a skilled performer can tell a long story without speaking a word.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: gestures—
choices.B: gestures
choices.C: gestures;
choices.D: gestures,

explanation.why: The clause "that a student learns first" tells which hand gestures the sentence is about, so it is essential and is not set off from "gestures" by any punctuation. The comma after "first" belongs to the separate nonessential phrase "each with its own Sanskrit name," which is set off by its own pair of commas.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A dash would set off the "that" clause as extra information, but the clause is essential.
explanation.B: Correct. No punctuation is needed because the "that" clause is essential: it identifies which gestures are meant.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The single-hand gestures" from the rest of its own clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma can't separate a noun from the essential "that" clause that identifies it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Over millions of years, a planet's gravity can slow a moon's spin until the moon rotates exactly once for each trip it makes around the planet, a state called tidal locking. A tidally locked moon always shows the same face to its planet, just as our own Moon always presents the same side to Earth. Such locking is common in the solar system. The moons known to be locked in this way ______ four largest moons, Saturn's giant moon Titan, and Neptune's moon Triton, along with dozens of smaller bodies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: include: Jupiter's
choices.B: include; Jupiter's
choices.C: include Jupiter's
choices.D: include, Jupiter's

explanation.why: In the last sentence, the subject is "The moons known to be locked in this way," the verb is "include," and the list that follows is the verb's object. No punctuation belongs between a verb and its object, even when the object is a list.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, and "The moons … include" is incomplete without its object.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; it can't separate a verb from its object.
explanation.C: Correct. No punctuation separates the verb "include" from the list that serves as its object.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "include" from its object.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians often refer to the years from 1718 to 1730 in the Ottoman Empire as the Tulip Era, a period when the court of Sultan Ahmed III, famous for its lavish garden parties, encouraged a fashion for rare tulip bulbs among the wealthy residents of ______ name itself was not used by people living at the time. It became popular only in the early twentieth century, when writers looking back on the period found the flower a convenient symbol of its elegance.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Istanbul, but the
choices.B: Istanbul: but the
choices.C: Istanbul but the
choices.D: Istanbul, but, the

explanation.why: The first sentence contains two independent clauses: "Historians often refer to the years … as the Tulip Era …" and "the name itself was not used by people living at the time." Despite the long first clause, the usual rule applies: a comma goes before a coordinating conjunction such as "but" that joins two independent clauses, and nothing separates the conjunction from its clause.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma and the coordinating conjunction "but" correctly join the two independent clauses.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon introduces an explanation or a list; it isn't used before a conjunction such as "but" that links two contrasting clauses.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When "but" joins two independent clauses, a comma is needed before it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The comma after "but" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Gulf Stream, a powerful ocean current, carries warm water from the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean along the eastern coast of North America and then, through its extensions, northeastward across the Atlantic. The heat that this water releases into the air above it as it travels toward the coasts of northwestern ______ often credited with keeping the region's winters milder than those at similar latitudes in North America, although some climate scientists argue that patterns of atmospheric circulation matter at least as much.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Europe; is
choices.B: Europe, is
choices.C: Europe—is
choices.D: Europe is

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is long: "The heat that this water releases into the air above it as it travels toward the coasts of northwestern Europe." Its verb is "is often credited." The clauses inside the subject are essential, so no punctuation separates the subject from its verb.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; here it would split the subject from its verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the subject "The heat …" from its verb "is."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A single dash can't separate a subject from its verb.
explanation.D: Correct. No punctuation separates the long subject from its verb "is often credited."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the dry plains of Iran, farmers have long drawn water from qanats, underground channels that carry groundwater by gravity alone from aquifers beneath distant hills to fields and villages. From the surface, a qanat looks like nothing more than a line of shafts dotting the ground. The ______ some of which run for dozens of kilometers and have been maintained by skilled diggers for generations, are built with a slope so slight that the water moves without eroding their walls.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: tunnels;
choices.B: tunnels
choices.C: tunnels,
choices.D: tunnels—

explanation.why: The clause "some of which run for dozens of kilometers and have been maintained … for generations" is extra information about "The tunnels." It closes with a comma before the verb "are built," so it must open with a comma after "tunnels."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The tunnels" from the rest of its own clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without an opening comma, the clause is not set off, and the comma before "are built" separates the subject from its verb.
explanation.C: Correct. The comma opens the pair of commas around the nonessential clause, matching the comma before "are built."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Extra information must be set off by matching marks; a dash can't open a clause that closes with a comma.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The telegram from the next station up the line was only six words long, and Mr. Okonjo read it twice before he understood it: the river had risen over the tracks. The evening train was already on its way. Every instinct told him to run down the platform shouting for help, but he did not do ______ he walked calmly to the signal lever, pulled it until the arm dropped to red, and only then allowed his hands to shake.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: that instead,
choices.B: that, instead,
choices.C: that. Instead;
choices.D: that; instead,

explanation.why: "Every instinct told him …, but he did not do that" is an independent clause, and "he walked calmly to the signal lever …" is another. "Instead" is a transitional word, not a conjunction, so the clauses need a semicolon before it, with a comma after it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation before "instead," the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Instead" is not a conjunction, so a comma before it can't join two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses; it can't separate the transitional word "Instead" from the rest of its own sentence.
explanation.D: Correct. The semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and the comma after "instead" sets off the transitional word.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Between roughly 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, gradual shifts in Earth's orbit strengthened the African monsoon, and much of what is now the Sahara was covered by grassland, lakes, and wetlands. Evidence for this "Green Sahara" comes from lake sediments, fossil pollen, and the rock art of the region. Paintings and engravings on cliffs in southern Algeria and Libya depict animals that could not survive in today's desert, such ______ elephants, hippopotamuses, and herds of cattle tended by people. As the monsoon weakened, the lakes dried up, and the people who had painted these scenes moved away.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: as—giraffes,
choices.B: as giraffes,
choices.C: as, giraffes,
choices.D: as: giraffes,

explanation.why: "Such as" introduces examples that are part of the same sentence. No punctuation goes between "such as" and the first example, "giraffes"; the commas that follow simply separate the items in the list.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A dash can't separate "such as" from the examples it introduces.
explanation.B: Correct. No punctuation separates "such as" from its first example, and the comma after "giraffes" separates the list items.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate "such as" from the examples it introduces.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause; it can't come between "such as" and its examples.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Hampi, in the Indian state of Karnataka, was once the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, which controlled much of southern India from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century. Among its most photographed monuments is a stone chariot in the courtyard of the Vittala Temple. The ______ which was built in the sixteenth century and whose carved stone wheels were once said to turn on their axles, is actually a shrine dedicated to Garuda, the eagle who carries the god Vishnu.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: chariot,
choices.B: chariot;
choices.C: chariot—
choices.D: chariot

explanation.why: The clause "which was built in the sixteenth century and whose carved stone wheels were once said to turn on their axles" is extra information about the chariot. It closes with a comma before the verb "is," so it must open with a comma after "chariot."
explanation.A: Correct. The comma opens the pair of commas around the nonessential clause, matching the comma before "is."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate the subject "The chariot" from the rest of its own clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Extra information must be set off by matching marks; a dash can't open a clause that closes with a comma.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without an opening comma, the clause is not set off, and the comma before "is" separates the subject from its verb.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Why would a major design museum devote an entire exhibition to what its curator called "the humblest tool in the ______ answer, according to the exhibition catalog, lies in the spoon's long history. Because nearly every culture has used some version of it, from carved wooden ladles to mass-produced stainless steel, the spoon offers an unusually clear record of how materials, manufacturing methods, and eating habits have changed over thousands of years. The exhibition includes more than four hundred spoons from six continents.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: kitchen"? The
choices.B: kitchen?" The
choices.C: kitchen." The
choices.D: kitchen," the

explanation.why: The whole first sentence is a question, but the quoted words, "the humblest tool in the kitchen," are not. In American English, a question mark goes outside the closing quotation mark when it belongs to the whole sentence rather than to the quotation. The next sentence then begins with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Correct. The question mark ends the whole question and goes outside the quotation mark, because the quoted words themselves are not a question.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Placing the question mark inside the quotation marks makes the curator's words a question, but only the full sentence is a question.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The first sentence asks a direct question ("Why would a major design museum …"), so it must end with a question mark, not a period.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma can't end the question or join it to the next independent clause; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In January 1973, a volcanic fissure opened on Heimaey, an island off the southern coast of Iceland, and lava soon began creeping toward the island's harbor, the base of its fishing industry. Residents and scientists responded with an unusual plan: they pumped enormous quantities of seawater onto the advancing ______ water chilled the outer edge of the flow until it hardened into a wall that helped hold back the molten rock behind it. When the eruption ended that summer, the harbor was still usable, and its entrance was even more sheltered than before.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: lava the
choices.B: lava, the
choices.C: lava, and, the
choices.D: lava; the

explanation.why: "They pumped enormous quantities of seawater onto the advancing lava" is an independent clause, and "the water chilled the outer edge of the flow …" is another. A semicolon can join two closely related independent clauses.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together (a run-on sentence).
explanation.B: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma and "and" could join the clauses, but the comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.
explanation.D: Correct. The semicolon correctly joins the two closely related independent clauses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A lichen may look like a single organism, but it is actually a partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually a green alga or a cyanobacterium. The fungus forms the lichen's body, anchoring it to a surface and shielding its partner from drying ______ partner uses sunlight to make sugars that nourish both organisms. This exchange allows lichens to colonize bare rock, tree bark, and other surfaces where neither partner could easily survive alone.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: out, while the
choices.B: out. While the
choices.C: out the
choices.D: out, the

explanation.why: "The fungus forms the lichen's body … from drying out" is an independent clause, and "the partner uses sunlight to make sugars" could also stand alone. The two must be joined correctly. Adding the subordinating conjunction "while" turns the second part into a dependent clause, which a comma can attach to the main clause.
explanation.A: Correct. "While" makes the second part a dependent clause, and a comma correctly attaches it to the independent clause before it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The period leaves "While the partner uses sunlight … both organisms" as a sentence fragment, because a "while" clause can't stand alone.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is a comma splice: a comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The rice terraces of the Ifugao people, which climb the steep mountainsides of northern Luzon in the Philippines, were long thought to be about 2,000 years old. Radiocarbon dates obtained from one terrace complex in the early 2010s, however, point to a far later start for its ______ one that roughly coincides with the arrival of Spanish colonizers in the islands in the sixteenth century—and some archaeologists now argue that terrace building expanded as communities moved into the highlands, beyond the reach of colonial rule.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: construction one
choices.B: construction, one
choices.C: construction—one
choices.D: construction; one

explanation.why: The phrase "one that roughly coincides with … the sixteenth century" is extra information describing the "far later start." It closes with a dash after "century," so it must open with a matching dash after "construction."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without an opening dash, the extra information runs straight into "construction," and the closing dash after "century" has nothing to match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Extra information that closes with a dash can't open with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.C: Correct. The dash opens the pair of dashes around the extra information, matching the dash after "century."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "one that roughly coincides … century" has no main verb of its own.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In early September 1859, the English astronomer Richard Carrington was sketching sunspots when he saw two patches of intensely bright white light flare briefly on the Sun's surface. About seventeen hours later, the most powerful geomagnetic storm on record struck Earth. Its effects reached across much of the ______ glowing as far south as the Caribbean and telegraph systems in Europe and North America failing, with some operators reporting sparks leaping from their equipment.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: world. Auroras
choices.B: world: auroras
choices.C: world; auroras
choices.D: world auroras

explanation.why: "Its effects reached across much of the world" is a complete independent clause. What follows, "auroras glowing … and telegraph systems … failing," is not a clause: "glowing" and "failing" are not main verbs. It lists the effects, and a colon after an independent clause correctly introduces such an explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The period leaves "Auroras glowing … from their equipment" as a sentence fragment, because "glowing" and "failing" can't serve as main verbs.
explanation.B: Correct. The colon follows an independent clause and introduces the details that explain how far the storm's effects reached.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "auroras glowing … failing" has no main verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the list of effects runs straight into "world," making the sentence confusing.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In ebru, the Turkish art of paper marbling, an artist sprinkles drops of pigment onto the surface of water thickened with a plant-based gum and then uses combs, brushes, or fine awls to coax the floating colors into swirling patterns. A sheet of paper laid gently on the water lifts the entire design in a single ______ result that can never be repeated exactly, since each pattern exists only until the paper takes it away.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: motion; a
choices.B: motion, a
choices.C: motion. A
choices.D: motion a

explanation.why: "A sheet of paper laid gently on the water lifts the entire design in a single motion" is a complete independent clause. The words that follow, "a result that can never be repeated exactly …," are a noun phrase that sums up and comments on that clause. Such a phrase is extra information and is attached to the clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a result that can never be repeated exactly" has no main verb of its own.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma sets off the phrase "a result that can never be repeated exactly," which adds a comment on the main clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The period leaves "A result that can never be repeated exactly … takes it away" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the phrase "a result that …" runs into "motion," and the sentence can't be read clearly.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Baltit Fort, which stands on a ridge above Karimabad in Pakistan's Hunza Valley, was home for centuries to the region's hereditary rulers, the Mirs. In the mid-twentieth century, the ruling family moved to a newer palace in the ______ the fort sat empty for decades while its timber-laced stone walls slowly cracked and sagged. A restoration led by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture finally stabilized the structure, and in 1996 it reopened as a museum.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: town, after it
choices.B: town, after which
choices.C: town. After which
choices.D: town; after which

explanation.why: "In the mid-twentieth century, the ruling family moved to a newer palace in the town" is an independent clause. The relative phrase "after which" turns the next part into a dependent clause that describes what happened after the move, and a comma correctly attaches that clause to the main clause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "After it the fort sat empty …" is an independent clause, so joining it to the first clause with only a comma creates a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma attaches the dependent clause beginning "after which" to the independent clause before it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The period leaves "After which the fort sat empty … cracked and sagged" as a sentence fragment, because a clause beginning with "after which" can't stand alone.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "after which the fort sat empty …" is a dependent clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Tropical pitcher plants of the genus Nepenthes catch insects in leaves shaped like deep cups that hold digestive fluid. One might expect the plants' slippery rims to be coated with wax, like the surfaces of many other leaves, but the rim's power to topple visitors turns out to come from something ______ thin film of water, from rain or from the plant's own nectar, that spreads across the rim's microscopic ridges and leaves an insect's feet nothing to grip.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: unexpected. A
choices.B: unexpected a
choices.C: unexpected; a
choices.D: unexpected: a

explanation.why: Everything before the blank, ending "turns out to come from something unexpected," is an independent clause. What follows, "a thin film of water … that spreads … and leaves …," is a long noun phrase whose verbs sit inside a relative clause, so it has no main verb. It identifies the "something unexpected," and a colon after an independent clause is the right mark to introduce it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The period leaves "A thin film of water … nothing to grip" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the noun phrase runs straight into "unexpected," and the sentence can't be read clearly.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a thin film of water …" is a noun phrase with no main verb.
explanation.D: Correct. The colon follows an independent clause and introduces the phrase that explains what the "something unexpected" is.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1942, the film actress Hedy Lamarr and the composer George Antheil received a US patent for a "Secret Communication System" meant to keep enemy forces from jamming the radio signals that guided torpedoes. Their idea, now known as frequency ______ to switch the signal rapidly among 88 frequencies in a pattern shared only by the transmitter and the receiver, a scheme inspired in part by the paper rolls that control player pianos. The US Navy did not adopt the design at the time.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: hopping was
choices.B: hopping; was
choices.C: hopping—was
choices.D: hopping, was

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is "Their idea," and its verb is "was." In between, "now known as frequency hopping" is extra information that renames the idea. It opens with a comma after "idea," so it must close with a comma before "was."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off from the main verb "was."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Their idea" from its verb "was," and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "idea," setting off the extra information so the subject connects to its verb "was."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For thirty-one years, Teodor Vasile had walked the aisles of the night train from the capital to the coast, and on his final run he moved more slowly than usual, as though memorizing each worn seat. Near dawn, a young passenger looked up from her book and asked whether the train was always so quiet. "Not ______ he said, glancing at the gray fields sliding past the window, "but the quiet is the part I will miss."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: always", he
choices.B: always," he
choices.C: always" he
choices.D: always"; he

explanation.why: Teodor's words are a single quoted sentence interrupted by "he said, glancing at the gray fields sliding past the window." The first part of the quotation must end with a comma to separate it from the words that identify the speaker, and in American English that comma goes inside the closing quotation mark.
explanation.A: Incorrect. In American English, a comma that ends a quoted phrase goes inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma separates the quotation from "he said," and it is placed inside the closing quotation mark, as American English requires.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma is needed to separate the quoted words from "he said"; without it, the quotation runs into the rest of the sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate a quotation from the words that identify its speaker; a semicolon belongs only between independent clauses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sea cucumbers, soft-bodied relatives of sea stars that live on the ocean floor, can change the stiffness of their body walls within seconds. When threatened, many species stiffen their skin so that they become difficult to bite or to pull from a ______ they need to squeeze through a narrow gap between rocks, they can soften the same tissue until it becomes remarkably pliable. Engineers have studied this ability while designing materials that switch between rigid and flexible states.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: crevice however, when
choices.B: crevice; however, when
choices.C: crevice, however when
choices.D: crevice, however, when

explanation.why: "When threatened, many species stiffen their skin … from a crevice" and "when they need to squeeze … they can soften the same tissue" are both independent clauses. "However" is a transition word, not a conjunction, so it can't join the clauses by itself. A semicolon must come before "however," and a comma after it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. With no punctuation before "however," the two independent clauses run together.
explanation.B: Correct. The semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and the comma after "however" sets off the transition from the clause that follows.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma before "however" still creates a comma splice, because "however" can't join two independent clauses.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Commas around "however" can't join two independent clauses; this creates a comma splice.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In 1888, the Irish-born teacher John Robert Gregg published a shorthand system that, after he moved to the United States, became the most widely used shorthand in the country for much of the twentieth century. Rather than distinguishing sounds by the thickness of a pen stroke, as some earlier systems did, Gregg built his writing ______ lines, curves based on the shapes of ordinary cursive handwriting, and small circles and hooks that stood for vowels.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: from: straight
choices.B: from straight
choices.C: from, straight
choices.D: from; straight

explanation.why: The preposition "from" takes the list "straight lines, curves …, and small circles and hooks" as its object. No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon must follow an independent clause, but "Gregg built his writing from" is not one; a colon can't separate a preposition from its object.
explanation.B: Correct. No punctuation is needed between the preposition "from" and the list that serves as its object.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the preposition "from" from its object.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon can't separate a preposition from its object, and "Gregg built his writing from" is not an independent clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For decades, the deadly bite of the Komodo dragon, the largest living lizard, was explained by a vivid but poorly tested idea: that the animal's mouth harbored bacteria so dangerous that bitten prey soon died of infection. A study published in 2009, however, described glands in the lizard's lower ______ secrete proteins that can prevent blood from clotting and lower blood pressure, suggesting that venom, rather than bacteria, helps it bring down prey as large as deer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: jaw; that
choices.B: jaw—that
choices.C: jaw that
choices.D: jaw, that

explanation.why: The clause "that secrete proteins …" tells which glands the study described, so it is essential to the sentence's meaning. Essential information is not set off by punctuation, and a clause beginning with "that" is never set off with a comma or dash.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "that secrete proteins …" is a dependent clause that can't stand alone.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A dash wrongly separates the essential clause from "glands in the lizard's lower jaw."
explanation.C: Correct. No punctuation is needed because "that secrete proteins …" is essential information identifying the glands.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma wrongly sets off the essential clause "that secrete proteins …" from the noun it identifies.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Human Development Index, introduced in 1990 in the first Human Development Report published by the United Nations, ranks countries not by income alone but by a combination of three dimensions: a long and healthy life, access to education, and a decent standard of living. The report was the project of the Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq, who, working closely with a team that included the Indian economist Amartya ______ that a country's progress should be judged by the real choices its people have rather than by a single figure such as national income.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Sen; argued
choices.B: Sen, argued
choices.C: Sen—argued
choices.D: Sen argued

explanation.why: In the clause "who … argued that a country's progress should be judged …," the subject "who" is separated from its verb "argued" by extra information: "working closely with a team that included the Indian economist Amartya Sen." That phrase opens with a comma after "who," so it must close with a comma before "argued."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate "who" from its verb "argued," and the words before it do not form an independent clause.
explanation.B: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "who," setting off the extra information so "who" connects to its verb "argued."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The extra information opens with a comma after "who," so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the extra information is never set off, and "Amartya Sen argued" wrongly seems to be its own subject and verb.

items.subject: science
items.passage: By the late 1920s, seismologists had concluded that Earth's core is liquid, partly because one kind of earthquake wave that cannot travel through liquids never reaches the far side of the planet. Records from a large 1929 earthquake in New Zealand, however, showed faint waves arriving at distances where the liquid-core model predicted almost none. Studying those records, the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann proposed in 1936 that the core contains a distinct inner ______ would bend and speed up passing waves enough to send some of them into that supposedly empty region.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: core; which
choices.B: core, this
choices.C: core, which
choices.D: core. Which

explanation.why: "Studying those records, the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann proposed in 1936 that the core contains a distinct inner core" is an independent clause. The next part describes that inner core. Beginning it with the relative pronoun "which" makes it a dependent clause, and a comma correctly attaches it to the noun it describes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "which would bend and speed up passing waves …" is a dependent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "This would bend and speed up passing waves …" is an independent clause, so joining it to the first clause with only a comma creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Correct. "Which" begins a dependent clause describing the inner core, and a comma correctly attaches that clause to the independent clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The period leaves "Which would bend … supposedly empty region" as a sentence fragment.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When Leonardo of Pisa, now known as Fibonacci, completed his Liber Abaci in 1202, most European merchants still kept their accounts in Roman numerals. Drawing on methods he had learned as a young man in North Africa, Leonardo showed readers how the nine "Indian figures" and the sign for zero could simplify the arithmetic of trade: converting between currencies, which varied from city to city; dividing profits among partners, often in unequal ______ converting weights and measures, a chore complicated by the many local standards then in use.
