explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together as a run-on sentence.
explanation.D: Correct. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction "so" correctly joins the two independent clauses.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ice cores drilled from the Antarctic ice sheet contain tiny bubbles of air that were sealed off as layers of old snow were slowly compressed into ice. Because each bubble preserves a sample of the atmosphere from the time it closed, the deepest cores allow scientists to measure carbon dioxide levels from roughly 800,000 years ago. The record from those ancient bubbles and the much younger ones above ______ that carbon dioxide levels today are higher than at any point in that long span.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them; shows
choices.B: them, shows
choices.C: them shows
choices.D: them—shows

explanation.why: The subject of the last sentence is "The record from those ancient bubbles and the much younger ones above them," and its verb is "shows." Even when a subject is long, no punctuation goes between the subject and its verb.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but it would split the subject from its verb "shows."
explanation.B: Incorrect. A single comma can't separate a subject from its verb, no matter how long the subject is.
explanation.C: Correct. No punctuation separates the long subject from its verb "shows."
explanation.D: Incorrect. A dash can't separate the subject from its verb "shows"; nothing here is being set off.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Built in the thirteenth century at Konark, on the coast of Odisha in eastern India, the Sun Temple was designed to resemble an enormous stone chariot for the sun god Surya, drawn by carved horses. Its twenty-four wheels—each nearly three meters across and covered with images of animals, dancers, and scenes of daily ______ thought by some scholars to have served as sundials, since the shadows cast by their spokes can be used to tell the time of day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: life; are
choices.B: life are
choices.C: life, are
choices.D: life—are

explanation.why: The subject "Its twenty-four wheels" is followed by extra information that describes the wheels and opens with a dash. That information must close with a matching dash before the verb "are thought." The commas inside the list "animals, dancers, and scenes of daily life" belong to the extra information and don't change this.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Its twenty-four wheels" from its verb, and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the extra information is never set off and runs into the verb "are thought."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Extra information that opens with a dash can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.D: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the extra information, so the subject "Its twenty-four wheels" connects to its verb "are thought."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Before the twelfth century, the stone walls of large European churches had to be thick and their windows relatively small, because the walls bore the full outward push of the heavy stone vaults overhead. Gothic builders found a way around this ______ shifting much of that push onto flying buttresses, external arches that carried the load down to piers standing away from the building, they were able to open the walls themselves to vast panels of stained glass.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: problem by:
choices.B: problem by
choices.C: problem, by
choices.D: problem: by

explanation.why: "Gothic builders found a way around this problem" is an independent clause, and so is "by shifting much of that push onto flying buttresses ..., they were able to open the walls." The second clause explains what the way around the problem was. A colon can join two independent clauses when the second explains the first.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A colon can't separate the preposition "by" from its object, "shifting much of that push."
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together as a run-on sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The commas leave two independent clauses, "Gothic builders found a way" and "they were able to open the walls," joined only by commas; this is a comma splice.
explanation.D: Correct. The colon joins the two independent clauses, and the second clause explains how the builders got around the problem.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Tomasz had promised to be the first seller in the square, so he was up long before dawn, checking the cart against the list his grandmother had dictated. Everything was there: three sacks of rye, ground the night before; a crate of eggs, each wrapped in ______ and the jar of plum preserves that she had insisted, over all his objections, would fetch the best price at the market in town.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: straw,
choices.B: straw
choices.C: straw:
choices.D: straw;

explanation.why: The colon introduces a list of three items, and each item contains its own comma: "three sacks of rye, ground the night before" and "a crate of eggs, each wrapped in straw." When list items contain commas, semicolons separate the items. A semicolon already follows the first item, so one must follow the second as well.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Because the items contain commas, a comma here would not clearly mark where the second item ends; the items must be separated by semicolons, as the first two are.
explanation.B: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the second and third items run together, and the eggs seem to be wrapped in straw "and the jar of plum preserves."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A colon can't separate items in a list, and the sentence already uses a colon to introduce the list.
explanation.D: Correct. The semicolon separates the second item from the third, matching the semicolon after the first item.

items.subject: science
items.passage: An insect rarely more than two centimeters ______ bombardier beetle defends itself with a chemical weapon. When threatened, it squeezes two compounds, hydroquinones and hydrogen peroxide, from separate storage sacs into a hardened chamber in its abdomen. There, enzymes trigger a violent reaction that heats the mixture to about the boiling point of water and blasts it out through an opening that the beetle can aim toward an attacker.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: long; the
choices.B: long: the
choices.C: long the
choices.D: long, the

explanation.why: "An insect rarely more than two centimeters long" is an introductory phrase that renames the subject, "the bombardier beetle." An introductory element like this is separated from the main clause by a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "An insect rarely more than two centimeters long" is only a phrase.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but "An insect rarely more than two centimeters long" is only a phrase.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a comma, the introductory phrase runs into the subject, and the sentence seems to describe "two centimeters long the bombardier beetle."
explanation.D: Correct. The comma separates the introductory phrase from the main clause "the bombardier beetle defends itself with a chemical weapon."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Fanny Mendelssohn, the older sister of the composer Felix Mendelssohn, was praised by many who heard her as an exceptional pianist, and she wrote more than 450 pieces of music, from short songs to a string quartet and a piano cycle depicting the months of the year. Although several of her early songs were printed under her brother's name and she published only a handful of works under her own before her death in ______ music has been widely performed and recorded since the late twentieth century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.D: 1847, but her

explanation.why: The sentence begins with "Although," so everything up to "her death in 1847" is one long dependent clause. It needs to be joined to the main clause, "her music has been widely performed and recorded," with a comma. The dependent clause already shows the contrast, so no other conjunction is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A period would leave "Although several of her early songs ... in 1847" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.B: Correct. A comma correctly links the long introductory "Although" clause to the main clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but the "Although" clause is dependent.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Although" already links the two parts of the sentence, so adding "but" leaves the sentence with two conjunctions doing one job, and no main clause stands on its own.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In January 1913, Srinivasa Ramanujan, a clerk in Madras with little formal training in advanced mathematics, mailed several pages of theorems to the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy. Some of the results were already known, but others were unlike anything Hardy had seen. After studying the pages with his colleague J. E. Littlewood, Hardy had to decide whether their author was a crank or a ______ soon concluded the latter and invited Ramanujan to Cambridge, where the two began one of the most productive partnerships in the history of mathematics.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: genius, he
choices.B: genius. He
choices.C: genius he
choices.D: genius? He

explanation.why: "Hardy had to decide whether their author was a crank or a genius" is a statement that reports a question indirectly; it is not itself a question, so it ends with a period. "He soon concluded the latter ..." is a new independent clause, so it must begin a new sentence (or be properly joined).
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join the two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.
explanation.B: Correct. The period ends the statement containing the indirect question, and "He soon concluded the latter" begins a new sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation, the two independent clauses run together as a run-on sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. An indirect question introduced by "whether" is part of a statement, so it ends with a period, not a question mark.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Dickinsonia—a flat, oval organism, marked with rib-like segments and sometimes more than a meter long, that lived on the seafloor more than 550 million years ______ long resisted classification: over the decades, paleontologists described it as a lichen, a giant single-celled organism, and a jellyfish-like animal. The debate shifted in 2018, when molecules derived from cholesterol, a compound characteristic of animals, were extracted from exceptionally well-preserved specimens collected in northwestern Russia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: ago,
choices.B: ago;
choices.C: ago—
choices.D: ago

explanation.why: The subject "Dickinsonia" is followed by a long description that opens with a dash, and the verb is "resisted." The description contains several commas of its own, but it began with a dash, so it must end with a matching dash before "long resisted classification."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The commas inside the description make a comma tempting, but extra information that opens with a dash can't close with a comma; the two marks must match.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Dickinsonia" from its verb "resisted," and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.C: Correct. The second dash closes the pair around the description, so the subject "Dickinsonia" connects to its verb "resisted."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing dash, the description is never set off, and "ago long resisted" runs the description into the main verb.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1850s, Chicago sat on ground so flat and so little above the level of Lake Michigan that water pooled in its unpaved streets and diseases such as cholera spread readily. The sewer plan that engineer Ellis Chesbrough proposed in 1855 was the first comprehensive one in the United States. Because the ground was too low for buried pipes to drain into the river by gravity, the plan called for laying the pipes on top of the existing streets and covering them with ______ property owners to raise their buildings, sometimes several stories of brick at a time, to the new street level.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: fill. Prompting
choices.B: fill, it prompted
choices.C: fill, prompting
choices.D: fill; prompting

explanation.why: The last sentence's main clause is "the plan called for laying the pipes on top of the existing streets and covering them with fill." What follows describes a result of that plan. A participial phrase beginning with "prompting" can express this result, and it is joined to the main clause with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A period would leave "Prompting property owners to raise their buildings ... to the new street level" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "It prompted property owners to raise their buildings" is an independent clause, and a comma alone can't join it to the main clause; this is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Correct. The comma attaches the participial phrase "prompting property owners to raise their buildings ..." to the main clause, describing a result of the plan.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "prompting property owners ..." is a phrase with no subject or main verb.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When a museum in Lyon opened its exhibition of twentieth-century textiles, the curator, Hélène Marchetti, displayed the weavings on open frames rather than behind glass, so that visitors could walk around each piece and study both sides. On the opening night, she defended the decision to a group of skeptical donors who had expected the works to be hung flat against the walls like paintings. "A textile is not a picture of a thing," she told ______ is the thing itself, and you have to be able to see how it was made."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them. It
choices.B: them, "it
choices.C: them "it
choices.D: them. "It

explanation.why: The quotation is interrupted by "she told them," but the two quoted parts are separate sentences: "A textile is not a picture of a thing" and "It is the thing itself, and you have to be able to see how it was made." Because the second part is a new independent clause, a period must follow the speaker tag, and the next quoted sentence begins with a capital letter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The period correctly ends the first sentence, but the words "It is the thing itself ..." are still Marchetti's, so they need an opening quotation mark; without it, the closing quotation mark at the end has no partner.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Joining the second complete quoted sentence to the first with a comma creates a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. With no punctuation after the speaker tag, the two independent clauses run together as a run-on sentence.
explanation.D: Correct. The period ends the first sentence after the speaker tag, and the capitalized "It" begins the second quoted sentence.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Selin's grandfather, who had sold spices from the same narrow stall in Istanbul's Egyptian Bazaar for half a century and who had, in all that time, never once raised his voice at a ______ merely lifted an eyebrow when the young merchant tried to overcharge him for a new set of brass scales. The merchant faltered, lowered his price, and then, as if on second thought, lowered it again. That single gesture, Selin later realized, had carried more reproach than any lecture could have.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: customer,
choices.B: customer—
choices.C: customer
choices.D: customer;

explanation.why: The subject of the first sentence is "Selin's grandfather," and its verb is "lifted." In between comes a long nonessential element made of two "who" clauses joined by "and." It opens with a comma after "grandfather," so it must close with a comma before "merely lifted"; the commas around "in all that time" sit inside the element and don't close it.
explanation.A: Correct. The closing comma matches the comma after "grandfather," so the subject connects to its verb "merely lifted."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The nonessential element opens with a comma, so it can't close with a dash; the two marks must match.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the nonessential element is never set off, and "merely lifted" seems to belong to "a customer" rather than to the grandfather.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Selin's grandfather" from its verb "lifted," and neither side would be an independent clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Cepheid variable stars brighten and dim in a regular rhythm, and in 1912 the astronomer Henrietta Swan Leavitt, studying Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, reported that the brighter stars took longer to complete each cycle. Because all the stars she examined lay at roughly the same distance from Earth, she could conclude that a Cepheid's period is linked to its true ______ astronomers to estimate how far away a Cepheid is by comparing its true brightness with its apparent brightness.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: luminosity, a relationship that allows
choices.B: luminosity; a relationship that allows
choices.C: luminosity a relationship that allows
choices.D: luminosity, this relationship allows

explanation.why: The sentence's last clause, "she could conclude that a Cepheid's period is linked to its true luminosity," is followed by a noun phrase, "a relationship that allows astronomers to estimate ...," that renames and sums up the link just described. Such a summary phrase is not a clause on its own, so it is attached with a comma.
explanation.A: Correct. The comma attaches the noun phrase that sums up the period-luminosity link to the end of the sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a relationship that allows astronomers ..." is a noun phrase; its verb "allows" sits inside the "that" clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without a comma, the summarizing phrase runs straight into "luminosity," and the sentence seems to say the period is linked to "luminosity a relationship."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "This relationship allows astronomers to estimate ..." is an independent clause, and a comma alone can't join it to the clause before; this is a comma splice.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The edicts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, carved on rocks and pillars across the Indian subcontinent in the third century BCE, became unreadable for centuries after the Brahmi script in which most of them were written fell out of use. Their decipherment in the 1830s drew on several kinds of evidence: coins that gave the same royal names in both Greek and Brahmi; short donor inscriptions from the stupa at ______ of which ended with the same two characters; and painstaking comparisons of letter shapes across hundreds of copied texts.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Sanchi; many
choices.B: Sanchi: many
choices.C: Sanchi many
choices.D: Sanchi, many

explanation.why: The colon introduces a list of three items separated by semicolons. The blank falls inside the second item, "short donor inscriptions from the stupa at Sanchi, many of which ended with the same two characters." Within that item, "many of which ..." is a nonessential clause about the inscriptions, so a comma, not a semicolon, sets it off.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The other semicolons make one tempting, but a semicolon here would split the second item in two, leaving "many of which ended with the same two characters" as a separate "item" that names no kind of evidence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A colon can't be used inside a list item to introduce a relative clause, and the sentence already uses a colon to introduce the list.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A nonessential clause beginning "many of which" must be set off with a comma; without one, the sentence seems to mention "Sanchi many."
explanation.D: Correct. The comma sets off the nonessential clause "many of which ended with the same two characters" inside the second item of the list.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Jørn Utzon's winning design for the Sydney Opera House, chosen in 1957, called for a cluster of soaring white shells, but for years no one could work out how to build them. The curves Utzon had first sketched followed no single geometry that engineers could readily calculate, so each rib would have needed its own costly mold. His solution, reached in 1961 after many rejected schemes, was to derive every ______ different in size and orientation, from the surface of one imaginary sphere, which meant that the ribs could be cast from a small set of standard molds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: shell, however
choices.B: shell; however,
choices.C: shell however
choices.D: shell—however

explanation.why: The phrase "however different in size and orientation" interrupts "to derive every shell ... from the surface of one imaginary sphere." It is nonessential, and it closes with a comma after "orientation," so it must open with a comma after "shell." Here "however" means "no matter how," not "but."
explanation.A: Correct. The comma after "shell" pairs with the comma after "orientation" to set off the interrupting phrase.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but it would cut "to derive every shell" off from the rest of its phrase, and "however different in size and orientation, from the surface ..." is not an independent clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Without an opening comma, the interrupting phrase is set off on only one side, and the comma after "orientation" is left without a partner.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The interrupting phrase closes with a comma after "orientation," so it can't open with a dash; the two marks must match.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many reef-building corals reproduce in a single burst each year, releasing bundles of eggs and sperm into the water over just a few nights. The timing is not ______ typically follows the full moon by several days, and within that window, colonies of the same species tend to release their bundles during the same hour or two after sunset, a synchrony that greatly increases the chance that eggs and sperm from different colonies will meet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: random: spawning
choices.B: random, rather, spawning
choices.C: random, which spawning
choices.D: random, spawning

explanation.why: "The timing is not random" is an independent clause, and what follows, "spawning typically follows the full moon by several days, and ... colonies ... tend to release their bundles ...," is also independent and explains why the timing is not random. A colon can join two independent clauses when the second explains the first.
explanation.A: Correct. The colon joins the two independent clauses, and the second one explains what the nonrandom timing looks like.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Rather" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so setting it off with commas still leaves two independent clauses joined only by commas, which is a comma splice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A "which" clause must have a gap that "which" fills, but "spawning typically follows the full moon" is already complete, so "which" has no role and the sentence is ungrammatical.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A comma alone can't join the two independent clauses; this is a comma splice.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For decades, models of Jupiter's interior assumed that the planet had formed around a small, compact core of rock and ice, which was later buried beneath a deep envelope of hydrogen and helium. Gravity measurements made by NASA's Juno spacecraft, which has orbited Jupiter since ______ that this picture is too simple: the core appears to be large and diffuse, with its heavy elements gradually mixing into the layers above rather than ending at a sharp boundary.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: 2016 suggest
choices.B: 2016, suggest
choices.C: 2016; suggest
choices.D: 2016, suggest,

explanation.why: The subject of the second sentence is "Gravity measurements made by NASA's Juno spacecraft," and its verb is "suggest." The clause "which has orbited Jupiter since 2016" is nonessential and opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma before "suggest." No punctuation then goes between "suggest" and its object, the clause beginning "that this picture is too simple."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Without a closing comma, the nonessential clause is never set off, and "suggest" seems to belong to the "which" clause.
explanation.B: Correct. The comma closes the nonessential clause, and nothing separates "suggest" from the "that" clause it introduces.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject "Gravity measurements" from its verb "suggest," and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The first comma is correct, but the second one separates the verb "suggest" from its object, the "that" clause.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In November 1974, at Hadar in the Afar region of Ethiopia, two researchers searching for fossils spotted a fragment of an arm bone on the slope of a gully. Over the following weeks, their team recovered several hundred pieces of bone representing about 40 percent of a single skeleton, later dated to roughly 3.2 million years ago. The researchers who celebrated the discovery at their camp that ______ the skeleton "Lucy," after the Beatles song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds," which was playing repeatedly on a tape recorder.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: night; named
choices.B: night—named
choices.C: night, named
choices.D: night named

explanation.why: The subject of the last sentence is "The researchers who celebrated the discovery at their camp that night," and its verb is "named." The "who" clause is essential: it tells which researchers the sentence means, so it is not set off with commas. With no opening comma after "researchers," no punctuation belongs before "named."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon would separate the subject from its verb "named," and neither side would be an independent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A dash can't separate the subject from its verb "named"; nothing here opens a pair of dashes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A long subject makes a comma tempting, but a single comma can't separate the subject from its verb "named," and the essential "who" clause needs no commas.
explanation.D: Correct. The essential "who" clause is not set off, so the long subject connects directly to its verb "named."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Carved over several centuries beginning around 600 CE, the Ellora Caves in the western Indian state of Maharashtra are among the most ambitious works of rock-cut architecture in the world. The site includes thirty-four principal caves associated with the Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain ______ was cut directly into a basalt cliff rather than built from separate blocks of stone. The largest, the Kailasa temple, was excavated from the top down, with workers removing an estimated 200,000 metric tons of rock.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: traditions, each of them
choices.B: traditions; each of which
choices.C: traditions, each of which
choices.D: traditions each of which

explanation.why: "The site includes thirty-four principal caves associated with the Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain traditions" is an independent clause. What follows must attach to it without forming a second independent clause. "Each of which was cut directly into a basalt cliff" is a dependent relative clause describing the caves, and it is set off with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Each of them was cut directly into a basalt cliff" is an independent clause, and a comma alone can't join it to the first; this is a comma splice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "each of which was cut ..." is a dependent relative clause.
explanation.C: Correct. The comma attaches the nonessential relative clause "each of which was cut ..." to the independent clause it describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A nonessential relative clause beginning "each of which" must be set off with a comma; without one, it runs straight into "traditions."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Miss Penhallow regarded the rain for some moments with the air of one who suspects the weather of a personal discourtesy. Her niece, who had long since learned that such silences came before a pronouncement, set down her teacup and waited. "Are we to understand, then, that the bridge is impassable and that we must remain at this inn until the river consents to ______ she asked the landlord, who, having no answer likely to satisfy her, merely bowed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: fall?" she
choices.B: fall"? she
choices.C: fall," she
choices.D: fall?," she

explanation.why: Miss Penhallow's words form a direct question ("Are we to understand ..."), so the quotation must end with a question mark. The question mark belongs to the quoted words, so it goes inside the closing quotation mark, and no comma is added before the speaker tag "she asked."
explanation.A: Correct. The question mark ends the quoted question inside the quotation marks, and the speaker tag follows with no comma.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The question is part of the quotation, so the question mark goes inside the closing quotation mark, not outside it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma before "she asked" is used for a quoted statement, but this quotation is a direct question and must end with a question mark.
explanation.D: Incorrect. When a quotation ends with a question mark, no comma follows it; using both marks is incorrect.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the low-lying wetlands of southern Bangladesh, where fields can remain underwater for months during the monsoon, farmers have for generations grown vegetables on beds that float. Each bed (a raft of water hyacinth and other aquatic plants, piled up to about a meter ______ slowly decomposes as the season goes on, releasing nutrients to the seedlings of okra, gourds, and leafy greens planted in its surface. When the waters recede, the remains of the raft can be spread on fields as fertilizer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: thick)
choices.B: thick,
choices.C: thick),
choices.D: thick

explanation.why: The subject "Each bed" is followed by an explanation in parentheses, and the verb is "decomposes." The parentheses must close after "thick," and because the parenthetical sits between a subject and its verb, no comma should follow the closing parenthesis.
explanation.A: Correct. The closing parenthesis ends the explanation, and the subject "Each bed" connects to its verb "decomposes" with no extra punctuation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The opening parenthesis is never closed, and a comma can't close a parenthetical that opens with a parenthesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The parenthesis is closed correctly, but the comma after it separates the subject "Each bed" from its verb "decomposes."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Without a closing parenthesis, the explanation never ends, and "decomposes" seems to belong inside the parentheses.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Under the Mongol Empire of the thirteenth century, official messengers traveled along a network of relay stations known as the yam, which stretched across much of Asia. Stations were spaced a few dozen kilometers apart along the major ______ a messenger carrying an urgent order could exchange an exhausted horse for a rested one and press on with little delay. Relayed in this way, news could cover far more ground in a single day than any one rider and horse could manage alone.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: routes; so that
choices.B: routes. So that
choices.C: routes, this meant
choices.D: routes, so that

explanation.why: "Stations were spaced a few dozen kilometers apart along the major routes" is an independent clause. "So that a messenger ... could exchange an exhausted horse for a rested one" is a dependent clause explaining the purpose of that spacing. A dependent clause like this is attached to the independent clause, here with a comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "so that a messenger ... could exchange ..." is a dependent clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A period would leave "So that a messenger ... press on with little delay" as a sentence fragment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "This meant a messenger ... could exchange an exhausted horse" is an independent clause, and a comma alone can't join it to the first; this is a comma splice.
explanation.D: Correct. The comma attaches the dependent "so that" clause to the independent clause it explains.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When Filippo Brunelleschi began work on the dome of Florence Cathedral in 1420, the enormous octagonal opening it was meant to cover had remained unroofed for years. The central ______ to vault a span of more than forty meters without the usual wooden framework, since no one could find, or afford, timbers long enough to hold up the masonry while its mortar set. His answer combined two nested shells with bricks laid in a herringbone pattern, which helped lock each new ring of brickwork in place.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: difficulty, was how
choices.B: difficulty was how
choices.C: difficulty was, how
choices.D: difficulty was: how

explanation.why: In "The central difficulty was how to vault a span ...," the subject is "difficulty," the linking verb is "was," and "how to vault a span of more than forty meters" completes the verb. No punctuation goes between a subject and its verb or between a verb and the words that complete it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the subject "The central difficulty" from its verb "was."
explanation.B: Correct. No punctuation separates the subject, the verb "was," and the phrase that completes it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A comma can't separate the verb "was" from the phrase "how to vault a span ..." that completes it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A colon must follow a complete independent clause, but "The central difficulty was" is unfinished without the words that complete "was."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most mammals keep their bodies at a steady, warm temperature, but the arctic ground squirrel is a striking exception. During its winter hibernation in Alaska and northern Canada, the squirrel's body temperature can drop below the freezing point of water, the lowest body temperature measured in any mammal. Even so, the animal does not freeze solid: every few weeks it wakes briefly, warms itself up by shivering, and then cools down again.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Arctic ground squirrels hibernate for longer periods than any other mammal in the far north.
choices.B: The arctic ground squirrel survives unusually low body temperatures while it hibernates.
choices.C: The arctic ground squirrel wakes every few weeks during winter to warm itself up.
choices.D: Most mammals cannot keep a steady body temperature in very cold climates.

explanation.why: The text opens by calling the arctic ground squirrel "a striking exception" to the steady body temperature of most mammals, then explains that during hibernation its temperature can fall below freezing. The last sentence adds how it survives this. The main idea must cover the whole text: the squirrel endures extremely low body temperatures in hibernation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never compares how long different mammals hibernate.
explanation.B: Correct. Every sentence supports this point: the squirrel is an exception, its temperature drops below freezing, and it still survives.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Waking every few weeks is one detail from the last sentence, not the main point of the whole text.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the opposite: most mammals do keep a steady, warm temperature.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries, weavers near Dhaka, in what is now Bangladesh, made a cotton cloth so fine and light that it was traded across Asia and Europe. The cloth, known as Dhaka muslin, was spun from a local cotton plant that grew along the banks of the Meghna River. By the early 1900s, however, the craft had disappeared, partly because cheaper machine-made fabric from Britain had replaced it in many markets.
items.stem: According to the text, what was one reason Dhaka muslin stopped being made?

choices.A: Its weavers left the region to look for work in European cities.
choices.B: The local cotton plant used to spin it became too costly to grow.
choices.C: The cloth was too delicate to survive long trade journeys.
choices.D: Cheaper fabric made by machines replaced it in many markets.

explanation.why: The question asks for a reason the craft ended. The last sentence gives it directly: the craft disappeared "partly because cheaper machine-made fabric from Britain had replaced it in many markets." The correct choice restates this in other words.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the cloth was traded to Europe, not that the weavers moved there.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text mentions the local cotton plant but never says it became expensive.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the cloth was traded across Asia and Europe, so it clearly survived long journeys.
explanation.D: Correct. "Cheaper fabric made by machines" restates "cheaper machine-made fabric from Britain," which the text names as a reason the craft disappeared.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Completed in the 120s CE, the dome of the Pantheon in Rome is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Its builders had no steel bars to strengthen the concrete, so they controlled the dome's weight in other ways. Near the base, where the structure carries the greatest load, the concrete contains heavy stone and the walls are several meters thick. Toward the top, the walls grow thinner, and the builders mixed in pumice, a light volcanic rock, so that the upper dome presses down far less on the structure below.
items.stem: Based on the text, why did the Pantheon's builders use pumice in the upper part of the dome?

choices.A: To reduce the weight that the top of the dome placed on the parts beneath it
choices.B: To make the upper walls of the dome thicker than the walls near its base
choices.C: To replace the steel bars that Roman builders usually placed in concrete
choices.D: To make the dome larger than any other concrete dome built in Rome at the time

explanation.why: The text says the builders "controlled the dome's weight" without steel. It then explains that they mixed in pumice, "a light volcanic rock, so that the upper dome presses down far less on the structure below." So the pumice was used to lighten the top of the dome and reduce the load on the lower parts.
explanation.A: Correct. The text states that pumice was used "so that the upper dome presses down far less on the structure below."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the walls grow thinner toward the top, not thicker.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the builders had no steel bars at all, so pumice could not be replacing a usual practice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text notes the dome's record size but never says pumice was used to achieve it.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Tomás had expected the work at his grandmother's pottery to be quick. On the first morning he shaped six bowls, each one lopsided, and pushed them aside in frustration. His grandmother said nothing; she simply cut the last bowl from the wheel and handed him a fresh lump of clay. By the end of the week, Tomás had made only two bowls, but he had stopped counting. He found himself listening to the hum of the wheel and the soft drag of his fingers through the wet clay, and he no longer glanced at the clock.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Tomás grows frustrated because his grandmother refuses to show him how to use the wheel.
choices.B: Tomás learns to shape bowls much more quickly as the week goes on.
choices.C: Tomás shifts from rushing his work to becoming absorbed in the process of making it.
choices.D: Tomás's grandmother is disappointed by the lopsided bowls he makes on the first morning.

explanation.why: At the start, Tomás expects the work "to be quick," makes six bowls, and is frustrated. By the end of the week he makes fewer bowls, has "stopped counting," and "no longer glanced at the clock." The text as a whole traces this change from hurrying to being absorbed in the work.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The grandmother says nothing, but the text never says she refuses to teach him; she hands him more clay to keep working.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Tomás actually makes fewer bowls by the end of the week (two, compared with six on the first morning).
explanation.C: Correct. This covers both the beginning (expecting quick work, frustration) and the end (stopping counting, ignoring the clock).
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text does not describe the grandmother's feelings about the bowls, and the point concerns Tomás's change.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the seasonally flooded forests of the Amazon basin, some trees drop their fruit into the water, where it is eaten by fish such as the tambaqui. Because seeds can pass through a fish's gut intact and be released far from the parent tree, ecologists have long suspected that these fish help disperse seeds. Tracking studies now suggest that the largest individuals, which swim farther and hold seeds longer, may carry seeds several kilometers. This finding has an uncomfortable implication: fishing tends to remove precisely the biggest fish, so even where tambaqui remain common, the forest may be losing its most effective long-distance seed dispersers, a loss that population counts alone would not reveal.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Fishing has made tambaqui rare in flooded forests by removing the species' largest individuals.
choices.B: Ecologists have long suspected that fish such as the tambaqui help spread the seeds of flooded-forest trees.
choices.C: Large tambaqui carry seeds farther than any other animal living in the Amazon's flooded forests.
choices.D: Fishing may reduce long-distance seed dispersal in flooded forests even where tambaqui remain common.

explanation.why: The text builds to its final sentence: because the largest tambaqui "may carry seeds several kilometers" and fishing "tends to remove precisely the biggest fish," the forest "may be losing its most effective long-distance seed dispersers" even "where tambaqui remain common." The main idea is this possible hidden effect of fishing on seed dispersal, stated with the text's own caution ("may").
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the loss could happen "even where tambaqui remain common," so it does not claim the fish have become rare.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is background from the second sentence; it leaves out the new finding about large fish and its implication.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text compares large tambaqui only with smaller tambaqui, not with every other animal in the forest.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the text's main point, including its hedge ("may") and the key condition that the fish can still be common.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Many illustrated manuscripts produced in the workshop of the Mughal emperor Akbar in the late sixteenth century carry small notes in their margins naming the artists involved. These notes frequently list more than one name for a single painting: one artist is credited with the design of the composition, another with the coloring, and occasionally a third with the faces. For art historians, the inscriptions complicate a habit inherited from the study of European painting, in which a work is attributed to a single master whose personal style it expresses. In Akbar's workshop, the notes suggest, a painting's distinctive qualities may have emerged from collaboration rather than from any one hand.
items.stem: According to the text, what do the notes in the margins of many manuscripts from Akbar's workshop indicate?

choices.A: Artists in Akbar's workshop, like European masters, were each credited with whole paintings.
choices.B: A single painting was often produced by several artists who handled different tasks.
choices.C: European painters had trained many of the artists who worked in Akbar's workshop.
choices.D: Every painting in Akbar's workshop was produced by at least three separate artists.

explanation.why: The text says the notes "frequently list more than one name for a single painting," with different artists credited for the design, the coloring, and "occasionally" the faces. So the notes show that paintings were often made by several artists with different jobs. Watch the qualifiers: "frequently" and "occasionally" rule out any choice that says "every."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The notes show the opposite: paintings were credited to more than one artist, which is why they complicate the European single-master habit.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates "more than one name for a single painting," with separate credits for design, coloring, and sometimes faces.
explanation.C: Incorrect. European painting is mentioned only as the source of art historians' habits, not as an influence on Akbar's artists.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A third artist is credited only "occasionally," and multiple names appear "frequently," not always.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mrs. Halloran had long prided herself on receiving bad news as she received the post: promptly, and without remark. When her brother's letter arrived announcing that the old family house at Kilrush was to be sold, she read it once at the breakfast table, folded it along its original creases, and asked the maid whether the bread had come. Only later, when she found herself in the garden at an hour she never went there, standing before the gooseberry bushes she had grown from cuttings taken at that very house, did she understand that she had been composing, all morning, a reply she had no intention of sending.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Mrs. Halloran is secretly relieved that the old family house at Kilrush is finally to be sold.
choices.B: Mrs. Halloran resents her brother for deciding to sell the house without asking her.
choices.C: Mrs. Halloran's calm response to the news hides, even from herself, how much it affects her.
choices.D: Mrs. Halloran's lifelong composure finally gives way when she breaks down in the garden.

explanation.why: Two parts of the text must be read together. At breakfast she reacts "without remark," folding the letter and asking about the bread. Later, standing by bushes grown from the house's cuttings, she realizes she has been "composing, all morning, a reply." The words "Only later ... did she understand" show that her calm surface hid her feelings even from her own awareness.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Her drift to the gooseberry bushes from the old house and her mental reply suggest she is unsettled by the sale, not relieved.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says the brother failed to consult her, and it does not reveal what her unsent reply says.
explanation.C: Correct. Her outward calm at breakfast contrasts with her later realization; "only later ... did she understand" shows the feeling was hidden even from her.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This overstates the garden scene: she quietly realizes something, but nothing suggests she breaks down.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: That Inca administrators used khipus, arrangements of knotted cords, to record numbers is not in dispute: the position and type of each knot correspond to a decimal system, and many khipus tally census figures or goods owed to the state. Whether some khipus also recorded language is a harder question. Spanish chroniclers of the sixteenth century reported that khipu keepers could "read" histories and family lines from the cords, yet such testimony, offered by observers who could not themselves interpret the cords, establishes only that keepers recited narratives while handling khipus, not that the narratives were encoded in them. A few surviving khipus whose cords vary in color and fiber far more than any numerical purpose would require have therefore drawn particular attention.
items.stem: Based on the text, why have certain surviving khipus drawn particular attention?

choices.A: Their variety of colors and fibers seems to exceed what recording numbers alone would require.
choices.B: They confirm chroniclers' reports that khipu keepers could read histories directly from cords.
choices.C: Their knots, unlike those of the census khipus, do not follow a decimal system of positions.
choices.D: Spanish observers saw keepers reciting narratives while handling these particular khipus.

explanation.why: The text says the chroniclers' reports cannot settle whether khipus recorded language. The last sentence, linked by "therefore," explains why some khipus stand out: their cords vary "far more than any numerical purpose would require." That extra variety is what makes them possible evidence of a non-numerical record.
explanation.A: Correct. This restates the final sentence: the variety goes beyond "any numerical purpose," which is why these khipus interest researchers asking whether khipus recorded language.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text calls the question of language open and says the reports prove less than they seem to; nothing confirms them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says these khipus' knots break from the decimal system; it points to color and fiber instead.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text discusses the chroniclers' testimony in general, not observations tied to these particular khipus.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The hoatzin, a pheasant-sized bird of the swampy forests of South America, usually builds its nest on branches that hang over water. When a snake or other predator comes near, a young hoatzin may simply drop out of the nest into the water below and swim away. Once the danger has passed, the chick climbs back up to the nest, gripping the branches with two small claws on each wing. These claws disappear as the bird grows up.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Snakes are the most common predators of birds in South American forests.
choices.B: Young hoatzins have a way to escape predators and then return to their nests.
choices.C: Hoatzins build their nests over water so that predators cannot reach the eggs.
choices.D: Adult hoatzins use the claws on their wings to climb through swampy forests.

explanation.why: The text explains what a young hoatzin does when a predator comes near: it drops into the water and swims away, and later it climbs back to the nest using claws on its wings. The main idea must cover both parts of this survival strategy, escaping and returning.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text mentions a snake as one possible predator but never compares predators of forest birds.
explanation.B: Correct. This covers the whole text: the chick escapes by dropping into the water and then climbs back up with its wing claws.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says where hoatzins nest but never says the nests keep predators from reaching eggs.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the claws disappear as the bird grows up, so adults do not use them.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every morning that spring, old Stavros carried a bucket of water up the hill to the olive sapling he had planted at the edge of his field. His neighbor laughed and pointed out that an olive tree can take many years to bear a full crop. Stavros only shrugged and nodded toward his granddaughter, who was chasing a goat through the tall grass. "The olives are not for me," he said. "They are for her."
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Stavros's granddaughter helps him water the olive sapling each morning.
choices.B: Stavros's neighbor persuades him that planting an olive tree is a waste of time.
choices.C: Stavros worries that his young olive tree will not survive the dry spring.
choices.D: Stavros tends a tree whose harvest he expects his granddaughter to enjoy.

explanation.why: The neighbor points out that an olive tree takes many years to produce a full crop. Stavros is not bothered: he nods toward his granddaughter and says, "The olives are not for me. . . . They are for her." The main idea is that he is caring for the tree for her future benefit.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The granddaughter is chasing a goat; the text says Stavros carries the water himself.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Stavros only shrugs at his neighbor and keeps caring for the tree, so he is not persuaded.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says Stavros worries about the tree surviving.
explanation.D: Correct. Stavros keeps watering the sapling even though it will take years to bear fruit, because the olives are "for her."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At Kalibangan, an archaeological site in the Indian state of Rajasthan, researchers uncovered one of the oldest plowed fields ever found. The field dates to about 2800 BCE. Its furrows were cut in two directions, crossing one another to form a grid. Farmers in the same region still plow some fields in this crisscross way today, so that they can grow two different crops in a single field.
items.stem: According to the text, what is notable about the furrows in the ancient field at Kalibangan?

choices.A: They were cut with a kind of plow that was later forgotten in the region.
choices.B: They are deeper than the furrows found at any other ancient site.
choices.C: They cross one another in a pattern that farmers in the region still use.
choices.D: They show that early farmers there grew only one crop in each field.

explanation.why: The text says the furrows were cut "in two directions, crossing one another to form a grid," and that farmers in the same region "still plow some fields in this crisscross way today." The correct choice restates both of these details.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the crisscross method is still used today, not that it was forgotten.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never compares the depth of these furrows with others.
explanation.C: Correct. The furrows form a crisscross grid, and the text says local farmers still plow some fields this way.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text links the crisscross pattern to growing two crops in a single field, not one.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Inuit artists in Kinngait, a small community in Nunavut, in northern Canada, had long been known for carving figures from stone. In the late 1950s, some of them began to experiment with printmaking, transferring their drawings onto stone blocks and printing them on paper. The new art form caught on quickly. Since 1959, Kinngait artists have released a collection of new prints nearly every year, and their work is now displayed in museums around the world.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Kinngait artists gave up stone carving entirely once they began making prints.
choices.B: Kinngait artists took up printmaking, which became a lasting success there.
choices.C: Printmaking in Kinngait began as a way to sell drawings to museums.
choices.D: Inuit artists in northern Canada have long carved figures from stone.

explanation.why: The text describes how Kinngait artists began making prints in the late 1950s and how the art form "caught on quickly," with new collections released nearly every year since 1959 and work shown in museums worldwide. The main idea is that printmaking became a lasting and successful practice in Kinngait.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says the artists stopped carving; it says they added printmaking.
explanation.B: Correct. This sums up the whole text: artists began printmaking, it caught on, and it has continued and gained wide recognition.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the prints are now in museums, not that printmaking began in order to sell to them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Stone carving is background from the first sentence; the text is mainly about printmaking.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the 1990s, divers off Amami Oshima, an island in southern Japan, began reporting strange circles in the sand of the seafloor. Each circle was about two meters across, with ridges and grooves running out from its center. Years later, scientists learned who made them: a male pufferfish only about 12 centimeters long. The fish builds each circle by swimming along the bottom and flapping its fins, and females lay their eggs in its center.
items.stem: According to the text, how does the male pufferfish make a sand circle?

choices.A: By swimming along the seafloor while flapping its fins
choices.B: By pushing sand into ridges with its mouth
choices.C: By working together with several female pufferfish
choices.D: By following grooves left in the sand by ocean currents

explanation.why: The question asks how the circle is made. The last sentence answers it directly: "The fish builds each circle by swimming along the bottom and flapping its fins." The correct choice restates this.
explanation.A: Correct. The text says the fish "builds each circle by swimming along the bottom and flapping its fins."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says the fish uses its mouth to move sand.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the male builds the circle; females only lay their eggs in its center.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the fish makes the ridges and grooves; it never mentions ocean currents.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Funmi had watched her mother sell fabric at the market in Lagos for years, but today the stall was hers for one hour. When a woman stopped to touch a roll of blue cloth, Funmi's voice came out as a whisper. She cleared her throat and tried again, louder this time, naming a price just as her mother would have. The woman nodded and counted out the money. Funmi folded the cloth with steady hands, grinning.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Funmi overcomes her nervousness and makes a sale on her own.
choices.B: Funmi's mother nervously watches her daughter speak with a customer.
choices.C: Funmi lowers the price of the cloth so that the woman will buy it.
choices.D: Funmi realizes that she would rather work somewhere other than the market.

explanation.why: At first Funmi's voice "came out as a whisper," showing she is nervous. She then speaks louder, names a price, makes the sale, and folds the cloth "with steady hands, grinning." The text as a whole shows her moving from nervousness to success on her own.
explanation.A: Correct. This covers the whole text: her nervous whisper at the start and her confident sale at the end.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says the mother is present or nervous; the stall is Funmi's for the hour.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Funmi names a price "just as her mother would have"; she does not lower it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Funmi ends the text grinning; nothing suggests she wants to work elsewhere.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 930 CE, chieftains from across Iceland began meeting each summer at Thingvellir, a wide valley in the southwest of the island. At this gathering, called the Althing, they settled disputes and agreed on laws that applied to everyone on the island. Because Iceland had no king, the Althing was the main way the island was governed. A parliament called the Althing still meets in Iceland today, making it one of the oldest such bodies in the world.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The Althing began as Iceland's lawmaking assembly in 930 CE and continues today.
choices.B: Thingvellir was chosen for the gathering because chieftains could reach it easily.
choices.C: Iceland's chieftains settled their disputes at Thingvellir in the year 930 CE.
choices.D: Iceland's chieftains met each summer mainly to choose a king for the island.

explanation.why: The text explains that the Althing began in 930 CE as a summer gathering where chieftains made laws and settled disputes, served as Iceland's main form of government, and still meets today. The main idea must cover both its origin and its long history.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures the whole text: the Althing's start as a lawmaking gathering and its survival to the present.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never explains why Thingvellir was chosen.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is only one detail, and the gatherings continued every summer rather than happening once.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says Iceland had no king; the Althing governed instead.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The gharial, a type of crocodile found in the rivers of northern India and Nepal, has an unusually long, thin snout lined with sharp teeth. This snout is well suited to the gharial's diet, which is made up almost entirely of fish. Because the snout is so narrow, it meets little resistance from the water. As a result, the gharial can sweep its head sideways quickly to snap up fish as they swim past.
items.stem: According to the text, why is the gharial's narrow snout useful?

choices.A: It lets the gharial crush the hard shells of turtles.
choices.B: It can be swung quickly through water to catch fish.
choices.C: It helps the gharial attract mates in the breeding season.
choices.D: It allows the gharial to stay hidden in shallow water.

explanation.why: The text says the narrow snout "meets little resistance from the water," so the gharial "can sweep its head sideways quickly to snap up fish." The snout is useful because it moves fast through water to catch fish.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the gharial eats almost entirely fish and never mentions turtles.
explanation.B: Correct. The narrow snout meets little resistance, so the gharial can sweep it sideways quickly to catch fish.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not discuss mating at all.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never says the snout helps the gharial hide.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Completed in 1885, the Home Insurance Building in Chicago rose ten stories, a great height for its time. Before then, the outer walls of a tall building had to carry its full weight, so the lower walls needed to be extremely thick. The Home Insurance Building was different: a frame made of iron and steel held up the structure. Its walls could therefore be thinner, and many historians consider it the first skyscraper.
items.stem: According to the text, how was the Home Insurance Building different from earlier tall buildings?

choices.A: Its outer walls were made thicker so that they could support more floors.
choices.B: It was the first building in Chicago to rise more than ten stories.
choices.C: It had more windows than any other office building of its time.
choices.D: Its weight was carried by a metal frame rather than by its walls.

explanation.why: The text says that in earlier tall buildings "the outer walls . . . had to carry its full weight," but in the Home Insurance Building "a frame made of iron and steel held up the structure." The difference is that a metal frame, not the walls, carried the load.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the opposite: because of the frame, its walls could be thinner.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the building had ten stories, not more than ten, and never ranks it among Chicago buildings.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions windows.
explanation.D: Correct. The text contrasts weight-bearing walls in earlier buildings with the iron and steel frame that held up this one.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every November, Jiho's grandmother made enough kimchi to last the whole winter. This year, for the first time, she handed Jiho a pair of rubber gloves. He rubbed the red pepper paste into each cabbage leaf the way she showed him, slowly at first and then faster. When he finished a head of cabbage, his grandmother inspected it, said nothing, and placed it in the big clay jar with her own. Jiho stood a little taller.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Jiho's grandmother decides to make less kimchi than usual this year.
choices.B: Jiho learns that kimchi must be stored in large clay jars during the winter.
choices.C: Jiho's grandmother criticizes the way he prepares the cabbage leaves.
choices.D: Jiho takes pride in being trusted to help with his grandmother's task.

explanation.why: For the first time, the grandmother gives Jiho gloves so he can help. When she puts his cabbage "in the big clay jar with her own," she shows she accepts his work, and "Jiho stood a little taller." The main idea is his pride at being trusted with this task.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says she makes less kimchi this year.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The clay jar is a small detail, and the text never says kimchi must be stored that way.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The grandmother says nothing and puts his cabbage with her own, which shows approval, not criticism.
explanation.D: Correct. This covers the whole text: Jiho is invited to help for the first time, his work is accepted, and he feels proud.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When people picture ancient pyramids, they usually think of Egypt. Yet Sudan, Egypt's southern neighbor, has even more of them. Nearly 200 pyramids stand at Meroë, once a capital of the Kingdom of Kush. Built over several centuries, mostly as tombs for Kushite kings and queens, they are much smaller than Egypt's famous pyramids at Giza, and their sides are much steeper.
items.stem: According to the text, how do the pyramids at Meroë compare with Egypt's pyramids at Giza?

choices.A: They are larger than the Giza pyramids but fewer in number.
choices.B: They were built many centuries before the pyramids at Giza.
choices.C: They are much smaller and have steeper sides.
choices.D: They were built for queens, while those at Giza were for kings.

explanation.why: The last sentence makes the comparison directly: the Meroë pyramids "are much smaller than Egypt's famous pyramids at Giza, and their sides are much steeper." The correct choice restates this.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the Meroë pyramids are much smaller, not larger.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says when the Giza pyramids were built, so it gives no basis for this comparison.
explanation.C: Correct. The text states that they are "much smaller" than the Giza pyramids and that "their sides are much steeper."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the Meroë pyramids were tombs for both kings and queens and says nothing about who was buried at Giza.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In parts of Africa, a small bird called the greater honeyguide helps people find honey. Honey hunters in Mozambique, for example, make a special trilling call as they walk through the bush. A honeyguide that hears the call often answers and then flies ahead, leading the hunters to a bees' nest hidden in a tree. After the people open the nest and take the honey, the bird feeds on the leftover beeswax.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Honey hunters in Mozambique have learned to imitate the songs of many birds.
choices.B: Honeyguides and human honey hunters work together in a way that helps both.
choices.C: Greater honeyguides feed mainly on the honey they find in bees' nests.
choices.D: Honeyguides answer calls made by people in nearly every part of the world.

explanation.why: The bird leads the hunters to a bees' nest, and the people open the nest, take the honey, and leave beeswax that the bird eats. The text as a whole describes this partnership, in which each side gains something.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The hunters make one special call; the text never says they imitate many birds.
explanation.B: Correct. The people get honey, and the bird gets the beeswax, so the cooperation helps both.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the people take the honey and the bird eats the leftover beeswax.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text describes this behavior only "in parts of Africa," so this claims far too much.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The American pika, a small, round-eared relative of rabbits, lives on rocky mountain slopes in western North America, where snow can cover the ground for more than half the year. Unlike marmots and many other mountain mammals, pikas do not hibernate. Instead, they spend the short summer gathering grasses and wildflowers, carrying them mouthful by mouthful to piles hidden beneath boulders. These stores, known as haypiles, supply the food a pika lives on during the long months when it stays active under the snow.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Pikas collect more summer food than any other mountain mammal.
choices.B: Pikas carry grasses and wildflowers to hidden piles beneath boulders.
choices.C: Like marmots, pikas spend the winter hibernating beneath boulders.
choices.D: Pikas stay active all winter by living on food they stored in summer.

explanation.why: The text contrasts pikas with mammals that hibernate: pikas "do not hibernate" but instead gather plants in summer, and these haypiles feed them while they stay "active under the snow." The main idea must connect the summer gathering to winter survival without hibernation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never compares how much food pikas and other mammals collect.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This describes how pikas gather food but leaves out why it matters, which is surviving the winter while active.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says that, unlike marmots, pikas do not hibernate.
explanation.D: Correct. This links the whole text: pikas skip hibernation and rely on summer haypiles to stay active through winter.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Bilal had always thought of the orchard outside Quetta as his uncle's place, somewhere to visit for a day at Eid and then forget. This summer, sent to help with the apricot harvest, he spent the first days counting the hours until his bus home. By the second week, though, he had learned which branches would bend without breaking and how to tell a ripe fruit by its softness under his thumb. On the last morning, when his uncle asked whether he would come back next year, Bilal was surprised to hear himself answer before the question was finished.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Bilal finds the apricot harvest more tiring than he had expected.
choices.B: Bilal agrees to return to the orchard only because his uncle insists.
choices.C: Bilal learns several useful skills during his second week in the orchard.
choices.D: Bilal goes from wanting to leave the orchard to wanting to return to it.

explanation.why: At first Bilal is "counting the hours until his bus home." By the end, he answers his uncle's invitation to return "before the question was finished," which shows eagerness. The text as a whole traces this change in his feelings about the orchard.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says the work tires him.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Bilal answers before his uncle even finishes asking, so he is eager, not pressured.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The skills he learns are a step in his change, not the main point of the whole text.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the change from counting the hours until he can leave to eagerly agreeing to come back.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In August 1858, after several failed attempts, workers finished laying a telegraph cable across the floor of the Atlantic Ocean, linking Ireland and Newfoundland. Celebrations broke out in cities on both sides of the ocean, and Queen Victoria sent a message of congratulations to US President James Buchanan. Yet the cable was disappointing in practice: her short message took more than sixteen hours to transmit, and within about three weeks the cable had stopped working entirely. A lasting connection across the Atlantic was not achieved until 1866.
items.stem: According to the text, what was true of the telegraph cable completed in 1858?

choices.A: It was the first of several cables that worked reliably across the Atlantic.
choices.B: It was celebrated mainly in Britain, which had paid for its construction.
choices.C: It carried messages across the Atlantic in minutes for a short time.
choices.D: It was widely celebrated, though it carried messages slowly and soon failed.

explanation.why: The text says "celebrations broke out in cities on both sides of the ocean," but then turns with "Yet": a short message took "more than sixteen hours," and the cable stopped working within about three weeks. The correct choice combines the celebration with these two problems.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The 1858 cable failed within weeks, and a lasting link came only in 1866.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Celebrations happened "on both sides of the ocean," and the text never says who paid for the cable.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says a short message took more than sixteen hours, not minutes.
explanation.D: Correct. The cable was celebrated widely, but it was very slow and stopped working within about three weeks.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The siku, a panpipe from the Andes of Bolivia and Peru, is made of cane tubes of different lengths bound together in rows. In its traditional form, the instrument's notes are divided between two separate sets of tubes, each held by a different musician: one set contains every other note of the scale, and the other contains the notes in between. To play a melody, the two musicians must alternate rapidly, so that neither one can perform the whole tune alone. Many Andean musicians describe this interlocking style as an expression of cooperation within a community.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The siku is made of cane tubes of different lengths bound into rows.
choices.B: Andean musicians favor the siku because it is easier to learn than other pipes.
choices.C: Each siku player performs a separate melody that blends with the other's tune.
choices.D: A traditional siku is built so that two players must share each melody.

explanation.why: Most of the text explains that a traditional siku splits the notes between two musicians, who must alternate so that "neither one can perform the whole tune alone," and the last sentence explains what this shared playing means to musicians. The main idea is that the instrument requires two players to work together on one melody.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This describes how the tubes are made, a detail from the first sentence, not the main point.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says the siku is easy to learn or compares it with other instruments.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The two players do not play separate melodies; they alternate notes of the same melody.
explanation.D: Correct. The text centers on how the siku's notes are split so that two musicians must alternate to play one tune.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Gardeners have long noticed that plants grown outdoors tend to be shorter and sturdier than those raised indoors. To test whether touch alone could produce this difference, horticulturist Ingrid Halvorsen grew two groups of basil seedlings under identical greenhouse conditions. Once a day, she gently brushed one group with a sheet of cardboard; the other group was left untouched. After four weeks, the brushed seedlings were about 20 percent shorter than the untouched ones, but their stems were thicker, and they bent less when placed in front of a fan.
items.stem: Based on the text, what did Halvorsen's experiment suggest about basil seedlings?

choices.A: They grow taller outdoors than they do in a greenhouse.
choices.B: Being touched regularly can make them shorter but sturdier.
choices.C: Wind affects their growth more strongly than being touched does.
choices.D: Being brushed daily causes them to produce more leaves.

explanation.why: Halvorsen kept all conditions the same except touch. The brushed seedlings ended up "about 20 percent shorter" with "thicker" stems that "bent less" in front of a fan. So the experiment suggests that touch alone can make seedlings shorter and sturdier.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says outdoor plants tend to be shorter, not taller, and the experiment was done entirely in a greenhouse.
explanation.B: Correct. The only difference between the groups was brushing, and the brushed plants were shorter with thicker, stiffer stems.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The experiment tested touch, not wind; the fan was used only to measure sturdiness afterward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions the number of leaves.
