items.subject: literature
items.passage: For thirty-one years, Captain Wiśniewski had steered the old ferry across the harbor in Gdańsk, and on the morning the new one entered service, he went down to the dock to watch. It was sleek and white, and it glided away without a single puff of black smoke. A young officer stood at its wheel, chatting easily with passengers. The captain had planned to find fault with something. Instead, as the ferry rounded the breakwater exactly where he would have turned it, he found himself nodding, and then, quietly, he raised a hand in salute.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The new ferry is cleaner and more modern than the one the captain steered.
choices.B: The captain, who expected to disapprove of the new ferry, ends up approving.
choices.C: The captain criticizes the young officer for steering the new ferry carelessly.
choices.D: The captain is relieved that he no longer has to steer the old ferry each day.

explanation.why: The text says the captain "had planned to find fault with something." Instead, when the ferry turns "exactly where he would have turned it," he nods and raises "a hand in salute." The main idea is this shift from expected disapproval to approval.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The description of the new ferry is a detail; the text focuses on the captain's reaction.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures the turn in the text from planning to find fault to quietly saluting.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The captain finds nothing to criticize; he salutes the officer's steering.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never says the captain feels relieved about retiring.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1720s and 1730s, Jai Singh II, the ruler of Jaipur in northwestern India, built several observatories, including one in his capital now known as the Jantar Mantar. Its instruments did not use telescopes; instead, they were giant structures of stone and brick, laid out to track the positions of the sun, moon, and stars. Their size served a purpose. On a larger instrument, each degree of the sky is spread over a longer distance, so observers could read positions more finely. The largest, a sundial nearly 27 meters tall, can show the local time to within a few seconds.
items.stem: According to the text, why were the instruments at the Jantar Mantar built so large?

choices.A: To hold the large telescopes used to track the sun, moon, and stars
choices.B: To make them visible to people throughout the city of Jaipur
choices.C: To show that Jaipur's observatory was grander than Jai Singh's others
choices.D: To allow observers to measure positions in the sky more precisely

explanation.why: The text says the instruments' "size served a purpose": on a larger instrument, "each degree of the sky is spread over a longer distance, so observers could read positions more finely." The size was meant to make measurements more precise.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the instruments "did not use telescopes."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says the instruments were meant to be seen across the city.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text mentions other observatories but never compares their size or grandeur.
explanation.D: Correct. The text explains that larger instruments spread each degree over a longer distance, allowing finer readings.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Bossa nova, which emerged in Rio de Janeiro in the late 1950s, grew out of samba, the lively dance music of Brazil's carnival. Yet the new style sounded strikingly different. Musicians such as the guitarist and singer João Gilberto reduced samba's crowd of drums to a gentle rhythm played on a single guitar, and they borrowed the rich, complex chords of American cool jazz. Singers, rather than projecting over a band, sang softly, almost as if speaking to one listener. The result was an intimate music that soon found eager audiences far beyond Brazil.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Bossa nova replaced samba as the main music of Brazil's carnival.
choices.B: Bossa nova turned elements of samba into a quieter, more intimate music.
choices.C: Bossa nova singers sang softly instead of projecting over a band.
choices.D: João Gilberto was the first musician in Brazil to play American jazz chords.

explanation.why: The text says bossa nova "grew out of samba" but "sounded strikingly different," then lists the changes: a gentle guitar rhythm, jazz chords, and soft singing. It concludes that the result was "an intimate music." The main idea must cover both its roots in samba and its transformation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says bossa nova replaced samba at carnival.
explanation.B: Correct. This covers the whole text: bossa nova came from samba but changed it into a quiet, intimate style.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Soft singing is only one of several changes the text describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says musicians borrowed jazz chords but never claims Gilberto was the first in Brazil to do so.

items.subject: science
items.passage: After shaping a ball of dung, a dung beetle rolls it away in a straight line, the quickest way to escape rivals that might steal it. Researchers in South Africa had already shown that the beetles can use the sun or moon to hold their course. But some beetles roll their balls straight even on moonless nights. To find out how, the researchers placed beetles in a planetarium, where they could control what appeared in the sky. When only the band of light from the Milky Way was shown, the beetles still traveled in fairly straight lines; under a completely dark dome, they wandered.
items.stem: According to the text, what did the planetarium experiment show?

choices.A: Dung beetles can steer by the moon but not by the Milky Way.
choices.B: Dung beetles can keep a straight course using the Milky Way's light alone.
choices.C: Dung beetles roll in straight lines even when the sky above is completely dark.
choices.D: Dung beetles roll their balls straighter indoors than they do outdoors.

explanation.why: In the planetarium, the researchers showed beetles only the Milky Way's band of light, and the beetles "still traveled in fairly straight lines." Under a completely dark dome, they wandered. So the experiment showed that the Milky Way alone is enough for the beetles to hold their course.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The beetles held a straight course when shown only the Milky Way, so they can use it.
explanation.B: Correct. With only the Milky Way visible, the beetles traveled fairly straight, which shows its light was enough.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Under a completely dark dome, the text says the beetles wandered.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares the beetles' paths indoors and outdoors.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Awa had spent weeks complaining that her older sister, Mariama, took up most of their shared bedroom in Dakar. Now Mariama's half of the room was nearly bare, her books and clothes packed into two suitcases for the university in Saint-Louis. Awa told herself she would finally have space to spread out. But that evening, sitting on her own bed, she realized she had not moved a single thing onto the empty shelves, and when Mariama called from the doorway to say goodnight, Awa asked her to sit down and talk a little longer.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Awa is eager to rearrange the bedroom as soon as her sister leaves.
choices.B: Mariama is nervous about leaving home to attend a distant university.
choices.C: Awa finds that she will miss her sister more than she had expected.
choices.D: Awa and Mariama have long argued about how to share their bedroom.

explanation.why: Awa expects to enjoy having more space, but she does not move anything onto the empty shelves and asks Mariama to "sit down and talk a little longer." These actions show that she is sadder about her sister's departure than she expected to be.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Awa only tells herself she will spread out; in fact she leaves the shelves empty.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never describes Mariama's feelings about leaving.
explanation.C: Correct. Awa's untouched shelves and her request that Mariama stay and talk show feelings she had not expected.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Awa's past complaints are background; the text focuses on her feelings as her sister leaves.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: During Japan's Edo period (1603–1868), many children of farmers, merchants, and craftspeople studied at terakoya, small private schools often run by a single teacher in a temple or a home. Pupils practiced writing characters, read practical texts such as letters and almanacs, and learned arithmetic on the abacus. Such schools multiplied rapidly in the last decades of the period, and historians generally agree that they helped make reading and writing common among ordinary people. Estimates of exactly how many people could read, however, vary widely, since few records measured literacy directly.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Terakoya probably spread literacy widely, though how widely is unclear.
choices.B: Terakoya records let historians measure Edo-period literacy rates precisely.
choices.C: Terakoya taught commoners' children arithmetic but not how to read.
choices.D: Most terakoya were run by a single teacher inside a temple.

explanation.why: The text says historians "generally agree" that terakoya "helped make reading and writing common among ordinary people," but then adds with "however" that estimates of literacy "vary widely" because few records measured it. The main idea must include both the agreement and the uncertainty.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures both the historians' general agreement and the uncertainty about exact numbers.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says few records measured literacy directly, so estimates vary widely.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says pupils practiced writing and read letters and almanacs, so reading was taught.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says terakoya were "often" run by one teacher "in a temple or a home"; this detail is also not the main point.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When Johann Sebastian Bach died in 1750, his music was already considered old-fashioned, and for decades afterward it was known mainly to musicians, who studied his keyboard pieces as exercises. That began to change in March 1829, when the twenty-year-old composer Felix Mendelssohn conducted Bach's St. Matthew Passion in Berlin, the work's first performance since Bach's own time. The concert drew a large audience and was repeated within weeks. In the years that followed, interest in Bach's music spread across Europe, and many of his works were published for the first time.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Mendelssohn was the first musician to study Bach's keyboard pieces.
choices.B: Bach's music was popular with large audiences throughout his own lifetime.
choices.C: Mendelssohn's performance helped revive wide interest in Bach's music.
choices.D: The 1829 performance of the St. Matthew Passion drew a large audience.

explanation.why: The text first explains that after 1750 Bach's music was known "mainly to musicians." It then says "that began to change" with Mendelssohn's 1829 performance, after which interest "spread across Europe." The main idea is the role of that performance in reviving broad interest in Bach.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says musicians had studied Bach's keyboard pieces for decades before 1829.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says his music was considered old-fashioned by the time he died and never describes large audiences in his lifetime.
explanation.C: Correct. This covers the whole text: Bach's music had faded from wide view, and Mendelssohn's performance began its revival.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The large audience is one detail; the text's point is the wider revival that followed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The hilsa, a silvery fish prized in Bangladeshi and Indian cooking, spends most of its life in the salty waters of the Bay of Bengal. To breed, however, adult hilsa swim upstream into large rivers such as the Padma and the Meghna, where they release their eggs in fresh water. Because so many fish gather in the rivers at once, catching them at this stage could sharply reduce the number of young produced. For that reason, Bangladesh bans hilsa fishing for a few weeks each autumn, during the peak of the breeding season.
items.stem: According to the text, why does Bangladesh ban hilsa fishing for part of each year?

choices.A: To stop the fish from swimming upstream into the Padma and the Meghna
choices.B: To protect the fish while they gather in rivers to breed
choices.C: To keep the price of hilsa high in local markets
choices.D: To let the fish return safely to the Bay of Bengal

explanation.why: The text says that because so many hilsa gather in the rivers to breed, catching them then "could sharply reduce the number of young produced." It adds, "For that reason," the fishing ban falls "during the peak of the breeding season." The ban protects the fish while they breed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Swimming upstream is a natural part of breeding; the ban protects this journey rather than stopping it.
explanation.B: Correct. The ban is timed to the breeding season, when catching the gathered fish would cut the number of young.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never discusses prices.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions the fish returning to the bay as the reason for the ban.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For a year, Teodora had copied the master's charts in his Lisbon workshop, tracing each bay and cape with a fine pen until her lines matched his exactly. This morning, though, a sailor who came in insisted that a sandbar now blocked the mouth of the river shown on the chart she was finishing. The master was away. Teodora hesitated, her pen above the paper, then asked the sailor to describe the sandbar's shape and position. Slowly, for the first time, she drew a line that appeared on no chart the master had ever made.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Teodora refuses to change the chart until her master returns to the workshop.
choices.B: Teodora learns from a sailor how sandbars form at the mouths of rivers.
choices.C: Teodora realizes that all of her master's charts are full of careless errors.
choices.D: Teodora moves from copying her master's work to relying on her own judgment.

explanation.why: At first Teodora copies the master's charts "until her lines matched his exactly." When the master is away and the sailor reports a new sandbar, she decides on her own to add it, drawing "a line that appeared on no chart the master had ever made." The text shows her shift from copying to independent judgment.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Teodora hesitates but then draws the sandbar while the master is still away.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The sailor describes the sandbar's shape and position, not how sandbars form.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sailor reports one new sandbar; the text never says the master's charts are full of careless errors.
explanation.D: Correct. This covers the whole text: a year of exact copying followed by her first independent change.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When Australia's six colonies united as one nation in 1901, a dispute arose over where its capital should be. Sydney and Melbourne, the two largest cities, were fierce rivals, and neither would accept the other as the seat of government. The solution was to build an entirely new city on a site between them. In 1912, an international competition to design the capital was won by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, whose plan arranged the city around a central lake. Construction moved slowly, however, and the lake was not filled until 1964.
items.stem: According to the text, why was a new city built to serve as Australia's capital?

choices.A: Neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as the capital.
choices.B: Australia's largest cities lacked space for government buildings.
choices.C: The Griffins proposed arranging the capital around a central lake.
choices.D: An international competition required the capital to be a new city.

explanation.why: The text says Sydney and Melbourne "were fierce rivals, and neither would accept the other as the seat of government," and then calls building a new city "the solution." The rivalry between the two cities is the reason a new capital was built.
explanation.A: Correct. Building a new city was "the solution" to the rivalry, since neither city would accept the other as capital.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never mentions a lack of space in either city.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true of the winning design, but it explains how the city was planned, not why it was built.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The competition came after the decision to build a new city; it did not cause that decision.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The ancient theater at Epidaurus, in southern Greece, was built in the fourth century BCE and could seat more than 12,000 people. It is famous for its sound: visitors today report that an actor speaking at normal volume on the stage can be heard clearly even from the highest rows. For centuries, this effect was credited simply to the theater's steep, bowl-like shape. More recently, however, some acoustic researchers have proposed that the rows of limestone seats also play a role, filtering out low-pitched background noise while reflecting the higher-pitched sounds of actors' voices.
items.stem: According to the text, what have some acoustic researchers proposed about the theater at Epidaurus?

choices.A: The theater's steep, bowl-like shape alone explains its remarkable sound.
choices.B: Actors there had to shout to be heard from the highest rows.
choices.C: The theater held more people than any other in ancient Greece.
choices.D: The theater's rows of seats help reduce low-pitched background noise.

explanation.why: The text says the effect was long credited "simply" to the theater's shape, but researchers have more recently proposed that the limestone seats "also play a role, filtering out low-pitched background noise." The correct choice restates this proposal.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is the older view; the researchers propose that the seats also play a role, so shape alone does not explain it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says an actor speaking "at normal volume" can be heard from the highest rows.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text gives the theater's size but never compares it with other Greek theaters.
explanation.D: Correct. The researchers propose that the rows of limestone seats filter out low-pitched background noise.

items.subject: science
items.passage: White-crowned sparrows are common songbirds across much of North America, but males in different areas sing noticeably different versions of their song, much as people in different regions speak with different accents. Studies have shown that these dialects are learned rather than inherited. A young male listens to the adult males around him during his first months of life and later practices until his song matches theirs. Males raised without ever hearing adult birds develop a simpler, unusual song instead.
items.stem: According to the text, how does a young male white-crowned sparrow come to sing the dialect of its area?

choices.A: By hearing nearby adult males early in life and later copying them
choices.B: By singing with other young males until they all agree on one version
choices.C: By inheriting the dialect that its own parents sang
choices.D: By moving to an area where its parents' dialect is common

explanation.why: The text says the dialects "are learned rather than inherited": a young male "listens to the adult males around him during his first months of life and later practices until his song matches theirs." The correct choice restates this process.
explanation.A: Correct. The young male listens to nearby adults in his first months and practices until his song matches theirs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says young males learn from adult males, not from one another.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the dialects are learned "rather than inherited."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never says young birds move to find their parents' dialect.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Sunita had grown up beside her father's printing press in Kathmandu, falling asleep to the rhythm of its clatter, but he had never let her touch it. Today, with a wedding order due by evening and his assistant sick, he pointed her toward the trays of metal letters without a word. Her fingers trembled as she set the first line backward, the way she had watched him do a thousand times. When the first card came off the press, her father held it to the light, studied it for a long moment, and handed her the next order.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Sunita is finally allowed to use the press and earns her father's trust.
choices.B: Sunita's father regrets letting her help with such an urgent order.
choices.C: Sunita's father carefully explains to her how to set the letters backward.
choices.D: Sunita discovers that setting type is much harder than it looked.

explanation.why: Sunita's father "had never let her touch" the press, but today he points her toward it. After studying her first card, he "handed her the next order," which shows he trusts her work. The text as a whole shows her being given this chance and succeeding.
explanation.A: Correct. This covers both the start (she was never allowed to touch the press) and the end (her father gives her more work).
explanation.B: Incorrect. After examining her card, her father hands her the next order, which shows approval rather than regret.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Her father points her to the letters "without a word"; she learned by watching him for years.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Her fingers tremble from nerves, but the text never says the work is harder than she expected; she sets the line correctly.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sleep is usually linked to the brain, and for a long time scientists studied it only in animals that have one. The upside-down jellyfish Cassiopea has no brain at all, only a loose network of nerve cells spread through its body. Yet a 2017 study found that at night these jellyfish pulse about a third less often than during the day and are slower to react when disturbed. When researchers kept them from resting at night, the jellyfish were less active the following day, much as a tired person would be. Such results suggest that something like sleep may not require a brain.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Cassiopea jellyfish are slower to react to disturbances at night than during the day.
choices.B: Scientists have now shown that sleep first evolved in brainless animals such as jellyfish.
choices.C: Jellyfish need more rest each night than animals that have brains do.
choices.D: Even an animal without a brain, such as Cassiopea, appears to show a sleep-like state.

explanation.why: The text sets up an expectation (sleep "is usually linked to the brain"), then describes a brainless jellyfish that pulses less at night, reacts more slowly, and is less active after being kept from resting. The last sentence draws the point together: "something like sleep may not require a brain." The main idea is that a brainless animal shows signs of sleep.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is one piece of evidence from the study, not the point the whole text makes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says only that sleep may not require a brain; it says nothing about where sleep first evolved.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares how much rest jellyfish need with how much other animals need.
explanation.D: Correct. Every detail in the text supports this point, and the choice keeps the text's caution ("appears," like the text's "may").

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Birch bark and palm leaf, the usual writing surfaces of early South Asia, rarely survive more than a few centuries, so most ancient texts from the region are known only through copies made long after the originals. That is why a discovery near Gilgit, in what is now northern Pakistan, has mattered so much to scholars. In 1931, local people found a cache of birch-bark Buddhist manuscripts inside the ruins of a stupa, where the dry mountain air had protected them for well over a thousand years. Some of the texts had previously been known mainly through Tibetan or Chinese translations. For these, the Gilgit manuscripts offer something no translation can: the Sanskrit wording itself, written down centuries before the copies scholars had relied on.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The Gilgit find gives scholars unusually early versions of texts otherwise known from later sources.
choices.B: Tibetan and Chinese translations of Buddhist texts are less accurate than scholars once believed.
choices.C: Birch bark lasted longer than palm leaf as a writing surface in the dry regions of early South Asia.
choices.D: Dry mountain air protected the birch-bark manuscripts near Gilgit for over a thousand years.

explanation.why: The text first explains a problem: most ancient South Asian texts survive only in much later copies. It then presents the Gilgit manuscripts as valuable because they are very old and, for some texts, preserve the original Sanskrit wording that was otherwise known mainly through translations. The main idea is the significance of the find as an early source.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures the whole argument: the find matters because it preserves early versions of texts that otherwise survive mainly in later copies or translations.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says only that translations cannot show the original wording; it never judges their accuracy.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text groups birch bark and palm leaf together as surfaces that rarely survive; it does not compare them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The dry air explains how the manuscripts survived, but this detail leaves out why the find matters.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The archerfish of Southeast Asian mangroves hunts by spitting: from just below the surface, it fires a jet of water that knocks insects off overhanging leaves. The feat is harder than it looks. Because light bends as it passes from air into water, an insect seen from below appears to sit somewhere other than where it actually is, and the size of that error changes with the angle of view. A fish that simply aimed at what it saw would therefore miss most shots taken at a slant. Archerfish, however, hit their targets from a wide range of angles, which indicates that they correct for the bending of light rather than aiming at the image they see.
items.stem: According to the text, why would an archerfish that aimed directly at the image it sees often miss its target?

choices.A: Light bending at the water's surface makes an insect appear away from its true position.
choices.B: Insects usually notice the fish below and move off the leaf before the jet of water arrives.
choices.C: The fish fires from too far below the surface for its jet to keep its force in the air.
choices.D: The fish can see an insect clearly only when the insect is directly above its head.

explanation.why: The text states that "because light bends as it passes from air into water, an insect seen from below appears to sit somewhere other than where it actually is." A fish aiming at that image "would therefore miss most shots taken at a slant." The reason for the miss is the displaced image caused by bending light.
explanation.A: Correct. This restates the text's explanation: bending light makes the insect appear displaced, so aiming at the image would miss.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says insects escape before the water arrives.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the fish fires "from just below the surface" and never mentions a loss of force.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says archerfish hit targets "from a wide range of angles," not only from directly below.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mr. Thorley proposed in the shrubbery, which he had evidently chosen for its privacy and which, Miss Vane could not help observing, he admired at some length before he arrived at his purpose. He spoke warmly of the beauty of the grounds, of the excellent condition of the home farm, and of the improvements a gentleman of energy might make to the east wing; he spoke, in short, of everything at Ashcombe but its mistress. When at last he paused for her answer, Eleanor thanked him with perfect civility. She was sensible, she said, of the honor he did the estate, and she was persuaded it would make him very happy; she only regretted that it could not accept him without her.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Eleanor accepts Mr. Thorley's proposal even though she privately doubts his motives.
choices.B: Mr. Thorley hopes to win Eleanor by promising to make improvements to the east wing of the house.
choices.C: Eleanor refuses Mr. Thorley because his proposal shows he is drawn chiefly to her estate.
choices.D: Eleanor is offended that Mr. Thorley chose such a private place in which to propose.

explanation.why: Mr. Thorley praises the grounds, the farm, and the house, speaking "of everything at Ashcombe but its mistress." Eleanor's polite reply is ironic: she thanks him for the honor he does "the estate" and regrets "that it could not accept him without her." In other words, she declines him because it is clearly the property, not she, that he wants.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Eleanor's reply, that the estate cannot accept him "without her," is a refusal, not an acceptance.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Mr. Thorley mentions possible improvements, but this detail misses Eleanor's response, which is the point of the passage.
explanation.C: Correct. The passage shows Mr. Thorley's attention fixed on the property and ends with Eleanor's ironic refusal on exactly that ground.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Eleanor notices the setting with amusement, but nothing suggests the choice of place offends her.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: For some two decades before he moved to New York in 1940, the Dutch painter Piet Mondrian worked within strict limits: straight black lines crossing at right angles, and flat areas of red, yellow, and blue set against white. Critics often described these canvases as calm, even static. Yet Broadway Boogie Woogie, which Mondrian completed in 1943, departs from that pattern in a telling way. The black lines are gone, replaced by bands of yellow broken into small squares of red, blue, and gray, so that the eye seems to skip from block to block. Many viewers see in the painting both the street grid of Manhattan and the driving rhythm of boogie-woogie piano music, which Mondrian loved, a sign that his rigorous method could absorb the energy of a new city.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Critics described Mondrian's paintings from before 1940 as calm and even static.
choices.B: In Broadway Boogie Woogie, Mondrian adapted his strict method to a new city's energy.
choices.C: After moving to New York, Mondrian gave up both straight lines and primary colors.
choices.D: Boogie-woogie music shaped Mondrian's art more strongly than any other influence ever did.

explanation.why: The text describes Mondrian's long-standing strict style, then shows how Broadway Boogie Woogie "departs from that pattern": colored, broken bands replace black lines, suggesting Manhattan's grid and the rhythm of boogie-woogie. The final clause states the point: his "rigorous method could absorb the energy of a new city." The main idea is that the painting adapts his method to New York.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is background about the earlier work, not the point the text builds toward.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures both the continuity (his strict method) and the change (it now conveys the city's energy).
explanation.C: Incorrect. The painting still uses straight bands and red, yellow, and blue; only the black lines are gone.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text mentions the music as one thing viewers see in the painting; it never ranks it above all other influences.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For three seasons Marisol had rebuilt the robot's lifting arm herself the night before every competition, and for three seasons the team had let her. This year, when the arm jammed during the final practice run, she was already reaching for her toolbox when Theo, a sophomore who rarely spoke at meetings, said quietly that the problem was the gear ratio, not the motor, and that he had sketched a fix weeks ago. Marisol nearly told him there was no time. Instead she watched him work, his hands slower than hers but sure, and when the arm swung up cleanly on the next run, she found herself wondering how many other sketches had stayed in notebooks because she had never asked to see them.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Marisol begins to suspect that doing everything herself has kept others' ideas unheard.
choices.B: Marisol resents that a younger teammate has solved a problem she was unable to solve herself.
choices.C: Theo has been waiting for a chance to show the team that he should replace Marisol as leader.
choices.D: The team's robot breaks down during the competition because its lifting arm jams again.

explanation.why: The passage contrasts Marisol's long habit of fixing the arm herself with the moment she lets quiet Theo try his fix. When it works, she wonders "how many other sketches had stayed in notebooks because she had never asked to see them." The main idea is her dawning recognition that her control has silenced teammates' ideas.
explanation.A: Correct. The final sentence shows Marisol realizing that her own habits may have kept teammates' ideas hidden.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Marisol watches Theo with interest and reflection, not resentment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nothing in the passage suggests Theo wants to replace Marisol.
explanation.D: Incorrect. After Theo's fix, the arm "swung up cleanly"; the passage does not describe a breakdown at the competition.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1833 a ship called the Tuscany left Boston carrying about 180 tons of ice cut from New England ponds, bound for Calcutta, a voyage of four months that crossed the equator twice. Many observers expected the cargo to arrive as water. Instead, more than half of it reached India still frozen, and the city soon built a special ice house to store later shipments. The trade depended on an unglamorous material: sawdust. Packed around the blocks, it slowed melting enough to make such voyages possible, and because New England's lumber mills produced it as waste, it cost shippers almost nothing. For decades, until machines that manufactured ice became common later in the century, much of Calcutta's ice came from frozen ponds on the other side of the world.
items.stem: According to the text, why was sawdust important to the ice trade between Boston and Calcutta?

choices.A: It replaced the ice house that Calcutta had built to store the shipments that came later.
choices.B: It let ships carry ice across the equator twice without needing to stop at any port along the way.
choices.C: It slowed the melting of the ice on long voyages while costing shippers very little to obtain.
choices.D: It was later replaced on ships by machines that kept the ice frozen for the whole voyage.

explanation.why: The text says that sawdust, "packed around the blocks, ... slowed melting enough to make such voyages possible," and that because lumber mills "produced it as waste, it cost shippers almost nothing." Both effectiveness and low cost made it important.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The ice house stored ice in Calcutta; sawdust did not replace it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never discusses stopping at ports during the voyage.
explanation.C: Correct. This combines the two reasons the text gives: sawdust slowed melting, and it was nearly free.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The machines mentioned manufactured ice, ending the trade; the text never says they were used on ships.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For about 150 years, lichens served as the textbook example of a two-partner partnership: a fungus provides structure and shelter, and an alga or cyanobacterium living among its threads supplies food through photosynthesis. Yet the model left puzzles. Two lichens in the genus Bryoria, for instance, differ strikingly, one producing a yellow toxic compound and the other not, even though their fungi and algae appeared genetically identical. In 2016, researchers reported that many lichens harbor a third partner, a yeast embedded in their outer layer, and that in Bryoria the yeast was far more abundant in the yellow form. The finding suggests that the classic two-partner picture may be incomplete and that overlooked members could account for differences among lichens.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A lichen consists of a fungus and an alga that supply each other with shelter and food.
choices.B: One of the two lichens in the genus Bryoria produces a yellow compound that is toxic.
choices.C: A newly found partner suggests that the long-accepted account of lichens may be incomplete.
choices.D: In many lichens, a yeast has replaced the alga as the partner that supplies most of their food.

explanation.why: The text presents the traditional two-partner model, points out a puzzle it could not explain, and then describes the discovery of a third partner, a yeast, that seems linked to the puzzle. The final sentence states the main idea: the classic picture "may be incomplete," and overlooked partners could explain differences.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is the traditional model that the text goes on to question; it leaves out the new finding that is the text's focus.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The yellow compound is part of one example, not the point of the whole text.
explanation.C: Correct. This captures the text's movement from the accepted model to the discovery that may show it is incomplete.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text adds the yeast as a third partner; it never says the yeast replaces the alga or supplies food.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Despite their name, the mud volcanoes of Hingol National Park, on the Makran coast of Pakistan's Balochistan province, have nothing to do with molten rock. The mud that oozes and bubbles from their cones is cool to the touch. These formations owe their existence instead to the region's geology. Off the coast, the Arabian Plate is sliding beneath the Eurasian Plate, and the collision squeezes thick layers of water-soaked sediment. Gas, much of it methane, collects in those layers under great pressure and forces mud upward through cracks until it spills out at the surface. The same forces can act suddenly: after a strong earthquake in 2013, a small island of mud rose from the sea near the port of Gwadar.
items.stem: According to the text, what causes mud to rise to the surface at the mud volcanoes of Hingol National Park?

choices.A: Seawater floods cracks in the ground during strong earthquakes and lifts it.
choices.B: Methane burning underground melts nearby sediment and drives it upward.
choices.C: Gas trapped under pressure in thick layers of squeezed sediment pushes it up.
choices.D: Molten rock rising from deep beneath the Arabian Plate heats the mud and lifts it.

explanation.why: The text explains that the plate collision "squeezes thick layers of water-soaked sediment" and that gas "collects in those layers under great pressure and forces mud upward through cracks." So pressurized gas in compressed sediment drives the mud to the surface.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The earthquake is mentioned as a sudden trigger near Gwadar; the text never says seawater floods cracks.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the gas is under pressure, not that it burns, and that the mud is cool.
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the text's explanation of how the mud reaches the surface.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the mud volcanoes "have nothing to do with molten rock" and that the mud is cool.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Few sounds are more closely tied to Argentine tango than the breathy, mournful voice of the bandoneon, a square, button-keyed relative of the accordion. Yet the instrument was not born in Buenos Aires. It was developed in Germany in the 1840s, and early sellers promoted it partly as an affordable substitute for the organ in small churches and partly for amateur folk music. Bandoneons reached the Río de la Plata region in the late nineteenth century, probably carried by sailors and immigrants, and tango musicians gradually made them central to their ensembles. For decades afterward, most of the bandoneons heard in Argentine dance halls were still manufactured in German factories.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Tango musicians preferred the bandoneon because it could be used in place of an organ.
choices.B: An instrument developed in Germany for other purposes came to define tango's sound.
choices.C: The bandoneon was invented by Argentine musicians who based it on the accordion.
choices.D: German factories built most of the instruments played in Argentina's tango ensembles.

explanation.why: The text opens with the bandoneon's close link to tango, then reveals ("Yet") that it was developed in Germany and promoted for churches and folk music before tango musicians adopted it. The main idea is this journey from a German instrument with other uses to the signature sound of tango.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The organ substitute was how early German sellers promoted it; the text never gives this as tango musicians' reason.
explanation.B: Correct. This joins the text's two halves: German origins for other uses and later central place in tango.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the instrument "was not born in Buenos Aires" but in Germany.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says most bandoneons were German-made, not most instruments in tango ensembles.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The Hallett Cornet Band had eleven members, four of whom could read music, and it practiced on Thursday evenings in the back of Pruett's feed store, among the sacks of oats. Mr. Pruett, who led it, held no illusions about its quality. When the Ladies' Aid suggested that the band might rest until it improved, he only shook his head. In a town of forty houses on a treeless plain, he said, a man could go a whole week hearing nothing but wind and the complaints of his neighbors; yet on the Fourth of July, when the band marched down the single street playing more or less the same tune, people came out of every door. It was not the music they came out for, Mr. Pruett said, and the band need not be good to give it to them.
items.stem: Based on the text, why does Mr. Pruett want the band to keep playing?

choices.A: He hopes the band's playing will drown out the complaints he hears from his neighbors.
choices.B: He expects the band to improve once more of its members have learned to read music.
choices.C: He wants to prove to the Ladies' Aid that the band plays better than they believe it does.
choices.D: He believes the band draws the isolated town together, whatever the quality of its music.

explanation.why: Mr. Pruett admits the band is poor ("held no illusions about its quality"), but he notes that in a lonely town people "came out of every door" when it marched. He says "it was not the music they came out for" and that the band "need not be good to give it to them." He values the band for bringing the community together.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The neighbors' complaints describe the dullness of town life; he never says the band should drown them out.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Mr. Pruett never predicts improvement; he argues the band need not be good.
explanation.C: Incorrect. He agrees the band is not good; he does not try to prove otherwise.
explanation.D: Correct. His argument is that the band gives the isolated town an occasion to come together, regardless of skill.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Standard economic models assume that adding an option nobody wants should not change how people choose among the options they already had. Research on the so-called decoy effect challenges that assumption. In one field study, economist Lerato Dube examined membership sales at a science museum that offered two plans: a basic plan for $60 a year and a family plan, with guest passes, for $110. When the museum added a third plan costing $105 that offered fewer benefits than the family plan, almost no one bought it, yet the share of buyers choosing the family plan rose from 31 percent to 47 percent. The unattractive new plan, Dube concluded, made the family plan look like a bargain by comparison.
items.stem: According to the text, what happened after the museum added the $105 plan?

choices.A: Few people chose the new plan, but a larger share of buyers chose the family plan.
choices.B: The share of buyers choosing the basic plan rose from 31 percent to 47 percent.
choices.C: Most buyers switched from the basic plan to the new plan, which offered more benefits.
choices.D: Total membership sales fell because visitors found the larger set of choices confusing.

explanation.why: The text reports that after the $105 plan was added, "almost no one bought it, yet the share of buyers choosing the family plan rose from 31 percent to 47 percent." The correct answer must state both parts of that result.
explanation.A: Correct. This restates the result: the new plan barely sold, while the family plan's share grew.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The figures 31 and 47 percent describe the family plan, not the basic plan.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says almost no one bought the new plan.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never says total sales fell or that buyers were confused.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Pteropods, often called sea butterflies, are swimming snails no bigger than a lentil, and in cold waters they can be extraordinarily abundant, serving as food for animals from small fish to salmon and whales. Their shells, however, are made of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate that dissolves more readily than most. As the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, its water becomes more acidic and less able to supply the carbonate that shell-builders need; samples collected in the Southern Ocean have already revealed pteropod shells with pitted, partly dissolved surfaces. Because so many predators depend on these tiny animals, researchers worry that harm to pteropods may not stay confined to pteropods.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Pteropod populations in the Southern Ocean have already collapsed as the ocean has warmed.
choices.B: Pteropods are more abundant in cold waters than in any other part of the world's oceans.
choices.C: Aragonite dissolves more readily than most other forms of calcium carbonate in the sea.
choices.D: Pteropods' vulnerability to more acidic water could also affect the animals that eat them.

explanation.why: The text explains that pteropods are important food for many animals, that their aragonite shells are especially vulnerable as seawater becomes more acidic, and that damage is already visible. It concludes that harm to pteropods "may not stay confined to pteropods." The main idea links the snails' vulnerability to its possible wider effects.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text reports pitted shells, not a population collapse, and it discusses acidity, not warming.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says pteropods can be abundant in cold waters but never compares them with every other region.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This explains why the shells are vulnerable, but it is only one step in the text's reasoning.
explanation.D: Correct. This combines the shells' vulnerability with the concern about predators that the text ends on, keeping its cautious "could."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The verses of the eighteenth-century Sindhi poet Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, collected in the Shah Jo Risalo, draw heavily on folk romances that his listeners already knew well, such as the tale of Sassui, who searches the desert for her lost husband, and that of Sohni, who crosses a river each night on a clay pot to meet her beloved. Yet Bhittai rarely retells these stories from beginning to end. He tends to pass over the familiar events and dwell instead on the heroine at a single moment of struggle, giving her a voice and following her doubts and resolve. In his hands, stories prized for their plots became explorations of longing and endurance, which helps explain why singers still perform the verses today.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Bhittai reshaped well-known folk stories by focusing on the inner experience of their heroines.
choices.B: Bhittai's audiences valued the plots of the old folk romances far more than his poems about them.
choices.C: Bhittai retold complete folk romances so that his listeners would remember their plots.
choices.D: The tale of Sassui is the most important of the stories retold in the Shah Jo Risalo.

explanation.why: The text says Bhittai drew on familiar romances but "rarely retells these stories from beginning to end," choosing instead to "dwell ... on the heroine at a single moment of struggle." As a result, plot-driven tales "became explorations of longing and endurance." The main idea is how he transformed the stories by centering the heroines' inner lives.
explanation.A: Correct. This sums up the text's contrast between the familiar plots and Bhittai's focus on the heroines' struggles.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the original stories were prized for their plots, but it never says listeners preferred them to Bhittai's poems.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says Bhittai rarely retells the stories completely, the opposite of this choice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Sassui is one of two examples; the text never ranks the stories.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Female loggerhead sea turtles often return to nest on or near the beach where they themselves hatched, sometimes after decades at sea. One leading hypothesis holds that hatchlings imprint on the magnetic signature of their home beach, the particular strength and angle of Earth's magnetic field there. Because Earth's field shifts slowly over time, the hypothesis makes a testable prediction: where the signatures of neighboring stretches of coast drift closer together, nesting turtles should crowd into a smaller area, and where the signatures drift apart, nests should spread out. An analysis of nineteen years of nesting records along the east coast of Florida found the predicted pattern, lending support to the hypothesis.
items.stem: According to the text, what does the magnetic imprinting hypothesis predict about stretches of coast whose magnetic signatures drift closer together?

choices.A: Fewer turtles should return to nest there than in earlier years.
choices.B: Turtles should begin nesting there far from the beaches of their birth.
choices.C: Turtle nests there should spread out over a longer stretch of coast.
choices.D: Nesting turtles there should become concentrated in a smaller area.

explanation.why: The text states the prediction directly: "where the signatures of neighboring stretches of coast drift closer together, nesting turtles should crowd into a smaller area." The correct choice must restate that crowding.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The hypothesis predicts where returning turtles nest, not that fewer of them return.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The hypothesis explains how turtles find their home area; it does not predict that they abandon it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nests spreading out is predicted where signatures drift apart, the opposite case.
explanation.D: Correct. "Crowd into a smaller area" means the nests become more concentrated.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The tram lurched, and Fenn, who had been thinking of nothing in particular, which is to say of the Hargreave account and its missing four shillings, caught at the strap and saw in the dark window his own face laid over the passing shops, the face of a man of forty, hat a little crooked. Was that what they saw at the office? Well. A boy across the aisle was eating an orange, peeling it in one long spiral, unhurried, as if the tram and the Hargreave account and all of London could wait, and quite suddenly Fenn was glad, absurdly glad, of the smell of it, sharp and sweet in the damp air, and of the boy, and even of the four shillings, which would turn up, which always turned up.
items.stem: Based on the text, what prompts Fenn's sudden change of mood?

choices.A: Discovering at last where the four shillings missing from the Hargreave account had gone
choices.B: Arriving at his office after a long and uncomfortable ride through the streets of London
choices.C: Seeing his reflection in the window and deciding that he looks younger than he had feared
choices.D: Watching a boy peel an orange slowly, as though nothing around him required any hurry

explanation.why: Fenn's worries (the account, his tired reflection) give way when he notices a boy peeling an orange "unhurried, as if the tram and the Hargreave account and all of London could wait." Right after this, "quite suddenly Fenn was glad ... of the smell of it ... and of the boy." The boy's calm, unhurried act triggers the change.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Fenn only expects the shillings to "turn up"; he has not found them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Fenn is still on the tram; the passage never shows him arriving at the office.
explanation.C: Incorrect. His reflection shows "a man of forty, hat a little crooked," and leads him to an uneasy question, not to relief.
explanation.D: Correct. The gladness follows directly from watching the unhurried boy and smelling the orange.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Beginning in the late 1500s, a broad-brimmed hat of beaver felt became a mark of status for European men. Beaver underfur was ideal for felt, since each hair carries tiny barbs that help the fibers lock tightly together into a dense, water-resistant material. But Europe's own beavers had been hunted until they were scarce, so hatters came to depend on pelts from North America. Over the next two centuries, demand for those pelts drew traders ever deeper into the continent's interior, shaped alliances between European companies and Indigenous trappers, and helped fund rival colonial ventures. The trade declined only in the mid-1800s, when silk hats came into fashion.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Indigenous trappers formed alliances to keep European traders out of the continent's interior.
choices.B: European demand for fashionable hats helped drive the growth of the North American fur trade.
choices.C: Europe's beavers became scarce once silk hats took the place of hats made of beaver felt.
choices.D: Beaver fur made better felt than any other material because each hair carries tiny barbs.

explanation.why: The text traces a chain of causes: beaver hats became fashionable in Europe, Europe's beavers were scarce, so hatters turned to North American pelts, and that demand drove traders inland, shaped alliances, and funded colonial ventures until silk hats replaced beaver. The main idea is that a fashion drove the North American fur trade.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says alliances formed between European companies and Indigenous trappers, not against traders.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures the cause-and-effect chain that the whole text follows.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Europe's beavers were scarce because of hunting; silk hats came centuries later and ended the trade.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says beaver fur was "ideal" for felt, not better than every other material, and this is only one supporting detail.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a human heart is damaged, the lost muscle is replaced by scar tissue, which cannot contract. A zebrafish, by contrast, can regrow as much as a fifth of its main pumping chamber within about two months. For years, researchers assumed that such repair must depend on a reserve of stem cells. Studies in which heart cells were genetically labeled, however, showed that most of the new muscle comes from mature heart muscle cells near the injury, which partly revert to a less specialized state and begin dividing again. Curiously, newborn mice show a similar ability during their first week of life before losing it, a hint that mammals may possess the capacity in a dormant form.
items.stem: According to the text, what did the studies using genetically labeled heart cells show about zebrafish?

choices.A: The fish can regrow its entire heart within about two months of an injury.
choices.B: Most new heart muscle comes from existing muscle cells that divide again.
choices.C: A reserve of stem cells near the injury produces most of the new heart muscle.
choices.D: Scar tissue in the heart gradually gains the ability to contract like muscle.

explanation.why: The text says researchers had "assumed" stem cells were responsible, "however" labeling studies "showed that most of the new muscle comes from mature heart muscle cells near the injury, which ... begin dividing again." The key restates that finding.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says zebrafish can regrow up to a fifth of one chamber, not the entire heart.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates what the labeling studies revealed about the source of new muscle.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is the earlier assumption that the labeling studies overturned.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text describes scar tissue only in human hearts and says it cannot contract.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764), now usually called the first Gothic novel, first appeared in disguise. Its title page presented the work as a translation of an Italian story printed in Naples in 1529, and its preface, signed by an invented translator, apologized for the superstitions of a less enlightened age. Reviewers welcomed it as a curious antique. When Walpole acknowledged his authorship in the second edition the following year, he also redefined the book's aim: it was, he explained, an attempt to blend two kinds of romance, the ancient, in which imagination ran free, and the modern, which imitated ordinary life. Some reviewers who had admired the supposed antique proved less charmed by a modern imitation.
items.stem: According to the text, how did some reviewers respond once Walpole acknowledged that he had written the novel?

choices.A: They thought less highly of the book than when they had believed it was centuries old.
choices.B: They praised him for blending ancient and modern kinds of romance in a single work.
choices.C: They insisted that the book must still be a translation of an Italian story printed in 1529.
choices.D: They objected that his preface had apologized for the superstitions of an earlier age.

explanation.why: The final sentence says that "some reviewers who had admired the supposed antique proved less charmed by a modern imitation." In other words, once they learned the book was new, their opinion of it dropped.
explanation.A: Correct. "Less charmed" after learning it was "a modern imitation" means they valued it less than before.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Blending the two kinds of romance is Walpole's stated aim; the text says some reviewers became less charmed, not that they praised this.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says reviewers doubted Walpole's admission.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The apology appeared in the first preface, and the text never says reviewers objected to it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Across the grasslands at the edge of the Namib Desert, millions of bare circles, each several meters wide and ringed by taller grass, dot the sand in a strikingly regular pattern. Two explanations for these "fairy circles" have long competed. One holds that sand termites, which are often found beneath them, kill the grass by eating its roots. The other proposes that the circles arise from the grasses themselves: where water is scarce, plants competing for moisture may organize into a pattern of bare patches whose stored water feeds the ring of grass around them. Computer models show that such competition can produce a similarly regular spacing, while field studies confirm that termites are present, so some researchers now suggest that both processes may play a part.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Sand termites produce fairy circles by eating the roots of grasses in the Namib Desert.
choices.B: Each of two competing explanations for fairy circles has support, and both may apply.
choices.C: Fairy circles store the water that sand termites need to survive in the Namib Desert.
choices.D: Computer models have proved that fairy circles can form without any termites at all.

explanation.why: The text describes the circles, presents two rival explanations (termites and competition among grasses), and notes evidence for each: field studies for termites, computer models for competition. It ends by saying "both processes may play a part." The main idea covers both explanations and this possible combination.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This states only one of the two explanations, and as settled fact.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures the competing explanations, the support for each, and the text's cautious conclusion.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the bare patches may supply water to the surrounding grass, not to termites.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The models show that competition "can produce" the pattern; they do not prove that termites play no role.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: It was past two when Harriet, alone at the eyepiece while her father slept in the next room, found the faint smudge where no smudge had been the night before. She knew at once what it was, and knew, too, the order of what must follow: the bell, her father's slippered haste upon the stair, the logbook, the letter to the Society in his close and confident hand, and in that letter, very likely, some graceful phrase about "my assistant." She did not ring the bell. For a quarter of an hour she sat with the cold brass against her brow and the comet entirely her own, unannounced, unclaimed, a secret between herself and the sky; and then, because she was her father's daughter and the hour was passing, she rose and rang.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Harriet looks forward to the letter in which her father will praise her as his skilled assistant.
choices.B: Harriet privately savors her discovery for a time, knowing it will soon be credited chiefly to him.
choices.C: Harriet hesitates to wake her father because she is not yet certain that the smudge is a comet.
choices.D: Harriet resents her father so bitterly that she considers keeping the comet a secret from him for good.

explanation.why: Harriet "knew at once" she had found a comet and foresees how it will be reported: in her father's letter, with her mentioned only as "my assistant." She waits a quarter of an hour with the comet "entirely her own, unannounced, unclaimed" before she dutifully rings the bell. The passage centers on this brief private ownership of a discovery that will publicly be his.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The phrase "my assistant" is presented with quiet irony, as a slight she expects, not praise she looks forward to.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures both her brief private enjoyment and her awareness of how credit will be assigned.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says she "knew at once what it was," so uncertainty is not why she waits.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Her delay lasts only a quarter of an hour, and she rings the bell out of loyalty; the passage does not show deep resentment or a plan to keep the secret.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For generations, economics textbooks offered the lighthouse as the model of a good that markets cannot supply: since a lighthouse's beam guides every passing ship whether or not its owner pays, no private builder, the reasoning went, could ever collect enough to cover costs. In 1974 the economist Ronald Coase challenged the example by turning to history. Many British lighthouses of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, he showed, had been built and operated by private individuals, who recovered their costs through fees charged to ships at nearby ports. Later historians added a qualification of their own: those fees could be collected only because the Crown had granted the operators the legal right to demand them. The lighthouse, then, illustrates neither purely private nor purely public provision, but a blend of the two.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: History undermines a textbook example without showing that private markets alone supplied lighthouses.
choices.B: Later historians showed that Coase was mistaken in claiming that some British lighthouses were private.
choices.C: Private lighthouse owners in Britain collected fees directly from ships as the ships passed their lights.
choices.D: Coase showed that private markets can supply any good that economists once believed required government.

explanation.why: The text moves in three steps: the textbook claim that markets cannot supply lighthouses, Coase's historical evidence of private lighthouses, and later historians' point that private fees depended on rights granted by the Crown. The conclusion, "a blend of the two," shows that the evidence undercuts the textbook example without supporting a purely market account.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures both the challenge to the textbook example and the qualification that rules out a purely private account.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The later historians added a qualification about the Crown's role; they did not deny that private operators existed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says fees were charged to ships at nearby ports, not as ships passed the lights.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Coase challenged one example; the text never says he showed that markets can supply every such good.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the nineteenth century, families of scroll painters from rural Bengal settled near the Kalighat temple in Calcutta and began producing single-sheet paintings for the pilgrims and visitors who crowded its lanes. The demands of this market shaped the art. Because the paintings were sold cheaply and in great numbers, the artists abandoned the detailed backgrounds of their village scrolls; working in watercolor on inexpensive mill-made paper, they rendered figures with a few sweeping, confident strokes against blank space. Alongside gods and goddesses, they began to depict the city itself, often satirically, from dandified clerks to quarreling couples. Ironically, the economy of means that commerce had imposed is precisely what some twentieth-century modernist painters in India would admire, praising Kalighat work for a boldness that slower, more polished traditions lacked.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Kalighat painters stop including detailed backgrounds in their work?

choices.A: Modernist painters of the period praised work that left large areas of the page blank.
choices.B: The inexpensive mill-made paper they used could not hold fine detail in watercolor.
choices.C: Their satirical scenes of city life called for simpler settings than religious subjects.
choices.D: The paintings were sold at low prices and had to be produced in large numbers.

explanation.why: The text gives the cause directly: "Because the paintings were sold cheaply and in great numbers, the artists abandoned the detailed backgrounds of their village scrolls." The market, not artistic theory or materials, drove the change.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The modernists' admiration came in the twentieth century, long after the style developed, so it could not have caused it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text mentions mill-made paper but never says it could not hold detail.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never links the simple backgrounds to the choice of subject.
explanation.D: Correct. This restates the cause that the text gives with "Because."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Magnetotactic bacteria, found in the mud of ponds and seafloors worldwide, build chains of tiny magnetite crystals inside their cells, and these chains turn each bacterium into a living compass needle that passively aligns with Earth's magnetic field. Why a microbe would need a compass is not obvious, since such bacteria travel only millimeters. The answer appears to lie in the field's direction: away from the equator, magnetic field lines tilt steeply into the ground. By swimming along them, a bacterium is guided downward, toward the low-oxygen layers of sediment it favors, rather than wandering in every direction. Consistent with this idea, most such bacteria in the Northern Hemisphere swim toward magnetic north, while most in the Southern Hemisphere swim toward magnetic south, the direction that, in each hemisphere, leads down.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Bacteria in the Southern Hemisphere build their magnetite chains quite differently from those in the north.
choices.B: Magnetic field lines tilt more steeply in the Northern Hemisphere than in the Southern Hemisphere.
choices.C: Following Earth's tilted magnetic field seems to guide these bacteria toward the sediment they favor.
choices.D: Magnetotactic bacteria use their magnetite chains as compasses to travel long distances.

explanation.why: The text raises a puzzle (why would a microbe that travels only millimeters need a compass?) and answers it: because field lines tilt into the ground, following them leads the bacteria down to the low-oxygen sediment they favor. The hemisphere difference is offered as evidence for this explanation. The main idea is the proposed purpose of the bacteria's magnetic sense.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says bacteria in the two hemispheres swim in different directions, not that they build their chains differently.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never compares how steeply the field lines tilt in the two hemispheres.
explanation.C: Correct. This states the text's answer to its central puzzle, with the text's own hedge ("appears").
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says these bacteria "travel only millimeters"; the compass matters for direction, not distance.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Miss Rowe's herbarium filled eleven volumes, and her nephew, who had lately taken up science at Cambridge, assured her that the county museum would be glad of it. She did not doubt it. The specimens were correctly named, neatly mounted, and labeled in the approved manner with place and date; a professor, he said, could not have done better. What she could not explain to him, and did not try to, was that the labels were for the professor and the plants were for herself. Bog asphodel, Cranmere, 14 July 1889: that was the summer her father had first let her walk the moor alone. Sea campion, Hartland, 1902: the week after the funeral. To give the volumes away would be correct, and generous, and rather like handing a stranger her diary.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Miss Rowe doubts that a county museum would want a collection assembled by an amateur.
choices.B: Miss Rowe's nephew hopes to earn credit with his teachers at Cambridge by arranging the collection's donation.
choices.C: Although her collection meets scientific standards, Miss Rowe values it chiefly as a record of her life.
choices.D: Miss Rowe keeps a diary that describes the places where she collected each of her specimens.

explanation.why: The text grants that the herbarium meets every scientific standard ("correctly named, neatly mounted, and labeled in the approved manner"), then turns: "the labels were for the professor and the plants were for herself." Each label recalls a moment of her life, and giving the volumes away would be "like handing a stranger her diary." The main idea is this gap between the collection's scientific and personal value.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says plainly, "She did not doubt it."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing suggests the nephew wants credit for himself; he simply praises the collection.
explanation.C: Correct. This captures the contrast between the collection's scientific quality and its private meaning for her.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The diary is a comparison; it is the herbarium itself that serves as a kind of diary.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When Supper at Emmaus surfaced in 1937, leading experts hailed it as a lost early masterpiece by Johannes Vermeer, and a Rotterdam museum paid a fortune for it. It was in fact the work of Han van Meegeren, a Dutch painter who later confessed to forging it and several other "Vermeers." To viewers today, the deception can seem baffling: the heavy-lidded, melancholy faces in his canvases look less like anything in Vermeer than like the illustrations and film stills of the 1930s. Some historians argue that this is exactly why the forgeries succeeded. A forger, on this view, reproduces not the old master but the old master his contemporaries imagine, and the features that flattered the expectations of 1937 became visible as period traits only once those expectations had faded.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Experts in 1937 lacked the scientific tools that would have quickly revealed Supper at Emmaus to be a forgery.
choices.B: Van Meegeren's forgeries may have succeeded because they matched what his era expected Vermeer to look like.
choices.C: Van Meegeren copied faces from 1930s films on purpose in order to mock the experts who praised him.
choices.D: Viewers today are generally better judges of Vermeer's style than the art experts of the 1930s were.

explanation.why: The text notes that van Meegeren's forgeries now look like 1930s images, then presents historians' explanation: a forger reproduces "the old master his contemporaries imagine," and those period features became visible "only once those expectations had faded." The main idea is that the forgeries fooled experts by fitting the expectations of their time.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never mentions scientific tools; its explanation concerns taste and expectations.
explanation.B: Correct. This states the historians' argument, which the whole text builds toward, with the text's hedge ("may").
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says the resemblance to film stills was deliberate or meant to mock anyone.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says period traits become visible once expectations fade, not that today's viewers are better judges in general.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Medieval Icelandic sagas mention a "sunstone" that could reveal the sun's position on an overcast day, and some researchers have proposed that Viking navigators actually used such a device. The most likely candidate is Iceland spar, a transparent form of calcite that splits light into two beams whose brightness depends on how the light is polarized; by rotating the crystal until both beams look equally bright, an observer can infer where the sun lies even behind clouds. Experiments have shown that the technique works to within a few degrees. Yet no such crystal has been recovered from any Viking-era site. The strongest physical evidence comes instead from an English ship that sank near the island of Alderney in 1592, where a calcite crystal lay beside the vessel's navigational instruments.
items.stem: Based on the text, why does the crystal found near Alderney offer only limited support for the idea that Viking navigators used sunstones?

choices.A: It may have been carried as cargo rather than used to help steer the ship.
choices.B: It comes from a ship that sank centuries after the Viking Age had ended.
choices.C: The sagas describe a sunstone that worked only on clear days, not overcast ones.
choices.D: Experiments show that calcite can locate the sun's position only very roughly.

explanation.why: The hypothesis concerns Viking navigators, but "no such crystal has been recovered from any Viking-era site." The best evidence comes from a ship that sank in 1592, long after the Viking Age. That crystal suggests calcite was used for navigation in the late 1500s, but it cannot show what Vikings did centuries earlier.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the crystal lay "beside the vessel's navigational instruments," which points toward navigational use, not cargo.
explanation.B: Correct. The date of the wreck is the gap: the evidence comes from long after the period the hypothesis is about.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the sagas describe a sunstone for "an overcast day."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the technique works "to within a few degrees," which supports rather than limits the idea.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Creole languages typically arise where people with no shared language are thrown together, as on colonial plantations: adults improvise a pidgin, a limited contact language, and children who grow up hearing it expand it into a full language with a complete grammar. Linguists have long noticed that creoles formed in widely separated places share certain grammatical habits, such as marking tense with separate small words placed before the verb. Some have taken these resemblances as evidence of an inborn human blueprint for grammar that children fall back on when the language around them is limited. Others counter that many of these creoles drew on related West African languages, whose shared features could simply have been passed along. Creoles whose speakers' languages had no such common source therefore carry special weight, since they can help separate the two explanations.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Most creole languages descend directly from West African languages rather than from pidgins.
choices.B: Pidgins become full languages only after adults add grammatical rules to them over several generations.
