choices.C: Creoles share grammatical features because children everywhere expand pidgins in the same inborn way.
choices.D: Linguists disagree about why creoles share features, and some creoles may help test the rival views.

explanation.why: After explaining how creoles form, the text presents a puzzle (shared features across distant creoles) and two competing explanations: an inborn grammar or features inherited from related West African languages. It ends by identifying which creoles could help decide between them. The main idea must include both the disagreement and the way to test it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says creoles grow out of pidgins and that many drew on West African languages, not that they descend directly from them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says children, not adults, expand pidgins into full languages.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This presents one side of the debate as settled fact.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures both rival explanations and the text's point about which evidence could separate them.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The rains had come early that year to Calcutta, and Bimal, who tutored the cloth merchant's son each afternoon in English grammar, arrived daily with his umbrella dripping and his temper short. The boy, Khokon, was hopeless with the subjunctive. He would gaze past the book at the courtyard, where water sheeted from the eaves, and announce, apropos of nothing, that the drain by the gate would overflow within the hour, or that the lane behind the warehouse would be knee-deep by evening. Bimal, who held a degree from the Presidency College, did not stoop to answer. It was only on the fourth afternoon, wading home along a lane Khokon had named, the water at his knees and his good shoes in his hand, that it occurred to him that he had been the pupil who would not attend.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Bimal realizes that he has dismissed knowledge of Khokon's that proves sound and useful.
choices.B: Bimal resents the cloth merchant for making him travel through the rain every afternoon.
choices.C: Khokon's predictions about the flooding prove mistaken, which embarrasses him.
choices.D: Khokon pretends not to understand English grammar so that his lessons will finish early.

explanation.why: Bimal scorns Khokon's remarks about where the water will rise and "did not stoop to answer." When he finds himself wading through a lane Khokon had predicted would flood, he realizes "he had been the pupil who would not attend," meaning he ignored what the boy could teach him. The main idea is this reversal in Bimal's understanding.
explanation.A: Correct. The final sentence shows Bimal recognizing that Khokon's practical knowledge was accurate and that he failed to heed it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Bimal's short temper is a detail; the passage never blames the merchant, and resentment is not its point.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Bimal wades through a lane Khokon had named, so the predictions proved correct.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing suggests Khokon is pretending; he is simply more interested in the rain.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The earliest surviving notation for Western chant, dating from the ninth and tenth centuries, consists of neumes: small marks written above the words that show whether the melody rises or falls and how notes are grouped, but not which pitches are sung or how far apart they lie. The system was less a failure of precision than a reflection of its purpose. Singers learned chants by ear over years of repetition; the neumes served to jog a memory already stocked with melodies. In the eleventh century, the monk Guido of Arezzo promoted a staff of horizontal lines on which each note's exact height could be fixed, allowing singers to learn a chant they had never heard. For melodies that fell out of use before staff notation spread, however, the older neumes alone cannot tell modern scholars how they sounded.
items.stem: Based on the text, why are modern scholars unable to determine how some early chants sounded?

choices.A: Those chants survive only in a notation meant to remind singers of melodies they knew.
choices.B: Guido of Arezzo's staff replaced the neumes before many chants had been written down.
choices.C: Singers of the ninth century deliberately altered the melodies each time that they performed them.
choices.D: The neumes did not show whether a melody rose or fell from one note to the next.

explanation.why: The text explains that neumes showed direction and grouping "but not which pitches are sung," because they were meant "to jog a memory already stocked with melodies." For chants that dropped out of use before staff notation, only these memory aids survive, so scholars cannot recover the exact melodies.
explanation.A: Correct. This combines the two parts of the text: what neumes were for and why they cannot reveal the lost melodies.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the problem concerns chants that fell out of use before staff notation spread; they were written down, but only in neumes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says singers changed the melodies; it says they learned them by ear.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says neumes did show whether the melody rises or falls; what they lacked was exact pitch.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Leafcutter ants can be seen marching through the tropical forests of Central and South America, each one carrying a piece of leaf much larger than its own head. Surprisingly, the ants do not eat these leaves. Instead, they chew them into a soft paste inside their nests and use the paste to grow a fungus. The fungus, not the leaf, is the colony's main food.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Leafcutter ants eat the leaves they cut once the leaves soften in the nest.
choices.B: Leafcutter ants collect leaves in order to grow the fungus that they eat.
choices.C: Leafcutter ants can carry pieces of leaf larger than their own heads.
choices.D: Leafcutter ants are the most common insects in tropical forests.

explanation.why: The text first describes ants carrying leaves, then explains the surprise: they "do not eat these leaves" but use them to grow a fungus, which is "the colony's main food." The main idea must cover this whole point: the leaves are used to grow the ants' food.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the ants "do not eat these leaves"; they eat the fungus grown on the paste.
explanation.B: Correct. This sums up the whole text: the ants gather leaves, turn them into paste, and grow the fungus they actually eat.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The size of the leaf pieces is one detail from the first sentence, not the main point.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares leafcutter ants with other insects.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Kofi had expected his aunt's bicycle shop to be quiet on a Saturday morning. Instead, customers were already waiting at the door when she unlocked it. One needed a new chain; another wanted a flat tire fixed. His aunt handed him a wrench and a tin of grease without a word. By noon his hands were black, his shirt was ruined, and he had repaired his first tire by himself.
items.stem: According to the text, how was the morning at the shop different from what Kofi had expected?

choices.A: The shop had run out of new chains and tires.
choices.B: His aunt would not let him work on any bicycles.
choices.C: His aunt asked him to open the shop by himself.
choices.D: Customers were already waiting when the shop opened.

explanation.why: The first sentence tells us what Kofi expected: a quiet Saturday morning. The next sentence begins with "Instead," which signals the difference: "customers were already waiting at the door when she unlocked it."
explanation.A: Incorrect. A customer needed a new chain, but the text never says the shop had none.
explanation.B: Incorrect. His aunt handed him tools, and he repaired a tire, so she clearly let him work.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says his aunt unlocked the shop; it never says Kofi opened it alone.
explanation.D: Correct. This restates the sentence that begins with "Instead": the shop was busy, not quiet, from the moment it opened.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The greater one-horned rhinoceros once roamed widely across the grasslands of northern India and Nepal. By the 1960s, however, hunting and the loss of grassland to farms had left only a small number in Nepal. In 1973, the government created Chitwan National Park and assigned guards to protect the animals. The effort has worked: a national count in 2021 found more than 700 of the rhinos in Nepal.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Protection efforts helped Nepal's rhinos recover after a sharp decline.
choices.B: Rhinos in Nepal are now protected mainly by farmers rather than by guards.
choices.C: The greater one-horned rhinoceros once lived widely in northern India and Nepal.
choices.D: Farms now cover most of the grassland where rhinos once lived in Nepal.

explanation.why: The text moves from a decline (only a small number of rhinos left by the 1960s) to a response (a national park with guards) to a result: "The effort has worked," with more than 700 rhinos counted in 2021. The main idea is that protection helped the population recover.
explanation.A: Correct. This covers the whole text: a sharp decline, protection in Chitwan, and a recovery to more than 700 rhinos.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the government assigned guards; farmers are mentioned only as a cause of lost grassland.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is background from the first sentence; it leaves out the decline and the recovery.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says grassland was lost to farms before the 1960s, but it never says farms cover most of it today.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A gamelan is a traditional Indonesian orchestra made up mostly of gongs, drums, and metal keyboard instruments, and its players are not expected to stand out as soloists. In one common Balinese technique, two musicians each play only some of the notes of a fast melody. Their parts fit together so closely that listeners hear a single, unbroken line. Neither part makes complete sense alone, so the music depends on every player fitting in with the others.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: In one technique, two musicians each play part of a fast melody.
choices.B: Listeners usually find gamelan melodies too broken up to follow.
choices.C: Gamelan musicians must train for many years before they may play solos.
choices.D: Gamelan music depends on players combining parts rather than playing alone.

explanation.why: The text says gamelan players are "not expected to stand out as soloists" and gives an example of two players whose parts fit together into one line. It ends by stating the point: "the music depends on every player fitting in with the others."
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is the example the text uses, not the larger point the example supports.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says listeners hear "a single, unbroken line," the opposite of a broken-up melody.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says players are not expected to be soloists; it says nothing about training for solos.
explanation.D: Correct. Both the opening claim and the example show that the music works only when players' parts combine.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1941, Swiss engineer George de Mestral returned from a walk in the Alps and noticed that small burrs, the seed cases of a plant called burdock, were stuck to his clothes and to his dog's fur. Looking at a burr under a microscope, he saw that it was covered in tiny hooks that caught on loops of thread and hair. Years later, he used this idea to create the hook-and-loop fastener now sold as Velcro.
items.stem: According to the text, what did de Mestral see when he looked at a burr under a microscope?

choices.A: Tiny hooks that could catch on thread and hair
choices.B: Loops of thread like the ones in his clothing
choices.C: Small holes that let it grip smooth fabric
choices.D: A sticky coating that held it to any surface

explanation.why: The second sentence answers the question directly: under the microscope, the burr "was covered in tiny hooks that caught on loops of thread and hair." The correct choice restates this.
explanation.A: Correct. This restates what de Mestral saw: tiny hooks that caught on thread and hair.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The loops were in the thread and hair; the burr itself had hooks.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions holes in the burr.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text explains the sticking with hooks, not with any sticky coating.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: From the rooftop, Sana could see dozens of kites rising over the old city of Lahore. Her own kite, the green one her brother had helped her build, kept dipping toward the water tanks below. Each time, she yanked the string too hard. Then she remembered her brother's advice and let the string out slowly. The kite steadied, caught the wind, and climbed until it was just one more bright square among the others.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Sana gets her kite to fly by following advice she had been given.
choices.B: Sana's brother flies his kite higher than anyone else in Lahore.
choices.C: Sana decides that her homemade kite cannot fly as well as the others.
choices.D: Sana watches the many kites that fill the sky above the old city.

explanation.why: Sana's kite keeps dipping while she yanks the string. The turning point comes when she "remembered her brother's advice and let the string out slowly"; after that, the kite "steadied" and "climbed." The main idea is that following the advice lets her fly the kite.
explanation.A: Correct. The passage shows a problem, the advice she remembers, and the kite's success once she follows it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The brother helped build the kite and gave advice, but he is not shown flying a kite at all.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Her kite ends up flying among the others, so the passage shows the opposite.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Seeing the other kites is only the opening detail, not what the passage is mainly about.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before 1840, letters in Britain were usually paid for by the person who received them, and the cost depended on how far the letter had traveled. Some people simply refused letters they did not want to pay for. In 1840, a reform proposed by teacher Rowland Hill took effect: senders paid in advance with a small stamp, and a light letter cost one penny to send anywhere in the country. Soon, far more letters were being mailed.
items.stem: Based on the text, why did the number of letters mailed in Britain most likely rise after 1840?

choices.A: People could now refuse letters they did not want.
choices.B: Senders paid one low price for any distance.
choices.C: Prices now depended on how far a letter traveled.
choices.D: Letters were now delivered faster than before.

explanation.why: The text describes the old system (receivers paid, and the cost depended on distance) and then the 1840 reform: senders paid in advance, and a light letter cost "one penny to send anywhere in the country." The rise in letters came right after this change, so the new single low price is the most likely reason.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Refusing letters was possible under the old system, before 1840, when receivers paid.
explanation.B: Correct. The reform set a single penny price for a light letter sent anywhere, and letter numbers then rose sharply.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Distance-based prices belong to the old system; after the reform, one penny covered any distance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions how fast letters were delivered.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Hummingbirds burn energy very quickly, and during the day they must feed every few minutes. At night, when they cannot feed, many hummingbirds enter a state called torpor. Their body temperature drops, and their heart rate slows sharply. This deep rest greatly reduces the amount of energy they use, helping them survive until morning, when they can feed again.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Hummingbirds sleep for more hours each night than other birds.
choices.B: Many hummingbirds survive the night by slowing their bodies to save energy.
choices.C: Hummingbirds must feed every few minutes during the day.
choices.D: Hummingbirds' heart rates rise sharply when they rest at night.

explanation.why: The text sets up a problem (hummingbirds use energy fast but cannot feed at night) and then explains the solution: torpor, in which body temperature and heart rate drop, which "greatly reduces the amount of energy they use." The main idea is how torpor helps them survive the night.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never compares hummingbirds' sleep with that of other birds.
explanation.B: Correct. This covers the problem and the solution: during torpor their bodies slow down, saving energy until morning.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Feeding every few minutes is a detail from the first sentence that sets up the main point.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says their heart rate "slows sharply," not that it rises.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Braille, the raised-dot system that lets blind people read by touch, was developed in France by Louis Braille, who lost his sight as a young child. As a student, he learned of a code of raised dots invented by an army officer, Charles Barbier, so that messages could be read in the dark. Braille found the code too complicated, so he simplified it. By age fifteen, he had created a system in which each letter fit under a single fingertip.
items.stem: According to the text, what did Louis Braille do with Barbier's code?

choices.A: He taught it to soldiers who needed to read at night.
choices.B: He simplified it to create an easier system.
choices.C: He replaced its raised dots with printed letters.
choices.D: He decided it was simple enough to use without changes.

explanation.why: The text says Braille "found the code too complicated, so he simplified it," creating a system in which each letter fit under one fingertip. The correct choice restates this.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Barbier invented the code for reading in the dark, but the text never says Braille taught soldiers.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates "he simplified it," which led to his own easier system.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Braille's own system still uses raised dots, as the first sentence says; nothing was replaced with printed letters.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Braille found the code "too complicated," so he did change it.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every evening, Lucía's grandfather sat on the harbor wall mending fishing nets, and every evening she watched. Today, he handed her the wooden needle and moved aside. Her first knots were clumsy; they slipped loose as soon as she pulled them tight. Her grandfather said nothing, only guided her fingers once through the loop. Slowly the knots began to hold, and when she looked up, he was smiling.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Lucía tries mending a net for the first time and, with quiet help, succeeds.
choices.B: Lucía's first knots slip loose as soon as she pulls them tight.
choices.C: Lucía's grandfather decides to stop fishing and gives his tools to her.
choices.D: Lucía's grandfather grows impatient with her clumsy, loose knots.

explanation.why: Lucía has always watched, but "Today" her grandfather hands her the needle. Her knots slip at first; he silently guides her fingers; then "the knots began to hold" and he smiles. The main idea is her first successful attempt, helped quietly by her grandfather.
explanation.A: Correct. This covers the whole passage: her first try, his silent help, and her success.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The slipping knots are only one moment; the passage goes on to show her improving.
explanation.C: Incorrect. He lets her use the needle for one evening; nothing suggests he is giving up fishing.
explanation.D: Incorrect. He stays quiet, guides her gently, and ends up smiling, so he is patient, not impatient.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Amazon rainforest looks like one of the most fertile places on Earth, yet much of its soil is poor in phosphorus, a nutrient that plants need to grow. Heavy rains wash the nutrient away. Part of the missing phosphorus arrives from an unexpected source: the Sahara Desert. Each year, winds carry millions of tons of dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic Ocean, and some of that phosphorus-rich dust falls on the rainforest.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: The Amazon's soil is richer in nutrients than the soil of most forests.
choices.B: Scientists plan to add phosphorus to the Amazon's soil to help plants grow.
choices.C: Dust from the Sahara helps supply a nutrient that the Amazon's soil lacks.
choices.D: Winds carry millions of tons of dust across the Atlantic Ocean each year.

explanation.why: The text explains a problem (the Amazon's soil is "poor in phosphorus" because rain washes it away) and then its surprising partial solution: phosphorus-rich dust blown from the Sahara. The main idea links the two: Saharan dust supplies a nutrient the soil lacks.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the forest only looks fertile; its soil is actually "poor in phosphorus."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text describes a natural process; it never mentions scientists adding phosphorus.
explanation.C: Correct. This connects both parts of the text: the soil's shortage of phosphorus and the dust that helps replace it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is one supporting detail; it leaves out why the dust matters to the rainforest.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, was a major center of learning in the 1400s and 1500s. Scholars there wrote and copied thousands of manuscripts on subjects such as astronomy, mathematics, medicine, and law. Many of these manuscripts survived for centuries because local families kept them in their homes, passing them down from parents to children. Today, libraries in the city work to preserve and study them.
items.stem: According to the text, how did many of Timbuktu's manuscripts survive for centuries?

choices.A: Scholars made fresh copies of them every few years.
choices.B: Families stored them at home and handed them down.
choices.C: They were sent to libraries in other countries.
choices.D: City libraries guarded them from the 1400s onward.

explanation.why: The third sentence gives the reason directly: the manuscripts survived "because local families kept them in their homes, passing them down from parents to children." The correct choice says the same thing in other words.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Scholars did write and copy manuscripts, but the text does not say that repeated copying is how they survived.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates the text's explanation: families kept the manuscripts at home and passed them down.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says the manuscripts left Mali.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says libraries preserve the manuscripts "today"; for centuries it was families who kept them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Sundarbans, a vast mangrove forest shared by Bangladesh and India, grows in muddy ground that is flooded by seawater twice a day. This mud holds very little oxygen, which plant roots need. Many of the forest's trees solve the problem with special roots called pneumatophores, which grow upward out of the mud like pencils. At low tide, these roots take in air for the rest of the tree.
items.stem: According to the text, what is the function of the pneumatophores?

choices.A: They take in air that the trees cannot get from the mud.
choices.B: They grow downward to reach oxygen deep in the soil.
choices.C: They store seawater for the trees to use at low tide.
choices.D: They hold the trees firmly in place in the soft mud.

explanation.why: The text names a problem, that the mud "holds very little oxygen," and says the trees "solve the problem" with pneumatophores, which "take in air for the rest of the tree." So their function is to supply air the mud cannot.
explanation.A: Correct. The roots take in air at low tide, solving the problem of oxygen-poor mud.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the roots grow "upward out of the mud," not downward.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The roots take in air, not seawater, and the text never mentions storing water.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never says these roots anchor the trees.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Lukas reached the station twenty minutes early and checked the arrivals board again and again. His older brother had been away at university in another city for almost a year. When the train finally pulled in, Lukas searched every window. Then he spotted a familiar wave from the third car. He had planned to act calm, but before the doors had fully opened, he was already running down the platform.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Lukas's brother has decided to leave university and move home.
choices.B: Lukas is so eager to see his brother that he cannot stay calm.
choices.C: Lukas plans to greet his brother calmly and manages to do so.
choices.D: Lukas worries that his brother's train will be canceled.

explanation.why: Every detail shows Lukas's eagerness: he arrives "twenty minutes early," checks the board "again and again," and searches every window. The last sentence confirms it: he "had planned to act calm" but is "already running down the platform."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says only that the brother has been away for a year, not that he is leaving university.
explanation.B: Correct. His early arrival, constant checking, and running down the platform all show an excitement he cannot hide.
explanation.C: Incorrect. He planned to act calm but ends up running, so he does not manage it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. He checks the board often, but nothing suggests he fears a cancellation.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Construction of the Sagrada Família, a church in Barcelona, Spain, began in 1882, and the architect Antoni Gaudí directed the work from 1883 until his death in 1926. Gaudí knew the building would not be finished in his lifetime, so he left detailed plaster models to guide later builders. Many of the models were broken in 1936, but workers patiently pieced the fragments back together. Today, builders use the repaired models along with computer design programs.
items.stem: According to the text, why did Gaudí leave detailed plaster models?

choices.A: He wanted to sell them to pay for the construction.
choices.B: He hoped to replace the models broken in 1936.
choices.C: He expected others to finish the building after him.
choices.D: He needed them to test his designs on computers.

explanation.why: The text gives the reason in one sentence: Gaudí "knew the building would not be finished in his lifetime, so he left detailed plaster models to guide later builders." The models were meant for the people who would continue the work.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never mentions selling the models or raising money.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Gaudí died in 1926, ten years before the models were broken.
explanation.C: Correct. He made the models because he knew later builders would have to complete the church.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Computer programs are used by builders "today," long after Gaudí's death.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Mehrgarh, on the Kachi Plain of Balochistan in Pakistan, is one of the earliest known farming villages in South Asia; people there grew barley and herded goats more than 8,000 years ago. The site is also known for a less expected discovery. In 2006, researchers reported that eleven molars from graves dated to roughly 7,500 to 9,000 years ago had small, neat holes drilled into them. Because the edges of the holes had been worn smooth by later chewing, the researchers concluded that the drilling was done on living people, an early form of dentistry.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Teeth found at Mehrgarh suggest that people there practiced an early form of dentistry.
choices.B: Mehrgarh is one of the earliest known farming villages in South Asia.
choices.C: Farming at Mehrgarh caused tooth decay that forced villagers to drill their teeth.
choices.D: Researchers found that the teeth from Mehrgarh had been drilled after their owners died.

explanation.why: After one sentence of background on farming, the text turns to "a less expected discovery" and spends the rest on it: drilled molars whose worn edges show the drilling was done on living people, which researchers read as "an early form of dentistry." That discovery is the text's main point.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures the discovery the text focuses on and the conclusion the researchers drew from it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is background from the first sentence; most of the text is about the drilled teeth.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says farming caused tooth decay or explains why the teeth were drilled.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The worn edges led researchers to conclude the opposite: the drilling was done while the people were alive.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Ngozi studied the board for a long time before tipping over her king, the sign that she had lost. Across the table, the regional champion, a man three times her age, shook her hand and was silent for a moment. Then he reset the pieces to where they had stood twenty moves earlier and pointed at her knight. "Here," he said quietly. "Here you almost had me." Ngozi left the hall having lost the game, but she was already replaying that move in her head, and she was smiling.
items.stem: Based on the text, why is Ngozi smiling as she leaves the hall?

choices.A: She has noticed a serious mistake the champion made late in the game.
choices.B: She believes the champion let her win part of the game out of kindness.
choices.C: She has learned from a strong opponent that she came close to beating him.
choices.D: She is relieved that the long and difficult tournament is finally over.

explanation.why: Ngozi loses, but the champion shows her a position from earlier in the game and tells her, "Here you almost had me." She leaves "replaying that move in her head" and smiling, so her smile comes from learning that she nearly beat a strong player.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The champion points to her knight twenty moves back, a chance she had, not a late mistake of his own.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing suggests the champion went easy on her; he simply points out where she nearly won.
explanation.C: Correct. The champion's words show her how close she came, and she leaves thinking about that move with a smile.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never says the tournament is over or that she feels relieved.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Wombats, burrowing marsupials native to Australia, are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped droppings. One might expect such a shape to be formed at the body's exit, the way a square nozzle shapes icing squeezed from a bag. In 2018, however, a team of researchers examining wombat intestines found that the cubes take shape earlier, inside the intestine itself, where some sections of the wall are stiffer than others. As the intestine contracts, these uneven walls press the contents into blocks with flat sides and fairly sharp corners.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Wombats' cube-shaped droppings are formed inside the intestine by walls of uneven stiffness.
choices.B: Wombats are burrowing marsupials that are native to the continent of Australia.
choices.C: Researchers now understand how the intestines of all animals shape their droppings.
choices.D: Wombats' droppings take their cube shape only at the body's exit, like icing from a nozzle.

explanation.why: The text introduces the wombat's unusual cube-shaped droppings, raises an expectation (the shape forms at the body's exit), and then, with "however," reports what researchers actually found: the cubes form inside the intestine, where uneven walls press the contents into blocks. The main idea is this finding about how the cubes form.
explanation.A: Correct. This states the researchers' finding, which is what the whole text builds toward.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This background detail leaves out the text's point about how the cube shape forms.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The research concerned wombats only; the text makes no claim about all animals.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the expectation that the 2018 research showed to be wrong.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When William Shakespeare died in 1616, only about half of his plays had appeared in print, often in cheap editions of uneven quality. Seven years later, two actors from his company, John Heminges and Henry Condell, gathered thirty-six of his plays into a single large volume now known as the First Folio. Without their effort, roughly eighteen plays, including Macbeth and The Tempest, might have been lost, since no earlier printed version of them is known to exist.
items.stem: Based on the text, what is the main reason the First Folio is considered important?

choices.A: It included every play that Shakespeare is known to have written.
choices.B: It corrected the errors found in cheap earlier editions of his plays.
choices.C: It was the first book to include any of Shakespeare's plays.
choices.D: It preserved many plays that had never been printed before.

explanation.why: The text's last sentence explains the volume's importance: without it, "roughly eighteen plays" might have been lost, because "no earlier printed version of them is known to exist." So the Folio matters mainly because it saved plays that had never been printed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the Folio contains thirty-six plays but never claims this was every play Shakespeare wrote.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text mentions that earlier editions were of uneven quality but never says the Folio corrected them.
explanation.C: Incorrect. About half of the plays had already appeared in print before Shakespeare died, so the Folio was not the first.
explanation.D: Correct. The text credits the Folio with saving about eighteen plays that had no earlier printed version.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In his treatise the Aryabhatiya, completed in 499 CE, the Indian mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata proposed that the stars only appear to move westward across the night sky. The real motion, he argued, is the Earth turning on its axis, much as a person in a moving boat sees trees on the shore seem to move backward. Most astronomers of his era, in India and elsewhere, held that the Earth stood still, and several later Indian scholars rejected his idea. The view that the Earth rotates gained wide acceptance only many centuries afterward.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Most astronomers in Aryabhata's era believed that the Earth stood still.
choices.B: Later Indian scholars improved Aryabhata's idea until it was widely accepted.
choices.C: Aryabhata was the first person in history to suggest that the Earth moves.
choices.D: Aryabhata argued that the Earth rotates, an idea that was not widely accepted in his time.

explanation.why: The text first presents Aryabhata's proposal that the Earth turns on its axis and then qualifies it: most astronomers of his era disagreed, later scholars rejected it, and the idea was widely accepted "only many centuries afterward." The main idea combines his claim with its cool reception.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is a supporting detail; it leaves out Aryabhata's own proposal, which is the text's focus.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says several later Indian scholars rejected the idea, not that they improved it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares Aryabhata with anyone earlier, so it does not support "first person in history."
explanation.D: Correct. This captures both parts of the text: Aryabhata's argument and the fact that it was not widely accepted for centuries.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Señor Ibarra had closed his tailor shop in Buenos Aires years ago, and he told anyone who asked that he did not miss it. So when his granddaughter brought him her torn winter coat, he grumbled that she should simply buy another. Still, he turned the coat over in his hands, studying the seam. By evening he had found his old spool of gray thread, cleared the kitchen table, and bent over the work, humming a tune she had not heard him hum in years.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A retired tailor regrets closing his shop and decides to open it once again.
choices.B: A granddaughter tears her winter coat and asks her grandfather to repair it.
choices.C: A retired tailor who claims not to miss his work seems to enjoy returning to it.
choices.D: A grandfather refuses to mend his granddaughter's coat because he has retired.

explanation.why: Ibarra says he does not miss tailoring and grumbles about the coat, but his actions tell a different story: he studies the seam, finds his old thread, and works while "humming a tune she had not heard him hum in years." The main idea is the contrast between what he claims and the pleasure he shows.
explanation.A: Incorrect. He enjoys one repair job, but nothing suggests he regrets closing the shop or plans to reopen it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is only the event that starts the passage; it leaves out how Ibarra responds.
explanation.C: Correct. This captures the contrast at the heart of the passage: his claim not to miss the work versus his evident pleasure in doing it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. He grumbles at first, but by evening he is mending the coat.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In April 1815, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, erupted with enormous force, sending vast amounts of ash and gas high into the atmosphere. The following year, people in Europe and North America lived through a strangely cold summer: frosts damaged crops in New England in June, and harvests failed in parts of Europe. At the time, few people suspected that the two events were linked. Only in the twentieth century did scientists show that particles from large eruptions can spread around the globe and block some sunlight, cooling distant regions.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A cold summer far from Tambora was likely caused by its eruption, a link recognized only later.
choices.B: The eruption of Mount Tambora caused frosts and crop failures across Indonesia in 1816.
choices.C: People in 1816 quickly realized that a distant volcanic eruption had cooled their summer.
choices.D: Frosts damaged crops in New England during June of the year after Tambora erupted.

explanation.why: The text pairs two events, the 1815 eruption and the cold summer that followed in Europe and North America, and then explains that the link between them was not understood until the twentieth century, when scientists showed how eruption particles can cool distant regions. The main idea combines the connection with the late recognition of it.
explanation.A: Correct. This joins the text's two parts: the eruption probably caused the distant cold summer, and scientists made the connection much later.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text describes cold and crop failures in Europe and North America, not in Indonesia.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says that at the time "few people suspected that the two events were linked."
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is one example of the cold summer; it leaves out the eruption's role and the later scientific explanation.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The moai of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), huge stone statues carved between roughly 1250 and 1500 CE, stand kilometers from the quarry where most of them were carved. Because the islanders had no wheels or large draft animals, the question of how the statues were moved long puzzled researchers. Oral traditions on the island say that the moai "walked." In 2012, archaeologists tested this idea with a concrete replica weighing more than four tons. Pulling on ropes tied to its head from alternating sides, a team of eighteen people rocked the upright statue forward, making it waddle along a path.
items.stem: According to the text, what did the 2012 test show?

choices.A: A small team using ropes could move an upright statue by rocking it.
choices.B: Every moai on the island was moved by being walked upright to its site.
choices.C: The island's stories of walking moai were invented by later visitors.
choices.D: The moai were most likely dragged from the quarry on wooden sleds.

explanation.why: The text describes the test in its last sentence: by pulling ropes "from alternating sides," eighteen people "rocked the upright statue forward, making it waddle along a path." The test showed that such a method could work, which fits the oral traditions that the moai "walked."
explanation.A: Correct. This restates the result: eighteen people with ropes moved an upright replica by rocking it forward.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A test with one replica shows the method was possible, not that every statue was moved this way.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The test supported the island's oral traditions rather than showing they were invented.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions sleds; the test moved the statue standing upright.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Nimali had imagined her grandfather's tea estate in the hills near Nuwara Eliya as a place of quiet green rows and slow mornings. Instead, on her first day, she was awake before dawn, following the pluckers up slopes so steep she had to grip the bushes to keep her balance. Her grandfather showed her how to pinch off only the top two leaves and a bud. By noon her basket held barely a handful, while the women around her had filled theirs twice. She did not complain; she only watched their hands more closely.
items.stem: Based on the text, how does Nimali respond to the difficulty of the work?

choices.A: She tries to improve by paying closer attention to the skilled pluckers.
choices.B: She complains to her grandfather that the slopes are too steep to work on.
choices.C: She asks her grandfather to give her an easier job somewhere on the estate.
choices.D: She regrets coming to the estate because it is not as quiet as she imagined.

explanation.why: The question asks how Nimali reacts to falling behind. The last sentence answers it: "She did not complain; she only watched their hands more closely." Watching the experienced women's hands suggests she is trying to learn their skill.
explanation.A: Correct. Watching the pluckers' hands "more closely" after falling behind shows she is trying to learn from them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text states directly that "She did not complain."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nimali never asks for a different job; she keeps watching and learning.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The estate differs from what she imagined, but the text never says she regrets coming.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The snapping shrimp, a sea creature only a few centimeters long, is among the loudest animals in the ocean, and large colonies of them can interfere with underwater sonar. For years, researchers assumed the sound came from the two halves of the shrimp's oversized claw striking each other. High-speed video and sound recordings told a different story. When the claw snaps shut, it shoots out a jet of water so fast that a bubble of very low pressure forms. The loud crack is made when that bubble collapses, not when the claw closes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Research showed that the shrimp's snap comes from a collapsing bubble, not the claw.
choices.B: Snapping shrimp are louder than any other animal that lives in the ocean.
choices.C: Large colonies of snapping shrimp can interfere with underwater sonar.
choices.D: The shrimp's crack is produced when the two halves of its claw strike together.

explanation.why: The text sets up an old assumption (the sound comes from the claw's halves striking) and then reports what high-speed video and recordings "told" instead: the crack comes from a collapsing low-pressure bubble. The main idea is this corrected explanation of the sound.
explanation.A: Correct. This states the text's central finding, which replaces the earlier assumption about the claw.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the shrimp is "among the loudest" animals, not the loudest of all.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sonar detail shows how loud the shrimp are, but it is not what the text is mainly about.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the old assumption that the newer research overturned.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Silent films were rarely watched in silence. In the 1910s and 1920s, most theaters employed a pianist or organist, and large city theaters sometimes hired full orchestras. Because musicians often had to match music to scenes they were seeing for the first time, film studios began sending out cue sheets: lists of a film's scenes with suggested pieces and moods for each. The sheets did not dictate every note, though, and many players continued to improvise, so the same film could sound quite different from one theater to the next.
items.stem: According to the text, why could the same silent film sound different from one theater to another?

choices.A: Studios sent each theater its own cue sheet with different music.
choices.B: Pianists in small theaters played louder to make up for having no orchestra.
choices.C: Cue sheets listed the exact notes each musician was expected to play.
choices.D: Many musicians improvised rather than playing set music note for note.

explanation.why: The final sentence gives the cause directly: cue sheets "did not dictate every note," and "many players continued to improvise, so the same film could sound quite different from one theater to the next." The word "so" links the improvising to the differences.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes cue sheets for each film, not different cue sheets for different theaters.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never discusses how loudly anyone played.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the cue sheets "did not dictate every note"; they suggested pieces and moods.
explanation.D: Correct. The text links the differences directly to musicians' improvising.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the early 1900s, the Harvard College Observatory hired women, known as "computers," to examine thousands of photographic plates of the night sky. The work was considered routine, and the pay was modest. Yet one of these women, Henrietta Swan Leavitt, noticed a pattern in a type of star whose brightness rises and falls: the longer such a star took to complete a cycle, the brighter it truly was. Her finding, published in 1912, later gave astronomers a way to measure distances to faraway stars and even to other galaxies.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Leavitt, hired for supposedly routine work, made a finding that helped astronomers measure great distances.
choices.B: Leavitt found that stars whose brightness rises and falls are farther away than other stars.
choices.C: Leavitt used her own finding to measure the distances to several galaxies beyond our own.
choices.D: The women hired as "computers" at Harvard were paid modest wages to examine photographs of the sky.

explanation.why: The text contrasts the job's low status ("considered routine," "modest" pay) with what Leavitt achieved through it, signaled by "Yet": she found a pattern that "later gave astronomers a way to measure distances." The main idea joins that contrast with the importance of her finding.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures the contrast between the routine job and the far-reaching discovery Leavitt made.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Leavitt linked a star's cycle length to its true brightness; the text never says such stars are farther away.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says her finding "later gave astronomers" a method; it does not say she measured galaxies herself.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This describes the working conditions in the first two sentences but leaves out Leavitt's discovery.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mei had agreed to help her uncle with his beehives only because her parents insisted. For the first hour she stood well back, flinching whenever a bee drifted near her veil. Her uncle worked slowly and spoke to the bees in a low voice, as if they were old friends. When he lifted out a frame heavy with honeycomb and offered it to her, she hesitated, then took it. The bees crawled calmly over the comb, and Mei, holding her breath, realized that her hands had stopped shaking.
items.stem: Based on the text, how do Mei's feelings change over the course of the text?

choices.A: She starts out confident but becomes nervous once the bees cover the comb.
choices.B: She starts out afraid of the bees but decides to keep bees of her own.
choices.C: She starts out fearful of the bees but grows calmer as she handles them.
choices.D: She starts out eager to help but grows bored by her uncle's slow work.

explanation.why: At first Mei stands "well back," "flinching" whenever a bee comes near. By the end, holding the comb, she realizes "her hands had stopped shaking." Her feelings move from fear toward calm.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the change: she begins nervous and ends calmer.
explanation.B: Incorrect. She becomes calmer, but nothing suggests she plans to keep bees herself.
explanation.C: Correct. Her flinching at the start and her steady hands at the end show fear giving way to calm.
explanation.D: Incorrect. She helps only because her parents insist, so she is not eager, and the text never mentions boredom.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Elephants communicate partly through rumbles so low in pitch that humans cannot hear them. These sounds, known as infrasound, lose little energy as they travel and can carry several kilometers. Researchers studying African elephants have also found that the rumbles send vibrations through the ground. Elephants appear to detect these vibrations with sensitive nerve endings in their feet and trunks, sometimes freezing in place and leaning forward as if listening. This ability may help herds keep track of distant groups that are far out of sight.
items.stem: Based on the text, why might elephants freeze in place and lean forward?

choices.A: To better sense vibrations traveling through the ground
choices.B: To hear airborne sounds too low for their ears to catch
choices.C: To rest their feet after walking several kilometers
choices.D: To produce low rumbles that travel through the ground

explanation.why: The text says elephants "appear to detect these vibrations with sensitive nerve endings in their feet and trunks," and that they freeze and lean forward "as if listening." Since the vibrations are sensed through the feet, this listening posture most likely helps them pick up the signals.
explanation.A: Correct. The text connects the freezing and leaning directly to detecting ground vibrations through the feet and trunk.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says humans cannot hear the rumbles; it never says elephants' ears cannot, and it ties the behavior to ground vibrations.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text gives no sign that the behavior has anything to do with tiredness.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The freezing is linked to detecting vibrations, not to making the rumbles.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Library of Alexandria, founded in Egypt in the third century BCE, is often remembered as having vanished in a single great fire. Ancient writers do report that books burned when fires set by Julius Caesar's forces spread through part of the city in 48 BCE. Many historians, however, think the library's end was slower and less dramatic. Over the centuries, royal support for scholars weakened, some scholars were driven out during political conflicts, and fewer new copies were made of the collection's papyrus scrolls, which decay with age.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Papyrus scrolls decay with age unless new copies of them are made.
choices.B: Many historians think the library declined gradually rather than in one fire.
choices.C: The library held more books than any other library in the ancient world.
choices.D: Fires set by Julius Caesar's forces destroyed the entire library in 48 BCE.

explanation.why: The text opens with a popular memory (the library "vanished in a single great fire"), grants that some books did burn in 48 BCE, and then, with "however," gives historians' view that the end "was slower and less dramatic," listing causes over centuries. The main idea is this gradual-decline view.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The decay of papyrus is one of several causes listed, not the main point.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures the contrast the text builds: the popular single-fire story versus historians' view of a slow decline.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares the library's size with that of other ancient libraries.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says only that some books burned in 48 BCE; it presents total destruction by one fire as the popular memory historians doubt.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Desert locusts spend much of their lives as solitary insects: shy, green, and inclined to avoid one another. When drought crowds them onto shrinking patches of vegetation, however, repeated contact with other locusts, particularly touches to the hind legs, can trigger a striking transformation. Within hours, crowded individuals become restless and attracted to one another, and over later generations they develop different colors and body proportions. Laboratory work has linked the initial change in behavior to a surge of the chemical messenger serotonin in the nervous system. The finding suggests that the swarms capable of stripping farmland across Africa and Asia are not a separate kind of locust but the same insects responding to the crowded conditions they encounter.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Drought is the main cause of the destructive locust swarms that strip farmland across Africa and Asia.
choices.B: Serotonin causes crowded locusts to change their color and body shape within just a few hours.
choices.C: Swarming locusts appear to be ordinary desert locusts that have changed in response to crowding.
choices.D: Solitary desert locusts are usually green and tend to avoid contact with other locusts.

explanation.why: The text describes how crowding, through repeated contact, switches solitary locusts into a different state, and its last sentence states the conclusion: swarms are "not a separate kind of locust but the same insects responding to the crowded conditions." The main idea must capture that link between crowding and swarming, not just one step in the process.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says drought crowds locusts together, but it presents contact with other locusts, not drought itself, as the trigger, and it never ranks drought as the main cause of swarms.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text links serotonin only to the "initial change in behavior"; changes in color and body proportions come "over later generations," not within hours.
explanation.C: Correct. This matches the text's conclusion that swarms are made up of the same insects transformed by crowded conditions.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This describes only the solitary phase in the first sentence and leaves out the transformation that the text is about.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: After her husband's death, Agnieszka Wróbel kept the clock shop open chiefly, she told the neighbors, so that the stock would not be wasted. She could not repair a mainspring and had no wish to learn. Yet each evening, once the shutters were drawn, she wound every clock on the walls, though no customer would come before morning to hear them, and set each one by the old regulator that Tadeusz had trusted above the railway time. When the apprentice suggested they let the unsold clocks run down to spare the springs, she told him sharply that a shop of stopped clocks was a shop for sale, and the matter was not raised again.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Agnieszka is determined to master the clock repairs that her husband once did.
choices.B: Agnieszka's nightly habits suggest a deeper attachment to the shop than she admits.
choices.C: Agnieszka keeps the shop open mainly so that her husband's stock can be sold off.
choices.D: Agnieszka resents the apprentice for trying to take control of the clock shop from her.

explanation.why: The first sentence gives Agnieszka's stated reason ("she told the neighbors") for keeping the shop open: not wasting the stock. The rest of the text undercuts that reason: she winds every clock each night when no one will hear them, sets them by the regulator her husband trusted, and refuses to let them stop because "a shop of stopped clocks was a shop for sale." Her actions reveal an attachment that her practical explanation does not admit.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says she "had no wish to learn" to repair a mainspring, which contradicts this choice.
explanation.B: Correct. Her careful nightly care for the clocks and her refusal to let them stop show an attachment beyond the practical reason she gives.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This takes her explanation to the neighbors at face value; her nightly winding of clocks no customer will hear shows that more than selling stock is at stake.
explanation.D: Incorrect. She answers the apprentice sharply once, but nothing suggests he is trying to take control of the shop or that she resents him.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The eleven medieval churches of Lalibela, in the highlands of northern Ethiopia, are often described as buildings, but in a strict sense almost none of them was built. Workers, probably in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, began with solid volcanic rock and removed material rather than adding it: they cut deep trenches to isolate a block, then hollowed the block into rooms, windows, and columns. Because nothing could be put back once it was removed, the method left little room for error, and some scholars infer that the plans must have been settled in detail before cutting began. Others caution that irregularities in several interiors suggest that designs were adjusted as the work proceeded.
items.stem: According to the text, why do some scholars infer that the plans for the churches were settled in detail before cutting began?

choices.A: The volcanic rock was too hard to allow any changes once the carving had started.
choices.B: Irregularities in several interiors show that workers kept to a single fixed design.
choices.C: Trenches had to be cut around each block before its interior could be hollowed.
choices.D: Rock removed during carving could not be restored if the workers made a mistake.

explanation.why: The text gives the reason directly with "Because": "nothing could be put back once it was removed," so the method "left little room for error," and from this some scholars infer that the plans were settled in advance. Keep track of who says what: the irregularities are evidence cited by other scholars for the opposite view.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never describes the rock as too hard to change; the problem was that removed material could not be replaced.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the irregularities suggest designs "were adjusted as the work proceeded," so they support the other scholars' view, not a fixed design.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is a true step in the method, but it is not the reason the text gives for the scholars' inference.
explanation.D: Correct. This restates the reason the text gives: because carved-away rock could not be put back, mistakes could not be undone.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Sculptures from Gandhara, a region centered on what is now northwestern Pakistan, are frequently cited as proof that Greek art shaped early images of the Buddha: many show robes falling in heavy folds and faces modeled in a manner reminiscent of Hellenistic statues. Yet most of these works date from the first to the fifth centuries CE, long after Greek rulers had lost power in the region, and their nearest stylistic parallels are often found in art of the Roman Empire, with which Gandhara traded. Some art historians therefore argue that "Greek influence" is a misleadingly simple label for a tradition that drew on several Mediterranean and local sources at once.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Some scholars think crediting Gandharan style to Greek art alone oversimplifies its sources.
choices.B: Gandharan sculptors copied Roman statues rather than Greek ones when carving the Buddha.
choices.C: Greek rulers lost power in Gandhara before its trade with the Roman Empire had begun.
choices.D: Gandharan sculptures show heavily folded robes and faces much like those of Hellenistic statues.

explanation.why: The text sets up a common claim (Gandharan sculpture proves Greek influence), then gives two complications: the dates fall "long after Greek rulers had lost power," and the closest parallels are "often" Roman. It concludes that some scholars see "Greek influence" as "a misleadingly simple label" for a tradition with "several Mediterranean and local sources." The main idea is that qualified argument.
explanation.A: Correct. This captures the scholars' conclusion, including its scope: the problem is treating Greek art as the single source.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This overstates the text, which says Roman parallels are "often" closest and that the tradition drew on several sources, not that sculptors simply copied Roman statues.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says Greek rulers had lost power before most of the sculptures were made, but it never says when trade with Rome began.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the evidence behind the common claim in the first sentence, not the point the text builds to.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1800, the naturalist Alexander von Humboldt described electric eels in a Venezuelan pool rising from the water to press themselves against horses that local fishers had driven in. For nearly two centuries, many biologists treated the account as an exaggeration, since eels were known to deliver their shocks while fully submerged. Experiments in the 2010s, however, showed that an eel confronting a partly submerged threat will indeed leap up and press its chin against it. Out of the water, the current that would otherwise spread into the surrounding water passes instead through the threat's body, so the shock it receives is stronger. The behavior, researchers suggest, may help eels defend themselves when shrinking dry-season pools leave them exposed.
items.stem: According to the text, why is an eel's shock stronger when the eel leaps up to press against a threat?

choices.A: Shrinking pools in the dry season leave eels more exposed to possible predators.
choices.B: Less current is lost to the surrounding water, so more passes through the threat.
choices.C: The eel can generate more electricity when part of its body is exposed to the open air.
choices.D: The surrounding water carries the eel's current directly into the threat's body.

explanation.why: The fourth sentence explains the mechanism: out of the water, "the current that would otherwise spread into the surrounding water passes instead through the threat's body, so the shock it receives is stronger." The shock is stronger because less current is lost to the water, not because the eel produces more.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is the situation in which the behavior may be useful, not the reason the shock is stronger.
explanation.B: Correct. This restates the text's explanation: current that would spread into the water passes through the threat instead.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says the eel produces more electricity in air; it says the same current is directed through the threat instead of spreading into the water.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says the water spreads the current away; leaping out of the water keeps it from doing so.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Accounts of the Ming dynasty's naval expeditions of the early 1400s, led by the admiral Zheng He, credit the largest "treasure ships" with lengths of roughly 120 meters, which would make them several times longer than the ships Columbus sailed decades later. Some historians accept the figure, noting that an enormous rudder post was excavated at the site of a former Ming shipyard. Others point out that the dimensions come from texts written long after the voyages and that wooden hulls of that length would have been extraordinarily difficult to keep from bending and leaking. What both sides agree on is that the fleets were vast overall, with dozens of ships and many thousands of crew members.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Wooden ships cannot be built longer than about 120 meters without bending and leaking.
choices.B: Some historians doubt reports of the ships' length because the reports were written much later.
choices.C: Historians dispute the size of Zheng He's largest ships but agree that his fleets were vast.
choices.D: A huge excavated rudder post has proved that Zheng He's largest ships were about 120 meters long.

explanation.why: The text presents a reported figure, then two camps: some historians accept it (citing the rudder post), and others doubt it (late sources, structural problems). The final sentence adds what "both sides agree on": the fleets were vast. A main idea must cover both the disagreement and the agreement.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says such hulls would have been "extraordinarily difficult" to keep sound, not impossible, and it makes no general claim about all wooden ships.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This gives only one side's argument and leaves out both the opposing view and the point of agreement.
explanation.C: Correct. This covers the whole text: the dispute over the largest ships' size and the shared view that the fleets were enormous.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The rudder post is evidence one side cites, not proof; the text presents the length as disputed.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For thirty-one years Haripada Sen had sorted the letters of Chandpur, and in retirement he had not lost the habit of meeting the morning mail boat. He no longer carried anything back from the landing; he simply stood at its edge while the new clerk, a young man from Comilla, counted out the bundles. Twice that winter the clerk misread a smudged address, and twice Haripada said nothing until the boat had gone, then mentioned, as if recalling an old story, a family by that name who had once lived beyond the tank. The letters reached their owners. The clerk thanked him the second time, and Haripada, embarrassed, spoke of the weather.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A retired postmaster misses the work of carrying the mail back from the landing.
choices.B: A young clerk depends on a retired postmaster to help him sort Chandpur's mail every morning.
choices.C: A retired postmaster quietly helps his successor while avoiding seeming to correct him.
choices.D: A retired postmaster resents the young clerk who has replaced him at the landing.

explanation.why: Haripada waits until the boat has gone, then offers the right information "as if recalling an old story," so his help never looks like a correction. When thanked, he is "embarrassed" and changes the subject. The text centers on this tactful, nearly hidden help.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says he no longer carries anything, but it never says he misses doing so.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Haripada helps only twice and does no sorting; he "simply stood" at the landing's edge.
explanation.C: Correct. His indirect hints and his embarrassment at being thanked show help given without any air of correction.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in his behavior suggests resentment; he helps the clerk and is embarrassed by thanks.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a whale dies in the open ocean, its carcass may sink to a seafloor where food is otherwise scarce. Studies of such "whale falls" describe a sequence of communities. Scavengers such as hagfish and sleeper sharks strip the soft tissue within months to a couple of years; worms and crustaceans then colonize the enriched sediment and exposed bones. The longest stage depends on the skeleton itself: as bacteria break down fats stored in the bones, they release sulfide, which other microbes use as a source of energy, supporting communities of animals for decades. Because some of these animals also live at hydrothermal vents, researchers have proposed that whale falls may serve as stepping stones for vent species spreading across the deep sea.
items.stem: According to the text, what makes it possible for a whale fall to support animals for decades?

choices.A: Animals from hydrothermal vents arrive at the carcass and gradually colonize its bones.
choices.B: Scavengers such as hagfish remove the whale's soft tissue slowly over many years.
choices.C: Microbes draw energy from sulfide released as bacteria break down fats in the bones.
choices.D: Food is otherwise scarce on the deep seafloor where the whale's carcass settles.

explanation.why: The fourth sentence explains the longest stage: bacteria break down fats in the bones and release sulfide, "which other microbes use as a source of energy, supporting communities of animals for decades." The decades-long support comes from this chain of microbial activity in the skeleton.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text only proposes that vent species might use whale falls as stepping stones; it does not say their arrival sustains the community.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says scavengers strip soft tissue "within months to a couple of years," which is quick, not slow over many years.
explanation.C: Correct. This restates the mechanism the text gives for the stage that lasts decades.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it explains why a whale fall matters, not what lets it support animals for decades.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In traditional Japanese indigo dyeing, or aizome, the blue does not come from a ready-made dye. Indigo leaves are first composted for months into a dark material called sukumo, which is then placed in a vat with lye made from wood ash. There, bacteria convert the insoluble indigo into a form that can soak into cloth; when the cloth is lifted out, contact with air turns it blue. Because the bacteria must be kept alive, dyers speak of feeding the vat and judge its condition by its smell and the look of its surface foam, and a neglected vat can fail entirely. Chemical agents can perform the same conversion in hours, yet many workshops still prefer the slower method.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Cloth dyed in an aizome vat turns blue only after it is lifted out and exposed to air.
choices.B: Traditional aizome relies on a living fermentation that dyers must tend with great care.
choices.C: The slow aizome method produces deeper shades of blue than any chemical process can.
choices.D: Chemical agents have now largely replaced bacteria in Japan's traditional indigo workshops.

explanation.why: The text explains that aizome depends on bacteria in the vat, which "must be kept alive": dyers "feed" the vat, check its smell and foam, and risk losing it if it is neglected. The last sentence adds that many workshops still choose this slow, living process. The main idea is that aizome depends on carefully tended fermentation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is one step in the process, not the point of the whole text.
explanation.B: Correct. This sums up the text's focus: the bacteria-driven process and the care needed to keep it working.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares the depth of color produced by the two methods.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says many workshops "still prefer the slower method," which contradicts this choice.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the Kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria, works in cast brass were long the property of the oba, or king. The casters belonged to a hereditary guild, the Igun Eronmwon, whose members lived together in a single quarter of Benin City and worked by royal commission. Between roughly the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, they produced hundreds of rectangular plaques showing court ceremonies, warriors, and foreign visitors, which once covered pillars of the royal palace. Much of the metal arrived as brass bracelets called manillas, traded by Portuguese merchants. The plaques thus record both the kingdom's internal order and its widening commercial ties, though the names of their individual makers have rarely survived.
items.stem: Based on the text, in what way do the plaques reflect the Kingdom of Benin's ties with the wider world?

choices.A: They depict foreign visitors and were cast largely from metal obtained in trade.
choices.B: They depict warriors and court ceremonies that reveal the kingdom's internal order.
choices.C: They covered the pillars of a palace built for Portuguese merchants in Benin City.
choices.D: They were cast by foreign artisans whose individual names have rarely survived.

explanation.why: The text says the plaques record "its widening commercial ties." Two details support that: the plaques show "foreign visitors," and much of their metal came as manillas "traded by Portuguese merchants." Only a choice built on those details answers the question.
explanation.A: Correct. This combines the two details that link the plaques to the outside world: their subject matter and their traded metal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is accurate, but it describes what the plaques show about the kingdom's internal order, not its outside ties.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The plaques covered pillars of the oba's royal palace; nothing says the palace was built for Portuguese merchants.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The casters were members of a hereditary guild living in Benin City, not foreign artisans.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Miss Pellow had been warned that the parsonage at Thornby was a dull house, and she arrived prepared to find it so. The drawing room was indeed plainly furnished, the curtains faded, and the vicar's welcome brief; yet she observed that every book upon the shelves had been read to softness at the spine, that the children's slates bore not copybook maxims but sums of a difficulty she had herself struggled with at fifteen, and that the youngest girl, introduced as shy, asked within the hour whether the moon had weather. By evening Miss Pellow had revised a good many of her expectations, and had begun, somewhat to her own alarm, to doubt whether she was equal to the place.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A governess finds the parsonage at Thornby just as dull and plain as she had been warned.
choices.B: A governess is charmed by the curiosity of the vicar's shy youngest daughter.
choices.C: A governess resolves to make the shabby parsonage more comfortable for the children.
choices.D: A governess finds a plain household far more intellectually demanding than she expected.

explanation.why: The text moves from expectation to surprise. Miss Pellow expects a "dull house," and the furnishings are plain, "yet" the worn books, difficult sums, and the youngest girl's question reveal lively minds. By evening she doubts "whether she was equal to the place." The main idea is this shift: the plain house turns out to challenge her.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Only the furnishings match the warning; the word "yet" introduces evidence that the household is far from dull.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The girl's question is one piece of evidence; it leaves out the books, the sums, and Miss Pellow's self-doubt.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says she plans to improve the house's comfort.
explanation.D: Correct. This captures the whole movement from expecting dullness to doubting she can meet the household's demands.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The purple frog of India's Western Ghats was not formally described by scientists until 2003, although people in the region had long known it. Its late recognition reflects its habits more than its rarity: the frog spends most of the year underground, where it feeds mainly on termites with its narrow, pointed snout, and it surfaces for only a few weeks during the monsoon to breed in temporary streams. Genetic studies indicate that its closest living relatives are small frogs found only in the Seychelles, islands in the Indian Ocean. The two lineages are thought to have diverged long ago, when India and the Seychelles were still joined as parts of the ancient supercontinent Gondwana.
items.stem: Based on the text, what is the main reason the purple frog went unrecognized by scientists for so long?

choices.A: It lives underground for most of the year and comes to the surface only briefly.
choices.B: Its closest living relatives are found only on islands in the Indian Ocean.
choices.C: It feeds almost entirely on termites, a food that few other kinds of frogs will eat.
choices.D: It is so rare that few people in the Western Ghats had ever encountered it.

explanation.why: The second sentence answers the question: the frog's late recognition "reflects its habits more than its rarity," and the colon introduces those habits, chiefly that it stays underground most of the year and surfaces "for only a few weeks." A frog that is seldom above ground is easy for scientists to miss.
explanation.A: Correct. This restates the habits the text gives as the reason: life underground with only brief appearances.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true according to the text, but it concerns the frog's ancestry, not why scientists overlooked it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says it feeds mainly on termites but never compares its diet with other frogs or links diet to its late discovery.
