explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that exports grew, which Qureshi takes for granted; it does not show which kind of shipping produced the growth.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but sea freight could exceed air freight every year without being the source of the growth.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Sea shipments rose by 36,000 tonnes, while air shipments rose by only 1,000, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows strong growth in sea shipments alongside nearly flat air shipments, which is exactly the pattern Qureshi describes.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Piano teachers often debate how students should divide their practice time. Music educator Camille Okafor had beginning piano students practice a new piece for the same total number of minutes each week, either in short daily sessions or in a single long session, and then tested how accurately they played it. Okafor reports that the two schedules produced nearly identical results while practice continued, but she argues that the daily schedule had an advantage that emerged only later: students who had practiced that way retained far more of the piece after a month without playing it.

data.title: Accuracy Playing a New Piece (percent of notes correct)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Okafor's argument?

choices.A: After two weeks of practice, students in the weekly group played slightly more accurately than students in the daily group.
choices.B: After the month without practice, the weekly group was more accurate than the daily group.
choices.C: Both groups played more accurately after four weeks of practice than they had after two weeks.
choices.D: After four weeks of practice the groups differed by 1 point, but a month later the daily group scored 18 points higher.

explanation.why: Okafor's argument has two parts: the schedules gave nearly identical results during practice, and the daily group retained far more a month later. Support must compare the two columns at the end of practice and again after the break. At four weeks the scores are 86 and 85 (1 point apart); after the month without practice they are 80 and 62 (18 points apart).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it fits only the first part of the argument and says nothing about the later advantage of daily practice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. After the break the daily group scored 80 and the weekly group 62, so this reverses the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows that both groups improved, not that the two schedules differed in how well students retained the piece.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows a near tie at the end of practice and a large gap after the break, matching both parts of Okafor's argument.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The shells of the grove snail, a common European land snail, range from pale yellow to dark brown. Dark shells absorb more sunlight than pale ones, so in exposed places they can cause their owners to overheat. Evolutionary biologist Marta Lindqvist marked hundreds of snails of each color, released them in three habitats on the Danish coast, and later recorded how many survived. She argues that the advantage of pale shells depends on exposure to the sun: it is substantial in open dunes but shrinks as the habitat becomes more shaded, nearly vanishing in woodland.

data.title: Survival of Marked Grove Snails by Shell Color and Habitat

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Lindqvist's argument?

choices.A: Pale shells' survival advantage was 27 points in open dunes, 11 points at the dune edge, and 2 points in woodland.
choices.B: Dark-shelled snails survived at a higher rate in woodland than they did in open dunes.
choices.C: Pale-shelled snails survived at a higher rate than dark-shelled snails in open dunes, at the dune edge, and in woodland.
choices.D: In woodland, dark-shelled snails survived at a higher rate than pale-shelled snails did.

explanation.why: Lindqvist's argument is about the size of the pale shells' advantage: large in open dunes, smaller with more shade, and nearly gone in woodland. The advantage is the gap between the two bars in each habitat. The gaps are 68 − 41 = 27 points, 61 − 50 = 11 points, and 57 − 55 = 2 points.
explanation.A: Correct. It tracks the gap between pale and dark shells across the three habitats and shows it shrinking from 27 points to almost nothing.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (55% versus 41%), but it describes dark shells alone and does not compare them with pale shells in each habitat.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that pale shells always did better, not that their advantage shrinks as shade increases.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In woodland, pale shells survived at 57% and dark shells at 55%, so this reverses the graph.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Ancient merchant ships in the Mediterranean carried wine and olive oil in amphorae, clay jars whose shapes reveal what they held. Because sunken wrecks preserve these cargoes, archaeologists can use them to trace changes in trade. Studying wrecks found off the coast of southern France, archaeologist Giulia Ferri argues that between the first century BCE and the second century CE, olive oil did not merely join wine as a major cargo but displaced it: as oil cargoes became more common, wine cargoes became correspondingly rarer.

data.title: Wrecks off Southern France by Main Cargo

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Ferri's argument?

choices.A: Wrecks carrying mainly olive oil outnumbered those carrying mainly wine in the first century CE, the middle period shown.
choices.B: More of the wrecks carried mainly olive oil than mainly wine in the second century CE.
choices.C: From the first century BCE to the second century CE, wine wrecks fell from 48 to 14 as oil wrecks rose from 9 to 37.
choices.D: The total number of wrecks in each period stayed between about 50 and 60.

explanation.why: Ferri claims not just that oil became common but that it displaced wine: oil cargoes rose while wine cargoes fell. Support must show both columns changing in opposite directions over time. Wine wrecks fell from 48 to 14, while oil wrecks rose from 9 to 37.
explanation.A: Incorrect. In the first century CE, 31 wrecks carried mainly wine and 22 mainly oil, so this reverses the table.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (37 versus 14), but a single period cannot show a change over time, let alone that wine declined as oil rose.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows wine cargoes declining while oil cargoes increased over the same span, which is the displacement Ferri describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (57, 53, and 51), but the total number of wrecks says nothing about which cargo was replacing which.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The flowers of a night-blooming cactus in the Sonoran Desert open at dusk and remain open until the following midmorning, so they are available both to hawk moths, which fly at night, and to bees, which begin foraging after sunrise. Botanist Inés Carrillo hypothesizes that the plant depends almost entirely on the moths for pollination and that the bees' morning visits, though frequent, contribute little to its seed production. To test this, she covered flowers with mesh bags during different periods, preventing visits at those times, and then recorded seed set. The results support Carrillo's hypothesis: ______

data.title: Seed Set in Cactus Flowers under Four Bagging Treatments

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: flowers open only at night set seed nearly as often as fully open flowers, while morning-only flowers rarely did.
choices.B: flowers open to all visitors had the highest seed set of any treatment, with 78% producing seed.
choices.C: flowers open only at night produced more seeds per fruit than flowers open to all visitors did.
choices.D: flowers open only in the morning were four times as likely to produce seed as flowers bagged throughout.

explanation.why: Carrillo's hypothesis has two parts: moths (night visitors) account for almost all pollination, and bees (morning visitors) add little. Support therefore needs the night-only treatment to come close to the fully open flowers and the morning-only treatment to fall far short. Night-only flowers set seed 71% of the time, close to the 78% for fully open flowers, while morning-only flowers did so only 12% of the time.
explanation.A: Correct. It compares each partial treatment with the fully open flowers and shows that night visits alone nearly match full access, while morning visits alone accomplish little.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but fully open flowers receive both moths and bees, so their seed set cannot show which visitor matters.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Night-only flowers averaged 389 seeds per fruit, fewer than the 412 for fully open flowers, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (12% versus 3%), but it highlights a contribution from morning visitors rather than showing that the plant depends almost entirely on moths.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When the public library system of a midsize American city stopped charging fines for overdue items in January 2014, critics warned that, without a penalty, borrowers would grow careless about returning items on time. Supporters had argued that fines mostly drove away the borrowers least able to pay them. Librarian and researcher Marisol Castellanos, analyzing the system's records, concludes not only that the critics' fear went unrealized but that the policy accomplished what its supporters had intended: ending fines drew back borrowers who had stayed away, many of them because of unpaid fines, without making borrowers any more likely to return items late.

data.title: Records of a City Library System

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Castellanos's conclusion?

choices.A: After fines ended, active borrowers rose from about 41,000 to nearly 51,000, while late returns stayed near 9% of items.
choices.B: The number of active borrowers increased in every year from 2012 to 2016.
choices.C: The share of items returned late was higher in 2014, the first full year without fines, than it had been in 2013, before fines ended.
choices.D: Active borrowers increased more from 2013 to 2014 than in any other one-year period shown.

explanation.why: Castellanos's conclusion joins two claims: ending fines brought borrowers back, and it did not make late returns more common. Support must use both columns across the change in 2014. Active borrowers rose from 40,600 in 2013 to 50,800 in 2016, while the share of late items stayed between 8.8% and 9.3% throughout.
explanation.A: Correct. It shows the rise in borrowers after 2013 together with a late-return rate that stayed near 9%, supporting both halves of the conclusion.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Active borrowers fell from 41,200 in 2012 to 40,600 in 2013, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true (9.3% versus 8.8%), but it seems to favor the critics, and it ignores the borrower figures and the return to about 9% afterward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (a rise of 6,300), but it addresses only the return of borrowers and says nothing about whether late returns became more common.

items.subject: science
items.passage: White-tailed deer in a Pennsylvania state park share their range with hikers, whose numbers on the park's trails more than triple on weekends. One might expect the deer simply to abandon the areas near the trails when hikers are most numerous. Wildlife biologist Owen Sutherland, who analyzed photographs from motion-triggered cameras placed along the trails, proposes a different account. The deer, he argues, do not so much leave the area on weekends as rearrange their schedules, avoiding the trails during the hours when hikers are present and making up for that avoidance after dark.

data.title: Average Deer Detections per Camera along Park Trails

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Sutherland's account?

choices.A: Summed across all six times shown, deer were detected less often on weekends, when hikers were most numerous, than on weekdays.
choices.B: Weekend detections peaked at 2 a.m., the time when weekday detections were at their lowest.
choices.C: On weekends, deer were detected less often than on weekdays at 6 a.m., 10 a.m., and 2 p.m.
choices.D: Weekend detections fell below weekday detections from 6 a.m. through 6 p.m. but rose above them at 10 p.m. and 2 a.m.

explanation.why: Sutherland's account is not merely that deer avoid the trails on weekends (the simple expectation he rejects) but that they shift their activity: fewer weekend detections during the day and more after dark. Support must compare the two lines in both daytime and nighttime hours. Weekend detections are lower at every time from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., but at 10 p.m. (17 versus 10) and 2 a.m. (15 versus 7) they exceed weekday detections.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (46 versus 58), but a lower weekend total, taken alone, fits the abandonment view that Sutherland rejects rather than his own account.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Weekend detections peaked at 10 p.m. (17), and weekday detections were lowest at 2 p.m. (6), so this misreads the graph.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but daytime avoidance alone fits the simple expectation that deer abandon the area; it does not show them making up for it after dark.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows both halves of the shift: lower weekend activity during hiking hours and higher weekend activity at night.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In northwestern Bangladesh, wheat is often sown after the rice harvest, so when the rice comes in late, so does the wheat. Late-sown wheat fills its grain during the hot weeks of March, and heat at that stage lowers yields. Agronomist Nusrat Jahan grew a standard wheat variety and a newer heat-tolerant variety side by side at four sowing dates. Jahan argues that farmers who sow early gain nothing by switching to the tolerant variety, but that for farmers who sow late, its advantage over the standard variety becomes larger the later the crop is sown.

data.title: Wheat Yields by Sowing Date in Northwestern Bangladesh

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Jahan's argument?

choices.A: From the earliest sowing date to the latest, the tolerant variety's yield fell by less than half as much as the standard variety's did.
choices.B: The tolerant variety produced a higher yield than the standard variety at every sowing date tested.
choices.C: Both varieties produced lower yields when sown on December 25 than when sown on November 10.
choices.D: The tolerant variety yielded no more than the standard one when sown in November but 0.4 and 0.7 tonnes more when sown in December.

explanation.why: Jahan's argument has two parts: the tolerant variety offers no gain at early sowing dates, and its advantage widens with later sowing. Support must compare the two bars at each date. In November the tolerant variety yields 3.5 versus 3.6 and 3.4 versus 3.4 (no gain), while in December it leads by 3.2 − 2.8 = 0.4 and then 2.9 − 2.2 = 0.7 tonnes per hectare.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (a drop of 0.6 versus 1.4), but comparing only the first and last dates cannot show that the tolerant variety offers no gain when sown early, the first half of Jahan's claim.
explanation.B: Incorrect. On November 10 the tolerant variety yielded less (3.5 versus 3.6), and on November 25 the yields were equal, so this misreads the graph.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows that late sowing hurts both varieties, not how the tolerant variety compares with the standard one.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows no advantage at the November dates and a growing advantage at the December dates, supporting both parts of Jahan's argument.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Until the early 1950s, most jazz recordings were issued on 78-rpm discs, which held only about three minutes of music per side, so musicians often had to trim their performances to fit. Once the long-playing record, or LP, became common, recorded performances grew much longer. Musicologist Rafael Oyelaran, who timed the sections of hundreds of studio recordings, argues that the added length was not distributed evenly across a performance: musicians devoted nearly all of the new time to improvised solos, while the written themes that open and close a piece remained about as long as they had been.

data.title: Average Length of Sections in Studio Jazz Recordings (minutes)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Oyelaran's argument?

choices.A: The average track recorded in 1955–1959 was more than twice as long as the average track recorded in 1945–1949.
choices.B: Of the 4.4 minutes added to the average track between 1945–1949 and 1955–1959, solos accounted for 4.2.
choices.C: In every period shown, musicians spent more time on improvised solos than they did on theme statements.
choices.D: Solos took up a larger share of the average track in 1945–1949 than they did in 1955–1959.

explanation.why: Oyelaran accepts that tracks got longer; his claim is about where the added time went: almost all of it to solos, with themes nearly unchanged. Support must compare the growth of the solo and theme columns with the growth of the whole track. From 1945–1949 to 1955–1959, tracks grew by 7.4 − 3.0 = 4.4 minutes, solos by 6.1 − 1.9 = 4.2 minutes, and themes by only 0.2 minutes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it shows only that tracks got longer, which the text already accepts, not which sections absorbed the added time.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows that nearly all of the added time went to solos, leaving theme statements almost unchanged.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but solos could outweigh themes in every period even if both had grown by similar amounts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Solos made up about 63% of a track (1.9 of 3.0 minutes) in 1945–1949 but about 82% (6.1 of 7.4) in 1955–1959, so this reverses the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Desert sunlight makes arid regions attractive for solar power, but dust that settles on panels blocks light and lowers their output, and washing panels is costly where water is scarce. At a test site in southern Jordan, engineer Dalia Haddad compared panels that were cleaned every week with panels that were never cleaned at all. Apart from one storm, the study period was entirely dry. At the end of April, the site received the only heavy rain of the six-month study. Haddad's data suggest that this single storm did much of the work of a cleaning crew: ______

data.title: Average Monthly Output of Test Panels in Southern Jordan

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: the output of the panels cleaned every week stayed between 94% and 96% of rated output in every month, both before and after the storm.
choices.B: the never-cleaned panels' output was higher in June than it had been in May.
choices.C: the never-cleaned panels' output, which trailed that of the cleaned panels by 20 points in April, came within 2 points of it in May.
choices.D: the never-cleaned panels' output fell by 7 percentage points in each month from January to April.

explanation.why: The statement claims that the late-April storm acted like a cleaning, so the data must show the uncleaned panels catching up with the cleaned panels right after the rain. That requires comparing the two lines before and after the storm. In April the gap was 94 − 74 = 20 points; in May it was 95 − 93 = 2 points.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the cleaned panels and shows nothing about what the storm did to the uncleaned ones.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Output of the never-cleaned panels fell from 93% in May to 86% in June, so this reverses the graph.
explanation.C: Correct. It compares the two kinds of panels just before and just after the storm and shows the uncleaned panels nearly matching the cleaned ones once the rain had fallen.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true (95, 88, 81, 74), but it shows the damage done by dust before the storm, not the recovery that the rain produced.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians have long debated how much the arrival of the railway shaped the growth of towns in nineteenth-century Germany, where thousands of kilometers of track were laid between 1840 and 1880. Skeptics point out that in one western region, towns without a railway station added more residents between 1850 and 1880 than towns with one did. Historian Wiebke Lorenz considers this comparison misleading, because the towns without stations were far larger to begin with. Measured relative to their starting size, she argues, the towns that had gained a station by 1855 grew about twice as fast as those that had not.

data.title: Average Population of Towns in One Western German Region

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Lorenz's argument?

choices.A: In every year shown, towns without a station were larger on average than towns with a station.
choices.B: From 1850 to 1880, towns with a station added more residents than towns without a station did.
choices.C: From 1850 to 1880, towns with a station grew by about 64%, while towns without one grew by about 33%.
choices.D: From 1850 to 1880, towns without a station added about 3,200 residents, while towns with a station added about 2,700.

explanation.why: Lorenz rejects comparing the number of residents added and instead compares growth relative to starting size, so support must express each group's growth as a percentage. Towns with a station grew from 4,200 to 6,900, an increase of 2,700, or about 64%; towns without one grew from 9,600 to 12,800, an increase of 3,200, or about 33%. The first rate is roughly twice the second.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it supports only Lorenz's point about starting size, not her claim about how fast each group grew.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Towns with a station added 2,700 residents, fewer than the 3,200 added by towns without one, so this reverses the table.
explanation.C: Correct. It compares growth relative to each group's starting size and shows towns with a station growing at about twice the rate of the others.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but it is the skeptics' comparison of residents added, which Lorenz calls misleading; it says nothing about growth relative to size.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A mushaira is a gathering at which Urdu poets recite their work before a live audience, which traditionally responds aloud to favorite lines. When a literary society in Karachi began streaming its annual mushaira online in 2015, some members worried that the stream would empty the hall. Cultural historian Sadia Mirza, who examined the society's attendance and viewing figures, argues that those worries proved unfounded and that the stream's growing audience came mainly from viewers outside Pakistan rather than from people in Pakistan who might otherwise have attended in person.

data.title: Audience for a Karachi Literary Society's Annual Mushaira

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Mirza's argument?

choices.A: In-person attendance rose in each year shown, from 3,100 in 2015 to 3,300 in 2019.
choices.B: In 2019, the mushaira's online viewers outnumbered its in-person attendees by more than seven to one.
choices.C: From 2015 to 2019, viewers abroad increased by about 16,000 and those in Pakistan by fewer than 2,000, while in-person attendance did not decline.
choices.D: Online viewers in Pakistan outnumbered online viewers abroad in every year shown.

explanation.why: Mirza's argument has two parts: the stream did not empty the hall, and the stream's growth came mainly from abroad rather than from within Pakistan. Support needs all three series. Viewers abroad rose from 2,200 to 18,500 (about 16,000), viewers in Pakistan rose from 4,000 to 5,900 (1,900), and in-person attendance went from 3,100 to 3,300.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it addresses only the first part of Mirza's argument, not where the stream's growing audience came from.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (24,400 versus 3,300), but the size of the online audience says nothing about where its growth came from or whether the hall emptied.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows that growth abroad far outpaced growth in Pakistan and that the hall did not empty, covering both parts of Mirza's argument.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Viewers abroad outnumbered viewers in Pakistan in 2017 (9,800 versus 5,100) and 2019 (18,500 versus 5,900), so this misreads the graph.

items.subject: science
items.passage: After Pacific salmon spawn and die, their decaying bodies release nitrogen carried from the ocean into the streams, and some of that nitrogen reaches the trees along the banks. Ecologist Hana Kowalczyk hypothesizes that this marine nitrogen speeds tree growth. Because waterfalls prevent salmon from swimming farther upstream, she compared trees below and above the falls on two Alaskan streams. She measured the share of leaf nitrogen that came from the ocean and, since soil moisture also affects growth, the moisture of the soil as well. Kowalczyk's data support her hypothesis while making soil moisture an unlikely alternative explanation: ______

data.title: Streamside Trees below and above Waterfalls on Two Alaskan Streams

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: trees below the falls on Stream 1 grew faster than trees in any other section of either stream, and their leaves held the most ocean nitrogen.
choices.B: on both streams, soil moisture was higher above the falls, where salmon cannot reach, than below the falls.
choices.C: trees along Stream 1 grew faster, on average, than trees along Stream 2 did.
choices.D: on both streams, trees below the falls grew faster and held more ocean nitrogen, yet soil there was moister on only one stream.

explanation.why: The statement makes two claims: the data support a link between marine nitrogen and growth, and they rule out soil moisture as the explanation. The completion must therefore show growth tracking nitrogen on both streams while moisture does not. Below the falls, growth (2.4 and 2.1 mm) and ocean nitrogen (22% and 18%) exceed the figures above the falls (1.5 and 1.4 mm; 3% and 2%), but soil was moister below the falls only on Stream 1 (31% versus 30%), not on Stream 2 (27% versus 33%).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but a single section cannot show a pattern across both streams, and it says nothing about soil moisture.
explanation.B: Incorrect. On Stream 1, soil moisture was 31% below the falls and 30% above them, so this misreads the table.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true (averages of 1.95 and 1.75 mm), but comparing the two streams ignores the below-versus-above comparison that the hypothesis depends on.
explanation.D: Correct. It shows growth and ocean nitrogen rising together below the falls on both streams while soil moisture follows no consistent pattern, which supports the hypothesis and undercuts the alternative.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Women now make up more than half of the medical students at a large public university in Chile but only about a quarter of its engineering students, and observers often cite the contrast as evidence that engineering has resisted change. Sociologist Paula Briones, examining the university's enrollment records since 1980, argues that this familiar contrast between the two fields conceals a reversal in their recent trajectories. Medicine, where women's share climbed rapidly from 1980 to 2000, has changed relatively little since then, she contends, whereas engineering, where change was slow over those two decades, has since gained more ground than medicine has.

data.title: Women's Share of Students in Two Fields at a Public University in Chile

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Briones's argument?

choices.A: Women's share of engineering students nearly tripled between 1980 and 2020.
choices.B: In every year shown, women made up a larger share of medical students than of engineering students.
choices.C: Women's share of medical students grew more from 2000 to 2020 than it had from 1980 to 2000.
choices.D: Medicine gained 23 points from 1980 to 2000 and then 4 points by 2020; engineering gained 7 points and then 9.

explanation.why: Briones's claim is about a reversal: medicine gained faster than engineering from 1980 to 2000, but engineering has gained more since 2000. Support must compare the gains of both fields in both periods. Medicine rose 23 points (28 to 51) and then 4 (51 to 55); engineering rose 7 points (9 to 16) and then 9 (16 to 25).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (9% to 25%), but it describes engineering over the whole period and cannot show that its pace overtook medicine's after 2000.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it is the familiar contrast that Briones says conceals the real pattern; it says nothing about how fast each field changed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Medicine gained 23 points from 1980 to 2000 but only 4 from 2000 to 2020, so this reverses the graph.
explanation.D: Correct. It gives both fields' gains in both periods and shows medicine ahead before 2000 and engineering ahead after, which is the reversal Briones describes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Tadpoles of many frog species grow deeper tails when predators are near, a change that helps them escape. Because dragonfly larvae prey on tadpoles, one might suppose that the mere presence of the larvae is enough to trigger the change. Ecologist Kwame Asante doubts this. He argues that tadpoles respond chiefly to chemical cues released when a predator eats other tadpoles, not to the presence of a predator as such, and still less to general disturbance. To test this, he raised tadpoles under four conditions and measured them after three weeks.

data.title: Tadpole Measurements after Three Weeks under Four Conditions

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Asante's argument?

choices.A: Stirring the water every day increased tail depth by only 0.1 mm compared with the control.
choices.B: Tadpoles kept near caged dragonfly larvae had deeper tails than control tadpoles, whether the larvae were fed snails or fed tadpoles.
choices.C: Tadpoles near larvae fed tadpoles had the shortest bodies but not the deepest tails of any group.
choices.D: Tails were 1.2 mm deeper with tadpole-fed larvae than with snail-fed larvae, more than twice the gap between snail-fed and control.

explanation.why: Asante's key claim is that the response comes chiefly from cues released when predators eat tadpoles, not from the predator's presence. The test of that is to compare the two predator conditions, which differ only in what the larvae ate, and to set that difference against the effect of presence alone. Larvae fed tadpoles produced tails 5.8 − 4.6 = 1.2 mm deeper than larvae fed snails, while snail-fed larvae raised tail depth only 4.6 − 4.1 = 0.5 mm above the control.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it rules out only general disturbance; it says nothing about whether presence or diet cues drive the response.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it treats both predator conditions alike, and the snail-fed result shows that presence alone has some effect, which does not help show that diet cues matter most.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Tadpoles near larvae fed tadpoles had the deepest tails (5.8 mm) of any group, so this misreads the table.
explanation.D: Correct. It isolates the effect of what the predator ate and shows that this effect is much larger than the effect of the predator's mere presence.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Painters in the seventeenth-century Dutch Republic turned out landscapes in enormous numbers, often working quickly in standardized formats, and in estate inventories from Amsterdam a landscape was, by the 1680s, valued at only a small fraction of what a history painting, depicting a scene from the Bible, mythology, or the past, would fetch. Art historian Femke Dijkstra, who compiled the values recorded in hundreds of such inventories, argues that this widening gap reflected changes in the market for landscapes alone: landscapes grew steadily cheaper, she contends, while the prices of history paintings scarcely moved.

data.title: Average Values of Paintings in Amsterdam Estate Inventories

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Dijkstra's argument?

choices.A: The average value of landscapes fell in every decade from the 1630s to the 1680s.
choices.B: The gap between the two kinds of painting widened mainly because history paintings became more expensive over the period.
choices.C: Landscapes fell from 24 to 11 guilders on average, while history paintings stayed between 58 and 63 guilders.
choices.D: History paintings were valued at least twice as highly as landscapes on average in every decade shown.

explanation.why: Dijkstra's argument explains the widening gap by pointing to one series only: landscapes fell while history paintings held steady. Support must describe both lines, showing a decline in one and stability in the other. Landscapes dropped from 24 to 11 guilders, while history paintings stayed between 58 and 63 guilders throughout.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it covers only half of the argument; the gap could also have widened partly because history paintings rose.
explanation.B: Incorrect. History paintings were worth 60 guilders in both the 1630s and the 1680s, so the gap widened because landscapes fell, the opposite of this choice.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows the decline in landscape values alongside nearly flat values for history paintings, which is exactly the pattern Dijkstra describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is true, but a constant ratio of at least two to one says nothing about which kind of painting changed in value.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the hills of central Nepal, the red flowers of the tree rhododendron, Nepal's national flower, have long marked the arrival of spring. Botanist Prakash Gurung compiled records of first flowering at two sites in the Annapurna region, one at 2,000 meters above sea level, among terraced farmland, and one at 3,200 meters, in high forest. Gurung argues that although rhododendrons now bloom earlier at both elevations than they did in 1990, the shift has been far greater at the higher site, a pattern he attributes to faster warming at high elevations.

data.title: Average First Flowering Date of Tree Rhododendrons in the Annapurna Region

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support Gurung's argument?

choices.A: At the lower site, rhododendrons first flowered earlier in 2020 than in any other year shown.
choices.B: In every year shown, rhododendrons at the higher site first flowered later in the year than those at the lower site.
choices.C: From 1990 to 2020, first flowering came 22 days earlier at the higher site but only 7 days earlier at the lower one.
choices.D: The gap between the first flowering dates at the two sites widened from 1990 to 2020.

explanation.why: Gurung's argument compares the size of the shift at the two sites: both now bloom earlier, but the higher site has shifted far more. Support must compare how much each line changed. A lower day number means earlier flowering: the higher site moved from day 128 to day 106 (22 days earlier), while the lower site moved from day 75 to day 68 (7 days earlier).
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes only the lower site and gives no comparison with the higher site.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it is expected at a colder site and says nothing about how much flowering has shifted at each elevation.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows that flowering moved earlier at both sites and that the shift at the higher site was about three times as large.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The gap shrank from 53 days (128 − 75) to 38 days (106 − 68), so this reverses the graph.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1840s and 1850s, travelers between Liverpool and New York could cross the Atlantic either on a sailing packet, a sailing ship that departed on a fixed schedule, or on a steamship. Because the prevailing winds over the North Atlantic blow from west to east, sailing ships took much longer on the westbound voyage to New York than on the eastbound return. Historian Aurelio Pinto argues that steam's advantage was therefore uneven: steamships saved travelers far more time on the westbound crossing, where sailing ships fought the wind, than on the eastbound one.

data.title: Average Crossing Times between Liverpool and New York (days)

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Pinto's argument?

choices.A: In both decades, steamships saved 21 or 22 days westbound but only 9 or 10 days eastbound.
choices.B: Sailing packets took 13 to 14 days longer to cross westbound than eastbound in both decades.
choices.C: Both kinds of ships made faster crossings in both directions in the 1850s than they had in the 1840s.
choices.D: In the 1850s, steamships' time advantage over sailing packets was greater eastbound than westbound.

explanation.why: Pinto's claim concerns the time steamships saved, which is the difference between packet and steamship times in each direction. Support must compute that saving for both directions and compare them. Westbound, steamships saved 37 − 16 = 21 days in the 1840s and 35 − 13 = 22 in the 1850s; eastbound, they saved only 23 − 14 = 9 and 22 − 12 = 10 days.
explanation.A: Correct. It compares the time steamships saved in each direction and shows the saving was more than twice as large westbound.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it repeats the premise about sailing ships and the wind; it does not compare sailing ships with steamships, which Pinto's claim requires.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is true, but improvement over time says nothing about whether steam's advantage differed by direction.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In the 1850s steamships saved 10 days eastbound but 22 days westbound, so this reverses the table.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the fynbos, the shrubland of South Africa's Western Cape, many plants keep seeds dormant in the soil for years and germinate only after a fire. Fires return to most patches of fynbos at intervals of a decade or more. A fire offers buried seeds two distinct signals: the heat that passes into the soil and the chemicals carried in smoke. Botanist Thandiwe Ndlovu exposed seeds of two fynbos plants, a reedlike restio and a legume, to heat alone, smoke alone, both, or neither. She concluded that the two species respond to different fire cues: ______

data.title: Germination of Two Fynbos Species after Four Treatments

items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: both species germinated at their highest rates when their seeds were exposed to heat and smoke together rather than to either cue alone.
choices.B: smoke alone raised the restio's germination from 6% of seeds to 48% of seeds.
choices.C: smoke alone raised the restio's germination from 6% to 48% but barely affected the legume's, whereas heat alone did the reverse.
choices.D: heat alone raised the restio's germination by more percentage points than smoke alone did.

explanation.why: Ndlovu's conclusion is a contrast: each species responds to a different cue. The completion must show each cue working for one species but not the other, which means comparing the single-cue bars with the untreated bars for both species. Smoke alone lifted the restio from 6% to 48% but the legume only from 4% to 5%, while heat alone lifted the legume from 4% to 55% but the restio only from 6% to 7%.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (51% and 57%), but it shows the two species behaving alike, which does nothing to show that they respond to different cues.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it describes one species and one cue; without the legume's results it cannot show that the species respond differently.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows smoke working for the restio but not the legume and heat working for the legume but not the restio, which is exactly the contrast Ndlovu draws.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Heat alone raised the restio only from 6% to 7%, while smoke alone raised it to 48%, so this reverses the graph.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Plants of the same species can look quite different depending on where they grow. On windy hilltops, for example, they tend to be shorter and have thicker stems than plants in sheltered valleys. Botanist Lena Fischer thinks the wind itself causes this difference. She hypothesizes that when a plant's stem is bent again and again, the plant responds by growing shorter and sturdier.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Fischer's hypothesis?

choices.A: Plants on windy hilltops produce fewer flowers than plants of the same species growing in valleys.
choices.B: Plants growing on windy hilltops are often damaged by strong storms during the winter.
choices.C: Indoor plants bent gently each day grew shorter and thicker than identical plants left alone.
choices.D: Valley soils hold more water than hilltop soils, which allows valley plants to grow taller.

explanation.why: Fischer's hypothesis is that repeated bending of the stem causes plants to grow shorter and sturdier. The strongest support would be a test in which bending is the only difference between two groups of plants. If the bent plants turn out shorter and thicker, bending is shown to cause the change.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Flower numbers have nothing to do with stem bending, height, or thickness.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Storm damage is a different effect of weather and says nothing about how bending changes growth.
explanation.C: Correct. Bending was the only difference between the two groups, and the bent plants grew shorter and thicker, just as Fischer predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This offers a different cause (water in the soil) for the height difference, so it would weaken the hypothesis rather than support it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the mid-1800s, trips to the seaside became common among British factory workers for the first time. Historian Kwame Asante argues that the main cause was cheap railway fares rather than rising wages. In his view, many workers could already afford a day away from work, but they had no affordable way to reach the coast until trains made the journey short and inexpensive.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Asante's argument?

choices.A: Where cheap trains to the coast already ran, workers' seaside trips became common only after wages rose.
choices.B: Seaside trips by workers increased sharply in towns soon after cheap train service to the coast began.
choices.C: Wealthy families had visited seaside resorts for many decades before railway lines reached the coast.
choices.D: Many seaside towns built new hotels and piers to attract the large numbers of visitors who arrived by train.

explanation.why: Asante claims that cheap trains, not higher wages, made seaside trips common. A finding weakens this if it shows that trains were not enough on their own and that wages made the difference. If trips stayed rare where cheap trains already ran and grew only once wages rose, wages look like the main cause.
explanation.A: Correct. Cheap trains were available but trips did not become common until wages rose, which points to wages, not fares, as the main cause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Trips rising right after cheap trains arrived would support Asante's argument, not weaken it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The argument is about factory workers; the habits of wealthy families do not bear on it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How resorts responded to visitors says nothing about whether fares or wages caused workers to travel.

items.subject: science
items.passage: House sparrows were once a familiar sight in South Asian cities, but residents of some neighborhoods in Karachi say they now see far fewer of them than in the past. Ornithologist Farah Siddiqui suspects that the main cause is a shortage of places to nest. Older houses had gaps under roofs and holes in walls where sparrows built their nests, whereas the smooth concrete and glass of newer buildings offer few such spaces.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Siddiqui's hypothesis?

choices.A: Sparrows in Karachi feed mainly on seeds and insects found in gardens and markets.
choices.B: Sparrow numbers fell by similar amounts in neighborhoods of older houses and in neighborhoods of new buildings.
choices.C: Several other bird species have also become less common in Karachi in recent decades.
choices.D: Sparrow numbers rose in an area after nest boxes were added to its new buildings but not in nearby areas.

explanation.why: Siddiqui's hypothesis is that sparrows declined because newer buildings offer few places to nest. If adding nesting places brings sparrows back in one area but not in similar areas without them, then a lack of nest sites was holding their numbers down. That is direct support.
explanation.A: Incorrect. What sparrows eat is unrelated to the hypothesis, which is about nesting sites.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If old houses with many nesting gaps lost sparrows just as fast, nest sites would not explain the decline; this weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Declines in other species could have many causes and do not show that sparrows lack nesting places.
explanation.D: Correct. Providing nest sites raised sparrow numbers only where they were added, which points to a shortage of nest sites as the cause.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When two languages come into close contact, speakers often borrow words from each other. Linguist Ngozi Eze has studied a coastal town where speakers of two languages have traded with each other for generations. She hypothesizes that the words most likely to be borrowed are those for things that were new to one community when the contact began, such as unfamiliar tools or foods, rather than words for familiar everyday ideas.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Eze's hypothesis?

choices.A: Speakers in the town use borrowed words more often when talking with traders than with family.
choices.B: Most borrowed words in the town name tools and foods that one group first encountered through trade.
choices.C: Words for body parts and family members are among the most often borrowed words in the town.
choices.D: Both languages spoken in the town have also borrowed many words from a third language used in schools.

explanation.why: Eze predicts that borrowed words will mostly name things that were new to one group when contact began, not familiar everyday ideas. A finding that most borrowings name tools and foods one group first met through trade matches this prediction exactly.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This concerns when people use borrowed words, not which kinds of words get borrowed.
explanation.B: Correct. Tools and foods first encountered through trade are exactly the "new" things Eze predicts will be borrowed most.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Body parts and family members are familiar everyday ideas, so heavy borrowing of these words would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Borrowing from a third language does not show which kinds of words the two trading communities borrow from each other.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Many nineteenth-century novels first reached readers in monthly installments, each containing several chapters. Literary scholar Henrik Lund argues that authors writing for this format deliberately shaped their stories around the installment breaks, saving moments of suspense for the end of each part so that readers would buy the next one. As evidence, Lund notes that in the serialized novels he examined, chapters that closed an installment ended on an unresolved situation far more often than chapters that fell in the middle of an installment did.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Lund's argument?

choices.A: Editors, not authors, chose where most installments would end, after each book was fully written.
choices.B: Readers of the period often discussed the latest installments of novels with friends and in letters to magazines.
choices.C: Authors' letters show that they planned in advance which chapter would close each installment of their novels.
choices.D: A few chapters in the middle of installments also ended on unresolved situations in some of the novels.

explanation.why: Lund's claim is about the authors' intentions: they deliberately placed suspense at the breaks. His evidence is a pattern (suspenseful endings cluster at breaks). If editors set the breaks after the books were written, authors could not have aimed suspense at them; the pattern would instead come from editors choosing suspenseful spots to cut. That offers another explanation for his evidence and undercuts his claim.
explanation.A: Correct. If the breaks were chosen by editors after the writing was done, the authors could not have shaped their stories around them, so the pattern Lund found has a different explanation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Readers' discussions show interest in the installments but say nothing about whether authors planned suspense around the breaks.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Authors planning the breaks in advance makes Lund's argument more likely, so this would support it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Lund says suspense came "far more often" at installment ends, not only there, so a few suspenseful mid-installment chapters fit his evidence.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Octopuses alternate between two states of sleep. In "quiet" sleep they are pale and still, but during brief bouts of "active" sleep their skin flickers through patterns of color and texture, and their eyes and arms twitch. Neuroscientist Aiko Tanabe hypothesizes that active sleep in octopuses serves a function similar to one proposed for dreaming in mammals: the strengthening of memories of recent experience. If so, she reasons, the skin patterns produced during active sleep should not be random but should reflect what the animal did while awake.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tanabe's hypothesis?

choices.A: Octopuses kept from active sleep for one night spent more time in active sleep the following night.
choices.B: The skin patterns that appeared during active sleep showed no relationship to the octopuses' waking activities.
choices.C: Patterns an octopus displayed in active sleep closely matched those it had used while hunting or hiding that day.
choices.D: Researchers have also observed a similar active sleep state in cuttlefish, which are close relatives of octopuses.

explanation.why: Tanabe's hypothesis makes a specific prediction: if active sleep strengthens memories of recent experience, the sleep patterns should reflect what the octopus did while awake. A finding that sleep patterns matched the octopus's patterns from earlier that day confirms this prediction directly.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Making up for lost active sleep suggests that active sleep matters to octopuses, but it does not show that it involves recent experience.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If the patterns had no link to waking activity, Tanabe's prediction would fail; this weakens her hypothesis.
explanation.C: Correct. Sleep patterns that match the day's hunting and hiding patterns are exactly the link to waking experience that Tanabe predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Finding active sleep in another species says nothing about what the octopus's sleep patterns reflect.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The sixteenth-century ruler Sher Shah Suri is remembered for the sarais, or roadside rest houses, that he built along the great road running across northern South Asia. Because the sarais offered free food and lodging to travelers, they are usually described as an investment in commerce. Historian Saad Hashmi contends, however, that commerce was at most a secondary concern: in his view, the sarais were placed chiefly to serve the relays of horses that carried official news and orders, and whatever benefit merchants gained followed from, rather than motivated, the choice of where to build them.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Hashmi's claim?

choices.A: Merchants traveling the road in that period often stayed at the sarais and praised the hospitality they found there.
choices.B: Sarais stood far closer together along busy market routes than along stretches that only the relays used.
choices.C: Horses for the relays that carried official news were kept at nearly every sarai along the road.
choices.D: Rulers who came after Sher Shah Suri built additional sarais specifically to encourage trade along the road.

explanation.why: Hashmi's claim is about motive, shown through placement: the sarais were located to serve the news relays, and merchants benefited only as a side effect. To weaken it, a finding must show that placement followed trade rather than the relays. If sarais were packed densely where markets were busy but sparse where only the relays ran, commerce, not the relays, appears to have guided where they were built.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Hashmi already grants that merchants benefited; he argues only that this benefit did not decide where sarais were built.
explanation.B: Correct. Placement that tracks trade routes rather than relay routes shows commerce shaping where sarais went, which contradicts Hashmi's claim.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Relay horses at nearly every sarai fits Hashmi's view that the sarais served the relays, so this would support him.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Later rulers' reasons for building sarais do not reveal why Sher Shah Suri placed his where he did.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In several Paleolithic caves in France and Spain, researchers have reported that painted images tend to cluster at spots where sound resonates or echoes strongly. Archaeologist Céline Marchand argues that the artists sought out these spots deliberately, perhaps because echoes held ritual significance for them. Skeptics point out, however, that resonance is strongest in narrow passages and small chambers, and that such spaces also offer the smooth, sheltered rock surfaces best suited to painting; on this view, the clustering could arise even if the artists paid no attention to sound at all.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Marchand's argument?

choices.A: In the caves studied, images appear far more often in narrow passages and small chambers than in large open halls.
choices.B: Many painted surfaces in the caves are smoother and better protected from moisture than nearby unpainted ones.
choices.C: Echoes are described as important in the ceremonies of several present-day societies that live near caves.
choices.D: Artists chose resonant spots far more often than nonresonant ones whose rock surfaces were equally suitable.

explanation.why: Marchand says artists chose resonant spots because of the sound. The skeptics offer another explanation: resonant spots also have the best painting surfaces, so the pattern might have nothing to do with sound. Support for Marchand must rule out that explanation by comparing spots whose surfaces are equally good. If artists still preferred the resonant ones, sound itself seems to have guided their choice.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Narrow passages and small chambers have both strong resonance and good surfaces, so this pattern fits the skeptics' explanation just as well as Marchand's.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Painted surfaces being smoother and more sheltered points to surface quality as the reason for the choice, which supports the skeptics instead.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The customs of present-day societies do not show what Paleolithic artists were thinking when they chose where to paint.
explanation.D: Correct. Because surface quality is held equal, the skeptics' explanation cannot account for the preference, so attention to sound, which is Marchand's claim, becomes the best explanation.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In spring, male woodpeckers drum rapidly on trees to claim a territory and attract a mate, and the sound can carry a long way through a forest. Ornithologist Ingrid Halvorsen has noticed that some woodpeckers drum on hollow branches or even on metal gutters instead of solid trunks. She hypothesizes that woodpeckers choose the drumming spots that produce the loudest sound.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Halvorsen's hypothesis?

choices.A: Female woodpeckers of some species also drum, though they usually do so less often than males do.
choices.B: Woodpeckers drummed on loud and quiet surfaces about equally often during the spring.
choices.C: Given a choice, woodpeckers drummed mostly on posts that rang loudly rather than on dull ones.
choices.D: Woodpeckers use their strong beaks both for drumming and for digging insects out of tree bark.

explanation.why: Halvorsen's hypothesis is that woodpeckers pick the spots that make the loudest sound. The best support would show woodpeckers, offered both loud and quiet surfaces, preferring the loud ones.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Which birds drum and how often does not show whether they prefer loud surfaces.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If woodpeckers used loud and quiet surfaces equally, they would not be choosing loud spots, so this would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Correct. Woodpeckers chose loud-sounding posts far more often than dull ones, which is exactly the preference Halvorsen predicts.
explanation.D: Incorrect. What else woodpeckers do with their beaks says nothing about how they choose drumming spots.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1300s, many towns in Europe began placing mechanical clocks on church towers and town halls. Historian Pieter Claes argues that merchants were the main reason for this change. In his view, merchants wanted a shared way to mark when markets opened and closed, so busy trading towns were the first to pay for public clocks.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Claes's argument?

choices.A: Some of the earliest public clocks struck a bell every hour instead of showing the time on a dial.
choices.B: Records from several trading towns show that merchants paid much of the cost of the first public clocks.
choices.C: Small farming towns with few merchants got public clocks as early as large trading towns did.
choices.D: Public clocks often had to be repaired, because their iron parts wore out quickly.

explanation.why: Claes says merchants drove the spread of public clocks, so trading towns got them first. A finding weakens this if towns without many merchants got clocks just as early, because then merchants could not have been the main reason.
explanation.A: Incorrect. How early clocks signaled the time does not show who wanted them or why.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Merchants paying for the first clocks would support Claes's argument, not weaken it.
explanation.C: Correct. If farming towns with few merchants got clocks as early as trading towns, merchants do not appear to be the main cause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Repairs to clocks say nothing about why towns first installed them.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Madhubani painting is a folk art from the Mithila region of Bihar, India, known for its bright colors and bold outlines. Art conservator Neha Jha has noticed that the colors in some older Madhubani paintings have faded badly, while the colors in others of the same age still look fresh. She hypothesizes that exposure to sunlight is the main cause of the fading.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Jha's hypothesis?

choices.A: Old paintings kept in dark storerooms stayed bright, while those near sunny windows faded.
choices.B: Madhubani paintings were first made on the walls of homes and later on paper and cloth.
choices.C: Some paintings kept in dim rooms faded just as much as paintings that hung in bright sunlight.
choices.D: Many Madhubani artists learned to paint from older relatives in their own villages.

explanation.why: Jha thinks sunlight is the main cause of fading. If paintings of the same age faded when they were near sunlight but stayed bright when kept in the dark, sunlight is the difference that matters.
explanation.A: Correct. The only paintings that faded were the ones exposed to sunlight, which is what Jha predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. What the paintings were made on does not show whether sunlight causes fading.
explanation.C: Incorrect. If paintings faded just as much without sunlight, sunlight would not be the main cause; this weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How artists learned to paint has nothing to do with why the colors fade.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Woodlice, also called pill bugs, are small land-dwelling relatives of crabs and shrimp. They are usually found in damp places, such as under logs and stones. Biologist Kenji Morita hypothesizes that woodlice seek out these places because their bodies lose water quickly, so they dry out if they stay in open air for long.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Morita's hypothesis?

choices.A: Woodlice placed in a dry, dark box lived just as long as woodlice placed in a damp, dark box.
choices.B: Woodlice feed mainly on dead leaves and rotting wood found on the forest floor.
choices.C: Woodlice are most active at night, when birds and other predators have trouble finding them.
choices.D: Given a tray with damp and dry halves, equally dark, most woodlice gathered on the damp side.

explanation.why: Morita's hypothesis has two parts: woodlice dry out easily, and so they seek damp places. A test in which dampness is the only difference between two areas, and woodlice choose the damp one, supports it directly.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If woodlice survived just as well in dry air, they would not need damp places to avoid drying out, so this weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.B: Incorrect. What woodlice eat says nothing about whether they seek damp places to avoid drying out.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This gives a reason for their timing (avoiding predators), not evidence that they seek moisture.
explanation.D: Correct. Darkness was the same on both sides, so the woodlice chose the damp side because of the moisture.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 2023, a coastal city began running buses late into the night on its main routes. Over the following year, the city's restaurants served more customers in the evening. Economist Valeria Quispe argues that the night buses caused this increase by making it easier for people to get home after a late dinner.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Quispe's argument?

choices.A: The city's night buses ran every thirty minutes from 10:00 p.m. until 2:00 a.m.
choices.B: Restaurants far from any night bus route gained evening customers just as fast as others.
choices.C: Bus fares in the city stayed the same before and after the night service began.
choices.D: Many diners surveyed at the city's restaurants said they had taken a night bus home after their meal.

explanation.why: Quispe says the night buses brought in more evening diners. If restaurants that the buses do not serve gained customers just as fast, the buses cannot explain the increase.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The bus schedule describes the service but does not show whether it brought in diners.
explanation.B: Correct. Restaurants with no night bus nearby grew just as quickly, so something other than the buses must be behind the increase.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Fares staying the same says nothing about whether the buses changed restaurant business.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Diners riding the night bus home would support Quispe's argument, not weaken it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Apple trees need insects to carry pollen from flower to flower before they can produce fruit. On a farm in New Zealand, entomologist Aroha Ngata noticed that the trees closest to the farm's beehives seemed to carry the most apples. She hypothesizes that placing more beehives in an orchard increases the number of apples its trees produce.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ngata's hypothesis?

choices.A: Honeybees visit many kinds of flowers besides apple blossoms, including clover and wild roses.
choices.B: The apple trees near the farm's beehives also received more water than trees elsewhere on the farm.
choices.C: The farm grows several varieties of apples, some of which ripen earlier than others.
choices.D: Orchards given extra hives produced more apples than similar orchards without extra hives.

explanation.why: Ngata claims that more beehives lead to more apples. The strongest support compares similar orchards that differ only in the number of hives and shows more fruit where hives were added.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Bees visiting other flowers does not show that adding hives increases the apple crop.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Extra water offers a different explanation for the large crop near the hives, so this would weaken the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. When different varieties ripen has nothing to do with whether beehives increase the number of apples.
explanation.D: Correct. Similar orchards differed in the number of hives, and the ones with extra hives produced more apples.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Music teacher Joseph Mensah teaches some of his students new songs by playing each song aloud and having them copy what they hear. He teaches his other students the same songs from written sheet music. Mensah hypothesizes that students who learn a song by ear remember it longer than students who learn it from sheet music.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Mensah's hypothesis?

choices.A: Students who learned from sheet music needed fewer lessons to learn each song than the other students did.
choices.B: Months after the lessons, both groups of students could play about the same number of songs from memory.
choices.C: Most of Mensah's students said they enjoyed learning by ear more than learning from sheet music.
choices.D: Months after the lessons, students who had learned by ear could play more of the songs from memory.

explanation.why: Mensah's hypothesis is about memory over time: learning by ear should help students remember songs longer. Support must show the by-ear group remembering more of the songs after time has passed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is about how quickly songs were learned, not how long they were remembered.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If both groups remembered equally, learning by ear would show no advantage; this weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Enjoying a method is different from remembering songs longer because of it.
explanation.D: Correct. After months, the by-ear students remembered more songs, which is what Mensah predicts.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Many picture books for young children repeat the same line again and again, such as a refrain that returns on every page. Literary scholar Fatima Zahra Benali argues that authors use these refrains to invite children to take part in the story. In her view, a repeated line lets children guess what comes next and say it along with the adult who is reading.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Benali's argument?

choices.A: Children usually listened quietly and rarely spoke when adults read books with refrains aloud.
choices.B: Picture books with refrains are often shorter than other picture books written for the same age group.
choices.C: Many authors of picture books draw the illustrations for their own stories.
choices.D: When adults read books with refrains aloud, children often said the refrain before the adult did.

explanation.why: Benali argues that refrains let children predict the next line and join in. Evidence that children actually say the refrain, even before the reader gets to it, supports her argument directly.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Children staying silent would suggest refrains do not get them to join in, which weakens the argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The length of the books says nothing about whether refrains invite children to take part.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Who draws the pictures has nothing to do with how refrains affect young listeners.
explanation.D: Correct. Children saying the refrain ahead of the reader shows that they predicted it and joined in, as Benali claims.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In winter, ravens in the forests of northern Canada often gather at the remains of deer and moose that wolves have killed. Wildlife biologist Marie Tremblay hypothesizes that ravens do not simply find these remains by chance. Instead, she thinks, the birds follow wolf packs while the wolves hunt so that they can reach each new kill quickly.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Tremblay's hypothesis?

choices.A: Tracked ravens traveled with wolf packs on hunting days and reached most kills within an hour.
choices.B: Ravens usually found wolf kills only after several days, long after the wolves had moved on.
choices.C: Wolves in the region usually hunt in packs of between five and ten animals during the winter.
choices.D: Ravens also eat insects, seeds, berries, and the food scraps that people leave behind.

explanation.why: Tremblay's hypothesis is that ravens follow hunting wolves to get to kills fast. Tracking data showing ravens moving with the packs and arriving at kills soon after supports both parts of the claim.
explanation.A: Correct. The ravens traveled with the wolves and reached kills quickly, just as Tremblay predicts.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Ravens arriving days later, after the wolves had left, suggests they were not following the packs; this weakens the hypothesis.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The size of wolf packs does not show whether ravens follow them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Ravens' other foods say nothing about whether they follow wolves.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Until the 1890s, many farm families in the United States had to travel to a post office in town to collect their mail. In 1896, the government began delivering mail directly to some rural homes. Historian Ruth Adler argues that this new service caused a rise in the number of farm families who subscribed to daily newspapers.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Adler's argument?

choices.A: Many farm families also used the delivery service to receive catalogs and letters from relatives.
choices.B: Daily newspapers of the 1890s often printed crop prices and weather reports that were useful to farmers.
choices.C: Subscriptions rose just as fast among farm families who still collected their mail in town.
choices.D: Subscriptions rose sharply in rural areas soon after home delivery of mail reached them.

explanation.why: Adler says home mail delivery caused more farm families to subscribe to newspapers. If families without home delivery increased their subscriptions just as fast, delivery cannot be the cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. What else families received by mail does not show whether delivery increased newspaper subscriptions.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This gives a reason farmers might want newspapers, but it does not test whether home delivery caused the rise.
explanation.C: Correct. Families without home delivery subscribed at the same growing rate, so the delivery service does not explain the rise.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Subscriptions jumping right after delivery began would support Adler's argument, not weaken it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Slugs can do serious damage to vegetable gardens by eating holes in the leaves of young plants. Many gardeners spread used coffee grounds around their lettuce plants to protect them. Horticulturist Bronwyn Davies hypothesizes that the grounds really do work, keeping slugs away from the plants they surround.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Davies's hypothesis?

choices.A: Slugs are most active on damp nights and hide under boards and stones during the day.
choices.B: Coffee grounds add small amounts of nutrients to the soil as they break down.
choices.C: Lettuce ringed with coffee grounds lost as many leaves to slugs as unprotected lettuce did.
choices.D: In a test, slugs turned back when they reached a ring of coffee grounds around a lettuce plant.

explanation.why: Davies's hypothesis is that coffee grounds keep slugs away from plants. If plants with grounds were damaged by slugs just as much as unprotected plants, the grounds are not keeping slugs away.
explanation.A: Incorrect. When slugs are active does not show whether coffee grounds repel them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Adding nutrients to soil is a different benefit and says nothing about slugs.
explanation.C: Correct. Protected and unprotected lettuce suffered the same slug damage, so the grounds did not keep slugs away.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Slugs turning back at the coffee grounds would support the hypothesis, not weaken it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Many older houses in Hyderabad, in the Sindh province of Pakistan, have a tall rooftop structure called a mangh, or wind catcher. Each mangh opens toward the direction from which the region's breeze usually blows. Architectural historian Kamran Soomro argues that builders added these structures mainly to cool the rooms below by directing the breeze down into them.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Soomro's argument?

choices.A: On hot afternoons, rooms under a mangh were several degrees cooler than similar rooms without one.
choices.B: Many of the older houses that have a mangh were built for families of wealthy merchants.
choices.C: Some newer buildings in the city have replaced their mangh with electric fans.
choices.D: When the breeze was blowing, rooms beneath a mangh stayed just as hot as rooms without one.

explanation.why: Soomro argues that the mangh was built to cool the rooms below by channeling the breeze. Measurements showing that rooms under a mangh are cooler than similar rooms without one support the claim that it served this cooling purpose.
explanation.A: Correct. Rooms under a mangh were measurably cooler, which fits the claim that the structure was built to cool them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Who owned the houses does not show what the mangh was for.
explanation.C: Incorrect. What later buildings did says nothing about whether the original mangh cooled rooms.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If rooms under a mangh were no cooler, the structure would not seem to serve a cooling purpose; this weakens the argument.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Hermit crabs protect their soft bodies by living inside empty snail shells, moving into new shells as they grow. A thick shell offers more protection from crabs that crush shells with their claws, but it is also heavier to carry. Marine biologist Lucía Fernández hypothesizes that hermit crabs adjust their choice of shell to the danger around them, selecting thicker shells when shell-crushing predators are nearby.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Fernández's hypothesis?

choices.A: When the scent of shell-crushing crabs was added to their tanks, hermit crabs chose thick shells more often.
choices.B: Hermit crabs on beaches with many shell-crushing crabs grow more slowly than hermit crabs on other beaches.
choices.C: Hermit crabs carrying thick shells moved more slowly across the sand than those carrying thin shells.
choices.D: Hermit crabs chose thick and thin shells equally often whether or not shell-crushing crabs were present.

explanation.why: Fernández claims that hermit crabs change their shell choice depending on whether shell-crushing predators are near. Support must show the choice itself shifting toward thick shells when signs of those predators appear.
explanation.A: Correct. The only change was the predators' scent, and the crabs responded by choosing thick shells more often.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Slower growth near predators is a different effect; it does not show that the crabs choose different shells.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This confirms that thick shells are costly to carry, which the text already states, but it says nothing about how crabs choose shells.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If shell choice did not change with predators, the crabs would not be adjusting to danger, so this weakens the hypothesis.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1850s and 1860s, sewing machines spread rapidly into American homes, even though a single machine could cost a large share of a family's yearly income. Historian Matteo Bellini argues that this spread depended mainly on installment plans, which let buyers take a machine home after a small first payment and pay the rest over many months. Without such plans, he contends, few households could have afforded a machine.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Bellini's argument?

choices.A: Many families who bought sewing machines used them to make clothing for their own use.
choices.B: Where no installment plans were offered, households bought machines at about the same rate as elsewhere.
choices.C: A garment that took many hours to sew by hand could be finished on a machine in a fraction of the time.
choices.D: Sales records show that most sewing machines bought for homes in this period were paid for in installments.

explanation.why: Bellini claims that installment plans were what made the spread of sewing machines possible. If households bought machines just as quickly where no such plans existed, the plans were not necessary, which undercuts his argument.
explanation.A: Incorrect. How families used their machines says nothing about how they managed to pay for them.
explanation.B: Correct. Machines spread just as fast without installment plans, so the plans could not have been the main reason for the spread.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This explains why families wanted machines, not whether installment plans made buying them possible.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Most machines being bought in installments fits Bellini's argument, so it would support rather than weaken it.
