Paleoclimatologist Henrik Aas links their decline to the climate of the time, which swung rapidly between cold and milder periods. Each cold spell, he argues, shrank the forests and grasslands on which Neanderthals depended, splitting their populations into small groups cut off from one another.
items.passage_b: Ancient DNA shows that late Neanderthals had very little genetic variety, a sign that they lived in small, scattered bands for many generations. Anthropologist Teresa Quispe argues that such groups were fragile: a few bad hunting seasons or the arrival of competing modern humans could have been enough to make them disappear.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Living in small, isolated groups left Neanderthals vulnerable to dying out.
choices.B: Competition with modern humans was the main cause of the Neanderthals' disappearance.
choices.C: Neanderthals had more genetic variety than early modern humans did.
choices.D: Rapid climate swings were the main reason Neanderthal populations became small.

explanation.why: Text 1 says cold spells split Neanderthals "into small groups cut off from one another," and links this to their decline. Text 2 says they lived "in small, scattered bands" that were "fragile" and could easily disappear. Both authors connect small, separated populations with the Neanderthals' extinction, though they differ on what caused it.
explanation.A: Correct. Both texts describe small, separated populations and link them to the Neanderthals' disappearance.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 mentions modern humans only as one possible final blow ("could have been"), and Text 1 does not mention them at all.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says late Neanderthals had "very little genetic variety," and neither text compares them with modern humans.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Only Text 1 blames climate swings; Text 2 explains the small groups using DNA evidence and never mentions climate.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Charles Dickens first ended Great Expectations (1861) with Pip and Estella meeting briefly and parting for good. When his friend, the novelist Edward Bulwer-Lytton, urged a happier conclusion, Dickens rewrote the final scene so that the two leave the ruined garden together. Many critics see this revision as a betrayal of the novel's sad, clear-eyed logic.
items.passage_b: The published ending is far less cheerful than its reputation suggests. Pip and Estella meet as two people worn down by years of disappointment, and the closing words, "I saw no shadow of another parting from her," are strangely hesitant; they describe what Pip did not see rather than what will happen. Read closely, the revised ending keeps the novel's somber tone and leaves the couple's future uncertain.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the critics' view of the revised ending in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that Dickens never wrote any ending other than the published one
choices.B: By suggesting that Bulwer-Lytton wrote the final scene of the novel himself
choices.C: By arguing that the revised ending is more uncertain and somber than critics suggest
choices.D: By agreeing that the revision gives the novel a simple, happy conclusion

explanation.why: Text 1 reports that critics see the revised ending as a happy betrayal of the novel's "sad, clear-eyed logic." Text 2 says the ending is "far less cheerful than its reputation suggests": the final words are "strangely hesitant," and the ending "keeps the novel's somber tone." So Text 2 would say the revision does not betray the novel's mood.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 discusses only the published ending and never denies that Dickens first wrote a different one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 1 says Bulwer-Lytton urged a change and Dickens rewrote the scene; neither text says Bulwer-Lytton wrote it.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 points to the worn-down characters and the hesitant final words to show that the ending stays somber.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 argues that the ending only seems happy; read closely, it is somber and uncertain.

items.subject: science
items.passage: As the climate warms, mountain glaciers around the world are losing ice. In the Himalayas, satellite images show that many glaciers have shrunk and pulled back over recent decades. Some writers conclude that every glacier in the high mountains of South and Central Asia is now retreating.
items.passage_b: In the Karakoram range of northern Pakistan, the record is surprisingly mixed. Since the 1990s, glaciologists have found that many glaciers there have stayed about the same size, and some have even grown slightly. Researchers are still testing explanations for this "Karakoram anomaly," such as heavier winter snowfall and cooler summers in the region, but none of them doubt that most of the world's glaciers are shrinking.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that satellite images of Himalayan glaciers are unreliable
choices.B: By rejecting the idea that most of the world's glaciers are losing ice
choices.C: By accepting the general trend while pointing out a region where it does not hold
choices.D: By claiming that glaciers in the Karakoram are growing faster than others are shrinking

explanation.why: Text 1 ends with the conclusion that "every glacier" in the high mountains of South and Central Asia is retreating. Text 2 reports that many Karakoram glaciers "have stayed about the same size" and some have grown, though no researcher doubts "that most of the world's glaciers are shrinking." So Text 2 accepts the overall trend but rejects the word "every."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 never questions the Himalayan satellite images; it discusses a different range.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says researchers do not "doubt that most of the world's glaciers are shrinking."
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 agrees that most glaciers are shrinking but gives the Karakoram as an exception to Text 1's claim about "every glacier."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says only that some Karakoram glaciers have grown "slightly"; it makes no comparison with the losses elsewhere.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Violins made by Antonio Stradivari in Cremona, Italy, around 1700 now sell for millions of dollars. Many musicians and collectors believe that these instruments produce a tone no modern violin can equal. Researchers have spent decades searching for the cause, proposing secrets in the wood Stradivari chose or in the varnish he applied.
items.passage_b: Before searching for the secret, it is worth asking whether the difference can be heard at all. In several blind tests, professional violinists wearing goggles that hid the instruments played old Italian violins, including ones by Stradivari, alongside fine new violins. Most players could not reliably tell which was which, and many preferred the sound of a new instrument.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief in Text 1?

choices.A: By questioning whether the tone of these violins is truly better than that of new ones
choices.B: By arguing that Stradivari's violins are worth far less than collectors pay
choices.C: By claiming that new violins sound better than old ones to every listener
choices.D: By agreeing that Stradivari's varnish explains the violins' superior tone

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the belief that Stradivari violins have a tone "no modern violin can equal." Text 2 asks "whether the difference can be heard at all" and reports that players in blind tests "could not reliably tell which was which." So Text 2 doubts that the tone is really superior.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2's blind tests suggest that players cannot reliably hear the difference Text 1 describes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 tests how the violins sound, not what they are worth; it never discusses their price.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says "many" players preferred a new violin, not every listener.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 questions whether there is any superior tone to explain, so it would not credit the varnish.

items.subject: science
items.passage: New Caledonian crows, found on islands in the South Pacific, are famous for making tools: they shape twigs and strips of leaf into hooks and probes that pull insects out of holes in wood. Young crows stay with their parents for up to two years, and ornithologist Mele Taufa argues that this long period of watching adults is how the birds learn to make and use tools.
items.passage_b: In one study, young New Caledonian crows were raised by people, with no adult crows to watch. Within a few months, the birds began poking sticks into crevices on their own. Their early tools were simple and clumsy compared with those of wild adults. The researchers concluded that the basic urge to use tools is inborn, though experience and observation may help the birds refine their skills.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that young crows cannot use tools until they have watched adults
choices.B: By arguing that young crows learn tool use mainly from crows other than their parents
choices.C: By suggesting that watching adults may refine tool use but is not where it begins
choices.D: By claiming that observation plays no part in how crows develop tool skills

explanation.why: Taufa argues in Text 1 that young crows learn tool use by watching adults. In Text 2, crows with "no adult crows to watch" still began using sticks, so the basic urge is "inborn," though "observation may help the birds refine their skills." Text 2 would say watching adults explains the refinement of tool use, not its origin.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The crows in Text 2 used sticks "on their own" with no adults to watch, the opposite of this choice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never compares learning from parents with learning from other crows.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 says the basic urge is inborn, while observation may help refine skills.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says observation "may help the birds refine their skills," so it does not rule observation out.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When the modern Olympic Games were founded in the 1890s, their organizers looked to ancient Greece for an ideal. Ancient athletes, they claimed, were amateurs who competed purely for honor, receiving nothing but a crown of olive leaves for victory. Professional sport, in this view, was a modern corruption of the Greek spirit.
items.passage_b: It is true that the official prize at Olympia was an olive crown. But historian Nikos Andreou points out that victors could expect far more once they returned home. Their cities rewarded them with cash, statues, and free meals for life, and at other Greek festivals winners received valuable prizes such as large jars of olive oil. The amateur athlete, Andreou concludes, was largely an invention of the modern Olympic movement.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the organizers' claim in Text 1?

choices.A: By pointing out that ancient winners in fact received valuable rewards
choices.B: By arguing that the modern Olympics should stop awarding prizes
choices.C: By agreeing that ancient athletes competed only for the honor of winning
choices.D: By claiming that olive crowns were never given to winners at Olympia

explanation.why: Text 1 reports the organizers' claim that ancient athletes received "nothing but a crown of olive leaves." Text 2 grants that the olive crown was the official prize but says winners received "cash, statues, and free meals for life" at home and valuable prizes elsewhere. So Text 2 would reject the image of the purely amateur Greek athlete.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 shows that victors received money and other valuable rewards from their cities and at other festivals.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 discusses ancient rewards and never recommends any change to the modern Games.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 lists cash, statues, meals, and olive oil as rewards, so athletes did not compete for honor alone.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says, "It is true that the official prize at Olympia was an olive crown."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the 1980s, conservators cleaned Michelangelo's frescoes on the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome, removing centuries of candle soot and old layers of glue. The ceiling that emerged was startlingly bright, full of vivid pinks, greens, and oranges. Art historian Chiara Bellandi argues that the cleaning revealed Michelangelo to be a far bolder colorist than scholars had believed.
items.passage_b: No one disputes that the cleaned ceiling looks dramatically brighter than it did before. Some critics, however, worry that the cleaning went too far. They argue that Michelangelo added final touches of shadow after the plaster had dried and that the solvents used may have stripped these away along with the dirt, leaving the colors harsher than he intended.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: The cleaning removed final touches of shadow that Michelangelo added himself.
choices.B: The cleaned ceiling looks much brighter than it did before the work began.
choices.C: The ceiling should be cleaned again to remove the remaining layers of glue.
choices.D: The colors now visible are the ones Michelangelo intended viewers to see.

explanation.why: Text 1 says the ceiling that emerged "was startlingly bright." Text 2 begins, "No one disputes that the cleaned ceiling looks dramatically brighter than it did before." The authors disagree about whether the cleaning was faithful to Michelangelo, but both accept that the ceiling is now much brighter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Only the critics in Text 2 raise this worry, and Text 1 treats the bright colors as Michelangelo's own.
explanation.B: Correct. Both texts state that the ceiling is much brighter after cleaning.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Neither text suggests further cleaning; Text 1 says the glue was removed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 1 suggests this, but Text 2 says the colors may be "harsher than he intended."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Woolly mammoths had vanished from nearly all of their mainland range by about 10,000 years ago, but a small population survived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean, until roughly 4,000 years ago. Paleontologist Sergei Volkov argues that the island's isolation protected the mammoths from human hunters, who did not reach Wrangel until after the animals were gone.
items.passage_b: Genetic studies of the last Wrangel Island mammoths reveal a population in poor health. Descended from a small group that was cut off when rising seas flooded the land around the island, the mammoths carried harmful mutations and had little genetic diversity. Geneticist Hana Novák suggests that this weakened population, which held on for thousands of years after its mainland relatives died out, may finally have been wiped out by a sudden event such as a disease outbreak.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Harmful mutations were the direct cause of the mammoths' extinction.
choices.B: Human hunters caused the final extinction of the Wrangel Island mammoths.
choices.C: The island's isolation protected the mammoths from human hunters.
choices.D: Mammoths survived on Wrangel Island long after they disappeared from the mainland.

explanation.why: Text 1 says mammoths survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago, long after they had vanished from the mainland. Text 2 says the population "held on for thousands of years after its mainland relatives died out." Both authors accept this late survival, though they focus on different reasons for it and for its end.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the mutations weakened the population but suggests that a sudden event finally wiped it out; Text 1 never mentions mutations.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 1 says hunters reached Wrangel only "after the animals were gone," and Text 2 suggests a sudden event such as disease.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only Text 1 makes this claim; Text 2 does not discuss hunters.
explanation.D: Correct. Both texts say the island's mammoths outlasted the mainland populations by thousands of years.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A familiar story holds that when Christopher Columbus proposed sailing west from Spain to Asia in the 1480s, most learned Europeans believed the Earth was flat. In this telling, scholars warned that his ships would fall off the edge of the world, and Columbus bravely proved them wrong in 1492.
items.passage_b: Educated Europeans of Columbus's time already knew that the Earth was round; Greek scholars had shown this nearly 2,000 years earlier, and one of them, Eratosthenes, had even estimated its size. The real argument concerned distance. Columbus's critics believed, correctly, that Asia lay much too far west for his ships to reach with the supplies they could carry. His voyage succeeded only because two continents unknown to Europeans lay in between.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the familiar story in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that Columbus's critics underestimated how far away Asia was
choices.B: By claiming that most Europeans of the time had never heard of Eratosthenes
choices.C: By agreeing that fear of a flat Earth delayed Columbus's voyage for years
choices.D: By explaining that the dispute was about the distance to Asia, not the Earth's shape

explanation.why: Text 1 tells the story that scholars feared Columbus would sail off a flat Earth. Text 2 says educated Europeans "already knew that the Earth was round" and that "the real argument concerned distance": critics thought Asia was too far away. Text 2 corrects the story by naming the true dispute.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the critics were correct that Asia was "much too far west," so they did not underestimate the distance.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says Greek scholars' knowledge was shared by educated Europeans; it never says how many people had heard of Eratosthenes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says educated Europeans knew the Earth was round, so it would reject any role for fear of a flat Earth.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 says the argument "concerned distance," since educated Europeans already knew the Earth was round.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries, historians called the period after the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE the "Dark Ages." In this view, as cities shrank and trade declined, Europeans lost much of the learning of the ancient world, and scholarship nearly died out until its revival in the 1300s and 1400s.
items.passage_b: Recent historians reject the label, or at least its gloom. Cities and long-distance trade did decline in much of western Europe, but monasteries from Ireland to Italy continued to copy and study ancient texts. Around 800, scholars at Charlemagne's court even promoted a clear new style of handwriting that made books easier to read, and many Roman works survive today only because they were copied during this period.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view of the period in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that ancient learning was lost during Charlemagne's reign
choices.B: By claiming that the early Middle Ages were a time of growth in every area of life
choices.C: By denying that cities and trade declined after the fall of Rome
choices.D: By accepting that some decline occurred while arguing that learning was preserved

explanation.why: Text 1 presents the view that learning "nearly died out" after Rome fell. Text 2 grants that "cities and long-distance trade did decline" but says monasteries kept copying ancient texts and that many Roman works "survive today only because" of copies made then. Text 2 concedes some decline but rejects the claim that learning vanished.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says scholars at Charlemagne's court helped preserve ancient works, the opposite of this choice.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 concedes decline in cities and trade, so it does not claim growth in every area.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 explicitly says cities and trade "did decline," so it does not deny this.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 admits that cities and trade declined but shows that monasteries and scholars preserved ancient learning.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When Emily Dickinson's poems were first published in 1890, four years after her death, the editors made many changes. Among other things, they replaced most of her frequent dashes with commas, periods, and semicolons. The editors believed these changes made the unusual poems easier for readers to follow, and the volume sold well.
items.passage_b: Readers of the 1955 edition, which restored the punctuation of Dickinson's manuscripts, met a different poet. Her dashes, many scholars argue, are not careless marks but part of the poems' meaning: they create pauses, leave thoughts open, and let a line point in more than one direction at once. Replacing them with ordinary punctuation made the poems tidier, but it also narrowed them.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the editors' changes in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the 1890 volume failed because readers found the poems confusing
choices.B: By agreeing that the changes brought the poems closer to Dickinson's intentions
choices.C: By claiming that Dickinson's manuscripts contained very few dashes
choices.D: By suggesting that the changes made the poems neater but lost some of their meaning

explanation.why: Text 1 says the editors replaced Dickinson's dashes to make the poems "easier for readers to follow." Text 2 says the dashes are "part of the poems' meaning" and that replacing them "made the poems tidier, but it also narrowed them." So Text 2 grants a gain in neatness but sees a loss in meaning.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 1 says the volume "sold well," and Text 2 never claims it failed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the dashes are part of the poems' meaning, so removing them moved the poems away from what Dickinson wrote.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the 1955 edition restored the punctuation of the manuscripts, including the dashes, so the manuscripts had many.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 calls the edited poems "tidier" but "narrowed," meaning they lost some of their range of meaning.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Dutch painter Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) left no written record of how he worked, but some art historians believe he used a camera obscura, a darkened box that projects an image through a lens. They point to features of his paintings that resemble optical effects, such as small, blurry dots of light on shiny surfaces, like those in an out-of-focus photograph.
items.passage_b: The resemblance is real, but it proves less than it seems. A painter with a sharp eye could notice how highlights glitter and soften and copy that effect by hand. Moreover, the list of Vermeer's possessions made after his death mentions no lenses or optical devices. Without such evidence, art historian Saskia Mertens argues, the camera obscura remains an interesting possibility rather than an established fact.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the belief of some art historians in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that the list of his possessions proves Vermeer never used the device
choices.B: By arguing that the camera obscura had not yet been invented in Vermeer's time
choices.C: By claiming that Vermeer's paintings show no effects resembling those of a lens
choices.D: By granting the visual similarity but arguing that it does not prove Vermeer used the device

explanation.why: Text 1 says some historians think Vermeer used a camera obscura because his paintings show lens-like effects. Text 2 agrees "the resemblance is real" but says a careful painter could create the effect by hand and that no optical devices appear among his possessions. Mertens calls the idea "an interesting possibility rather than an established fact."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 treats the idea as still "an interesting possibility," so it does not claim proof that Vermeer never used one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never discusses when the camera obscura was invented.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 begins by saying "the resemblance is real," so it does not deny the effects.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 accepts the resemblance but says it "proves less than it seems."

items.subject: science
items.passage: An octopus has roughly 500 million neurons, but about two-thirds of them lie not in its brain but in its eight arms. An arm can still touch, taste, and grasp food even after it has been separated from the body. For neurobiologist Ilse Vandermeer, this distribution implies a striking division of labor: the central brain issues only broad commands, such as "reach toward that crab," and leaves the arms to work out every detail of a movement for themselves.
items.passage_b: Octopus arms are undeniably capable of acting on their own, but that capacity does not show that they always do. In one experiment, octopuses learned to steer a single arm through a transparent maze toward food that they could see but that the arm could not reach by touch or taste until the very end. Because the arm's own senses offered no guide to the route, success depended on the brain watching the arm and correcting its path along the way.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim about the central brain in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that octopus arms actually contain far fewer neurons than Text 1 indicates
choices.B: By claiming that in the maze experiment the arm, not the brain, worked out the route
choices.C: By rejecting the idea that an octopus's arms can sense and respond to their surroundings
choices.D: By arguing that it overlooks cases in which the brain guides an arm's movements closely

explanation.why: Text 1 says the brain issues "only broad commands" and leaves "every detail" to the arms. Text 2 grants that arms can act on their own but describes a maze task in which "success depended on the brain watching the arm and correcting its path." So Text 2 would say Text 1's claim misses cases of close central control.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 never discusses how many neurons the arms contain.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses Text 2's point: the arm's senses "offered no guide to the route," so the brain had to guide it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 calls the arms "undeniably capable of acting on their own," so it does not reject their ability to sense and respond.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2's maze experiment shows the brain directing an arm step by step, which the claim that the brain issues "only broad commands" leaves out.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In nineteenth-century Calcutta, painters known as patuas set up stalls near the Kalighat temple and sold watercolors to the pilgrims who crowded its lanes. Art historian Rohini Sen argues that the paintings' famous look, with bold, sweeping outlines, flat washes of color, and almost no background, was shaped above all by this market. Pilgrims wanted inexpensive keepsakes, and a style that could be executed in minutes allowed a painter to produce dozens of works a day.
items.passage_b: The demands of a crowded temple market surely encouraged speed, and speed helps account for the economy of the Kalighat line. But a market explanation says little about what the patuas chose to paint. Alongside gods and goddesses, they produced sharp scenes of contemporary city life: a fashionably dressed gentleman admiring his own reflection, a wife ordering her husband about. Such images suggest painters who were commenting on a changing society, not merely supplying souvenirs.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Sen in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting it as an account of the paintings' style but not of their subject matter
choices.B: By contending that the patuas' scenes of city life sold better than their religious images
choices.C: By arguing that the bold Kalighat line reflects social commentary rather than a need for speed
choices.D: By rejecting the claim that pilgrims bought Kalighat paintings as inexpensive keepsakes

explanation.why: Text 2 agrees that the market "encouraged speed" and that speed "helps account for the economy of the Kalighat line," so it accepts Sen's explanation of the style. It then says the market explanation "says little about what the patuas chose to paint," pointing to satirical city scenes. Text 2 therefore accepts the argument for style but finds it incomplete for subject matter.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 grants that market pressure explains the quick, bold style but says it does not explain the choice of satirical subjects.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about which kinds of paintings sold better.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 credits speed for the "economy of the Kalighat line"; it links social commentary to the subjects, not to the line.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not dispute that pilgrims bought the paintings; it accepts that the temple market shaped the style.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Did ancient Greeks and Romans read silently? Many historians have doubted it, pointing to a famous passage in Augustine's Confessions, written around 400 CE. Augustine describes his surprise at watching Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, read with his eyes moving over the page while his voice remained still. If silent reading so impressed a highly educated man, these historians conclude, it must have been a rare skill in the ancient world.
items.passage_b: Augustine's account deserves a closer look. He does not say he had never seen anyone read silently; he wonders why Ambrose read that way, guessing that the bishop wished to rest his voice or to avoid being drawn into discussions by listeners. What struck Augustine may have been less the practice itself than Ambrose's choosing it in a setting where visitors expected to hear the text and talk about it. Several earlier Greek writers, moreover, mention people reading letters without a sound.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the historians' conclusion in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that Ambrose read silently to rest his voice, as Augustine's account proves
choices.B: By claiming that most ancient readers preferred reading silently to reading aloud
choices.C: By suggesting that the passage shows surprise at Ambrose's choice, not at a rare skill
choices.D: By agreeing that silent reading was rare but disputing that Augustine was surprised by it

explanation.why: The historians reason that Augustine's surprise shows silent reading was "a rare skill." Text 2 argues that what struck Augustine "may have been less the practice itself than Ambrose's choosing it" in a setting where listeners expected to hear the text, and it adds earlier evidence of silent reading. Text 2 thus reinterprets the surprise rather than accepting it as evidence of rarity.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says Augustine was "guessing" at Ambrose's reasons, so it would not say his account proves them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 shows only that silent reading was not unknown; it never claims most readers preferred it.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 suggests that Augustine was struck by Ambrose's decision to read silently in that setting, not by a skill few people had.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not deny Augustine's surprise, and it does not agree that silent reading was rare; it questions exactly that conclusion.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a rat runs a maze, particular neurons in its hippocampus fire in a sequence that tracks its route. During the deep sleep that follows, the same sequences often fire again, compressed into a fraction of a second. Neuroscientist Kwabena Mensah argues that this "replay" is how the day's experiences are consolidated into lasting memories, and he regards it as the main reason that sleep is indispensable to learning.
items.passage_b: Replay is not confined to sleep. Rats pausing at the end of a maze run, fully awake, also fire compressed sequences of these neurons, sometimes tracing routes they have just taken and sometimes routes they have yet to try. Replay may well support memory, but if it occurs during quiet waking as well as during sleep, it cannot by itself explain why sleep in particular is so important for learning.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view held by Mensah in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the idea that replay plays any part in the formation of lasting memories
choices.B: By questioning whether the sequences seen during sleep truly match the rat's earlier route
choices.C: By agreeing that sleep is indispensable to learning because replay occurs only during sleep
choices.D: By allowing that replay may aid memory while doubting it explains sleep's special role

explanation.why: Text 2 says "Replay may well support memory," so it does not reject Mensah's view of what replay does. But because replay also happens "during quiet waking," Text 2 says it "cannot by itself explain why sleep in particular is so important." Text 2 accepts one part of Mensah's view and rejects the other.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says replay "may well support memory," so it does not deny replay any role.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never questions that sleep sequences match the earlier route.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2's main point is that replay does not occur only during sleep.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 allows that replay may help memory but argues that, since it also occurs while rats are awake, it cannot explain why sleep matters so much.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At its height in the sixteenth century, the Arsenal of Venice, the city's state shipyard, employed thousands of workers and could fit out war galleys with remarkable speed. Visitors described hulls being towed along a canal past a row of windows, from each of which workers handed out oars, ropes, weapons, or provisions in turn. For economic historian Marco Ferrante, such accounts show that the Arsenal anticipated the modern assembly line by centuries.
items.passage_b: The Arsenal's sequence of stations and its stocks of ready-made fittings do resemble later factory methods. Yet the resemblance can be pressed too far. The assembly line's defining feature was the division of work into simple, repeated motions that unskilled workers could learn quickly. The Arsenal, by contrast, depended on master shipwrights, caulkers, and oar makers who trained for years and exercised judgment throughout the building of a ship.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim made by Ferrante in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that the Arsenal's master shipwrights invented the methods of the assembly line
choices.B: By disputing the visitors' accounts of hulls being fitted out as they were towed along a canal
choices.C: By granting a resemblance but arguing that the Arsenal's skilled workers weaken the comparison
choices.D: By contending that the Arsenal built galleys more slowly than later factories produced goods

explanation.why: Text 2 concedes that the Arsenal's stations and fittings "do resemble later factory methods," then warns that "the resemblance can be pressed too far." Its reason is that the assembly line relied on simple tasks for unskilled workers, whereas the Arsenal relied on highly trained craftsmen. So Text 2 accepts part of Ferrante's claim and rejects the full comparison.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 uses the shipwrights' skill to separate the Arsenal from the assembly line, not to credit them with inventing it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts the "sequence of stations"; it never doubts the visitors' descriptions.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 admits the similarity in how work was sequenced but says the Arsenal's reliance on long-trained craftsmen makes it unlike an assembly line.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not compare the Arsenal's speed with that of later factories.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the 1880s, meteorologists in India noticed that winters with unusually heavy snow in the Himalayas tended to be followed by weak summer monsoons. The idea makes physical sense: snow-covered land reflects sunlight and spends energy on melting, so it warms slowly in spring, weakening the land-sea temperature contrast that draws moist ocean air inland. Climatologist Priya Raghavan argues that Eurasian snow cover therefore remains one of the most dependable signals for forecasting the monsoon.
items.passage_b: The link between snow and the monsoon is physically plausible, and in some decades it has held up well. But a forecasting signal is only as good as its consistency, and this one has been erratic: in several recent decades the correlation between spring snow cover and monsoon rainfall weakened or nearly vanished, apparently because other influences, such as conditions in the tropical Pacific, came to dominate. A link that fades and returns cannot be called dependable.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Raghavan in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the tropical Pacific is the only reliable guide to monsoon rainfall
choices.B: By claiming that heavy Himalayan snow is usually followed by unusually strong monsoons
choices.C: By rejecting the physical explanation of how snow cover could weaken the monsoon
choices.D: By granting that the link is plausible but denying that it is a dependable signal

explanation.why: Text 2 opens by calling the snow-monsoon link "physically plausible," so it accepts the reasoning in Text 1. It then argues that the correlation has "weakened or nearly vanished" in recent decades and concludes that such a link "cannot be called dependable," which is the very word Raghavan uses. Text 2 accepts the mechanism but rejects the claim of reliability.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 mentions the tropical Pacific only as one of the "other influences"; it never calls it the only reliable guide.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never claims that heavy snow leads to strong monsoons; it says only that the snow-monsoon correlation has been inconsistent.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 calls the link "physically plausible," so it does not reject the explanation.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 accepts that the link makes physical sense but says its inconsistency in recent decades keeps it from being a dependable signal.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For years, studies seemed to show that bilingual children outperform monolingual peers on tests of executive control, such as switching rapidly between tasks or ignoring distracting information. Psychologist Leila Haddad explains the pattern by pointing to bilinguals' daily experience: because both languages are always active in the mind, speakers must constantly suppress one while using the other, and this practice, she argues, strengthens general mental control.
items.passage_b: Haddad's proposed mechanism is ingenious, but it may be explaining an effect that is not there. Many early studies tested small groups, and studies that found no difference were less likely to be published. When later studies tested thousands of children and accounted for factors such as family income, the bilingual advantage on executive control tasks largely disappeared. Before asking why bilinguals have such an advantage, researchers should establish that they do.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation offered by Haddad in Text 1?

choices.A: By accepting that the advantage is real but doubting that large studies are able to detect it
choices.B: By questioning whether the advantage that the explanation is meant to account for really exists
choices.C: By claiming that bilingual children actually perform worse than monolingual children on such tests
choices.D: By arguing that constantly suppressing one language tires speakers instead of strengthening them

explanation.why: Text 2 says Haddad's mechanism "may be explaining an effect that is not there," because in large, careful studies "the bilingual advantage ... largely disappeared." Its closing sentence asks researchers to "establish that they do" have the advantage before explaining it. Text 2 thus doubts the finding that the explanation rests on.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses Text 2: the large studies are its evidence that the advantage may not be real.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 argues that larger studies fail to find the advantage, so the explanation may be accounting for something that does not exist.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the advantage "largely disappeared," not that bilingual children do worse.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not offer a different effect of language suppression; it questions whether there is an advantage to explain.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Gothic cathedrals such as Chartres owe their soaring, light-filled interiors to an engineering device: the flying buttress. These external arches carry the outward thrust of a high stone vault across open air to massive piers set away from the building. With the walls relieved of much of that load, builders could make them thinner and fill them with large expanses of stained glass. The buttress, in this view, is a structural solution and nothing more.
items.passage_b: No one doubts that flying buttresses did essential structural work; without them, the great windows of Gothic churches could not have stood. Yet medieval masons did not leave them plain. They carved the arches with tracery, set statues in niches along the piers, and added ornament that served no structural purpose. To treat the buttress purely as engineering is to ignore how deliberately its builders made it part of the building's display.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Flying buttresses were first built as decoration and only later took on structural work.
choices.B: Medieval masons regarded flying buttresses as purely structural devices.
choices.C: The carving on flying buttresses was added to help them resist the thrust of the vault.
choices.D: Flying buttresses made it possible for builders to use larger windows.

explanation.why: Text 1 says that with buttresses carrying the vault's thrust, builders could "fill [the walls] with large expanses of stained glass." Text 2 agrees that "without them, the great windows of Gothic churches could not have stood." Both authors therefore accept that buttresses allowed larger windows; they disagree only about whether the buttress was also display.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Neither text says buttresses began as decoration; both treat their structural work as essential.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 1 presents the buttress as purely structural, but Text 2 argues that masons deliberately made it part of the display.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the ornament "served no structural purpose," so it would reject this.
explanation.D: Correct. Both texts say buttresses let builders open the walls for great windows of stained glass.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On cold nights, many hummingbirds enter torpor, a state in which body temperature and metabolic rate drop sharply. Because a hummingbird burns energy so quickly that it could starve overnight, ornithologist Tadeusz Kowal describes torpor as an emergency measure. Birds resort to it, he argues, only when their fat reserves have fallen too low to fuel a night at normal body temperature.
items.passage_b: Ecologist Ana Mamani weighed hummingbirds at dusk on a high Andean slope and then recorded their body temperatures through the night. Birds of every species she studied entered torpor, including individuals that had gone to roost carrying ample fat. Mamani suggests that at such altitudes torpor is less a last resort than a routine strategy: by spending the night in torpor, a bird can save its reserves for the demands of the following day.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Kowal in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that only Andean species of hummingbirds are able to enter torpor
choices.B: By citing evidence that hummingbirds with sufficient reserves also enter torpor
choices.C: By agreeing that torpor is an emergency measure for hummingbirds at high altitudes
choices.D: By disputing that hummingbirds burn energy fast enough to risk starving overnight

explanation.why: Kowal claims hummingbirds use torpor "only when their fat reserves have fallen too low." Text 2 reports that torpor occurred even in "individuals that had gone to roost carrying ample fat," and Mamani calls torpor "less a last resort than a routine strategy." Text 2 would answer Kowal with evidence against his "only when" claim.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 studied Andean birds but never says other hummingbirds cannot enter torpor; Text 1 says many do.
explanation.B: Correct. Mamani's well-fed birds entered torpor too, which contradicts the claim that torpor occurs only when reserves run low.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 calls torpor at high altitude "less a last resort than a routine strategy," the opposite of an emergency measure.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 never questions how quickly hummingbirds burn energy.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The dry zone of ancient Sri Lanka supported cities such as Anuradhapura through a vast system of reservoirs, known locally as tanks, and the channels that linked them. Some tanks, built under royal sponsorship, covered many square kilometers. Historian Nimal Jayawardena argues that so extensive a system could only have been planned and maintained by a powerful central state, which organized labor and decided how water was shared across the countryside.
items.passage_b: The great royal reservoirs were indeed state projects. But most of the dry zone's tanks were small village reservoirs arranged in cascades along shallow valleys, each catching the overflow of the one above it. Records of local water rights suggest that these tanks were added a few at a time over generations and that villages themselves maintained them and divided their water. The system as a whole may owe as much to accumulated local effort as to central planning.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Jayawardena in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that it overlooks the many small tanks that villages built and ran themselves
choices.B: By agreeing that the cascades reflect central planning while doubting the royal tanks' size
choices.C: By denying that any of Sri Lanka's ancient reservoirs were built under royal sponsorship
choices.D: By claiming that the village cascades held more water than the great royal reservoirs did

explanation.why: Text 2 agrees that "the great royal reservoirs were indeed state projects," but it points out that "most of the dry zone's tanks" were village reservoirs that villages "themselves maintained." It concludes that the system "may owe as much to accumulated local effort as to central planning." Text 2 would say Jayawardena's "only" claim ignores this local part of the system.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 argues that most tanks were village works, built gradually and managed locally, which Jayawardena's account of a centrally run system leaves out.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 credits the cascades to local effort, not central planning, and never questions the size of the royal tanks.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that the great reservoirs were state projects.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 compares the number of village tanks, not how much water they held.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Between about 800 and 950 CE, many of the great cities of the southern Maya lowlands, such as Tikal, were largely abandoned. Sediment layers from lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula record a series of severe droughts in the same period. For paleoclimatologist Eva Brandt, the match in timing is decisive: prolonged drought, she argues, destroyed the farming on which these cities depended and was the cause of their collapse.
items.passage_b: The droughts were real and severe, but their effects were not uniform. Several cities in the northern Yucatán, a region that was drier to begin with, grew and flourished during these same decades; Chichen Itza reached its height then. If drought alone determined the fate of Maya cities, the north should have suffered first. The southern collapse more likely resulted from drought acting on societies already strained by warfare and political rivalry.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion reached by Brandt in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that warfare, rather than drought, was the sole cause of the southern collapse
choices.B: By claiming that northern cities flourished because they received more rain than the south
choices.C: By questioning whether the lake sediments accurately record droughts in that period
choices.D: By arguing that drought was likely one contributing cause rather than the sole cause

explanation.why: Text 2 accepts that "the droughts were real and severe" but notes that northern cities flourished despite them, so "drought alone" cannot explain the southern collapse. It proposes instead "drought acting on societies already strained by warfare and political rivalry." Text 2 keeps drought as a cause but denies that it was the only one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 does not drop drought; it describes drought combining with warfare and rivalry.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the north was "drier to begin with," so it would not claim the north got more rain.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says "the droughts were real and severe," so it does not question the sediment record.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 treats drought as one factor that worked together with warfare and political strain, not as the single cause Brandt claims.

items.subject: science
items.passage: About 1.9 million years ago, Homo erectus appeared with a larger brain, smaller teeth, and a smaller gut than its ancestors had. Anthropologist Hamid Zand attributes these changes to cooking: cooked food is softer and yields more energy with less chewing and digestion, which would have freed energy for a growing, costly brain. In his view, the control of fire must therefore have begun at roughly the time this species arose.
items.passage_b: Cooking certainly makes food easier to digest, and its benefits for a large-brained animal are clear. The difficulty lies in the archaeological record. Traces of fire at a few sites may be about a million years old, but clear evidence that hominins used fire routinely, in hearths found again and again across many sites, appears only around 400,000 years ago, long after Homo erectus emerged.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view held by Zand in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that Homo erectus did not in fact have a larger brain than its ancestors
choices.B: By rejecting the claim that cooked food provides more energy than raw food does
choices.C: By questioning whether routine fire use is old enough to explain the changes
choices.D: By claiming that hominins never used fire at all before about 400,000 years ago

explanation.why: Text 2 agrees that cooking's "benefits for a large-brained animal are clear," so it does not attack Zand's reasoning about energy. Its objection is timing: routine fire use appears only "around 400,000 years ago, long after Homo erectus emerged" about 1.9 million years ago. Text 2 doubts that fire was controlled early enough to cause those changes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 never disputes the anatomical changes described in Text 1.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says "Cooking certainly makes food easier to digest," accepting this part of Zand's view.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 argues that clear evidence of routine fire use comes far too late to account for changes seen 1.9 million years ago.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 mentions fire traces "about a million years old," so it does not say hominins never used fire earlier.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For much of the twentieth century, the standard account held that the first people to reach the Americas walked south from Beringia through an ice-free corridor that opened between the two vast ice sheets covering what is now Canada. Archaeologist Ruth Calloway still regards that inland route as the most likely path, noting that it led directly to the grasslands of the interior, where herds of large game could have sustained migrating hunters.
items.passage_b: The inland route faces a problem of timing. Studies of ancient plant and animal remains suggest that the corridor could not have supported travelers until roughly 13,000 years ago, yet people were already living at Monte Verde, in southern Chile, more than a thousand years earlier. A coastal route, along shores rich in fish, shellfish, and seaweed, would have been open sooner and would have offered food the whole way.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view held by Calloway in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the corridor opened early but denying that it offered enough large game
choices.B: By claiming that the first people to reach the Americas did not come from Beringia
choices.C: By arguing that people reached South America before the inland route was usable
choices.D: By suggesting that hunters on the interior grasslands later moved to the Pacific coast

explanation.why: Text 2's objection is "a problem of timing": the corridor could not support travelers until about 13,000 years ago, "yet people were already living at Monte Verde ... more than a thousand years earlier." If people were in Chile before the corridor was usable, they must have come another way. Text 2 uses that date to challenge Calloway's preferred route.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says the corridor could not support travelers until late, so it does not agree that it was usable early.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 offers a different route, not a different starting point; it never denies that people came from Beringia.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 notes that Monte Verde was occupied more than a thousand years before the corridor could support travelers.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about hunters moving from the grasslands to the coast.

items.subject: science
items.passage: European robins can orient by Earth's magnetic field, but how they sense it has long been debated. One leading hypothesis locates the sensor in cryptochrome, a light-sensitive protein in the retina, in which magnetic fields could alter chemical reactions. Biophysicist Jonas Lindgren considers the question settled, citing experiments in which weak radio-frequency noise, too feeble to affect an iron-based magnetic sensor, nonetheless left caged robins unable to orient.
items.passage_b: The radio-frequency results are striking, and they fit the cryptochrome hypothesis well. They are, however, evidence about what disrupts the compass, not a direct observation of the compass itself. Researchers have shown that cryptochrome made from the robin's genes responds to magnetic fields in the laboratory, but no one has yet demonstrated that the protein performs this role inside the retina of a living, orienting bird. Until then, the case remains strong but incomplete.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the position taken by Lindgren in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that robins rely on the position of the sun rather than on magnetic fields
choices.B: By arguing that the radio-frequency experiments in fact point to an iron-based sensor
choices.C: By granting that the evidence favors the hypothesis while denying that it proves it
choices.D: By rejecting the hypothesis because cryptochrome does not respond to magnetic fields

explanation.why: Lindgren says the question is "settled." Text 2 agrees the results "fit the cryptochrome hypothesis well" but notes that no one has shown cryptochrome working "inside the retina of a living, orienting bird," so the case is "strong but incomplete." Text 2 accepts the evidence as support while denying that it settles the matter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 does not discuss the sun or doubt that robins use magnetic fields.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the results fit the cryptochrome hypothesis; it never links them to an iron-based sensor.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 calls the case "strong but incomplete," agreeing the evidence supports cryptochrome while rejecting Lindgren's claim that the question is settled.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 reports that cryptochrome "responds to magnetic fields in the laboratory," so it does not reject the hypothesis on those grounds.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Before the 1840s, painters usually stored oil paint in pig bladders, which were difficult to seal and to carry. The collapsible metal tube, patented in 1841, kept paint fresh and portable, and art historian Clara Duvall argues that it made Impressionism possible: freed from the studio, painters such as Claude Monet could set up their easels outdoors and record shifting light directly in front of their subjects.
items.passage_b: Portable paint certainly encouraged painting outdoors, and the Impressionists made much of their work in the open air. Yet the image of the Impressionist completing every canvas on the spot is misleading. Monet, for instance, began his paintings of Rouen Cathedral in front of the building but reworked many of them for months in his studio. The tube changed where a painting could begin; it did not end the role of the studio.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Monet's paintings of Rouen Cathedral show that the tube freed painters from the studio.
choices.B: The metal paint tube made it easier for painters to work outdoors.
choices.C: Most Impressionist paintings were completed in the studio rather than outdoors.
choices.D: Before 1841, painters were unable to work outdoors at all.

explanation.why: Text 1 says the tube "kept paint fresh and portable" so painters could work outdoors. Text 2 agrees that "Portable paint certainly encouraged painting outdoors." The authors differ on how far the studio lost its role, but both accept that the tube made outdoor painting easier.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 uses the Rouen Cathedral paintings to show the studio's continuing role, the opposite of this claim.
explanation.B: Correct. Both texts agree that portable tube paint encouraged painters to work in the open air.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says only that the idea of finishing every canvas outdoors is misleading; it does not say most were finished in the studio, and Text 1 would disagree.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 1 says paint in bladders was hard to carry, not that outdoor work was impossible, and Text 2 does not address the point.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: George Eliot's Middlemarch (1871–1872) opens by comparing its heroine, Dorothea Brooke, to Saint Theresa, a woman whose longing for a great life found a great outlet. Dorothea's longing finds none. By the novel's close she has married Will Ladislaw and given herself to his career and their family, and the narrator concedes that her influence was not widely visible. For critic Hana Kubová, the ending thus registers a defeat: a society that offered women no grand vocation reduced an epic nature to a merely private one.
items.passage_b: Readers who see only loss in Dorothea's fate overlook the claim with which Eliot ends the book. The narrator insists that the good of the world depends partly on "unhistoric acts" performed by people who lived faithfully and left no famous name, and that Dorothea's effect on those around her was "incalculably diffusive." The novel laments the narrowing of her opportunities, but it refuses to equate an obscure life with a wasted one.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of the ending in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that Eliot meant Dorothea's marriage to fulfill her longing for a great life
choices.B: By denying that the novel presents Dorothea's opportunities as limited by her society
choices.C: By granting that her prospects narrowed but denying that her life amounts to a defeat
choices.D: By arguing that Dorothea's influence was in fact widely visible to those around her

explanation.why: Text 2 agrees that "The novel laments the narrowing of her opportunities," so it accepts part of Kubová's reading. But it points to the narrator's praise of "unhistoric acts" and of Dorothea's "incalculably diffusive" effect, and says the novel "refuses to equate an obscure life with a wasted one." Text 2 therefore rejects the conclusion that the ending registers a defeat.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 does not say the marriage fulfilled her epic longing; it argues that a life of quiet influence still has worth.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the novel "laments the narrowing of her opportunities," so it accepts that her society limited her.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 accepts that her prospects were narrowed but argues that the ending honors, rather than mourns, an obscure but influential life.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 calls her influence "diffusive" and her life "obscure"; it values her influence without claiming it was widely visible.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Among the earliest sculptures to show the Buddha in human form are works from Gandhara, a region in what is now northwestern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan. Their figures wear heavy, deeply folded robes and have wavy hair and calm, idealized faces strikingly like those of Greek statues. Art historian Farhan Siddiqi traces these features to the Greek kingdoms that ruled the region in the centuries after Alexander the Great's campaigns, arguing that Gandharan sculptors inherited a Hellenistic tradition planted there by those rulers.
items.passage_b: That Gandharan sculpture draws on Greco-Roman models is beyond question; what remains open is the route. The Greek kingdoms of the region had disappeared by around the start of the Common Era, whereas most Gandharan Buddhas were carved during the following centuries, when the region traded extensively with the Roman Empire. The closest parallels to Gandharan drapery and portrait heads, moreover, are found not in earlier Hellenistic work but in the art of Roman provinces from that later period.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Siddiqi in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that the Greek kingdoms themselves commissioned the earliest Gandharan Buddhas
choices.B: By questioning whether Gandharan sculpture resembles Greco-Roman art in any meaningful way
choices.C: By accepting the sculptures' classical character while proposing another source for it
choices.D: By suggesting that artists from Rome traveled to Gandhara to carve the sculptures themselves

explanation.why: Text 2 says it is "beyond question" that Gandharan sculpture draws on Greco-Roman models, so it accepts the resemblance Siddiqi describes. Its disagreement is over "the route": the Greek kingdoms were gone before most of the sculptures were carved, and the best parallels lie in later Roman provincial art. Text 2 keeps the classical influence but traces it to Roman-era contact instead of the Greek kingdoms.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is closer to Text 1's view; Text 2 notes that the Greek kingdoms had disappeared before most Gandharan Buddhas were made.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 calls the debt to Greco-Roman models "beyond question."
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 agrees the sculptures look classical but argues that the influence came through later trade with the Roman world, not from the earlier Greek rulers.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 points to trade and artistic parallels, not to Roman artists working in Gandhara.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Every twenty years, the main sanctuaries of the Ise Grand Shrine in Japan are rebuilt from new timber on a site beside the old ones, after which the previous buildings are dismantled. The practice has continued, with some interruptions, for some 1,300 years. To conservation theorist Mark Ellery, who holds that a monument's authenticity resides in the original material surviving from its making, the shrine is a remarkable tradition but not an ancient building, since nothing that stands there today is more than two decades old.
items.passage_b: Ellery's standard works well for a cathedral whose stones were laid once, but it assumes that every culture locates a building's value in the same place. At Ise, what is preserved is the design, the carpentry techniques passed from master to apprentice, and the ritual of renewal itself; letting old timber stand would break the very tradition that makes the shrine what it is. Judged by what its builders aim to keep, the shrine is among the most faithfully preserved structures in the world.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the judgment of the shrine in Text 1?

choices.A: By contending that his standard ignores what the shrine's tradition actually seeks to preserve
choices.B: By rejecting the idea that original material matters to the authenticity of any building
choices.C: By disputing Text 1's account of how often the shrine is rebuilt and for how long
choices.D: By agreeing that only original material confers authenticity but claiming that Ise retains some

explanation.why: Text 2 says Ellery's standard "assumes that every culture locates a building's value in the same place." At Ise, what is kept is "the design, the carpentry techniques ... and the ritual of renewal," so judged by "what its builders aim to keep," the shrine is faithfully preserved. Text 2 argues that a material-based standard misses what this tradition preserves.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 argues that the shrine preserves design, skill, and ritual rather than timber, so a standard based on original material misjudges it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says Ellery's standard "works well for a cathedral," so it does not reject the importance of material everywhere.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts the facts of the rebuilding and argues only about how to judge them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not claim any original material survives, and it denies that material is the only measure of authenticity.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On New Year's Day 1995, instruments on the Draupner platform in the North Sea recorded a single wave about 26 meters high amid seas in which the typical large waves were less than half that height. Such rogue waves were once dismissed as sailors' exaggerations. Physicist Lucia Ferreira argues that they arise mainly through a nonlinear process in which one wave in a group steadily draws energy from its neighbors, growing far beyond what the simple overlapping of waves would predict.
items.passage_b: That rogue waves are real, and that they tower over the typical waves around them, is no longer in doubt; their origin is less settled. Analyses of thousands of ocean wave records have found that most rogue waves occur about as often as would be expected if many ordinary waves, traveling at different speeds and in different directions, simply happened to pile up at one place and moment. Energy-stealing instabilities, which grow strongly in laboratory tanks, may be weakened at sea, where waves spread in many directions.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Rogue waves can be far taller than the typical large waves around them.
choices.B: Nonlinear instabilities are as powerful in the open sea as they are in laboratory tanks.
choices.C: The Draupner wave is the tallest wave that has ever been recorded in the open ocean.
choices.D: Rogue waves form mainly when waves traveling in different directions happen to pile up.

explanation.why: Text 1 describes the Draupner wave as about 26 meters high where typical large waves were "less than half that height." Text 2 says it is "no longer in doubt" that rogue waves "tower over the typical waves around them." The authors disagree about how rogue waves form, but both accept that they greatly exceed the surrounding waves.
explanation.A: Correct. Both texts treat rogue waves as real and far larger than the ordinary waves around them; they disagree only about the cause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 suggests these instabilities "may be weakened at sea," so its author would not agree.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Neither text claims the Draupner wave is the tallest ever recorded.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the view suggested in Text 2; Text 1 argues that rogue waves arise mainly through a nonlinear process instead.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In the final chapter of Edith Wharton's The Age of Innocence (1920), Newland Archer, now a widower in his late fifties, sits on a bench outside the Paris apartment of Ellen Olenska, the woman he loved and gave up decades earlier. He sends his son up to see her but does not follow, and at last walks back to his hotel alone. Critic Teodor Varga reads the scene as the final proof of Archer's timidity: offered one last chance at the life he wanted, he retreats once more, as he always has, from anything that might disturb his habits.
items.passage_b: The bench scene is easy to read as one more retreat, but Wharton has prepared for it with care. In the pages just before it, Archer reflects that his long marriage, however unexciting, held real duty and even a kind of dignity, and that he has missed something in life without wholly regretting what he chose instead. Seen against that reckoning, his decision to stay below looks less like a failure of nerve than like a recognition that the Ellen he has carried in memory cannot be recovered by climbing a staircase.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of the scene in Text 1?

choices.A: By attributing Archer's choice to a wish to stay loyal to the memory of his late wife
choices.B: By maintaining that Archer's earlier reflections make his choice seem considered
choices.C: By arguing that Archer's choice shows the timidity that defined the whole of his life
choices.D: By rejecting the view that Archer ever gave up Ellen for the sake of social convention

explanation.why: Varga sees the scene as "final proof of Archer's timidity." Text 2 grants that it is "easy to read as one more retreat" but points to Archer's reflections "in the pages just before it" and concludes that his choice "looks less like a failure of nerve than like a recognition" that the remembered Ellen cannot be recovered. Text 2 uses the earlier reflections to recast the choice as considered.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 mentions his marriage's duty and dignity, but it explains the choice by the gap between the remembered Ellen and the real one, not by loyalty to his wife.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 argues that Archer's reckoning with his past makes staying below a thoughtful recognition rather than a failure of nerve.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is Varga's reading in Text 1, which Text 2 argues against.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 does not deny that Archer gave Ellen up decades earlier; it reinterprets only his final decision.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Black Death, which swept across Europe between 1347 and 1351, killed perhaps a third or more of the continent's population. In England, the surviving laborers found themselves in demand: despite laws that tried to hold wages at preplague levels, pay rose, and over the following century serfdom largely disappeared. Economic historian Signe Dahl draws a general lesson from this outcome. When labor becomes scarce, she argues, the bargaining power of workers inevitably rises and the bonds of servitude weaken.
items.passage_b: Demographic shock alone cannot explain what happened next, because the shock did not produce the same result everywhere. In parts of eastern Europe, where labor was also in short supply, landowners responded over the following two centuries by tying peasants more firmly to their estates, a development historians call the "second serfdom." Whether scarcity empowered workers seems to have depended on whether lords were organized and strong enough to restrict peasants' movement.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the general lesson drawn by Dahl in Text 1?

choices.A: By suggesting that laws limiting wages worked far better in eastern Europe than they did in England
choices.B: By claiming that serfdom in England survived the plague largely unchanged
choices.C: By rejecting the idea that the plague had any lasting effect on European laborers
choices.D: By pointing to a case in which labor scarcity led to stronger rather than weaker servitude

explanation.why: Dahl claims that scarce labor "inevitably" strengthens workers and weakens servitude. Text 2 describes eastern Europe, "where labor was also in short supply," yet landowners tied peasants "more firmly to their estates." That single counterexample shows the outcome was not inevitable but depended on the power of lords.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 credits lords' power to restrict peasants' movement, not wage laws.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not challenge Text 1's account of England; it adds a contrasting case from eastern Europe.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says the plague's effects differed by region, not that it had no lasting effect.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2's account of the "second serfdom" in eastern Europe is a case where scarcity was followed by harsher, not looser, servitude.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On Earth, nearly all the oxygen in the atmosphere is produced by photosynthesis; without living things to replenish it, oxygen would react with rocks and volcanic gases and largely disappear. Astrobiologist Mireille Fontaine therefore argues that if telescopes detect abundant oxygen in the atmosphere of an Earth-sized planet orbiting another star, astronomers will have found strong evidence of life.
items.passage_b: Oxygen's link to life on Earth is not a law of nature. On a planet orbiting a small, active red dwarf star, intense ultraviolet light could split water molecules high in the atmosphere; the light hydrogen would escape to space, leaving oxygen behind, possibly in large amounts, on a world with no life at all. Oxygen would become persuasive only alongside other clues, such as methane, a gas that reacts with oxygen and should soon vanish unless something keeps replenishing both.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Fontaine in Text 1?

choices.A: By rejecting the claim that photosynthesis produces nearly all of Earth's atmospheric oxygen
choices.B: By claiming that methane, rather than oxygen, is the most reliable single sign of life
choices.C: By suggesting that planets orbiting red dwarf stars are unlikely to keep their atmospheres
choices.D: By arguing that oxygen on its own could mislead, since it might build up without any life

explanation.why: Fontaine treats abundant oxygen by itself as strong evidence of life. Text 2 describes how oxygen could accumulate "on a world with no life at all" and says oxygen "would become persuasive only alongside other clues." Text 2 would therefore say oxygen alone is not enough.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 speaks of "Oxygen's link to life on Earth" and does not dispute it; it denies only that the link must hold elsewhere.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 values methane only together with oxygen; it does not call methane by itself the most reliable sign.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2's red dwarf planet keeps its oxygen; nothing suggests such planets lose their atmospheres.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 shows how a lifeless planet could build up oxygen, so oxygen without other clues would not be strong evidence of life.

items.subject: science
items.passage: About 74,000 years ago, the Toba volcano on the island of Sumatra erupted with a force unmatched in the last two million years, spreading ash as far as India. Anthropologist Owen Trask argues that the eruption plunged the planet into a volcanic winter lasting years and that the resulting famine reduced early human populations to a few thousand individuals, a bottleneck that he believes can still be detected in the limited genetic diversity of living humans.
items.passage_b: At Jwalapuram, in southern India, a thick layer of Toba ash lies between deposits containing stone tools. The tools above the ash closely resemble those below it in style and manufacture, suggesting that the same population went on living and working in the valley after the eruption. A disaster severe enough to reduce humanity to a few thousand people should have left a clearer break in the record. If the region's toolmakers weathered Toba, the eruption's role in shaping human genetic diversity is open to doubt.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the argument made by Trask in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the limited genetic diversity of living humans has no known explanation
choices.B: By denying that ash from the Toba eruption reached as far as the Indian subcontinent
choices.C: By agreeing that a volcanic winter occurred but arguing that it lasted only a few months
choices.D: By citing archaeological continuity that casts doubt on a population-wide catastrophe

explanation.why: Trask claims Toba's volcanic winter shrank human populations to a few thousand. Text 2 reports that tools above and below the Toba ash at Jwalapuram are alike, "suggesting that the same population went on living" there, and says such a disaster "should have left a clearer break in the record." Text 2 uses this continuity to cast doubt on the catastrophe Trask describes.
