explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 doubts that Toba explains human genetic diversity but does not say the diversity has no explanation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 describes a thick layer of Toba ash in southern India, so it accepts that the ash reached India.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 never discusses how long a volcanic winter lasted.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 points to unbroken toolmaking at Jwalapuram as evidence against a disaster that nearly wiped out humanity.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Russian speakers must distinguish between two basic color terms, goluboy for lighter blues and siniy for darker ones, where English speakers use only "blue." In experiments, Russian speakers are faster than English speakers at telling apart two shades that fall on opposite sides of the goluboy-siniy boundary. Linguist Alina Petrova takes this as evidence that the language one speaks reshapes perception itself, so that Russian speakers literally see a sharper division among blues.
items.passage_b: Studies of this effect contain a revealing detail. When Russian speakers perform the same color task while silently rehearsing a string of numbers, a task that occupies verbal memory, their advantage at the goluboy-siniy boundary disappears; a demanding visual task of similar difficulty does not erase it. Language, these results suggest, speeds discrimination by being called on in the moment, as speakers covertly name what they see, rather than by permanently changing what their eyes deliver.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the interpretation offered by Petrova in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that language has no influence on how quickly speakers tell colors apart
choices.B: By denying that Russian speakers are faster than English speakers at telling the shades apart
choices.C: By accepting the advantage but tracing it to naming in the moment, not altered perception
choices.D: By arguing that the advantage reflects visual training rather than knowledge of Russian

explanation.why: Text 2 does not question that Russian speakers have an advantage; it notes that the advantage "disappears" when verbal memory is occupied but not when a visual task is added. It concludes that language helps "by being called on in the moment ... rather than by permanently changing what their eyes deliver." Text 2 accepts the finding but rejects Petrova's claim that perception itself is reshaped.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says language "speeds discrimination," so it does not deny language any influence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 refers to "their advantage" as a real result; it questions only what causes it.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 accepts the faster discrimination but explains it as silent naming during the task rather than a lasting change in what speakers see.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 links the advantage to verbal naming, and a visual task does not erase it, so visual training is not its explanation.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For decades, archaeologists debated whether farming spread into Europe through the movement of people or the movement of ideas. Ancient DNA has largely settled the question, according to geneticist Pieter Hollander. Skeletons of early farmers in central Europe carry ancestry derived mostly from farming populations of Anatolia and very little from the hunter-gatherers who lived there before them. Farming, Hollander concludes, came to Europe chiefly with incoming farmers who displaced the earlier inhabitants.
items.passage_b: The genetic results from central Europe are clear, and they confirm that migrating farmers carried agriculture into much of the continent. But Europe is large. Around the eastern Baltic, ancient genomes from communities that took up pottery and, in time, some farming practices show mostly local hunter-gatherer ancestry for many centuries after the change. There, at least, new ways of life seem to have spread largely through foragers adopting them, a pattern that samples drawn mainly from central Europe could not reveal.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion reached by Hollander in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that the central European genomes in fact show mostly local hunter-gatherer ancestry
choices.B: By accepting it for central Europe while noting a region where it does not appear to hold
choices.C: By claiming that farming spread through Europe mainly through the movement of ideas
choices.D: By suggesting that the farmers of Anatolia learned agriculture from European hunter-gatherers

explanation.why: Text 2 says the central European results "are clear" and "confirm that migrating farmers carried agriculture into much of the continent," so it accepts Hollander's conclusion there. It then points to the eastern Baltic, where local foragers seem to have adopted new practices themselves. Text 2 limits the conclusion rather than overturning it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 calls the central European results "clear" and accepts them; the local ancestry it describes comes from the Baltic.
explanation.B: Correct. Text 2 agrees that migration explains farming in central Europe but describes the eastern Baltic as an exception.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 says migrating farmers brought agriculture to "much of the continent"; it treats spread by ideas as a regional exception.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says nothing about where Anatolian farmers learned agriculture.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Beneath many forests, the threads of mycorrhizal fungi link the roots of neighboring trees into shared networks. In experiments in which researchers supply a large tree with carbon dioxide containing a traceable form of carbon, some of that carbon later turns up in nearby seedlings. Forest ecologist Maren Holt interprets such results as evidence that older trees use these fungal networks to nourish young ones, an exchange she believes helps seedlings survive in the deep shade of the forest floor.
items.passage_b: Labeled carbon does move from tree to seedling; the questions are how much and by what path. In most field studies, the amounts detected in seedlings are small, often too small to make a measurable difference to their growth. And because carbon could also travel through the soil or through roots that touch directly, finding it in a seedling does not show that the fungal network carried it there. Experiments that block each possible route in turn are needed before the network can be credited with nourishing anything.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the interpretation offered by Holt in Text 1?

choices.A: By contending that the results do not establish that the networks meaningfully feed seedlings
choices.B: By agreeing that the networks feed seedlings but doubting that this helps them survive in shade
choices.C: By denying that labeled carbon supplied to a large tree is ever found in nearby seedlings
choices.D: By claiming that seedlings get most of their carbon from the soil rather than from older trees

explanation.why: Text 2 accepts that "Labeled carbon does move from tree to seedling" but raises two problems: the amounts are "often too small to make a measurable difference," and the carbon could have traveled "through the soil or through roots that touch directly." Until other routes are ruled out, the network cannot "be credited with nourishing anything." Text 2 says the evidence falls short of Holt's interpretation.
explanation.A: Correct. Text 2 argues that the amounts are small and the route unproven, so the results do not show that the networks nourish seedlings in any meaningful way.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not agree that the networks feed seedlings; it says that has not been shown.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 states that labeled carbon "does move from tree to seedling."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 mentions the soil only as one possible route for the labeled carbon; it makes no claim about where seedlings get most of their carbon.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Before printing, every copy of a book was made by hand, and each scribe introduced errors of his own, so that no two manuscripts of a long text were identical. Historian Gérard Lemaire argues that the printing press, introduced in Europe in the mid-fifteenth century, changed this by fixing texts. Once type was set, hundreds of copies could be pulled from it in the time a scribe needed for one, and readers in distant cities could, for the first time, cite the same words on the same page.
items.passage_b: Printing did make it possible to produce many copies far faster than any scribe could. But early printed editions were less uniform than they appear. Printers routinely corrected errors while a sheet was being run, without discarding the sheets already printed, and then bound corrected and uncorrected sheets together. Surviving copies of a single edition, such as Shakespeare's First Folio of 1623, therefore often differ from one another. The stability we associate with print was a slow achievement of later practice, not an immediate effect of the press.
items.stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?

choices.A: Early printers seldom corrected errors once a book's type had been set.
choices.B: The stability of printed texts developed gradually through later printing practices.
choices.C: Copies of a single early printed edition were usually identical to one another.
choices.D: Printing allowed copies of a book to be produced far more quickly than by hand.

explanation.why: Text 1 says hundreds of copies could be printed "in the time a scribe needed for one." Text 2 agrees that printing made it possible "to produce many copies far faster than any scribe could." The authors disagree about whether early print fixed texts, but both accept that printing was much faster than hand copying.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says printers "routinely corrected errors" during a print run.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is Text 2's view; Text 1 presents fixed texts as an effect of the press itself.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 1 implies this, but Text 2 says copies of one edition "often differ from one another."
explanation.D: Correct. Both texts state that printing produced copies much faster than scribes could.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a honeybee colony outgrows its hive, thousands of bees leave with the old queen and cluster on a branch while scouts search for a new home. Returning scouts perform waggle dances advertising the sites they have found, and bees that have inspected a better site dance for it longer. Over several days, dances for inferior sites die out. Biologist Rafael Moreno argues that the swarm reaches its decision when the dancers achieve consensus, all advertising the same site, at which point the swarm takes flight.
items.passage_b: The dances clearly do the work of comparing sites: better sites recruit more inspectors. But the trigger for departure lies elsewhere. Scouts visiting a candidate site keep track, apparently by how often they encounter one another, of how many bees are present there. Once that number passes a threshold, they return and begin preparing the swarm to fly, sometimes while dances for rival sites are still under way. The choice is settled by a quorum at the site, not by unanimity on the cluster.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the account of how the swarm reaches its decision in Text 1?

choices.A: By claiming that dances for inferior sites always continue until the swarm takes flight
choices.B: By rejecting the idea that waggle dances help the swarm compare possible nest sites
choices.C: By agreeing that dances compare sites but locating the decision in a quorum at the site
choices.D: By arguing that a swarm departs only after every scout has inspected the chosen site

explanation.why: Text 2 agrees that "The dances clearly do the work of comparing sites." But it says departure is triggered when the number of scouts at one site "passes a threshold," "sometimes while dances for rival sites are still under way." So the decision comes from a quorum at the site, not the consensus among dancers that Moreno describes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says rival dances continue only "sometimes"; it does not say they always last until departure.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the dances "clearly do the work of comparing sites."
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 keeps the dances' role in comparing sites but argues that a quorum of scouts at a site, not unanimous dancing, settles the choice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says a threshold number of bees at the site is enough; it never requires every scout to visit.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Where did human language begin? Psychologist Naomi Adler argues that it began in the hands. Chimpanzees and other great apes, she notes, use dozens of gestures flexibly: an individual adjusts its gestures to the attention of its audience and repeats or changes them when it is not understood. Their vocal calls, by contrast, appear largely fixed and tied to emotional states. Because flexible, intentional signaling is a precondition for language, Adler concludes that language must have first emerged as gesture and only later shifted to speech.
items.passage_b: The contrast between flexible ape gestures and rigid ape calls was once widely accepted, but it has softened. Field studies now show that chimpanzees produce some calls selectively, calling more when companions seem unaware of a danger than when they already know of it, and captive orangutans have learned to produce new sounds by imitation. If vocal signaling in apes is more controllable than once thought, the case for a gesture-only stage loses its main support, and language may have drawn on hand and voice together from the start.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the conclusion reached by Adler in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that great apes adjust their gestures to the attention of their audience
choices.B: By rejecting the idea that flexible, intentional signaling is a necessary precondition for language
choices.C: By claiming that human language began as speech and only later came to include gesture
choices.D: By arguing that it rests on a contrast between gesture and voice that newer evidence weakens

explanation.why: Adler's conclusion depends on the contrast between flexible gestures and "largely fixed" calls. Text 2 says that contrast "has softened," citing chimpanzees that call selectively and orangutans that learn new sounds, so "the case for a gesture-only stage loses its main support." Text 2 attacks the premise about ape calls rather than the importance of flexible signaling.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that ape gestures are flexible; it questions only how rigid their calls are.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 never questions this premise; it disputes the claim that only gestures met it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Text 2 suggests hand and voice worked "together from the start," not that speech came first.
explanation.D: Correct. Text 2 argues that apes' calls are more controllable than Adler assumes, which undercuts the contrast her conclusion relies on.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Anton Chekhov's story "The Lady with the Dog" (1899) begins with Dmitri Gurov, a jaded Moscow banker who regards women with contempt, starting an affair at a seaside resort that he expects to forget within weeks. Instead, back in Moscow, he cannot stop thinking of Anna, and by the end he recognizes that only now, as his hair turns gray, has he truly fallen in love. Critic Elif Arslan reads the story as a tale of redemption: love has transformed a cynic into a man capable of tenderness.
items.passage_b: Gurov's change of heart is genuine; Chekhov leaves no doubt that he has come to love Anna. What the story withholds is any sense that this love has delivered him. Its final scene finds the lovers in a Moscow hotel room, still meeting in secret, still married to others, and still unable to imagine how they might live openly. They feel that a solution must be near, yet both understand that the hardest part has barely begun. A reading that ends in redemption completes a story that Chekhov deliberately leaves open.
items.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading of the story in Text 1?

choices.A: By denying that Gurov comes to feel genuine love for Anna by the end of the story
choices.B: By suggesting that the story's open ending reveals Chekhov's disapproval of the affair
choices.C: By granting that Gurov changes but denying that the story resolves his situation
choices.D: By claiming that the lovers find a way to live together openly in the story's final scene

explanation.why: Text 2 agrees that "Gurov's change of heart is genuine," accepting part of Arslan's reading. It objects that the story "withholds any sense that this love has delivered him": the lovers are still hiding, and "the hardest part has barely begun." A redemption reading, Text 2 says, "completes a story that Chekhov deliberately leaves open."
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says Chekhov "leaves no doubt that he has come to love Anna."
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says the ending is open, but it never says Chekhov disapproves of the affair.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 accepts that Gurov truly changes but says calling it redemption imposes an ending that the open final scene withholds.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the lovers are "still unable to imagine how they might live openly."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: At exactly noon, the old clocks in Mr. Adeyemi's repair shop ______ all at once, filling the narrow room with chimes, bells, and the cry of a wooden cuckoo. His new apprentice, Tunde, still jumps at the sound every day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: rings
choices.B: ring
choices.C: is ringing
choices.D: has rung

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "clocks," which is plural; "in Mr. Adeyemi's repair shop" only tells where the clocks are. A plural subject needs a plural verb, and the rest of the passage is in the simple present ("jumps"), so "ring" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Rings" is singular and agrees with "shop," but the subject is the plural "clocks."
explanation.B: Correct. The plural verb "ring" agrees with the plural subject "clocks."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Is ringing" is singular, but the subject "clocks" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Has rung" is singular, but the subject "clocks" is plural.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Louvre in Paris first opened as a public museum in 1793, during the French Revolution. Today, ______ collection holds hundreds of thousands of objects, so only a small fraction of them can be displayed at any one time.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it's
choices.B: their
choices.C: its
choices.D: its'

explanation.why: The blank must show that the collection belongs to the Louvre, a single museum. The possessive form of "it" is "its," with no apostrophe.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "It's" is a contraction of "it is" or "it has"; "it is collection" makes no sense.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Their" is plural, but it refers to the Louvre, which is singular.
explanation.C: Correct. "Its" is the singular possessive pronoun, showing the collection belongs to the Louvre.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Its'" is not a word in Standard English; the possessive "its" never takes an apostrophe.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Rosetta Stone, found in Egypt in 1799, records a single royal decree in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic, and ancient Greek. Because the scholars who studied it could already read Greek, the stone gave ______ a way to work out the meaning of the other two scripts, though fully deciphering the hieroglyphs still took more than twenty years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them
choices.B: it
choices.C: they
choices.D: him

explanation.why: The ones who were given a way to work out the other scripts are "the scholars," a plural noun. The pronoun is also the object of "gave," so it must be the plural object pronoun "them."
explanation.A: Correct. "Them" is plural, matching "scholars," and is the object form needed after "gave."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but it must refer to the plural "scholars"; the stone did not give a way to itself or to the Greek text.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "They" is a subject pronoun; after the verb "gave," the object form "them" is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Him" is singular and refers to no one in the text; the antecedent "scholars" is plural.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before 1869, traveling from New York to San Francisco meant a long wagon journey or a sea voyage of several months. When the first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah, in May of that year, it ______ the trip to about a week. The celebrations, however, largely ignored the thousands of Chinese immigrant workers who had built much of the line through the Sierra Nevada.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: shortens
choices.B: has shortened
choices.C: will shorten
choices.D: shortened

explanation.why: The sentence describes a single finished event at a stated past time: "When the first transcontinental railroad … was completed … in May of that year" (1869). The other verbs in the passage, such as "was completed" and "ignored," are also in the past, so the simple past "shortened" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present tense "shortens" doesn't fit an event the text places in 1869.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present perfect "has shortened" isn't used with a specific finished past time such as "in May of that year."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The future "will shorten" doesn't fit an event that already happened in 1869.
explanation.D: Correct. The simple past "shortened" matches the past time "in May of that year" and the past-tense verbs around it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The 1977 discovery of hydrothermal vents along the Galápagos Rift, where scientists aboard the submersible Alvin found tube worms, clams, and crabs crowded around openings in the seafloor roughly 2,500 meters below the surface, ______ one of the most consequential findings in modern biology. It showed that entire communities of animals can depend on bacteria that draw energy from chemicals rather than from sunlight.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: remain
choices.B: remains
choices.C: have remained
choices.D: are

explanation.why: Strip away the long modifiers and the sentence reads "The 1977 discovery … remains one of the most consequential findings." The subject is the singular noun "discovery"; "vents," "scientists," "worms," "clams," "crabs" and "openings" all sit inside phrases that describe it. A singular subject needs the singular verb "remains."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Remain" is plural and seems to agree with nearby plural nouns such as "vents" or "openings," but the subject is the singular "discovery."
explanation.B: Correct. The singular verb "remains" agrees with the singular subject "discovery."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have remained" is plural, but the subject "discovery" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Are" is plural, but the subject "discovery" is singular.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In the 1840s, many reviewers judged a novel differently depending on whether they believed its author was a man or a woman. Publishing under the pen name Currer Bell, a name she chose partly because it did not reveal her sex, ______ Reviewers soon began guessing about who the mysterious author really was.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Charlotte Brontë's novel Jane Eyre was published in 1847 and quickly became a success.
choices.B: the novel Jane Eyre was published by Charlotte Brontë in 1847 and quickly became a success.
choices.C: Charlotte Brontë released Jane Eyre in 1847, and the novel quickly became a success.
choices.D: in 1847 Jane Eyre, a novel by Charlotte Brontë, appeared and quickly became a success.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Publishing under the pen name Currer Bell, a name she chose …" describes the person who published. An introductory modifier applies to the subject that comes right after it, so that subject must be Charlotte Brontë herself, not her novel.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "Charlotte Brontë's novel Jane Eyre," so the sentence says the novel was publishing under a pen name and chose it; the modifier dangles.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "the novel Jane Eyre," so the novel, not Brontë, seems to be publishing under the pen name.
explanation.C: Correct. "Charlotte Brontë" comes right after the introductory phrase, so she is the one publishing under the pen name she chose.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "Jane Eyre," the novel, so the introductory phrase wrongly describes the book as the one choosing a pen name.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Gitanjali (Song Offerings), the 1912 collection of devotional poems that Rabindranath Tagore translated from his own Bengali verse into spare English prose and that so impressed the Irish poet W. B. Yeats that Yeats agreed to write its introduction, ______ Tagore the Nobel Prize in Literature the following year, making him the first non-European writer to receive the award.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: earning
choices.B: having earned
choices.C: to earn
choices.D: earned

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "Gitanjali (Song Offerings)"; everything from "the 1912 collection" to "its introduction" is a long description of it, and the verbs inside it ("translated," "impressed," "agreed") belong to the "that" clauses. The sentence still needs its own main verb, so the blank must be a finite verb: "earned."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Earning" is a participle, not a main verb, so the sentence would have no main verb and would be a fragment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Having earned" is a participle phrase, not a main verb, so the subject "Gitanjali" would be left without a verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "To earn" is an infinitive, which can't serve as the main verb of a sentence.
explanation.D: Correct. The past-tense verb "earned" gives the subject "Gitanjali (Song Offerings)" its main verb and fits the past time of the passage.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper on a dry plaster wall in Milan in the 1490s, experimenting with a technique that, unlike traditional fresco, did not bind the pigment into wet plaster; within a few decades the paint had begun to flake. A team of conservators spent more than twenty years, from 1978 to 1999, cleaning the mural. The ______ choice to strip away centuries of earlier retouching, and to fill the resulting gaps with pale watercolor rather than reconstruct Leonardo's lost brushwork, divided critics.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: conservator's
choices.B: conservators'
choices.C: conservators
choices.D: conservators's

explanation.why: The choice belonged to "a team of conservators," so the word in the blank must be plural and possessive. A plural noun that already ends in s forms its possessive by adding only an apostrophe: "conservators'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Conservator's" is the possessive of one conservator, but the text says the work was done by a team of conservators.
explanation.B: Correct. "Conservators'" is the plural possessive, showing that the choice belonged to the whole team.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Conservators" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it doesn't show that the choice belonged to them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession; "conservators's" is not standard.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Hummingbirds can hover in place in front of a flower and can even fly backward. To stay in the air this way, the wings of a small hummingbird ______ remarkably fast. In some species, they beat more than 50 times per second, so quickly that they look like a blur to the human eye.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: is moving
choices.B: move
choices.C: moves
choices.D: has moved

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "wings," which is plural; "of a small hummingbird" only tells whose wings they are. A plural subject needs a plural verb, and the passage is in the simple present ("beat," "look"), so "move" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Is moving" is singular, but the subject "wings" is plural.
explanation.B: Correct. The plural verb "move" agrees with the plural subject "wings."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Moves" is singular and seems to agree with "hummingbird," but the subject is the plural "wings."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Has moved" is singular, but the subject "wings" is plural.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Thangkas are detailed Buddhist paintings on cloth made in Nepal, Tibet, and other parts of the Himalayas. Traditional thangka painters often make ______ own colors by grinding minerals into fine powders: malachite gives a rich green, and azurite gives a deep blue. The powders are then mixed with a glue made from animal hide.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them
choices.B: their
choices.C: his
choices.D: its

explanation.why: The people who make the colors are "painters," a plural noun. The blank needs a possessive pronoun that refers to them, so the plural possessive "their" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Them" is an object pronoun, not a possessive one; "make them own colors" is not Standard English.
explanation.B: Correct. "Their" is the plural possessive pronoun, matching "painters."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "His" is singular, but the antecedent "painters" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Its" is singular and refers to a thing, but the antecedent "painters" is plural and refers to people.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The ancient Phoenicians, who lived along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean Sea, became famous for a deep purple dye. To make it, workers crushed huge numbers of murex sea snails and collected a liquid from the ______ glands. Because thousands of snails were needed for a small amount of dye, purple cloth was extremely expensive.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: snail's
choices.B: snails
choices.C: snails'
choices.D: snails's

explanation.why: The glands belong to the snails, and the text says workers crushed "huge numbers" of them, so the owner is plural. A plural noun that ends in -s shows possession with an apostrophe after the s: "snails'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Snail's" is singular possessive, but the glands came from many snails, not one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Snails" is plural but not possessive; the glands belong to the snails, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.C: Correct. "Snails'" is the plural possessive, showing the glands belong to many snails.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Snails's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Last Saturday, Hana woke up before sunrise to help her grandfather at the farmers' market. She carried crates of peaches to his stall, wrote prices on small chalkboards, and ______ change for customers until almost noon. By the time they packed up, only one crate of peaches was left.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: will count
choices.B: counted
choices.C: counts
choices.D: has counted

explanation.why: The story happened "last Saturday," and the blank is the third verb in a list that already uses the simple past: "carried," "wrote," and ______. The verb must also be in the simple past, so "counted" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Will count" is future tense, but the events already happened.
explanation.B: Correct. "Counted" is simple past, matching "carried" and "wrote" and the time "last Saturday."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Counts" is present tense, but the events took place last Saturday and the other verbs in the list are past tense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Has counted" is present perfect, which does not fit a finished event at a specific past time like "last Saturday."

items.subject: science
items.passage: The kiwi, a flightless bird found only in New Zealand, hunts mostly at night. Unlike other birds, it has its nostrils at the very tip of its long, thin bill, which helps it find food it cannot see. Poking its bill deep into the soil, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the kiwi sniffs out worms and insects.
choices.B: the soil gives the kiwi the smell of worms and insects.
choices.C: the kiwi's sense of smell finds worms and insects.
choices.D: worms and insects are sniffed out by the kiwi.

explanation.why: The phrase "Poking its bill deep into the soil" describes whoever is doing the poking, so the words right after the comma must name that one: the kiwi. Only one choice places "the kiwi" directly after the introductory phrase.
explanation.A: Correct. "The kiwi" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear the kiwi pokes its bill into the soil.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This choice says the soil poked its bill into the soil, which makes no sense.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This choice says the kiwi's sense of smell poked its bill into the soil; the modifier must describe the bird itself.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This choice places "worms and insects" after the phrase, which says the worms and insects poked their bill into the soil.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Taiko is a style of Japanese drumming in which groups of performers strike large drums with heavy wooden sticks. The deep sound of the biggest drums ______ through the whole concert hall, and audience members often say they can feel each beat in their chests.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: travel
choices.B: travels
choices.C: are traveling
choices.D: have traveled

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "sound," which is singular; "of the biggest drums" only describes the sound. A singular subject needs a singular verb, and the passage is in the present tense ("say," "can feel"), so "travels" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Travel" is plural and seems to agree with "drums," but the subject is the singular "sound."
explanation.B: Correct. The singular verb "travels" agrees with the singular subject "sound."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are traveling" is plural, but the subject "sound" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Have traveled" is plural, but the subject "sound" is singular.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Hatshepsut, one of the few women to rule ancient Egypt as pharaoh, reigned for about twenty years in the 1400s BCE. During that time, she ordered many temples and monuments to be built. Among ______ most famous projects is a temple at Deir el-Bahari, near the city of Thebes, whose rows of columns rise in terraces against tall cliffs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: their
choices.B: hers
choices.C: she
choices.D: her

explanation.why: The projects belong to Hatshepsut, one woman, so the blank needs a singular possessive pronoun that can come before a noun ("most famous projects"). That pronoun is "her."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Their" is plural, but the antecedent "Hatshepsut" is one person.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Hers" stands alone ("the idea was hers") and cannot come directly before a noun such as "projects."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "She" is a subject pronoun, not a possessive one; "she most famous projects" is not Standard English.
explanation.D: Correct. "Her" is the singular possessive form used before a noun, matching "Hatshepsut."

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Himalayas hold thousands of glaciers, huge masses of ice that move slowly down mountain valleys. Each summer, the ______ meltwater flows into rivers such as the Indus, the Ganges, and the Brahmaputra. Farms and cities far downstream in Pakistan, India, and Bangladesh depend in part on this water.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: glaciers
choices.B: glaciers'
choices.C: glaciers's
choices.D: glacier's

explanation.why: The meltwater comes from the "thousands of glaciers," so the owner is plural. A plural noun ending in -s shows possession with an apostrophe after the s: "glaciers'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Glaciers" is plural but not possessive; an apostrophe is needed to show the meltwater belongs to them.
explanation.B: Correct. "Glaciers'" is the plural possessive, showing the meltwater comes from many glaciers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Glaciers's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Glacier's" is singular possessive, but the meltwater comes from thousands of glaciers.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the mid-1900s, bald eagles nearly disappeared from much of the United States. The pesticide DDT made the shells of their eggs so thin that many broke before the chicks could hatch. After DDT was banned in 1972, the number of nesting pairs ______ steadily, and in 2007 the bald eagle was removed from the list of threatened and endangered species.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: increased
choices.B: increasing
choices.C: to increase
choices.D: having increased

explanation.why: The clause "the number of nesting pairs ______ steadily" has a subject ("the number") but needs a main verb. Only a finite verb can serve as the main verb of a clause, and the passage tells past events, so "increased" is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. "Increased" is a finite past-tense verb, giving the clause the main verb it needs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Increasing" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the clause would have no main verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "To increase" is an infinitive and cannot serve as the main verb of the clause.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Having increased" is a participle phrase, not a finite verb, so the clause would have no main verb.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Anna Mary Robertson Moses spent most of her life working on farms in New York and Virginia. Taking up painting seriously in her late seventies, ______ Her bright, detailed scenes of country life were being shown in New York galleries within just a few years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: she became famous as "Grandma Moses."
choices.B: fame came to her under the name "Grandma Moses."
choices.C: her paintings of rural life made her famous as "Grandma Moses."
choices.D: the name "Grandma Moses" became well known.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Taking up painting seriously in her late seventies" describes the person who took up painting, so that person must be named right after the comma. Only one choice begins with "she," meaning Moses.
explanation.A: Correct. "She" (Moses) comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear she took up painting.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This choice says fame took up painting; the modifier must describe Moses herself.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This choice says her paintings took up painting, which makes no sense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This choice says the name "Grandma Moses" took up painting, which makes no sense.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Sigiriya is a massive rock in central Sri Lanka where King Kashyapa built a palace in the late 400s CE. Partway up the rock, the paintings on a sheltered wall ______ elegant women holding flowers. Protected from the rain by overhanging stone, their colors have stayed bright for about 1,500 years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: is showing
choices.B: show
choices.C: has shown
choices.D: shows

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "paintings," which is plural; "on a sheltered wall" only tells where they are. A plural subject needs a plural verb, so "show" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Is showing" is singular, but the subject "paintings" is plural.
explanation.B: Correct. The plural verb "show" agrees with the plural subject "paintings."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Has shown" is singular, but the subject "paintings" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Shows" is singular and seems to agree with "wall," but the subject is the plural "paintings."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When the rain started on our walk home from school, my friend Priya opened her large green umbrella and held it over both ______ and herself. We walked the last six blocks pressed close together, splashing through puddles and laughing every time a gust of wind tried to turn the umbrella inside out.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: me
choices.B: I
choices.C: mine
choices.D: myself

explanation.why: The narrator is the object of the preposition "over" ("over both ______ and herself"). An object needs the object pronoun "me." "Herself" works because Priya is the subject, but the narrator is not the subject of this clause.
explanation.A: Correct. "Me" is the object pronoun needed after the preposition "over."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "I" is a subject pronoun, but the blank is the object of "over."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Mine" is possessive ("the umbrella is mine"); nothing here is owned by the narrator.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Myself" is reflexive and can be used only when "I" is the subject of the same clause; here the subject is Priya.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Guggenheim Museum Bilbao in northern Spain, designed by the architect Frank Gehry, opened in 1997. Much of the ______ curving exterior is covered in thin titanium panels that seem to change color with the weather and the light. The museum quickly became one of the most widely recognized buildings of its time.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: buildings's
choices.B: buildings'
choices.C: buildings
choices.D: building's

explanation.why: The curving exterior belongs to one building, the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao. A singular noun shows possession with an apostrophe and s: "building's."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Buildings's" is not a Standard English form.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Buildings'" is plural possessive, but the text describes a single building.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Buildings" is plural and not possessive; the exterior belongs to one building.
explanation.D: Correct. "Building's" is the singular possessive, showing the exterior belongs to the one museum.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: On June 16, 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova ______ the first woman to travel into space. During her flight aboard Vostok 6, which lasted almost three days, she orbited Earth 48 times. Before training as a cosmonaut, she had worked in a textile factory and practiced parachute jumping as a hobby.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has become
choices.B: will become
choices.C: became
choices.D: becomes

explanation.why: The sentence describes an event on a specific past date, June 16, 1963, and the rest of the passage uses the past tense ("lasted," "orbited"). The simple past "became" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Has become" is present perfect, which does not fit an action tied to a specific past date.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Will become" is future tense, but the event is in the past.
explanation.C: Correct. "Became" is simple past, matching the specific past date and the other past-tense verbs.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Becomes" is present tense, but the event happened in 1963.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1941, after a walk in the Swiss countryside, engineer George de Mestral noticed burdock burrs stuck to his dog's fur. Studying them under a microscope, ______ He later used this idea to design Velcro, a fastener made of one strip of fabric with tiny hooks and another with tiny loops.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: de Mestral's microscope showed tiny hooks on the burrs.
choices.B: de Mestral saw that the burrs were covered in tiny hooks.
choices.C: tiny hooks were found covering the burrs.
choices.D: the burrs were seen to be covered in tiny hooks.

explanation.why: The phrase "Studying them under a microscope" describes the person who did the studying, so that person must be named right after the comma. Only one choice begins with "de Mestral."
explanation.A: Incorrect. This choice says the microscope studied the burrs; "de Mestral's" only describes the microscope, which is the subject.
explanation.B: Correct. "De Mestral" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear he studied the burrs.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This choice says tiny hooks did the studying, which makes no sense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This choice says the burrs studied themselves under a microscope.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Nakshi kantha is a quilting tradition from Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal. Women stitch together layers of old cotton saris and then cover the cloth with colorful embroidery. A single quilt, decorated with flowers, fish, and scenes from village life, often ______ several months to finish.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are taking
choices.B: take
choices.C: have taken
choices.D: takes

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "quilt," which is singular; the phrase between the commas only describes it. A singular subject needs a singular verb, and the passage is in the present tense, so "takes" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are taking" is plural, but the subject "quilt" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Take" is plural and seems to agree with "flowers," "fish," or "scenes," but the subject is the singular "quilt."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have taken" is plural, but the subject "quilt" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular verb "takes" agrees with the singular subject "quilt."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Young sunflower plants follow the Sun across the sky. Each morning, the growing plants face east, and during the day ______ slowly turn toward the west. At night, they swing back to the east to wait for sunrise. Once the plants are fully grown, however, most of them stop moving and face east all day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: they
choices.B: its
choices.C: them
choices.D: it

explanation.why: The blank is the subject of the verb "turn," and it refers to "the growing plants," which is plural. The plural subject pronoun "they" is correct; the passage itself uses "they" for the plants in the next sentence.
explanation.A: Correct. "They" is the plural subject pronoun, matching "plants."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Its" is a singular possessive, not a subject pronoun.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Them" is an object pronoun, but the blank is the subject of "turn."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but it must refer to the plural "plants"; "it slowly turn" also lacks agreement.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: As the train slowed to a stop, Amira pressed her face to the window, searching the crowded platform for her older brother. When she finally spotted him waving a handmade sign with her name on it, she ______ her bag and hurried toward the door.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: to grab
choices.B: grabs
choices.C: grabbing
choices.D: grabbed

explanation.why: In the clause "she ______ her bag and hurried toward the door," the blank and "hurried" are two main verbs joined by "and." The blank needs a finite verb in the same simple past tense as "hurried" and "spotted," so "grabbed" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "To grab" is an infinitive and cannot serve as the main verb after "she."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Grabs" is present tense, but the story is told in the past ("slowed," "spotted," "hurried").
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Grabbing" is a participle, not a finite verb, so "she grabbing her bag" has no main verb.
explanation.D: Correct. "Grabbed" is a finite past-tense verb, matching "hurried" and the rest of the story.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Leafcutter ants do not eat the leaves they carry back to their nests. Instead, workers chew the pieces into a pulp on which they grow a fungus, and it is the fungus that the ants eat. Each colony raises its own fungus garden, and the ______ survival depends on keeping that garden healthy, so smaller workers constantly remove mold and waste from it while larger ones guard the nest.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: colonies
choices.B: colonys'
choices.C: colonies'
choices.D: colony's

explanation.why: The sentence begins "Each colony raises its own fungus garden," so the survival being discussed belongs to one colony. A singular noun shows possession with an apostrophe and s: "colony's." The earlier plural nouns ("ants," "workers," "nests") are a distraction.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Colonies" is plural and not possessive, but the survival belongs to one colony.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Colonys'" is not a Standard English form; the singular possessive of "colony" is "colony's."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Colonies'" is plural possessive, but "Each colony" and "its own" show that one colony is meant.
explanation.D: Correct. "Colony's" is the singular possessive, matching "Each colony" and "its own fungus garden."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the early 1400s, most writing in Korea was done in Chinese characters, which took years to master, so relatively few ordinary people could read. Hoping to change this, ______ The original script had 28 letters, each designed to be simple to learn, and the Korean alphabet used today keeps 24 of them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: King Sejong's new alphabet, now known as Hangul, was introduced in 1446.
choices.B: a new alphabet, now known as Hangul, was introduced by King Sejong in 1446.
choices.C: King Sejong introduced a new alphabet, now known as Hangul, in 1446.
choices.D: the introduction of a new alphabet, now known as Hangul, came from King Sejong in 1446.

explanation.why: "Hoping to change this" describes someone who hoped, so the noun right after the comma must name that person, King Sejong. An alphabet, an introduction, or a possessive like "King Sejong's" cannot do the hoping.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject here is "alphabet"; "King Sejong's" only describes it, so the sentence says the alphabet did the hoping.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This choice places "a new alphabet" after the phrase, saying the alphabet hoped to change things.
explanation.C: Correct. "King Sejong" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear he is the one who hoped to change this.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This choice says "the introduction" hoped to change things; the modifier must describe a person.

items.subject: science
items.passage: India's summer monsoon usually reaches the southern state of Kerala first and then spreads north over the following weeks. The arrival of the monsoon rains on the Kerala coast, which forecasters at the India Meteorological Department watch closely each year, typically ______ around June 1, although the date can vary by a week or more. For many farmers, this arrival signals that planting season is near.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: occur
choices.B: have occurred
choices.C: are occurring
choices.D: occurs

explanation.why: Strip away the modifiers and the sentence reads "The arrival … typically occurs around June 1." The subject is the singular "arrival"; "rains," "forecasters," and the other nouns sit inside phrases that describe it. A singular subject needs the singular verb "occurs," which also fits a yearly pattern described in the present tense.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Occur" is plural and seems to agree with "rains" or "forecasters," but the subject is the singular "arrival."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Have occurred" is plural, but the subject "arrival" is singular.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are occurring" is plural, but the subject "arrival" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular verb "occurs" agrees with the singular subject "arrival."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Before a concert begins, the members of an orchestra tune ______ instruments to a single note, usually an A played by the principal oboist. The oboe is given this job partly because its clear, penetrating tone is easy for everyone on stage to hear and partly because the pitch of an oboe is harder to adjust quickly than that of many other instruments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: their
choices.C: his or her
choices.D: one's

explanation.why: The people who tune the instruments are "the members," a plural noun; "of an orchestra" only says which members. The pronoun must be plural and possessive, so "their" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Its" is singular and seems to refer to "orchestra," but the subject doing the tuning is the plural "members."
explanation.B: Correct. "Their" is the plural possessive pronoun, matching "members."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "His or her" is singular, but the antecedent "members" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "One's" refers to a general, unnamed person, not to the specific plural noun "members."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1271, the young Venetian Marco Polo set out for Asia with his father and his uncle, both merchants. By the time he returned to Venice in 1295, he ______ more than two decades traveling and working in lands ruled by the Mongol emperor Kublai Khan. A few years later, an account of his journeys, written down with the help of a writer named Rustichello, began to circulate across Europe.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has spent
choices.B: spends
choices.C: will have spent
choices.D: had spent

explanation.why: The phrase "By the time he returned to Venice in 1295" sets a moment in the past, and the years of travel were finished before that moment. An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect, so "had spent" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Has spent" is present perfect, which connects to the present, but the time frame here ends in 1295.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Spends" is present tense, but the events took place in the 1200s.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Will have spent" is future perfect, but the passage describes events that are already in the past.
explanation.D: Correct. "Had spent" is past perfect, showing the travels were completed before his return in 1295.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the Waitomo Caves of New Zealand, the dark ceilings sparkle with thousands of tiny blue-green lights. The lights are produced by the glowing larvae of a fungus gnat, each of which hangs sticky threads of silk below its nest. Attracted by the glow in the darkness, ______ The larvae then reel in the threads and eat their catch.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the larvae trap small flying insects in the dangling threads.
choices.B: the larvae's threads catch small flying insects.
choices.C: small flying insects become trapped in the dangling threads.
choices.D: the dangling threads trap small flying insects.

explanation.why: The phrase "Attracted by the glow in the darkness" describes whatever is attracted, and it is the insects, not the larvae or the threads, that fly toward the light. So "small flying insects" must come right after the comma.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This choice says the larvae are attracted by the glow, but the larvae produce the glow; the insects are drawn to it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject here is "threads"; "the larvae's" only describes them, so the sentence says the threads are attracted by the glow.
explanation.C: Correct. "Small flying insects" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear the insects are attracted by the glow.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This choice says the threads are attracted by the glow, which makes no sense.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Grand Trunk Road is one of the oldest and longest roads in Asia, running from Bangladesh across northern India and Pakistan to Kabul in Afghanistan. In the 1540s, the ruler Sher Shah Suri rebuilt and extended much of the route. Along the ______ length, he had shade trees planted, wells dug, and inns called sarais built at regular intervals so that travelers and merchants could rest safely.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: roads
choices.B: roads'
choices.C: road's
choices.D: roads's

explanation.why: The length belongs to one road, the Grand Trunk Road. A singular noun shows possession with an apostrophe and s, so "road's" is correct. The plural nouns later in the sentence ("trees," "wells," "sarais") do not change who owns the length.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Roads" is plural and not possessive; the length belongs to a single road.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Roads'" is plural possessive, but the text describes one road.
explanation.C: Correct. "Road's" is the singular possessive, showing the length belongs to the Grand Trunk Road.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Roads's" is not a Standard English form.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: On the last night of the festival, Mei and her grandmother carried their paper lanterns down to the river. Each of the lanterns that Grandmother had folded that afternoon ______ marked with a wish written in tiny characters along its lower edge. As the lanterns drifted away on the dark water, Mei tried to guess which glowing shape held her own wish.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have been
choices.B: are
choices.C: were
choices.D: was

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "Each," which is singular; "of the lanterns that Grandmother had folded" only says which ones. A singular subject needs a singular verb, and the story is told in the past tense, so "was" is correct. The singular "its lower edge" confirms that one lantern at a time is meant.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural, but the subject "Each" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Are" is plural, and it is also present tense in a story told in the past.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Were" is plural and seems to agree with "lanterns," but the subject is the singular "Each."
explanation.D: Correct. The singular past-tense verb "was" agrees with the singular subject "Each" and fits the past-tense story.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Ibn Khaldun, a scholar born in Tunis in 1332, served as an official at several North African courts before withdrawing from public life to write a history of the world. Completed in 1377 as the introduction to that history, ______ In it, he argued that a dynasty draws its strength from the loyalty that binds its founding group, a bond that tends to weaken over several generations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the Muqaddimah examines why dynasties rise and fall.
choices.B: the question of why dynasties rise and fall is examined in the Muqaddimah.
choices.C: why dynasties rise and fall is examined by Ibn Khaldun in the Muqaddimah.
choices.D: Ibn Khaldun examined in the Muqaddimah why dynasties rise and fall.

explanation.why: The phrase "Completed in 1377 as the introduction to that history" describes a piece of writing, so the noun right after the comma must name that writing: the Muqaddimah. Ibn Khaldun himself was not "completed" as an introduction.
explanation.A: Correct. "The Muqaddimah" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear the book was completed in 1377.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This choice says "the question" was completed in 1377 as an introduction; the modifier must describe the book.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This choice says a question ("why dynasties rise and fall") was completed as the introduction, which makes no sense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This choice places "Ibn Khaldun" after the phrase, saying the scholar himself was completed as an introduction.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Among seahorses, it is the male, not the female, that becomes pregnant. During mating, the female places her eggs into a pouch on the front of the male's body, where they are fertilized. The father then carries the developing young in ______ pouch for several weeks, and when they are ready, he releases dozens or even hundreds of tiny seahorses into the water.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: their
choices.B: hers
choices.C: his
choices.D: her

explanation.why: The pouch belongs to "the father," one male seahorse, and the passage later refers to him as "he." The singular masculine possessive "his" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Their" is plural, but the pouch belongs to the father, a single animal, not to the young.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Hers" stands alone and cannot come before a noun; it also refers to the female rather than the father.
explanation.C: Correct. "His" is singular and masculine, matching "the father" and "he."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Her" refers to the female, but the text says the pouch is on the male's body.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Abdur Rahman Chughtai, a painter who spent most of his life in Lahore, developed a graceful style that drew on Mughal and Persian traditions of miniature painting. In 1927, Chughtai, by then already admired for his delicate watercolors, ______ Muraqqa-e-Chughtai, a lavish edition of the Urdu poetry of Mirza Ghalib illustrated with his own paintings. The book brought his art to a wide audience across South Asia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: publishing
choices.B: having published
choices.C: to publish
choices.D: published

explanation.why: The subject "Chughtai" is followed by a descriptive phrase set off by commas, and then the sentence needs its main verb. Only a finite verb can be the main verb, and the event happened in 1927, so the simple past "published" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Publishing" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Having published" is a participle phrase, not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "To publish" is an infinitive and cannot serve as the main verb of the sentence.
explanation.D: Correct. "Published" is a finite past-tense verb, giving the subject "Chughtai" the main verb it needs.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ecologists Ines Duarte and Kwame Asante wanted to know what red foxes living in cities actually eat. Over two years, they collected and analyzed hundreds of fox droppings from parks and gardens in a large European city. The two ______ results surprised many residents: although the foxes did eat food scraps left by people, earthworms, insects, and small rodents made up a large part of their diet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: researchers'
choices.B: researcher's
choices.C: researchers
choices.D: researchers's

explanation.why: The results belong to the two ecologists, Duarte and Asante, so the owner is plural ("The two"). A plural noun ending in -s shows possession with an apostrophe after the s: "researchers'."
explanation.A: Correct. "Researchers'" is the plural possessive, showing the results belong to both ecologists.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Researcher's" is singular possessive, but "The two" shows there are two researchers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Researchers" is plural but not possessive; the results belong to the researchers, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Researchers's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Velvet worms are soft-bodied animals, usually just a few centimeters long, that hunt insects and spiders on the damp floors of tropical forests. Rather than chase their prey, they capture it from a distance. When an insect comes close, the two large slime glands inside a velvet worm's body ______ a sticky fluid through small openings beside the mouth. The fluid shoots out in fast, wobbling jets, and within seconds it hardens into a net of threads that holds the victim in place.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: is squirting
choices.B: squirt
choices.C: squirts
choices.D: has squirted

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "glands," which is plural; "inside a velvet worm's body" only tells where the glands are. A plural subject needs a plural verb, and the passage describes a repeated habit in the simple present ("comes," "shoots," "hardens"), so "squirt" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Is squirting" is a singular verb, but the subject "glands" is plural.
explanation.B: Correct. The plural verb "squirt" agrees with the plural subject "the two large slime glands."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Squirts" is singular and seems to agree with the nearby noun "body," but the subject is the plural "glands."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Has squirted" is a singular verb, but the subject "glands" is plural.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: A Balinese gamelan is an ensemble made up mostly of bronze percussion instruments, such as gongs and metallophones with rows of metal keys. Many of the keyed instruments are built and tuned in pairs, with one member of each pair set slightly higher in pitch than the other. Musicians strike the two instruments of a pair at the same moment, and ______ slightly different sound waves combine into a rapid, shimmering pulse that Balinese musicians call ombak, or "wave."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: their
choices.B: they're
choices.C: it's
choices.D: its

explanation.why: The sound waves belong to "the two instruments of a pair," which is plural. A plural antecedent needs the plural possessive pronoun "their." The singular nouns "gamelan" and "pair" are nearby, but each instrument produces its own wave, and it is the two instruments whose waves combine.
explanation.A: Correct. "Their" is the plural possessive pronoun, matching "the two instruments."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "They're" means "they are"; "they are slightly different sound waves combine" is not grammatical, and a possessive is needed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; "it is slightly different sound waves" makes no sense, and a possessive is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Its" is singular, but the waves belong to the plural "two instruments."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Every working day in Mumbai, India, about five thousand delivery workers known as dabbawalas carry home-cooked lunches from people's homes to their offices and bring the empty tins back in the afternoon. The service dates to the 1890s, and it still relies mostly on bicycles, handcarts, and suburban trains. Each tin is marked with a short code of letters, numbers, and colors, and the ______ ability to read these codes at a glance allows them to sort tens of thousands of tins in railway stations within minutes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: dabbawalas'
choices.B: dabbawala's
choices.C: dabbawalas's
choices.D: dabbawalas

explanation.why: The ability belongs to the delivery workers as a group: there are "about five thousand" of them, and the sentence goes on to say the ability "allows them" to sort the tins. A plural noun ending in -s shows possession with an apostrophe after the s, so "dabbawalas'" is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. "Dabbawalas'" is the plural possessive, showing that the ability belongs to all the workers.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Dabbawala's" is singular possessive, but the text describes thousands of workers, referred to later as "them."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Dabbawalas's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Dabbawalas" is plural but not possessive; the ability belongs to the workers, so an apostrophe is needed.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mary Anning grew up in Lyme Regis, on the southern coast of England, where the crumbling cliffs are full of fossils. Around 1811, when she was about twelve years old, her brother Joseph found the skull of a large marine reptile, and over the following months Mary uncovered much of the rest of the skeleton. The animal, which was later classified as an ichthyosaur, ______ to a group of sea-dwelling reptiles that had died out millions of years earlier, and the find helped persuade scientists that entire kinds of animals could disappear.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: having belonged
choices.B: to belong
choices.C: belonging
choices.D: belonged

explanation.why: The subject of the sentence is "The animal"; "which was later classified as an ichthyosaur" is a description of it, and "was" belongs to that clause. The main clause still needs its own verb, so the blank must be a finite verb, and the past-tense narrative calls for "belonged."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Having belonged" is a participle phrase, so the sentence would still lack a main verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "To belong" is an infinitive, which cannot serve as the main verb of a clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Belonging" is a participle, not a main verb, so the main clause would have no verb.
explanation.D: Correct. "Belonged" is a finite past-tense verb that gives the subject "The animal" its main verb.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: All winter, Ines and her younger sister Clara had argued about what to grow in the small plot behind their apartment building. In the end they agreed on beans, tomatoes, and a single row of sunflowers along the fence. Kneeling in the damp soil on the first warm morning of April, ______ while Clara followed behind with a watering can, humming to herself.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Ines pressed each bean seed into a shallow hole
choices.B: Ines's hands pressed each bean seed into a shallow hole
choices.C: the shallow holes received the bean seeds that Ines pressed into them
choices.D: each bean seed was pressed by Ines into a shallow hole

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Kneeling in the damp soil" describes a person. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be the one who was kneeling: Ines.
explanation.A: Correct. "Ines" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that she was the one kneeling.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject here is "hands," not Ines; hands cannot kneel, so the modifier is misplaced.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "the shallow holes" the subject, so the sentence says the holes were kneeling.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This makes "each bean seed" the subject, so the sentence says the seed was kneeling in the soil.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: China's Grand Canal is the longest artificial waterway in the world. Its first great expansion came under the Sui dynasty in the early 600s CE, when Emperor Yang ordered huge numbers of laborers to dig new channels and connect older ones. The resulting network of waterways, which linked the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers, ______ used to ship grain from the fertile south to the capital and to the armies stationed in the north.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are
choices.B: were
choices.C: have been
choices.D: was

explanation.why: The subject is "network," a singular noun; "of waterways" and the clause "which linked the Yellow and Yangtze Rivers" both describe it. A singular subject needs a singular verb, and the passage describes events in the 600s, so the past-tense "was" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are" is plural, but the subject "network" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Were" is plural and seems to agree with "waterways" or "Rivers," but the subject is the singular "network."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural, but the subject "network" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular past-tense verb "was" agrees with the singular subject "network."

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Himalayan monal, the national bird of Nepal, lives in mountain forests and meadows from eastern Afghanistan to Bhutan. The male is one of the most colorful pheasants in the world, with feathers that shine metallic green, purple, and copper in the sunlight. Female monals, by contrast, are mostly mottled brown, a color that hides ______ from foxes, eagles, and other predators while they sit on their eggs on the ground.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it
choices.B: them
choices.C: him
choices.D: her

explanation.why: The birds being hidden are "Female monals," a plural noun, and the same sentence refers to them as "they" and "their." The pronoun is the object of "hides," so the plural object pronoun "them" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but the antecedent "Female monals" is plural; the color does not hide itself.
explanation.B: Correct. "Them" is plural, matching "Female monals" and the later "they" and "their."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Him" is singular and refers to a male, but the antecedent is the plural "Female monals."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Her" is singular, but it must refer to the plural "Female monals."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Construction of the Sagrada Família, a basilica in Barcelona, Spain, began in 1882, and the architect Antoni Gaudí took charge of the project the following year. When Gaudí died in 1926, only a small part of the building was complete. Since then, architects have relied on his surviving models and drawings to continue the work, and the ______ eighteen planned towers have been rising one by one for decades.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: basilicas's
choices.B: basilicas
choices.C: basilica's
choices.D: basilicas'

explanation.why: The towers belong to one building, the Sagrada Família. A singular noun shows possession with an apostrophe and s, so "basilica's" is correct. The plural "towers" is what is owned, not the owner.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Basilicas's" is not a Standard English form.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Basilicas" is plural and not possessive; the towers belong to one basilica.
explanation.C: Correct. "Basilica's" is the singular possessive, showing that the towers belong to the Sagrada Família.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Basilicas'" is plural possessive, but the text describes a single basilica.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Once a year, Mr. Haddad drove his old van into the hills to tune the only piano in the village of San Isidro. This year, a landslide blocked the main road, and he had to take a long detour through the valley. By the time he finally reached the school, the children ______ in the courtyard for nearly two hours, and several of them ran to the gate to help him carry his heavy case of tools.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are waiting
choices.B: had been waiting
choices.C: wait
choices.D: will have waited

explanation.why: The story is told in the past tense ("drove," "reached," "ran"). The waiting began before Mr. Haddad arrived and continued up to that past moment, which "By the time he finally reached" signals. An action that continued up to a point in the past takes the past perfect progressive, "had been waiting."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present progressive "are waiting" doesn't fit a story told in the past.
explanation.B: Correct. "Had been waiting" shows that the waiting went on before and up to the past moment when he arrived.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present tense "wait" doesn't fit a story told in the past.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The future perfect "will have waited" refers to the future, but the arrival already happened.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1947, Norwegian explorer Thor Heyerdahl set out to show that people from South America could have reached the islands of Polynesia by sea in ancient times.
