Built from nine balsa logs lashed together with hemp rope, ______ After 101 days at sea, the raft ran aground on a reef in the Tuamotu Islands, roughly 6,900 kilometers from where the voyage began.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Heyerdahl's voyage west from Peru across the Pacific took place on the raft Kon-Tiki.
choices.B: west from Peru across the Pacific sailed Heyerdahl and five crew members on the raft Kon-Tiki.
choices.C: the raft Kon-Tiki carried Heyerdahl and five crew members west from Peru across the Pacific.
choices.D: Heyerdahl and five crew members sailed west from Peru across the Pacific on the raft Kon-Tiki.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Built from nine balsa logs lashed together with hemp rope" describes the raft. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be the raft itself.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "voyage," but a voyage cannot be built from logs and rope.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The words right after the comma are "west from Peru," and the subject that follows is "Heyerdahl and five crew members," not the raft, so the modifier is left without the noun it describes.
explanation.C: Correct. "The raft Kon-Tiki" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that the raft was built from balsa logs.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This makes "Heyerdahl and five crew members" the subject, so the sentence says the men were built from balsa logs.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Papua New Guinea, which occupies the eastern half of the island of New Guinea, is one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth. Many of its valleys are separated by steep mountains and dense forest, so neighboring communities developed their own ways of speaking over thousands of years. Today, the number of distinct languages used across the country ______ more than 800, according to most estimates, and many of them are spoken by only a few thousand people.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are
choices.B: have been
choices.C: is
choices.D: were

explanation.why: The subject is "the number," which is singular; "of distinct languages used across the country" describes it. "The number of" takes a singular verb, and "Today" calls for the present tense, so "is" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are" is plural and seems to agree with "languages," but the subject is the singular "number."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural, but the subject "number" is singular.
explanation.C: Correct. The singular present-tense verb "is" agrees with "the number" and fits "Today."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Were" is plural, but the subject "number" is singular; it is also past tense, which conflicts with "Today."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Mimar Sinan served as chief architect of the Ottoman Empire for about fifty years in the sixteenth century, and he is credited with designing more than three hundred buildings, including mosques, bridges, and public baths. He also trained a generation of younger architects in his workshop. Several of these students went on to have major careers of ______ own; one of them, Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa, designed the Sultan Ahmed Mosque in Istanbul, completed in 1616.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: one's
choices.B: their
choices.C: its
choices.D: his

explanation.why: The careers belong to "Several of these students," a plural group. A plural antecedent needs the plural possessive pronoun "their." The singular names nearby, Sinan and Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa, are not the ones whose careers are being described.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "One's" refers to a general, unnamed person, but the antecedent is the specific plural "students."
explanation.B: Correct. "Their" is plural, matching "Several of these students."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Its" is singular and refers to a thing, but the antecedent is the plural "students."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "His" is singular, but the careers belong to the plural "Several of these students."

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a honeybee forager finds a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a waggle dance on the vertical surface of the honeycomb. Other workers crowd around and follow her movements closely. The angle of the ______ waggling run, measured from straight up, shows the direction of the flowers relative to the Sun, and the length of each run indicates how far away they are.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: dancers
choices.B: dancers'
choices.C: dancer's
choices.D: dancers's

explanation.why: Only one bee performs the dance: the forager, referred to as "she" and "her." The waggling run belongs to that single dancer, so the singular possessive, an apostrophe and s, is needed: "dancer's."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Dancers" is plural and not possessive; the run belongs to one dancer.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Dancers'" is plural possessive, but only one bee is dancing; the "Other workers" are watching.
explanation.C: Correct. "Dancer's" is the singular possessive, showing that the run belongs to the one forager.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Dancers's" is not a Standard English form.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1979, the Pakistani physicist Abdus Salam shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Sheldon Glashow and Steven Weinberg for work showing that two of nature's fundamental forces, electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force, are aspects of a single force. By the time he received the prize, Salam ______ an institute in Trieste, Italy, where physicists from developing countries could spend time doing research alongside leading scientists.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: will found
choices.B: has founded
choices.C: founds
choices.D: had already founded

explanation.why: "By the time he received the prize" points to a moment in the past (1979), and the founding happened before that moment. An action completed before another past event takes the past perfect, "had already founded."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The future "will found" places the founding after the prize, but "By the time" shows it came before.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present perfect "has founded" connects an action to the present, but the sentence sets it before a past moment.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present tense "founds" doesn't fit an event that happened before 1979.
explanation.D: Correct. The past perfect "had already founded" shows the founding came before he received the prize.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Greenland sharks swim slowly through the cold, dark waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans. Because the sharks lack hard bones that record yearly growth, scientists estimated their ages by dating proteins in the lenses of their eyes, which form before birth. Growing only about a centimeter each year, ______ The same study suggested that some individuals live for more than 270 years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the sharks may need around 150 years to reach adulthood, scientists concluded.
choices.B: scientists concluded that the sharks may need around 150 years to reach adulthood.
choices.C: around 150 years may be needed for the sharks to reach adulthood, scientists concluded.
choices.D: the sharks' adulthood may take around 150 years to arrive, scientists concluded.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Growing only about a centimeter each year" describes the sharks. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be "the sharks."
explanation.A: Correct. "The sharks" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that the sharks are the ones growing slowly.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This makes "scientists" the subject, so the sentence says the scientists grow about a centimeter each year.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject here is "around 150 years," so the sentence says a period of time is growing.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject here is "adulthood," not the sharks; adulthood does not grow a centimeter a year.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When Leila's family cleared out her grandmother's house, Leila volunteered to sort through the attic. Most of the boxes held old clothes and chipped dishes, but under a stack of quilts she found a small wooden trunk. Inside, a bundle of letters that her grandfather had mailed home during his years as a merchant sailor ______ tied with a faded blue ribbon, the envelopes soft from being opened and reread.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have been
choices.B: were
choices.C: are
choices.D: was

explanation.why: The subject is "a bundle," which is singular; "of letters" and the clause "that her grandfather had mailed home ..." describe it. A singular subject needs a singular verb, and the story is told in the past tense ("cleared," "found"), so "was" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural, but the subject "bundle" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Were" is plural and seems to agree with "letters," but the subject is the singular "bundle."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are" is plural, but the subject "bundle" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular past-tense verb "was" agrees with "a bundle" and fits the past-tense story.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Kathak is a classical dance form of northern India and Pakistan known for its rapid spins and complex rhythmic footwork. Performers wear ghungroo, strings of small brass bells wrapped around the ankles. The bells, often more than a hundred on each ankle, are a demanding part of the art: dancers spend years learning to strike the floor in ways that make ______ ring loudly, softly, or even one at a time.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them
choices.B: itself
choices.C: they
choices.D: it

explanation.why: The things that ring are "The bells," a plural noun. The pronoun is the object of "make," so it must be the plural object pronoun "them."
explanation.A: Correct. "Them" is plural, matching "The bells," and is the object form needed after "make."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Itself" is singular and reflexive, but it must refer to the plural "bells," and the subject of the clause is "dancers," not the bells.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "They" is a subject pronoun; after the verb "make," the object form "them" is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but the things that ring are the plural "bells," not the floor or the art.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Most of the roughly three thousand runestones that survive in Sweden were raised in the tenth and eleventh centuries as memorials, and their inscriptions typically name both the person who sponsored the stone and the relative being honored. Because traces of pigment have been detected on a number of them, scholars now think that many were once brightly painted. The ______ original colors, which would have made the carved letters easier to read from a distance, have almost entirely worn away, leaving the gray surfaces familiar from museum photographs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: stones
choices.B: stones'
choices.C: stones's
choices.D: stone's

explanation.why: The colors belong to the many runestones that scholars think were painted, not to one particular stone: the text speaks of "many" stones and "gray surfaces." A plural noun ending in -s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone, so "stones'" is correct. The singular "the stone" earlier refers to the stone in a typical inscription, not to the owner of these colors.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Stones" is plural but not possessive; the colors belong to the stones, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.B: Correct. "Stones'" is the plural possessive, showing that the colors belong to the many painted stones.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Stones's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Stone's" is singular possessive, but the colors belong to many stones, as "many were once brightly painted" and "surfaces" show.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In experiments begun in 1909 in Ernest Rutherford's laboratory at the University of Manchester, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden aimed a beam of alpha particles at a sheet of gold foil far thinner than a sheet of paper. According to the model of the atom then widely accepted, in which positive charge was spread thinly throughout each atom, the particles should ______ through the foil with, at most, slight deflections. Instead, a small fraction bounced off at sharp angles, a result that Rutherford explained in 1911 by proposing that an atom's positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: had passed
choices.B: passed
choices.C: have passed
choices.D: passing

explanation.why: After a helping verb such as "should," English uses the base form of a verb ("should pass") or, for an expectation about the past, "have" plus the past participle ("should have passed"). The sentence describes what the old model predicted about experiments already done, so "should have passed" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Should had passed" is not grammatical; after "should," the base form "have" is required, not "had."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Should passed" is not grammatical; "should" must be followed by a base form, not a past-tense verb.
explanation.C: Correct. "Should have passed" correctly combines "should" with "have" and the past participle to describe a past expectation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Should passing" is not grammatical; a helping verb like "should" cannot be followed by an -ing form alone.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: According to a story first printed in 1802, some sixty years after the fact, Johann Sebastian Bach wrote the Goldberg Variations for a sleepless count whose young harpsichordist, Johann Gottlieb Goldberg, was to play them at night. Many scholars doubt the tale, noting that the published score carries no dedication to the count and that Goldberg was then only about fourteen. Published in 1741 as an aria followed by thirty variations, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: a harpsichord with two keyboards is required by the work, several of whose variations call for the player's hands to cross.
choices.B: Bach's plan for the work called for a harpsichord with two keyboards, and several variations require the player's hands to cross.
choices.C: Bach designed the work for a harpsichord with two keyboards, and several variations require the player's hands to cross.
choices.D: the work was designed for a harpsichord with two keyboards, and several of its variations require the player's hands to cross.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Published in 1741 as an aria followed by thirty variations" describes the composition. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be the work itself.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This makes "a harpsichord" the subject, so the sentence says the instrument was published as an aria and variations.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "plan," not the work; Bach's plan was not what was published as an aria and variations.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "Bach" the subject, so the sentence says Bach was published as an aria with thirty variations.
explanation.D: Correct. "The work" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that the composition was what was published in 1741.

items.subject: science
items.passage: To learn how quickly plastic pollution reaches the deep ocean, a team led by marine geologist Tomasz Wierzbicki analyzed sediment cores drilled from the floor of a submarine canyon off the coast of Portugal. In layers deposited since the 1960s, the concentration of microplastic fibers, most of them shed from synthetic clothing during washing, ______ roughly in step with global plastic production, a pattern suggesting that the fibers settle within years rather than centuries. The team cautions, however, that canyons may funnel debris downslope faster than the open seafloor does.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: rises
choices.B: rise
choices.C: are rising
choices.D: have risen

explanation.why: Strip away the modifiers and the main clause reads "the concentration ... rises roughly in step with global plastic production." The subject is the singular noun "concentration"; "fibers" sits inside the phrase "of microplastic fibers," and "most of them shed from synthetic clothing" is an aside about the fibers. A singular subject needs the singular verb "rises."
explanation.A: Correct. The singular verb "rises" agrees with the singular subject "concentration."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Rise" is plural and seems to agree with "fibers" or "them," but the subject is the singular "concentration."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are rising" is plural, but the subject "concentration" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Have risen" is plural, but the subject "concentration" is singular.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Founded in what is now the Indian state of Bihar around the fifth century CE, Nalanda grew into one of the largest centers of Buddhist learning in Asia, drawing students from as far away as Korea and Central Asia. Much of what historians know about daily life there comes from Xuanzang and Yijing, two Chinese monks who studied at Nalanda in the seventh century. The accounts that ______ wrote after returning to China describe crowded lecture halls, demanding admission tests, and a curriculum that ranged from philosophy and logic to medicine.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: they
choices.B: them
choices.C: he
choices.D: it

explanation.why: The accounts were written by "Xuanzang and Yijing," two people, so the pronoun must be plural. It is also the subject of "wrote" in the clause "that ___ wrote," so the subject form "they" is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "They" is plural, matching "Xuanzang and Yijing," and is the subject form needed before "wrote."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Them" is an object pronoun, but the blank is the subject of "wrote."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "He" is singular, but the accounts were written by two monks, Xuanzang and Yijing.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It" is singular and would refer to Nalanda, but a place did not write the accounts; the two monks did.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In parts of southern Africa, fungus-farming termites build mounds of soil that can rise more than two meters above the ground, though the insects themselves live in a nest beneath the mound rather than inside its tall chimney. Researchers once assumed that the chimney worked like a simple exhaust pipe. Measurements now suggest instead that daily swings in outdoor temperature drive air to circulate through the mound's porous walls, flushing out carbon dioxide and keeping the ______ underground gardens of fungus at a fairly steady humidity.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: termites'
choices.B: termites's
choices.C: termites
choices.D: termite's

explanation.why: The fungus gardens belong to the termites of the colony, a plural group ("the insects themselves live in a nest"). A plural noun ending in -s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone, so "termites'" is correct. The singular possessive "mound's" nearby refers to a different owner.
explanation.A: Correct. "Termites'" is the plural possessive, showing that the gardens belong to the insects of the colony.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Termites's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Termites" is plural but not possessive; the gardens belong to the termites, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Termite's" is singular possessive, but the gardens are tended by many termites, not one.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: In the final round of the regional championship, Adaeze Okafor sat motionless for twenty minutes while her clock ran down, studying a position that looked hopeless to everyone watching. At last she pushed a pawn forward, a move so quiet that her opponent barely glanced at it. Only later, replaying the game with her coach, did she see how narrow her escape had been: if she ______ her bishop instead, as she had nearly done, her opponent could have trapped her king in three moves.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: would have moved
choices.B: moves
choices.C: has moved
choices.D: had moved

explanation.why: The sentence imagines a past event that did not happen (she did not move the bishop), and the result clause uses "could have trapped." In Standard English, the "if" clause of an unreal past condition uses the past perfect: "if she had moved." "Would have" belongs only in the result clause, never in the "if" clause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Would have moved" cannot appear in the "if" clause of a conditional; it belongs in the result clause.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present tense "moves" doesn't fit a past situation that never happened.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present perfect "has moved" doesn't fit a past situation that never happened.
explanation.D: Correct. The past perfect "had moved" is the standard form for the "if" clause of an unreal past condition.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci arrived in China in 1582 and spent nearly three decades there, eventually mastering classical Chinese. He had studied mathematics and astronomy in Rome before sailing east. Working with Chinese scholars, including the mathematician Li Zhizao, he produced a world map that combined European geographic knowledge with Chinese sources and place names. Printed in Beijing in 1602 on six large panels, ______ a choice that most likely made the unfamiliar map more acceptable to its Chinese readers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Ricci and his collaborators placed China near the center rather than at the edge, as many European maps did,
choices.B: the map placed China near the center rather than at the edge, as many European maps did,
choices.C: Ricci's decision placed China near the center rather than at the edge, as many European maps did,
choices.D: China was placed near the center rather than at the edge, as many European maps did,

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Printed in Beijing in 1602 on six large panels" can describe only the map. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be "the map."
explanation.A: Incorrect. This makes "Ricci and his collaborators" the subject, so the sentence says the people were printed on six panels.
explanation.B: Correct. "The map" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that the map was what was printed on six panels.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "decision"; a decision cannot be printed on panels.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This makes "China" the subject, so the sentence says the country was printed in Beijing on six panels.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Book of Kells, an illuminated manuscript of the four Gospels now held at Trinity College Dublin, was made around 800 CE on roughly 340 leaves of calfskin vellum. Its pages are crowded with interlaced knots, spirals, and tiny animals, some so intricate that they can be fully appreciated only with a magnifying glass. Despite centuries of study, neither the names of the monks who produced it nor the exact place where the work was begun ______ known with certainty, though many scholars favor a monastery on the Scottish island of Iona.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: is
choices.B: were
choices.C: are
choices.D: have been

explanation.why: When two subjects are joined by "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. Here the closer subject is "the exact place," which is singular, so the verb must be singular. The present-tense "favor" shows that the sentence describes what is known today, so "is" is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. The singular verb "is" agrees with "the exact place," the subject closer to the verb.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Were" is plural, but the nearer subject "place" is singular.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are" is plural and agrees with "names," but with "neither ... nor" the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the singular "place."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural, but the nearer subject "place" is singular.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Saharan silver ants leave their nests at midday, when the surface of the desert sand can exceed 60°C and most other animals stay hidden. Their bodies are covered in tiny hairs with a triangular cross-section that reflect much of the sunlight striking them and help radiate excess heat. Even so, the ants must keep their trips short, racing across the sand in search of insects that have died in the heat. Their timing is no accident: the lizards that usually prey on ______ have by then retreated into the shade.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it
choices.B: them
choices.C: themselves
choices.D: they

explanation.why: The animals the lizards prey on are the ants, a plural noun used throughout the passage. The pronoun is the object of the preposition "on," so it must be the plural object pronoun "them."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but it must refer to the plural "ants"; the lizards do not prey on the sand or the shade.
explanation.B: Correct. "Them" is plural, matching "the ants," and is the object form needed after "on."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Themselves" is reflexive and would refer back to the subject "the lizards," saying that lizards prey on lizards.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "They" is a subject pronoun; after the preposition "on," the object form "them" is needed.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every summer since he was twelve, Faraz had worked at his uncle's tea stall in Qissa Khwani Bazaar, the old storytellers' market in Peshawar, carrying cups of green tea to the shopkeepers nearby. He had learned to pour from a height without spilling, to remember who took cardamom and who did not, and, above all, to listen. By late afternoon the benches filled with older ______ voices as they argued, in Pashto and Urdu, about cricket scores, the price of cloth, and whose grandfather had told a story best.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: mens
choices.B: man's
choices.C: men's
choices.D: mens'

explanation.why: The voices belong to several older men, as "they argued" shows. "Men" is an irregular plural that does not end in -s, so it forms its possessive by adding an apostrophe and s: "men's."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Mens" is not a Standard English word, and it lacks the apostrophe needed to show possession.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Man's" is singular possessive, but the voices belong to several men who "argued."
explanation.C: Correct. "Men's" is the possessive of the irregular plural "men," showing that the voices belong to the older men.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Mens'" is not a Standard English form; "men" is already plural, so it takes 's, not s'.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: According to the usual account, in late 1946 or early 1947 Bedouin shepherds searching for a stray goat near Qumran, on the northwestern shore of the Dead Sea, entered a cave and found clay jars holding ancient scrolls. Over the next decade, archaeologists and local searchers recovered fragments of roughly nine hundred manuscripts from eleven caves in the area. The oldest of these texts, written mostly in Hebrew and Aramaic on parchment and papyrus, ______ to the third century BCE, about a thousand years earlier than most previously known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: to date
choices.B: dating
choices.C: having dated
choices.D: date

explanation.why: The subject of the last sentence is "The oldest of these texts"; "written mostly in Hebrew and Aramaic on parchment and papyrus" is a description of them, not a verb. The sentence still needs a main verb, so the blank must be a finite verb: "date."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "To date" is an infinitive, which cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Dating" is a participle, so the sentence would have no main verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Having dated" is a participle phrase, so the sentence would still lack a main verb.
explanation.D: Correct. "Date" is a finite verb that gives the subject "The oldest of these texts" its main verb.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The star-nosed mole, which lives in the wetlands of eastern North America, is nearly blind, yet it finds food with remarkable speed, whether digging through moist soil or hunting underwater. At the tip of its snout is a star-shaped ring of twenty-two fleshy rays covered with tens of thousands of tiny touch receptors. Tapping the ground around the animal roughly ten times per second, ______ allowing the mole to identify and swallow a small worm or insect larva in well under a second.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the mole's brain receives a detailed picture of every surface the star touches,
choices.B: the mole's brain is sent a detailed picture of every surface the star touches,
choices.C: a detailed picture of every surface the star touches is sent to the mole's brain,
choices.D: the star sends a detailed picture of every surface it touches to the mole's brain,

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Tapping the ground around the animal roughly ten times per second" describes the star on the mole's snout. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be "the star."
explanation.A: Incorrect. This makes "the mole's brain" the subject, so the sentence says the brain taps the ground.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This makes "the mole's brain" the subject again, so the brain is said to be tapping the ground.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "a detailed picture" the subject, so the sentence says the picture taps the ground.
explanation.D: Correct. "The star" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that the star is what taps the ground.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Saturn's rings look solid from a distance, but they are made of countless separate pieces. The particles that make up the ring system, each following its own orbit around the planet, ______ composed overwhelmingly of water ice, which is why the rings reflect so much sunlight. Measurements of the rings' mass by the Cassini spacecraft have led some scientists to propose that the rings formed within the last few hundred million years, although others argue that the rings could be far older and have simply been kept clean of darker dust.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: was
choices.B: has been
choices.C: are
choices.D: is

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "The particles," which is plural. "That make up the ring system" and "each following its own orbit around the planet" both describe the particles, and the singular words inside them ("system," "each," "its") do not change the subject. A plural subject needs the plural verb "are," which also fits the present-tense description.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Was" is singular, and its past tense also clashes with the present-tense description; the subject "particles" is plural.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Has been" is singular, but the subject "particles" is plural.
explanation.C: Correct. The plural verb "are" agrees with the plural subject "The particles."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Is" is singular and seems to agree with "system" or "each," but the subject is the plural "particles."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Pansori, a Korean form of musical storytelling, requires only two performers: a singer, who narrates a long tale through song, speech, and gesture, and a drummer, who keeps time on a barrel drum and calls out short shouts of encouragement known as chuimsae. A complete performance of a single story can last several hours. Audiences are expected to take part as well, and experienced listeners time ______ own shouts carefully, calling out at the end of a phrase rather than in the middle of one, so that the cries spur the singer on instead of interrupting the song.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: one's
choices.B: their
choices.C: his or her
choices.D: its

explanation.why: The shouts belong to "experienced listeners," a plural noun. A plural antecedent needs the plural possessive pronoun "their." The singular nouns nearby, such as "the singer" and "a drummer," are not the ones timing these shouts.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "One's" refers to a general, unnamed person, but the antecedent is the specific plural "listeners."
explanation.B: Correct. "Their" is plural, matching "experienced listeners."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "His or her" is singular, but the antecedent "experienced listeners" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Its" is singular and refers to a thing, but the shouts belong to the plural "listeners."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Kot Diji, a site near the town of Khairpur in Sindh, Pakistan, was occupied for centuries before the rise of great Indus cities such as Mohenjo-daro, and it gave its name to a distinctive style of early pottery. Excavations in the 1950s uncovered a settlement on a low mound protected by a massive wall of limestone blocks and mud brick. Archaeologists still debate what threat prompted the early ______ investment in such costly defenses; layers of ash between the early and later levels have been read as evidence of conflict, though accidental fires may account for them as well.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: inhabitant's
choices.B: inhabitants
choices.C: inhabitants's
choices.D: inhabitants'

explanation.why: A wall around a whole settlement was the work of the community, so the investment belongs to many people, the early inhabitants. A plural noun ending in -s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone, so "inhabitants'" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Inhabitant's" is singular possessive, but a settlement and its massive wall belonged to many residents, not one.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Inhabitants" is plural but not possessive; the investment belongs to the inhabitants, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Inhabitants's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.D: Correct. "Inhabitants'" is the plural possessive, showing that the investment was made by the settlement's residents.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On the morning of June 30, 1908, an enormous explosion shook a remote forest near the Podkamennaya Tunguska River in Siberia. Because the region was so isolated, no scientific team reached it until 1927, when an expedition led by the mineralogist Leonid Kulik finally arrived. Kulik found no crater. Instead, millions of trees, stripped of their branches and pointing away from a central area, ______ flattened across more than 2,000 square kilometers, evidence that most researchers now attribute to a comet or asteroid that burst apart in the air before reaching the ground.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: lay
choices.B: lain
choices.C: laid
choices.D: laying

explanation.why: The sentence needs a main verb for the subject "millions of trees," and the meaning is that the trees were resting on the ground, which is the verb "lie." The past tense of "lie" is "lay," which fits the past-tense narrative ("found," "arrived"). "Laid" is the past tense of "lay," a different verb that means to put something down and needs an object.
explanation.A: Correct. "Lay," the past tense of "lie," gives the subject a main verb and correctly says the trees were resting on the ground.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Lain" is the past participle of "lie" and cannot be the main verb without a helping verb such as "had."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Laid" is the past tense of "lay," which means to put something down and requires an object; the trees were not putting anything down.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Laying" is a participle of "lay" (to put something down), so the sentence would have no main verb.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For forty-one years Endre Varga had cut and stitched suits in a narrow shop above a bakery, and when his eyesight began to fail, he sold his machines and hung his shears on a nail by the door, where they gathered dust for three years. Then his granddaughter announced her engagement. Having sworn on the day he closed the shop that he would never again accept an order, ______ He spent the next six weeks at his kitchen table, working slowly beside the window, where the light was best.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: a wedding suit for his granddaughter's fiancé was the one order that Mr. Varga could not refuse.
choices.B: Mr. Varga's decision to make a wedding suit for his granddaughter's fiancé surprised everyone.
choices.C: the request from his granddaughter's fiancé surprised Mr. Varga, who accepted it anyway.
choices.D: Mr. Varga surprised himself by agreeing to make a wedding suit for his granddaughter's fiancé.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Having sworn on the day he closed the shop that he would never again accept an order" describes a person: the tailor who made the vow. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be Mr. Varga himself.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This makes "a wedding suit" the subject, so the sentence says the suit had sworn never to accept an order.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "decision," not Mr. Varga; "Mr. Varga's" only describes the decision, which did not swear anything.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "the request" the subject, so the sentence says the request had sworn never to accept an order.
explanation.D: Correct. "Mr. Varga" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that he is the one who had sworn.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Fires were a constant danger in ancient Rome, where crowded apartment blocks of wood and brick lined narrow streets. In 6 CE, the emperor Augustus created the vigiles, a force made up largely of freed slaves who served as both firefighters and night watchmen. The force was divided into seven cohorts, and each of these units, which numbered several hundred men and kept stations in different parts of the city, ______ responsible for two of Rome's fourteen districts. Armed with buckets, axes, and hand-operated pumps, the vigiles could do little against the largest blazes but probably kept many smaller ones from spreading.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: were
choices.B: are
choices.C: have been
choices.D: was

explanation.why: The subject of the second clause is "each," which is singular; "of these units" and the clause "which numbered several hundred men and kept stations ..." describe it. "Each" takes a singular verb, and the passage is in the past tense, so "was" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Were" is plural and seems to agree with "units" or "men," but the subject is the singular "each."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Are" is plural, but the subject "each" is singular; it is also present tense in a passage about ancient Rome.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural, but the subject "each" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular past-tense verb "was" agrees with "each" and fits the past-tense passage.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mudskippers are fish that spend much of their lives out of the water, skipping across tropical mudflats at low tide to feed, defend territories, and court mates. Their adaptations for life in air are numerous. The gills of most fish collapse when exposed to air, their thin filaments sticking together, but in a mudskipper ______ stay open because the fish holds a mouthful of water in enlarged chambers around them. A mudskipper also absorbs oxygen directly through its skin and the lining of its mouth, which is why it must roll in puddles regularly to keep moist.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: they
choices.C: it
choices.D: them

explanation.why: The things that "stay open" are the gills, a plural noun, as the plural verb "stay" and the later "around them" confirm. The pronoun is the subject of "stay," so it must be the plural subject pronoun "they."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Its" is a possessive and needs a noun after it; it cannot be the subject of "stay."
explanation.B: Correct. "They" is plural, matching "gills," and is the subject form needed before "stay."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but the antecedent "gills" is plural, and "it stay" does not agree.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Them" is an object pronoun, but the blank is the subject of "stay."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Violins made by Antonio Stradivari in Cremona in the late 1600s and early 1700s are among the most valuable instruments in the world, and many musicians have long believed that their tone cannot be matched. In several double-blind experiments conducted since 2010, however, professional soloists wore modified goggles so that they could not see which instrument they were playing. Most could not reliably tell old Italian violins from new ones, and the ______ stated preferences often favored the modern instruments, a result that has challenged, though hardly ended, the belief in an irreproducible Cremonese sound.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: soloists
choices.B: soloists'
choices.C: soloists's
choices.D: soloist's

explanation.why: The preferences belong to the professional soloists who took part in the experiments, a plural group ("Most could not reliably tell"). A plural noun ending in -s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone, so "soloists'" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Soloists" is plural but not possessive; the preferences belong to the soloists, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.B: Correct. "Soloists'" is the plural possessive, showing that the preferences belong to the many players tested.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Soloists's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Soloist's" is singular possessive, but many soloists took part and stated preferences.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When Marc Isambard Brunel began digging beneath the River Thames in London in 1825, no one had ever built a tunnel under a navigable river. To keep the soft riverbed from collapsing, he used a tunneling shield, an iron frame in which workers excavated the soil in small sections, one at a time. Even so, the river broke through more than once, and the project took eighteen years. When the tunnel finally opened in 1843, it was used only by people on foot, even though Brunel ______ it to carry horse-drawn carriages; the company had run out of money for the long ramps that vehicles would have needed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has designed
choices.B: designs
choices.C: will design
choices.D: had designed

explanation.why: The design work happened before the tunnel opened in 1843, which is itself a past event ("it was used"). An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect, so "had designed" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present perfect "has designed" links the action to the present, but the sentence places it before a past event.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present tense "designs" doesn't fit a design made before a past event in 1843.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The future "will design" places the design after the opening, but the tunnel was already built.
explanation.D: Correct. The past perfect "had designed" shows that the design came before the tunnel opened and was used only by pedestrians.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most of the tea grown in the hills around Darjeeling, in the Indian state of West Bengal, comes from the small-leaved Chinese variety of the tea plant rather than the larger-leaved Assam variety common in the plains. Cool temperatures at elevations of up to about 2,000 meters slow the bushes' growth, which is thought to concentrate the compounds that give the leaves their aroma. Picked in March and April, soon after the bushes end their winter dormancy, ______ which is one reason it often sells for more than tea from later harvests.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the first flush of tender new shoots yields a tea with a light, flowery taste,
choices.B: the light, flowery taste of the first flush of tender new shoots is prized by growers,
choices.C: a light, flowery taste is what growers prize in the first flush of tender new shoots,
choices.D: growers prize the first flush of tender new shoots for its light, flowery taste,

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Picked in March and April, soon after the bushes end their winter dormancy" describes what is picked: the new shoots of the first flush. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be "the first flush of tender new shoots."
explanation.A: Correct. "The first flush of tender new shoots" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that the shoots are what was picked.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "taste"; a taste is not something that can be picked.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "a light, flowery taste" the subject, so the sentence says the taste was picked.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This makes "growers" the subject, so the sentence says the growers were picked in March and April.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When Tomasz inherited his great-uncle's farmhouse, he expected to find little of value inside: the roof leaked, the stove was cracked, and the furniture had long since been sold. He spent his first week pulling up the warped boards of the upstairs bedroom, intending to replace them before winter. Beneath the loosest of the boards, in a hollow carved into the wooden beam below, ______ a rusted tin box tied shut with wire and a small bundle of letters addressed to a woman Tomasz had never heard of.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: is
choices.B: was
choices.C: has been
choices.D: were

explanation.why: The last sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb. "Beneath the loosest of the boards" and "in a hollow carved into the wooden beam below" are prepositional phrases, not the subject. The subject is "a rusted tin box ... and a small bundle of letters"; two subjects joined by "and" are plural, and the story is in the past tense, so "were" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Is" is singular, but the compound subject is plural; it is also present tense in a past-tense story.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Was" is singular and seems to agree with "box" or "hollow," but the subject is the compound "a rusted tin box ... and a small bundle of letters."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Has been" is singular, but the compound subject is plural.
explanation.D: Correct. The plural past-tense verb "were" agrees with the compound subject joined by "and."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Dresden Codex, a folding book of bark paper painted by Maya scribes several centuries before the Spanish arrived in the Americas, is one of only four Maya books known to have survived. Among its pages is a table that predicts when Venus would rise as the morning star, a cycle of about 584 days, and that adjusts those predictions to correct for small errors that build up over time. The table is generally credited to Maya astronomers, ______ careful records of the planet's movements must have been kept over many generations for such corrections to be possible.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: which
choices.B: whose
choices.C: whom
choices.D: who's

explanation.why: The blank begins a clause that describes "Maya astronomers" and tells what belonged to them: their careful records. The relative pronoun that shows possession is "whose."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Which" refers to things rather than people and cannot show possession here; "which careful records ... must have been kept" leaves the clause without a link to the astronomers.
explanation.B: Correct. "Whose" is the possessive relative pronoun, showing that the records belonged to the astronomers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Whom" is an object pronoun and cannot show possession; "whom careful records" is ungrammatical.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Who's" is a contraction of "who is" or "who has"; "who is careful records" makes no sense.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Each autumn, a Clark's nutcracker may bury tens of thousands of pine seeds in several thousand small caches scattered across mountain slopes in western North America, and months later, often under snow, it recovers a large share of them. In laboratory studies with several captive birds, researchers placed landmarks near hidden seeds and later moved them a short distance; the ______ searches shifted by the same distance as the landmarks, suggesting that the birds remember each cache by its position relative to nearby objects. Seeds that are never retrieved can sprout, so some pine forests depend heavily on the nutcrackers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: nutcrackers
choices.B: nutcrackers'
choices.C: nutcrackers's
choices.D: nutcracker's

explanation.why: The searches belong to the "several captive birds" in the laboratory studies, a plural group, as "the birds remember" confirms. A plural noun ending in -s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone, so "nutcrackers'" is correct. The singular "a Clark's nutcracker" in the first sentence describes a wild bird in general, not the birds in the experiment.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Nutcrackers" is plural but not possessive; the searches belong to the birds, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.B: Correct. "Nutcrackers'" is the plural possessive, showing that the searches belong to the several birds tested.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Nutcrackers's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Nutcracker's" is singular possessive, but the experiment used several birds.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Pakistani artist Sadequain, who lived from 1930 to 1987, is remembered both as a painter and as a calligrapher who turned verses of Urdu and Persian poetry into bold, angular images. Many of his best-known works were produced on a monumental scale, including large murals for public buildings in Pakistan and India. At the time of his death, Sadequain ______ on a vast painting for the ceiling of Frere Hall in Karachi; the unfinished work, which depicts the earth and the heavens, can still be seen there today.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: works
choices.B: has been working
choices.C: was still working
choices.D: will be working

explanation.why: "At the time of his death" refers to a moment in 1987, and the work was in progress at that moment, as "the unfinished work" shows. An action in progress at a specific past moment takes the past progressive, "was still working."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present tense "works" doesn't fit an action at a past moment, the time of his death in 1987.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present perfect progressive "has been working" suggests the work continues into the present, but Sadequain died in 1987.
explanation.C: Correct. The past progressive "was still working" shows that the painting was in progress when he died.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The future progressive "will be working" refers to the future, but the event is in the past.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance was launched in 1912 at a shipyard in Sandefjord, Norway, under the name Polaris, and Shackleton bought it in 1914. Built for polar cruises and renamed by Shackleton after his family's motto, Fortitudine vincimus ("By endurance we conquer"), ______ In January 1915, the ship became trapped in the pack ice of the Weddell Sea, which slowly crushed it over the following months. All of the crew survived, and the wreck was finally located in 2022, about three kilometers below the surface.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Shackleton's plan was to sail the Endurance to Antarctica and then cross the continent on foot.
choices.B: an attempt to cross Antarctica on foot began when the Endurance left Britain in August 1914.
choices.C: the Endurance left Britain in August 1914, carrying an expedition that hoped to cross Antarctica on foot.
choices.D: Shackleton sailed the Endurance from Britain in August 1914, intending to cross Antarctica on foot.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Built for polar cruises and renamed by Shackleton after his family's motto" describes the ship. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be "the Endurance."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "plan," not the ship; "Shackleton's" only describes the plan, which was not built or renamed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This makes "an attempt" the subject, so the sentence says the attempt was built for polar cruises.
explanation.C: Correct. "The Endurance" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that the ship was built and renamed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This makes "Shackleton" the subject, so the sentence says Shackleton was built for polar cruises and renamed by himself.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Because lichens absorb water and nutrients directly from the air and rain, many species are highly sensitive to sulfur dioxide, a pollutant released by burning coal. During the industrial era, these species vanished from the centers of many European cities. The return of several pollution-sensitive lichens to the bark of trees in London and other British cities since the late twentieth century ______ that sulfur dioxide levels have fallen sharply, although ecologists note that some of the newcomers thrive on nitrogen pollution from traffic, so the lichens tell a more complicated story than simple recovery.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: suggest
choices.B: have suggested
choices.C: are suggesting
choices.D: suggests

explanation.why: Strip away the modifiers and the sentence reads "The return ... suggests that sulfur dioxide levels have fallen sharply." The subject is the singular noun "return"; "lichens," "trees," and "cities" all sit inside prepositional phrases that describe it. A singular subject needs the singular verb "suggests."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Suggest" is plural and seems to agree with "lichens" or "cities," but the subject is the singular "return."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Have suggested" is plural, but the subject "return" is singular.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are suggesting" is plural, but the subject "return" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular verb "suggests" agrees with the singular subject "The return."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: I had been at Harwood scarcely a fortnight before Mr. Pell began to call upon us with a regularity that the whole parish remarked. My aunt, who had buried two husbands and had no intention of acquiring a nephew-in-law she disliked, received him in the front parlor with a courtesy so exact that it amounted to a rebuke. It had been settled, by an understanding never once spoken aloud between my aunt and ______, that his attentions were to be met with civility and returned with nothing warmer; and so, each Thursday, I poured his tea, admired his opinions of the weather, and wished him safely home.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: I
choices.B: me
choices.C: mine
choices.D: myself

explanation.why: The blank is part of the compound object of the preposition "between" ("between my aunt and ___"). The object of a preposition must be an object pronoun, so the narrator refers to herself as "me." A quick test is to remove "my aunt and": "between ... me" is correct, not "between ... I."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "I" is a subject pronoun, but the blank is the object of the preposition "between."
explanation.B: Correct. "Me" is the object pronoun needed after the preposition "between."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Mine" is a possessive pronoun meaning "belonging to me," which makes no sense as one of the two people sharing the understanding.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Myself" is reflexive and is used only when "I" is the subject of the same clause; here the subject is "It," so the object form "me" is needed.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Medieval manuscripts were usually copied by hand, often in monastic workshops, and the margins of surviving books sometimes preserve remarks that their makers never intended for posterity. Alongside corrections and doodles, historians have cataloged brief notes in which a copyist grumbles about cold fingers, poor ink, or the length of the text still to be finished. Such notes, scattered across hundreds of manuscripts written in many different hands, have encouraged scholars to treat the ______ complaints not as isolated outbursts but as evidence of shared working conditions: long hours, scarce light, and the physical toll of writing for days on end.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: scribe's
choices.B: scribes's
choices.C: scribes
choices.D: scribes'

explanation.why: The complaints come from "hundreds of manuscripts written in many different hands," so they belong to many scribes, and the point of the sentence is that the working conditions were "shared." A plural noun ending in -s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone, so "scribes'" is correct. The singular "a copyist grumbles" describes a typical note, not the owner of all the complaints.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Scribe's" is singular possessive, but the complaints were written by many people in "many different hands."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Scribes's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Scribes" is plural but not possessive; the complaints belong to the scribes, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.D: Correct. "Scribes'" is the plural possessive, showing that the complaints belong to the many copyists.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1980, the physicist Luis Alvarez, his son, the geologist Walter Alvarez, and their colleagues proposed that an asteroid impact had caused the mass extinction that ended the age of the dinosaurs, citing an unusually high concentration of iridium in a thin layer of clay found around the world. Ironically, the crater that would eventually be tied to that impact ______ already been noticed two years earlier by geophysicists surveying for oil on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, but their findings drew little attention outside the oil industry, and the link between the buried structure and the extinction was not established until 1991.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: had
choices.B: has
choices.C: have
choices.D: having

explanation.why: The subject is "the crater"; "that would eventually be tied to that impact" describes it. The noticing happened in 1978, "two years earlier" than the 1980 proposal, which is itself in the past. An action completed before another past event takes the past perfect, so the sentence needs "had already been noticed."
explanation.A: Correct. "Had" forms the past perfect "had already been noticed," placing the discovery before the 1980 proposal, and it works with the singular subject "crater."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Has" forms the present perfect, which cannot be used with a specific past time such as "two years earlier" than 1980.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have" is plural and present, but the subject "crater" is singular and the event is in the past.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Having" is a participle, so the main clause would have no finite verb.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The first part of Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote, published in Madrid in 1605, was so popular that readers waited impatiently for more adventures of the deluded knight and his practical squire, Sancho Panza. Cervantes, who was nearly sixty when the first part appeared, worked slowly on a continuation. Another writer, however, moved faster than Cervantes did. Stung by the appearance in 1614 of an unauthorized sequel written under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda, whose true identity remains unknown, ______ Some scholars suspect that the insult hurried Cervantes to finish the book.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Cervantes openly mocked the impostor in his own second part, published in 1615, even letting Don Quixote meet a character from the false book.
choices.B: mockery of the impostor fills the genuine second part that Cervantes published in 1615, which even lets Don Quixote meet a character from the false book.
choices.C: the genuine second part, which Cervantes published in 1615, openly mocks the impostor, even letting Don Quixote meet a character from the false book.
choices.D: Cervantes's genuine second part, published in 1615, openly mocks the impostor, even letting Don Quixote meet a character from the false book.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Stung by the appearance in 1614 of an unauthorized sequel" describes a person who felt insulted: Cervantes. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be Cervantes himself, not his book.
explanation.A: Correct. "Cervantes" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that he is the one who was stung.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This makes "mockery" the subject, so the sentence says the mockery was stung by the sequel.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This makes "the genuine second part" the subject, so the sentence says the book was stung by the sequel.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "second part"; "Cervantes's" only describes the book, so the sentence says the book was stung.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Spread across a low ridge near the town of Thatta in Sindh, Pakistan, the Makli necropolis holds hundreds of thousands of graves dating from the fourteenth to the eighteenth centuries, when Thatta was a prosperous port and capital. Its monuments, built for rulers, scholars, and merchants of successive dynasties, combine carved stone in the styles of Gujarat with glazed brick and tile from Persia and Central Asia. The sandstone tomb of the Samma ruler Jam Nizamuddin II, together with the dozens of smaller tombs clustered around it, ______ what many historians regard as the clearest illustration of this blending.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: provide
choices.B: provides
choices.C: have provided
choices.D: are providing

explanation.why: The subject is "The sandstone tomb," which is singular. A phrase beginning with "together with" (like "along with" or "as well as") adds information but does not join subjects the way "and" does, so it does not make the subject plural. A singular subject needs the singular verb "provides."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Provide" is plural, treating "together with the dozens of smaller tombs" as part of the subject, but only "and" creates a compound subject.
explanation.B: Correct. The singular verb "provides" agrees with the singular subject "The sandstone tomb."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have provided" is plural, but the subject "tomb" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Are providing" is plural, but the subject "tomb" is singular.

items.subject: science
items.passage: African lungfish inhabit shallow lakes and swamps that may shrink or disappear entirely during the dry season, and the fish have evolved a striking way to wait out the drought. As the water recedes, the lungfish burrow into the soft mud at the bottom. There, as the mud hardens around them, each fish, curled with its tail over its head and breathing air through an opening to the surface, wraps ______ in a cocoon of dried mucus that keeps its body from losing moisture. Inside, the animal's metabolism slows dramatically, and it can survive this way for months, or in some cases years, until the rains return.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: themselves
choices.C: them
choices.D: itself

explanation.why: The subject of "wraps" is "each fish," which is singular, and the fish wraps its own body, so the pronoun must refer back to the subject. A pronoun that refers back to the subject of its own clause is reflexive, and the singular reflexive for an animal is "itself." The plural "lungfish" and "them" earlier in the sentence belong to a different clause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Its" is a possessive and needs a noun after it; "wraps its in a cocoon" is ungrammatical.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Themselves" is plural, but the subject of "wraps" is the singular "each fish."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Them" is plural and not reflexive; it would mean the fish wraps something else, such as the mud, rather than its own body.
explanation.D: Correct. "Itself" is singular and reflexive, referring back to the subject "each fish."

items.subject: science
items.passage: The gharial, a slender-snouted crocodilian now found mainly along the Chambal River in northern India and in a few rivers of Nepal, is critically endangered, partly because the sandbanks where females lay their eggs are disturbed by sand mining and dams. After hatching, the young often gather in large groups near the nesting banks, and observers have described adult males remaining near these groups for weeks. Some researchers suggest that the ______ survival may depend partly on such guarding, though whether the males actively protect the young or merely share a favorable stretch of river has not been established.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: hatchling's
choices.B: hatchlings'
choices.C: hatchlings
choices.D: hatchlings's

explanation.why: The survival in question belongs to the young gharials that "gather in large groups," a plural group of hatchlings. A plural noun ending in -s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone, so "hatchlings'" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Hatchling's" is singular possessive, but the text describes large groups of young, not one hatchling.
explanation.B: Correct. "Hatchlings'" is the plural possessive, showing that the survival belongs to the many young in the groups.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Hatchlings" is plural but not possessive; the survival belongs to the hatchlings, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Hatchlings's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Marta had checked her coat pockets three times before the line reached the gangway, each time producing the same useless collection of receipts, a pencil stub, and the key to an apartment she had already given up. Behind her, a family of five shifted their suitcases with pointed sighs. The ticket officer, a gray-haired man who had plainly heard every possible excuse in his thirty years at the harbor, listened to hers without expression and then insisted that she ______ aside so that the others could board, though he added, more gently, that the last ferry of the evening would not leave for another hour.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: stood
choices.B: standing
choices.C: stands
choices.D: stand

explanation.why: After a verb of demand or urging such as "insisted" used to give an order, Standard English uses the subjunctive: the base form of the verb, with no -s and no change for past tense ("insisted that she stand"). The context shows an order, since he wanted her out of the way "so that the others could board." (British writers often use "should stand" instead, but in American English the base form is standard.)
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Stood" would mean he claimed she had already stood aside; to express his demand, the subjunctive "stand" is needed.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Standing" is a participle, so the clause "that she ___ aside" would have no verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Stands" is the ordinary present tense; after "insisted that" expressing a demand, the base form "stand" is required.
explanation.D: Correct. The base form "stand" is the subjunctive required after "insisted that" when it expresses a demand.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the 1940s, working with corn plants at Cold Spring Harbor on Long Island, New York, the geneticist Barbara McClintock noticed that some kernels bore streaks and spots of color that the genetics of the day could not easily explain. Puzzled by the way these patterns appeared and disappeared across generations of her own carefully controlled crosses, ______ When she presented the idea in 1951, many colleagues found it baffling, and decades passed before similar "jumping genes" were found in other organisms; in 1983, she received an unshared Nobel Prize.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: certain genetic elements, McClintock concluded, could move from one position on a chromosome to another, switching nearby genes on and off.
choices.B: the conclusion McClintock reached was that certain genetic elements could move from one position on a chromosome to another, switching nearby genes on and off.
choices.C: McClintock concluded that certain genetic elements could move from one position on a chromosome to another, switching nearby genes on and off.
choices.D: McClintock's conclusion was that certain genetic elements could move from one position on a chromosome to another, switching nearby genes on and off.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Puzzled by the way these patterns appeared and disappeared" describes a person: the scientist who was puzzled. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be McClintock herself.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "certain genetic elements"; "McClintock concluded" is only an interrupting phrase, so the sentence says the genetic elements were puzzled.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This makes "the conclusion" the subject, so the sentence says the conclusion was puzzled.
explanation.C: Correct. "McClintock" comes right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that she was the one who was puzzled.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "conclusion"; "McClintock's" only describes it, so the sentence says the conclusion was puzzled.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When the Ballets Russes presented The Rite of Spring in Paris on May 29, 1913, few in the audience were prepared for Igor Stravinsky's pounding, dissonant score or for Vaslav Nijinsky's choreography, in which dancers stamped and hunched rather than leaping gracefully. Accounts of the evening differ, and some details have surely grown in the retelling. Most witnesses agree, however, that so loud ______ the jeering, the whistling, and the shouted arguments among rival groups of spectators that the dancers could barely hear the orchestra, and Nijinsky had to call out the counts to them from the wings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has been
choices.B: is
choices.C: were
choices.D: was

explanation.why: The clause "so loud ___ the jeering, the whistling, and the shouted arguments" is inverted: the verb comes before its subject. The subject is the series "the jeering, the whistling, and the shouted arguments," and items joined by "and" form a plural subject. The passage describes a past evening, so the plural past-tense "were" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Has been" is singular, but the compound subject is plural.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Is" is singular, but the compound subject is plural; it is also present tense in a description of a past event.
explanation.C: Correct. The plural past-tense verb "were" agrees with the compound subject "the jeering, the whistling, and the shouted arguments."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Was" is singular and seems to agree with "the jeering," the first item, but the whole compound subject joined by "and" is plural.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Nan Madol, off the southeastern coast of the Pacific island of Pohnpei, consists of nearly one hundred artificial islets built on a coral reef from long, naturally formed columns of basalt stacked crosswise like the logs of a cabin, with coral rubble filling the spaces between them. Some of the columns weigh several tons, and how they were quarried and moved remains uncertain. The complex was the seat of the Saudeleur rulers, ______ local oral tradition describes as increasingly harsh overlords until they were overthrown, according to the same tradition, sometime around the early seventeenth century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: which
choices.B: who
choices.C: whom
choices.D: whose

explanation.why: Inside the clause that describes the rulers, the subject is "local oral tradition" and the verb is "describes"; the rulers are the ones being described, the object of "describes." The object form of the relative pronoun for people is "whom" (compare "tradition describes them"). In everyday speech "who" is often used here, but formal Standard English, which the SAT tests, requires "whom."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Which" refers to things, not people, and the Saudeleur rulers were people.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Who" is the subject form, but the rulers are the object of "describes"; the subject of that verb is "local oral tradition."
explanation.C: Correct. "Whom" is the object form, needed because the rulers are the ones that tradition describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Whose" shows possession, but nothing in the clause belongs to the rulers; "whose local oral tradition describes as ... overlords" leaves "describes" without an object.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the Dutch Republic of the seventeenth century, a painter who wished to sell work openly in a city such as Delft or Haarlem was generally required to join that city's Guild of Saint Luke, an association of painters and related craftsmen. Because each city maintained its own guild, regulations varied from place to place; nevertheless, the ______ common requirements, among them a period of apprenticeship and the payment of an entrance fee, help explain why so many Dutch painters trained locally and remained in the towns where they had first enrolled.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: guilds'
choices.B: guilds's
choices.C: guilds
choices.D: guild's

explanation.why: The requirements are described as "common," meaning shared by the many city guilds, and the sentence contrasts them with regulations that "varied from place to place." The owner is therefore plural, and a plural noun ending in -s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone: "guilds'." The singular "that city's Guild" and "its own guild" refer to one city at a time.
explanation.A: Correct. "Guilds'" is the plural possessive, showing that the shared requirements belonged to the many city guilds.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Guilds's" is not a Standard English form; a plural ending in -s takes only an apostrophe.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Guilds" is plural but not possessive; the requirements belong to the guilds, so an apostrophe is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Guild's" is singular possessive, but requirements that are "common" across cities belong to many guilds, not one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In September 1991, two hikers crossing a glacier in the Ötztal Alps, near the border between Austria and Italy, came upon a human body partly frozen into the ice.
