The man, later nicknamed Ötzi, turned out to have died about 5,300 years earlier, and his clothing, copper ax, and bow have since given archaeologists an unusually detailed view of life in Copper Age Europe. For years, researchers assumed that he had died of exposure in a sudden storm. Not until 2001, a decade after the discovery, ______ an X-ray examination reveal a stone arrowhead lodged beneath his left shoulder, evidence that he had in fact been shot.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: had
choices.B: has
choices.C: did
choices.D: was

explanation.why: When a sentence begins with a negative phrase such as "Not until 2001," the subject and helping verb are inverted, as in a question. The main verb that follows is the base form "reveal," and the helping verb that pairs with a base form in the past tense is "did": "did an X-ray examination reveal."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Had" must be followed by a past participle ("had revealed"), not the base form "reveal."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Has" must be followed by a past participle, and the present perfect does not fit the specific past year 2001.
explanation.C: Correct. "Did" pairs with the base form "reveal" to form the past tense in this inverted sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Was" must be followed by an -ing form or a past participle, not the base form "reveal."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The scholar al-Biruni, born in Khwarazm in Central Asia in 973, spent years in the lands of the Ghaznavid rulers, whose territory then extended into the Punjab; while there, he used a hilltop near Nandana, in the Salt Range of present-day Pakistan, to estimate the size of Earth. Unlike most earlier foreign writers on India, who had relied on travelers' reports, he sought out Indian scholars and their books. Having learned Sanskrit well enough to read works of astronomy and philosophy in the original, ______ Historians still consult it as a source on eleventh-century South Asia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: a detailed study of Indian astronomy, philosophy, and customs, drawing directly on those texts, was completed by al-Biruni around 1030.
choices.B: al-Biruni's detailed study of Indian astronomy, philosophy, and customs was completed around 1030 and drew directly on those texts.
choices.C: al-Biruni completed around 1030 a detailed study of Indian astronomy, philosophy, and customs that drew directly on those texts.
choices.D: around 1030 there appeared al-Biruni's detailed study of Indian astronomy, philosophy, and customs, which drew directly on those texts.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Having learned Sanskrit well enough to read works ... in the original" describes a person who learned a language. A modifier at the start of a sentence applies to the subject that comes right after the comma, so that subject must be al-Biruni himself, not his book.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This makes "a detailed study" the subject, so the sentence says the study learned Sanskrit.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "study"; "al-Biruni's" only describes it, so the sentence says the study learned Sanskrit.
explanation.C: Correct. "Al-Biruni" is the subject right after the introductory phrase, so it is clear that he is the one who learned Sanskrit.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The sentence uses "there appeared," so the subject is the study, not al-Biruni; the modifier is left describing a book that learned Sanskrit.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Arctic terns make the longest known migration of any animal. Each year, these small gray-and-white seabirds ______ from their nesting grounds in the far north to the edge of Antarctica and back again. Because they follow winding routes over the ocean, a single round trip can cover more than 70,000 kilometers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has flown
choices.B: fly
choices.C: is flying
choices.D: flies

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "seabirds," a plural noun ("these small gray-and-white seabirds"). A plural subject needs a plural verb, and the passage describes something that happens "each year," so the simple present "fly" fits.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Has flown" is singular, but the subject "seabirds" is plural.
explanation.B: Correct. The plural verb "fly" agrees with the plural subject "seabirds."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Is flying" is singular, but the subject "seabirds" is plural.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Flies" is a singular verb, but the subject "seabirds" is plural.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Ralli quilts are made by women in Sindh, Pakistan, and in nearby regions. To make one, a quilter cuts old cotton cloth into small pieces and then carefully sews ______ together in bright patterns of squares and triangles. A finished quilt can take months of work and is often given as a gift at a wedding.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: them
choices.C: they
choices.D: it

explanation.why: The pronoun names the things the quilter sews together: the "small pieces" of cloth. "Pieces" is plural, and the pronoun is the object of the verb "sews," so the plural object pronoun "them" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Its" is a singular possessive that must come before a noun; it can't stand alone as the object of "sews."
explanation.B: Correct. "Them" is plural, matching "pieces," and is the object form needed after "sews."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "They" is a subject pronoun; after the verb "sews," the object form "them" is needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but it must refer to the plural "pieces."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Giraffes feed mostly on the leaves of acacia trees, which are protected by long, sharp thorns. A ______ tongue can be about 45 centimeters long, and it is tough enough to reach between the thorns. The animal curls its tongue around a bunch of leaves and pulls them off the branch without being badly hurt.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: giraffe's
choices.B: giraffes
choices.C: giraffes's
choices.D: giraffes'

explanation.why: The blank must show that the tongue belongs to a giraffe. The article "A" and the words "the animal" and "its tongue" show that one giraffe is meant, so the singular possessive "giraffe's" is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. "Giraffe's" is the singular possessive, showing that the tongue belongs to one giraffe.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Giraffes" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it doesn't show that the tongue belongs to the animal.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Giraffes's" is not a standard form; a plural ending in s takes only an apostrophe, and here the noun should be singular anyway.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Giraffes'" is a plural possessive, but "A" and "the animal" show that only one giraffe is meant.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In October 1911, Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and four companions left their base camp on the coast of Antarctica with sleds pulled by dogs. On December 14 of that year, after nearly two months of travel across the ice, the five men ______ the South Pole, becoming the first people known to stand there.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: reached
choices.B: will reach
choices.C: reach
choices.D: reaching

explanation.why: The sentence describes a finished event on a specific past date, "December 14" of 1911, and the passage is told in the past tense ("left"). The sentence also needs a main verb for the subject "the five men," so the simple past "reached" is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. The simple past "reached" gives the subject its main verb and matches the past time of the passage.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The future "will reach" doesn't fit an event that already happened in 1911.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present tense "reach" doesn't fit an event the passage places in 1911.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Reaching" is not a main verb, so the subject "the five men" would be left without one and the sentence would be incomplete.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Marisol had promised her music teacher that she would not be late for another lesson. Hurrying down the steep hill with her violin case, ______ Without slowing down, she pulled her coat over the case to keep it dry and began to run.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Marisol felt the first drops of rain on her face.
choices.B: the first drops of rain fell on Marisol's face.
choices.C: Marisol's face was hit by the first drops of rain.
choices.D: the rain began to fall on Marisol's face.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Hurrying down the steep hill with her violin case" describes a person. The subject that comes right after the comma must be the one doing the hurrying, and only Marisol can hurry down a hill carrying a violin case.
explanation.A: Correct. "Marisol" comes right after the introductory phrase, so she is the one hurrying down the hill.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "the first drops of rain," so the sentence says the raindrops were hurrying down the hill with a violin case.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "Marisol's face," so the sentence says her face was hurrying down the hill; the modifier must describe Marisol herself.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "the rain," so the sentence says the rain was carrying the violin case down the hill.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Rohtas Fort, near the city of Jhelum in Pakistan, was built in the 1540s to control an important route through the hills. The massive stone walls of the fort ______ for about four kilometers, and twelve gates allow travelers to pass through them. Today the fort is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: is stretching
choices.B: stretch
choices.C: stretches
choices.D: has stretched

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "walls," which is plural; "of the fort" only tells whose walls they are. A plural subject needs a plural verb, so "stretch" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Is stretching" is singular, but the subject "walls" is plural.
explanation.B: Correct. The plural verb "stretch" agrees with the plural subject "walls."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Stretches" is singular and seems to agree with "fort," but the subject is the plural "walls."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Has stretched" is singular, but the subject "walls" is plural.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A sea star that loses an arm to a predator can often grow a new one over several months. In a few species, something even more surprising can happen: the lost arm can grow into a whole new sea star, as long as ______ still includes a piece of the animal's central body.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it
choices.B: them
choices.C: they
choices.D: those

explanation.why: The pronoun refers to "the lost arm," the thing that must still include a piece of the central body. "Arm" is singular, and the pronoun is the subject of "includes," so the singular subject pronoun "it" is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "It" is singular, matching "the lost arm," and agrees with the singular verb "includes."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Them" is plural and is an object pronoun, but the blank needs a singular subject for "includes."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "They" is plural, but it must refer to the singular "arm."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Those" is plural, but it must refer to the singular "arm."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In bunraku, a form of puppet theater from Japan, each large puppet is moved by three performers at once. One controls the head and right arm, another the left arm, and a third the feet. The three ______ movements must be so closely matched that the audience sees a single living character instead of three people.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: performers
choices.B: performer's
choices.C: performers's
choices.D: performers'

explanation.why: The blank must show that the movements belong to the three performers. "Three" shows that the noun is plural, and a plural noun ending in s shows possession with an apostrophe after the s: "performers'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Performers" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it doesn't show that the movements belong to them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Performer's" is the possessive of one performer, but "three" shows that several performers are meant.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Performers's" is not standard; a plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession.
explanation.D: Correct. "Performers'" is the plural possessive, showing that the movements belong to all three performers.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Venus flytrap is a plant that catches insects with leaves shaped like small open jaws. Inside each leaf are tiny trigger hairs. When an insect touches these hairs twice within a short time, the leaf ______ shut in a fraction of a second, trapping the insect inside.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: snaps
choices.B: to snap
choices.C: having snapped
choices.D: snapping

explanation.why: The main clause "the leaf ______ shut" needs a main (finite) verb for its subject, "the leaf." The passage is in the present tense ("touches"), so the present-tense verb "snaps" is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. "Snaps" is a main verb in the present tense that agrees with the singular subject "the leaf."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "To snap" is an infinitive, which can't serve as the main verb of a clause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Having snapped" is a participle, not a main verb, so the sentence would be incomplete.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Snapping" is not a main verb, so the clause "the leaf snapping shut" would have no main verb.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Found in the cool mountain forests of Nepal, Bhutan, and parts of India and China, ______ Because this food provides little energy, the animal spends many hours a day feeding and much of the rest of its time asleep in the trees.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: most of the red panda's diet is bamboo leaves.
choices.B: bamboo is the main food of the red panda.
choices.C: the red panda eats mostly bamboo leaves.
choices.D: bamboo leaves make up most of the red panda's diet.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Found in the cool mountain forests of Nepal, Bhutan, and parts of India and China" describes the animal. The subject right after the comma must therefore be "the red panda," not its food or its diet.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "most of the red panda's diet," so the phrase describes the diet rather than the animal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "bamboo," so the phrase describes the plant rather than the red panda.
explanation.C: Correct. "The red panda" comes right after the introductory phrase, so the phrase clearly describes the animal.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "bamboo leaves," so the sentence says the leaves are the thing found in those forests and described by the phrase, not the red panda.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Grandpa Osei has written to pen pals around the world for fifty years. Every Saturday, the stack of letters on his kitchen table ______ a little taller, and every Sunday he sits down with a cup of tea to answer them one by one, in neat blue ink.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: grow
choices.B: have grown
choices.C: are growing
choices.D: grows

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "stack," which is singular; "of letters on his kitchen table" only describes the stack. A singular subject needs a singular verb, and the passage uses the simple present for a habit ("sits"), so "grows" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Grow" is plural and seems to agree with "letters," but the subject is the singular "stack."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Have grown" is plural, but the subject "stack" is singular.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are growing" is plural, but the subject "stack" is singular.
explanation.D: Correct. The singular verb "grows" agrees with the singular subject "stack."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: On December 17, 1903, near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first successful flights in a powered airplane. The first flight lasted only 12 seconds, but by the end of the day, the brothers had kept ______ machine in the air for nearly a minute.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: his
choices.C: their
choices.D: they're

explanation.why: The machine belongs to "the brothers," a plural noun. A plural antecedent needs the plural possessive pronoun "their."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Its" is singular and refers to a thing, but the owners are the plural "brothers."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "His" is singular, but the machine belongs to both brothers.
explanation.C: Correct. "Their" is the plural possessive pronoun, matching "the brothers."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "They're" is a contraction of "they are"; "they are machine" makes no sense.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In India's national parks, researchers count tigers with camera traps, cameras that take a photo whenever an animal walks past. Because each ______ pattern of stripes is unique, much like a human fingerprint, scientists can compare photos and tell individual tigers apart without ever handling them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: tigers
choices.B: tigers's
choices.C: tigers'
choices.D: tiger's

explanation.why: The blank must show that the pattern of stripes belongs to a tiger. The word "each" shows that one tiger at a time is meant, so the singular possessive "tiger's" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Tigers" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it doesn't show possession, and "each" needs a singular noun.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Tigers's" is not a standard form; plural nouns ending in s take only an apostrophe, and "each" needs a singular noun.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Tigers'" is a plural possessive, but "each" requires a singular noun.
explanation.D: Correct. "Tiger's" is the singular possessive, matching "each" and showing that the pattern belongs to one tiger.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Japanese artist Katsushika Hokusai made his woodblock print The Great Wave off Kanagawa around 1831. It shows a huge wave curling over three small boats, with Mount Fuji in the distance. Since then, copies of the image ______ on everything from posters and book covers to coffee mugs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have appeared
choices.B: to appear
choices.C: appearing
choices.D: will appear

explanation.why: The phrase "Since then" describes something that began in the past (around 1831) and continues up to the present. That meaning calls for the present perfect, and the plural subject "copies" needs "have," so "have appeared" is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. The present perfect "have appeared" fits "Since then" and agrees with the plural subject "copies."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "To appear" is an infinitive, which can't serve as the main verb of the sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Appearing" is not a main verb, so the subject "copies" would be left without one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The future "will appear" doesn't fit "Since then," which points to a period from the past up to now.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Setting out from his hometown of Tangier, in Morocco, in 1325 at the age of twenty-one, ______ That pilgrimage turned out to be only the first stage of his travels, which eventually carried him as far as India and China. He did not settle back in Morocco for about twenty-four years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Ibn Battuta's first journey took him across North Africa to Mecca.
choices.B: a journey across North Africa to Mecca was begun by Ibn Battuta.
choices.C: Ibn Battuta traveled across North Africa on his way to Mecca.
choices.D: North Africa was crossed by Ibn Battuta on his way to Mecca.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Setting out from his hometown of Tangier ... at the age of twenty-one" describes a person. The subject right after the comma must be that person, Ibn Battuta.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "Ibn Battuta's first journey," so the sentence says the journey was twenty-one and set out from its hometown.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "a journey," so the phrase wrongly describes the journey as setting out from its hometown at twenty-one.
explanation.C: Correct. "Ibn Battuta" comes right after the introductory phrase, so he is the one setting out from Tangier at twenty-one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "North Africa," so the sentence says North Africa set out from Tangier.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In 1932, the Mexican painter Diego Rivera began a cycle of murals for the Detroit Institute of Arts in Michigan. The cycle, which includes 27 panels showing workers on the assembly lines of the city's car factories, ______ all four walls of a large indoor courtyard. Some local critics attacked the murals when they were unveiled in 1933, but the museum kept them, and they are now regarded as among Rivera's finest works.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: covers
choices.B: have covered
choices.C: are covering
choices.D: cover

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "The cycle," which is singular. The clause between the commas ("which includes 27 panels showing workers on the assembly lines of the city's car factories") is full of plural nouns, but none of them is the subject, so the verb must be the singular "covers."
explanation.A: Correct. The singular verb "covers" agrees with the singular subject "cycle."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Have covered" is plural, but the subject "cycle" is singular.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are covering" is plural, but the subject "cycle" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Cover" is plural and seems to agree with nearby nouns such as "panels" or "factories," but the subject is the singular "cycle."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For weeks, Amaru carried his grandfather's wooden flute in his coat pocket without daring to play it. The instrument was older than the house, and the tiny birds carved along ______ side had been worn smooth by decades of fingers. When he finally raised it to his lips one evening, the first note came out thin and shaky, yet his grandfather, listening from the doorway, smiled.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: they're
choices.B: its
choices.C: their
choices.D: it's

explanation.why: The side belongs to "The instrument" (the flute), which is singular, not to the birds carved on it. A singular thing as owner needs the singular possessive pronoun "its," with no apostrophe.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "They're" means "they are" and is plural; "along they are side" makes no sense.
explanation.B: Correct. "Its" is the singular possessive pronoun, showing that the side belongs to the instrument.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Their" is plural and seems to refer to "birds," but the birds are carved along the side of the instrument, which is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; "along it is side" makes no sense.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Oxpeckers, small birds of sub-Saharan Africa, spend much of their lives perched on large mammals such as giraffes, buffalo, and rhinoceroses, picking off ticks and other pests. For a long time, these ______ habits were seen as a simple service to the mammals. More recent studies, however, have shown that oxpeckers also peck at open wounds, keeping them from healing, and drink the animals' blood.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: birds
choices.B: birds'
choices.C: bird's
choices.D: birds's

explanation.why: The blank must show that the habits belong to the oxpeckers. The word "these" shows the noun is plural, and a plural noun ending in s shows possession with an apostrophe after the s: "birds'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Birds" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it doesn't show that the habits belong to the birds.
explanation.B: Correct. "Birds'" is the plural possessive, matching "these" and showing that the habits belong to the oxpeckers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Bird's" is the possessive of one bird, but "these" requires a plural noun, and the text discusses oxpeckers as a group.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Birds's" is not standard; a plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Construction of the Taj Mahal in Agra, India, began in 1632, the year after the death of Mumtaz Mahal, the wife of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. By the time the main tomb was essentially finished around 1643, thousands of workers ______ on it for more than a decade. The project was still not complete, however: work on the surrounding buildings and gardens continued for about ten more years.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: working
choices.B: had worked
choices.C: work
choices.D: have worked

explanation.why: The phrase "By the time the main tomb was essentially finished around 1643" sets a point in the past. Work that went on before and up to that past point needs the past perfect, so "had worked" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Working" is not a main verb, so the clause "thousands of workers working on it" would have no main verb.
explanation.B: Correct. The past perfect "had worked" shows that the work took place before the past moment named by "By the time ... 1643."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present tense "work" doesn't fit events that the passage places in the 1630s and 1640s.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The present perfect "have worked" connects the past to the present, but this action ended at a past point, "around 1643."

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The trail markers had vanished an hour earlier, buried under fresh snow, and the wind was rising. Squinting at the faded map in his gloved hands, ______ Nothing on the paper matched the ridge in front of him. With the light starting to fail, he folded the map, turned back toward the valley, and decided that pride was not worth a night on the mountain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Yerlan searched for the pass that the guide had described.
choices.B: the guide's directions to the pass made no sense to Yerlan.
choices.C: the pass that the guide had described was nowhere to be seen.
choices.D: Yerlan's search for the pass that the guide had described failed.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Squinting at the faded map in his gloved hands" describes a person. The subject right after the comma must be that person, so the sentence must begin with "Yerlan," not with the pass, the directions, or his search.
explanation.A: Correct. "Yerlan" comes right after the introductory phrase, so he is the one squinting at the map.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "the guide's directions," so the sentence says the directions were squinting at the map.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "the pass," so the sentence says the pass was squinting at the map.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "Yerlan's search," not Yerlan, so the sentence says his search had gloved hands and was squinting.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A coral reef is built by colonies of tiny animals called polyps. Each of the polyps that make up a reef ______ large numbers of microscopic algae inside its tissues, and the algae supply the polyp with much of its food. When the surrounding water stays too warm for too long, however, the polyps expel the algae, and the coral turns white, a process known as bleaching.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have housed
choices.B: houses
choices.C: are housing
choices.D: house

explanation.why: The subject of the verb is "Each," which is singular; "of the polyps that make up a reef" only tells which group is meant. The singular "its tissues" and "the polyp" later in the sentence confirm this, so the singular verb "houses" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Have housed" is plural, but the subject "Each" is singular.
explanation.B: Correct. The singular verb "houses" agrees with the singular subject "Each."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are housing" is plural, but the subject "Each" is singular.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "House" is plural and seems to agree with "polyps," but the subject is the singular "Each."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1804, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out to explore the lands west of the Mississippi River for the United States. During the expedition's first winter, the leaders hired a French Canadian trader as an interpreter, and his wife, a young Shoshone woman named Sacagawea, joined the group as well. When the explorers reached Shoshone territory the next summer, Lewis and Clark relied on ______ to help them trade for the horses they needed to cross the Rocky Mountains.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: herself
choices.B: hers
choices.C: her
choices.D: she

explanation.why: The pronoun refers to Sacagawea and comes after the preposition "on," so it is an object. The object form of "she" is "her."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Herself" is a reflexive pronoun, which needs to refer back to a female subject in the same clause, but the subject here is "Lewis and Clark."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Hers" is a possessive pronoun meaning "the one belonging to her," which makes no sense here.
explanation.C: Correct. "Her" is the object pronoun, used after the preposition "on" to refer to Sacagawea.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "She" is a subject pronoun; after the preposition "on," the object form "her" is needed.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: When Hagia Sophia was completed in Constantinople (present-day Istanbul) in 537 CE, visitors marveled at a huge dome that seemed to float above the floor. That impression comes partly from the forty windows set around ______ base, which let in a ring of light. The original dome did not last, however; it collapsed in 558, after earthquakes had weakened it, and was rebuilt with a taller shape.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its'
choices.B: their
choices.C: it's
choices.D: its

explanation.why: The base belongs to the dome, which is singular, not to the windows set around it. The singular possessive pronoun for a thing is "its," with no apostrophe.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Its'" is not a word in Standard English; the possessive "its" never takes an apostrophe.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Their" is plural and seems to refer to "windows," but the base belongs to the singular "dome."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; "around it is base" makes no sense.
explanation.D: Correct. "Its" is the singular possessive, showing that the base belongs to the dome.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When the power failed during the storm, Farida's family gathered in the kitchen. Her father lit the old oil lamp that ______ on the top shelf, unused, since her great-grandmother's time. The storm rattled the windows all night, yet no one complained; for the first time in months, they played cards together by the lamp's yellow light until the children fell asleep at the table.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: sitting
choices.B: had sat
choices.C: sits
choices.D: has sat

explanation.why: The story is told in the past tense ("failed," "gathered," "lit"). The lamp's sitting on the shelf began long before the father lit it and lasted up to that past moment, so the past perfect "had sat" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Sitting" is not a main verb, so the clause beginning with "that" would have no verb.
explanation.B: Correct. The past perfect "had sat" shows an action that lasted until a moment in the past, when the father lit the lamp.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present tense "sits" doesn't fit a story told in the past tense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The present perfect "has sat" connects to the present, but the lamp's time on the shelf ended at a past moment, when the father lit it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Born into slavery in Maryland around 1822, ______ Rather than stay in safety, she returned to Maryland about thirteen times over the next decade, guiding roughly seventy people to freedom along the network of secret routes and safe houses known as the Underground Railroad. Later, during the Civil War, she worked for the Union army as a nurse, a scout, and a spy.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Harriet Tubman escaped to Philadelphia in 1849.
choices.B: Philadelphia was where Harriet Tubman fled in 1849.
choices.C: Harriet Tubman's escape to Philadelphia came in 1849.
choices.D: the year 1849 was when Harriet Tubman escaped to Philadelphia.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Born into slavery in Maryland around 1822" describes a person. The subject right after the comma must be that person, Harriet Tubman, not her escape, a year, or a city.
explanation.A: Correct. "Harriet Tubman" comes right after the introductory phrase, so she is the one who was born into slavery.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "Philadelphia," so the sentence says the city was born into slavery.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "Harriet Tubman's escape," so the sentence says her escape was born into slavery.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "the year 1849," so the sentence says a year was born into slavery.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: On the top shelf of the pantry in Teodora's house, behind rows of jars filled with pickled peppers, ______ a small tin box of old photographs. Her grandchildren have guessed for years what else it might hold, such as love letters or a map to forgotten land. Whenever they ask, however, Teodora only smiles and offers them another slice of cake.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: sit
choices.B: are sitting
choices.C: sits
choices.D: have sat

explanation.why: In this sentence the subject comes after the verb: what sits on the shelf is "a small tin box," which is singular. The plural nouns before the blank ("rows," "jars," "peppers") are part of introductory phrases, not the subject, so the singular verb "sits" is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Sit" is plural and seems to agree with "jars" or "peppers," but the subject is the singular "box."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Are sitting" is plural, but the subject "box" is singular.
explanation.C: Correct. The singular verb "sits" agrees with the singular subject "a small tin box," which follows the verb.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Have sat" is plural, but the subject "box" is singular.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Indian flying fox, one of the largest bats in the world, is found across South Asia, from Pakistan to Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. By day, the bats hang in noisy colonies from tall trees; at night, they fly long distances to feed on fruit. Seeds that pass through ______ bodies are often dropped far from the parent tree, so the animals help new trees take root across the countryside.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: it's
choices.B: its
choices.C: their
choices.D: they're

explanation.why: The bodies belong to the bats, which the passage refers to with the plural "the bats" and "they." A plural antecedent needs the plural possessive pronoun "their."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; "through it is bodies" makes no sense.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Its" is singular and seems to refer to "The Indian flying fox," but the nearest antecedent is the plural "the bats" ("they fly"), and "bodies" is plural.
explanation.C: Correct. "Their" is the plural possessive pronoun, matching "the bats."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "They're" means "they are"; "through they are bodies" makes no sense.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country in which women could vote in national elections. Petitions organized by Kate Sheppard and other campaigners gathered more than 30,000 signatures, and in September of that year, the ______ right to vote became law. Women could not stand for election to Parliament, however, until 1919, and the first woman was not elected to Parliament until 1933.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: women's
choices.B: womens'
choices.C: women
choices.D: woman's

explanation.why: The blank must show that the right to vote belongs to women as a group. "Women" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive is formed by adding an apostrophe and s: "women's."
explanation.A: Correct. "Women's" is the possessive of the irregular plural "women."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Womens'" is not a word; the plural is "women," and its possessive is "women's."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Women" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it doesn't show that the right belongs to them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Woman's" is the possessive of one woman, but the right was granted to women as a group.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The mbira, an instrument from Zimbabwe made of thin metal keys attached to a wooden board, ______ by plucking the keys with the thumbs and one finger. Although it is sometimes called a "thumb piano," it has little in common with a piano: its sound comes from vibrating metal rather than struck strings, and players often set it inside a large hollow gourd that makes its tone louder.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: having been played
choices.B: is played
choices.C: to be played
choices.D: being played

explanation.why: The subject "The mbira" needs a main verb, and the descriptive phrase between the commas does not provide one. The mbira is the thing that receives the action, and the passage is in the present tense, so the present passive "is played" is correct.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Having been played" is a participle phrase, not a main verb, so the sentence would be incomplete.
explanation.B: Correct. "Is played" is a main verb in the present tense, giving the subject "The mbira" a verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "To be played" is an infinitive, which can't serve as the main verb of a sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Being played" is a participle, not a main verb, so the subject "The mbira" would have no verb and the sentence would be a fragment.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Humpback whales have several ways of catching the small fish they eat, and one of the most remarkable is called bubble-net feeding. Swimming in a slow upward spiral beneath a school of small fish, ______ The whale, sometimes joined by others from its group, then surges up through the center of the ring with its mouth wide open. Not every population of humpbacks uses this technique, however; it is best known among whales that feed in the waters off Alaska.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: a ring of bubbles is released by a humpback whale, trapping the fish like a net.
choices.B: the fish are trapped by a ring of bubbles that a humpback whale releases.
choices.C: a ring of bubbles from a humpback whale traps the fish like a net.
choices.D: a humpback whale releases a ring of bubbles that traps the fish like a net.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Swimming in a slow upward spiral beneath a school of small fish" describes the whale. The subject right after the comma must be "a humpback whale," not the bubbles or the fish.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "a ring of bubbles," so the sentence says the bubbles were swimming in a spiral beneath the fish.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "the fish," so the sentence says the fish were swimming beneath a school of small fish, which makes no sense.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "a ring of bubbles," so the phrase describes the bubbles rather than the whale.
explanation.D: Correct. "A humpback whale" comes right after the introductory phrase, so the whale is the one swimming in the spiral.

items.subject: science
items.passage: When a shark or other predator bites at a hagfish, the eel-shaped animal releases a small amount of mucus from glands along its body, and within a fraction of a second the mucus expands in seawater into a large mass of slime that can clog the attacker's gills. The surprising strength of this slime, according to biologists who have studied the glands of several hagfish species, ______ from thousands of protein threads, each far thinner than a human hair, that unspool from specialized cells and lace the mucus together.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: are coming
choices.B: have come
choices.C: come
choices.D: comes

explanation.why: Strip out the interrupting phrases ("according to biologists who have studied the glands of several hagfish species") and the core sentence is "The surprising strength of this slime ______ from thousands of protein threads." The subject is the singular noun "strength"; "slime," "biologists," "glands" and "species" all sit inside phrases that describe or interrupt it. A singular subject needs the singular verb "comes."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Are coming" is plural, but the subject "strength" is singular.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Have come" is a plural verb form, so it doesn't agree with the singular subject "strength."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Come" is a plural verb; it seems to match the nearby plural nouns "biologists" or "species," but the subject is the singular "strength."
explanation.D: Correct. The singular verb "comes" agrees with the singular subject "strength."

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Dholavira, a Harappan city built more than 4,000 years ago on an island in the salt flats of the Rann of Kutch in present-day Gujarat, India, received little rain, and the two streams that flowed past it ran for only part of the year. To get through the long dry months, the city's residents cut a series of large reservoirs into the bedrock and built dams and channels on the streams to steer the seasonal runoff into ______. Archaeologists regard this system as one of the most sophisticated examples of water management in the ancient world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: itself
choices.B: it
choices.C: them
choices.D: its

explanation.why: The runoff was steered into the things built to hold water: "a series of large reservoirs." That antecedent is plural ("reservoirs"), so the pronoun must be the plural object pronoun "them." Don't be pulled toward a singular noun closer to the blank, such as "bedrock" or "runoff"; runoff can't be steered into bedrock or into itself.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Itself" is a singular reflexive pronoun; the sentence would say the runoff was steered into the runoff, and it doesn't match the plural "reservoirs."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "It" is singular, but the water was steered into the plural "reservoirs."
explanation.C: Correct. The plural pronoun "them" refers back to the plural antecedent "reservoirs."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Its" is a possessive form, which must be followed by a noun ("its banks"); it can't stand alone as the object of "into."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Linear B, a script used on Crete and the Greek mainland during the Late Bronze Age, baffled scholars for half a century after thousands of clay tablets inscribed with it were unearthed at the palace of Knossos. Many experts assumed that it recorded an unknown, non-Greek language. In 1952, however, Michael Ventris, an English architect who had studied the script since boyhood, showed that the ______ signs stood for syllables of an early form of Greek. The decoded texts proved to be mostly palace records of livestock, textiles, and other goods.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: tablets'
choices.B: tablets
choices.C: tablets's
choices.D: tablet's

explanation.why: The signs belong to the thousands of clay tablets mentioned earlier, so the word in the blank must be both plural and possessive. A plural noun that already ends in s forms its possessive by adding only an apostrophe: "tablets'."
explanation.A: Correct. "Tablets'" is the plural possessive, showing that the signs belong to the many tablets.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Tablets" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it doesn't show that the signs belong to the tablets.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession; "tablets's" is not a standard form.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Tablet's" is the possessive of a single tablet, but the text refers to thousands of tablets.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In December 1994, three cave explorers squeezing through a narrow passage above the Ardèche River in southern France entered a cave whose walls were covered with hundreds of images of lions, rhinoceroses, horses, and mammoths. The paintings were astonishingly well preserved because a rockfall ______ the cave's original entrance many thousands of years earlier, shielding the chambers from weather, animals, and later human visitors. Radiocarbon dates from charcoal used in some of the drawings suggest that they are more than 30,000 years old.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: would seal
choices.B: has sealed
choices.C: had sealed
choices.D: seals

explanation.why: The passage describes a past situation (the paintings "were" well preserved in 1994) and explains it with an action that happened before that situation, "many thousands of years earlier." An action completed before another past time takes the past perfect: "had sealed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Would seal" points to a time after the past moment being described, but the rockfall came before the paintings were found, not after.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The present perfect "has sealed" links a past action to the present; it can't be used with a specific earlier time such as "many thousands of years earlier" in a sentence set in the past.
explanation.C: Correct. The past perfect "had sealed" shows that the rockfall came before the past situation described in the sentence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Seals" is present tense, but the rockfall happened thousands of years before the past events in the passage.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Göbekli Tepe, a hilltop site in southeastern Turkey, has forced archaeologists to rethink the origins of monumental building. Raised around 9500 BCE, thousands of years before the invention of writing or the wheel, ______ The builders appear to have been hunter-gatherers, a conclusion that challenges the long-held view that only settled farming societies could organize projects on such a scale.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: visitors to the site can see massive T-shaped limestone pillars, some taller than five meters, carved with foxes, boars, and vultures.
choices.B: the carvings of foxes, boars, and vultures cover massive T-shaped limestone pillars at the site, some taller than five meters.
choices.C: archaeologists have found massive T-shaped limestone pillars at the site, some taller than five meters, carved with foxes, boars, and vultures.
choices.D: the site's massive T-shaped limestone pillars, some taller than five meters, are carved with foxes, boars, and vultures.

explanation.why: An introductory modifier describes whatever noun comes right after the comma. "Raised around 9500 BCE" describes something that was set upright long ago, which can only be the stone pillars. So the subject that follows must be the pillars themselves.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Placing "visitors" right after the modifier says modern visitors were raised around 9500 BCE, which makes no sense.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject "the carvings" comes right after the modifier, but carvings are cut into stone, not raised; the modifier is meant for the pillars.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Placing "archaeologists" right after the modifier says the archaeologists were raised around 9500 BCE, so the modifier dangles.
explanation.D: Correct. The subject "the site's massive T-shaped limestone pillars" comes right after the modifier, so the pillars are what was raised around 9500 BCE.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1976 the Hōkūleʻa, a double-hulled voyaging canoe built by the Polynesian Voyaging Society, sailed about 4,000 kilometers from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti. Its course was set by Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Micronesia who read the rising and setting points of stars, the direction of ocean swells, and the flight of seabirds. Neither a magnetic compass nor modern navigational charts ______ used to guide the canoe, and the voyage strengthened the case that ancient Polynesians had deliberately navigated such distances rather than drifting to new islands by chance.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has been
choices.B: is
choices.C: was
choices.D: were

explanation.why: When two subjects are joined by "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. Here the closer subject is "modern navigational charts," which is plural, and the passage is set in the past, so the verb must be the plural past form "were."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Has been" is singular, so it doesn't agree with the nearer subject, the plural "charts."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Is" is singular, so it doesn't agree with the plural "charts," and it is also in the present tense.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Was" agrees with the farther subject, "a magnetic compass," but with "neither ... nor" the verb must agree with the nearer subject, the plural "charts."
explanation.D: Correct. The plural past-tense verb "were" agrees with the nearer subject, "modern navigational charts," and fits the 1976 setting.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The superb lyrebird of southeastern Australia is famous for its mimicry. During the breeding season, an adult male clears a patch of forest floor, raises his long, lacy tail over his head, and sings a medley that can include the calls of kookaburras, whipbirds, and dozens of other species. Young males, however, do not hatch knowing these imitations. Researchers who have recorded birds over many years think that much of ______ repertoire is learned gradually by listening to older males singing nearby.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: their
choices.C: his
choices.D: they're

explanation.why: The pronoun refers to the birds whose repertoire is learned: "Young males," a plural noun. A plural antecedent needs the plural possessive pronoun "their." The singular "his" is tempting because the earlier sentence describes one adult male, but that male is not the one doing the learning.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Its" is singular, so it can't refer to the plural antecedent "young males."
explanation.B: Correct. The plural possessive "their" agrees with the plural antecedent "young males."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "His" is singular and seems to refer to the adult male described earlier, but the learners are the plural "young males."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "They're" is a contraction of "they are," not a possessive pronoun; "much of they are repertoire" makes no sense.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Nyatapola Temple in Bhaktapur, Nepal, completed in 1702 during the reign of King Bhupatindra Malla, rises five stories above the city's main square and is among the tallest pagoda-style temples in the country. Pairs of carved stone guardians line the steep stairway that climbs its five-tiered platform. The temple survived powerful earthquakes in 1934 and 2015 that badly damaged many nearby buildings, and many observers attribute part of its stability to the ______ broad, stepped base, which spreads the structure's weight over a wide area.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: temples'
choices.B: temple
choices.C: temples
choices.D: temple's

explanation.why: The broad, stepped base belongs to one building, the Nyatapola Temple. A singular noun shows possession with an apostrophe plus s: "temple's." The passage names only one temple, so a plural form doesn't fit.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Temples'" is a plural possessive, but the base belongs to one temple, not several.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Temple" has no apostrophe, so it doesn't show that the base belongs to the temple; "the temple broad, stepped base" is not standard.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Temples" is a plain plural; it neither shows possession nor matches the single temple in the passage.
explanation.D: Correct. "Temple's" is the singular possessive, showing that the base belongs to the one temple.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Esther stood at the rail of the night ferry and watched the harbor lights of her hometown shrink to a thin bright line. Her brother had offered to drive her to the port and wait with her until the boarding call, but she had insisted on taking the bus alone. Now, with the black water widening between them, she understood that if she ______ his offer, she would have had one more hour to tell him what she had never managed to say.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: had accepted
choices.B: would have accepted
choices.C: accepted
choices.D: has accepted

explanation.why: The sentence imagines a past that didn't happen: Esther refused the ride, and the result clause says "she would have had one more hour." A condition contrary to past fact takes the past perfect in the "if" clause, paired with "would have" in the result clause: "if she had accepted ..., she would have had."
explanation.A: Correct. The past perfect "had accepted" correctly pairs with "would have had" to describe an unreal past condition.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Would have" belongs in the result clause, not in the "if" clause; "if she would have accepted" is not standard.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The simple past "accepted" is used for unreal present or future conditions ("if she accepted, she would have"), so it clashes with the past result "would have had."
explanation.D: Incorrect. The present perfect "has accepted" doesn't fit a story told in the past or a condition that never happened.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Arctic ground squirrels hibernate for up to eight months of the year in burrows beneath the tundra of Alaska and northern Canada. Curled in a tight ball in its frozen burrow, ______ Every few weeks, though, the animal shivers itself back to a normal temperature for less than a day before cooling again, a costly process whose purpose researchers are still investigating.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the squirrel can let its body temperature fall below the freezing point of water, to about −3°C, without its blood turning to ice.
choices.B: the body temperature of the squirrel can fall below the freezing point of water, to about −3°C, without its blood turning to ice.
choices.C: the squirrel's body temperature can fall below the freezing point of water, to about −3°C, without its blood turning to ice.
choices.D: a drop in body temperature below the freezing point of water, to about −3°C, can occur in the squirrel without its blood turning to ice.

explanation.why: The phrase "Curled in a tight ball in its frozen burrow" describes the animal itself; only a squirrel can curl into a ball. An introductory modifier must be followed directly by the noun it describes, so the main clause must begin with "the squirrel."
explanation.A: Correct. "The squirrel" comes right after the modifier, so it is clearly the squirrel that is curled in a tight ball.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject is "the body temperature," so the modifier wrongly describes a temperature as curled in a ball.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "the squirrel's body temperature," so the sentence says a temperature is curled in a ball; a possessive like "squirrel's" doesn't make the squirrel the subject.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject is "a drop in body temperature," which can't be curled in a burrow, so the modifier dangles.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Each autumn the hill town where Lucía Ferreyra grew up holds a pottery competition that draws entries from three provinces. The rules have hardly changed in sixty years. The jury, made up of three retired potters from neighboring villages and a visiting curator from the regional museum, ______ every entry by hand before any discussion begins, turning each bowl over to inspect its base for hairline cracks and tapping its rim to hear whether the firing was even.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: examines
choices.B: examine
choices.C: have examined
choices.D: are examining

explanation.why: The subject is "The jury"; the long phrase "made up of three retired potters ... and a visiting curator" only describes it. "Jury" is a collective noun, and here the jury acts as a single body that follows the same rules every year. In American English a collective noun acting as one unit takes a singular verb, and the passage describes a regular routine, so the present-tense "examines" fits.
explanation.A: Correct. The singular verb "examines" agrees with the collective noun "jury" acting as one body and fits the yearly routine described.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Examine" is plural; it seems to agree with "potters," but the subject is the collective noun "jury," which acts as a unit and takes a singular verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Have examined" is plural, so it doesn't agree with the singular subject "jury."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Are examining" is plural, so it doesn't agree with the singular subject "jury."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Rongorongo, a script of carved glyphs that survives on about two dozen wooden tablets and staffs from Rapa Nui (Easter Island), most of them collected by European visitors in the late 1800s, has resisted every attempt at decipherment. By the time outsiders became interested in the glyphs, few if any islanders could still read them. Scholars therefore continue to debate whether ______ records full sentences of the Rapa Nui language or serves mainly as a memory aid for people reciting chants.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: they
choices.B: them
choices.C: it
choices.D: itself

explanation.why: The thing that either "records full sentences" or "serves as a memory aid" is the script, "Rongorongo," a singular noun named at the start. The blank is the subject of the clause, so it needs a singular subject pronoun: "it." The plural nouns "tablets," "staffs" and "glyphs" are tempting, but they are not what the scholars are debating, and the singular verbs "records" and "serves" confirm a singular subject.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "They" is plural, but the antecedent is the singular "Rongorongo"; "they records" also breaks agreement.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Them" is plural and is an object pronoun, so it can't serve as the subject of "records."
explanation.C: Correct. The singular subject pronoun "it" refers back to "Rongorongo" and agrees with "records" and "serves."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Itself" is a reflexive pronoun, which can't act as the subject of a clause.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At its height in the twelfth century, Angkor, the capital of the Khmer Empire in what is now Cambodia, was laced with canals and moats and flanked by enormous rectangular reservoirs called barays. The West Baray alone stretches about 8 kilometers from end to end. Some archaeologists argue that the ______ main purpose was to store monsoon water for irrigating rice fields during the dry season; others contend that they served chiefly religious and symbolic functions, representing the oceans that surround the mythical center of the world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: reservoirs
choices.B: reservoirs'
choices.C: reservoir's
choices.D: reservoirs's

explanation.why: The main purpose under debate belongs to all of the barays, and the next clause refers to them with the plural "they." So the word in the blank must be plural and possessive. A plural noun ending in s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone: "reservoirs'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Reservoirs" is a plain plural; without an apostrophe it can't show that the purpose belongs to the reservoirs.
explanation.B: Correct. "Reservoirs'" is the plural possessive, matching the many barays that the later "they" refers to.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Reservoir's" is singular possessive, but the debate concerns all the barays, as the plural "they" shows.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession, so "reservoirs's" is not standard.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Somapura Mahavihara, in the Paharpur area of northwestern Bangladesh, was founded in the late eighth century by Dharmapala, a king of the Pala dynasty, and grew into one of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalayas, with more than 170 cells for monks arranged around a vast courtyard. By the time British surveyors described its ruins in the nineteenth century, the monastery ______ abandoned for hundreds of years, and its towering central temple lay buried beneath a great mound of earth and brick.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: has been
choices.B: had been
choices.C: is
choices.D: was being

explanation.why: The time marker "By the time British surveyors described its ruins in the nineteenth century" sets a past moment, and the abandonment had already lasted for hundreds of years before then. A state that continued up to a past moment is expressed with the past perfect: "had been."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The present perfect "has been" connects a situation to the present, but the sentence measures the abandonment up to a moment in the nineteenth century.
explanation.B: Correct. The past perfect "had been" shows that the abandonment lasted up to the past moment when the surveyors arrived.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The present tense "is" doesn't fit a sentence set in the nineteenth century and conflicts with the past-tense "lay."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Was being abandoned" says the abandonment was still in progress, which contradicts "for hundreds of years" and the ruins already lying buried.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A cuttlefish can change the color and pattern of its body in less than a second, matching sand, rock, or seaweed closely enough to vanish from view. Layered over light-reflecting cells and packed with millions of tiny elastic sacs of pigment called chromatophores, ______ Because each sac is stretched open or squeezed shut by muscles wired directly to the brain, a new pattern can ripple across the animal almost instantly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: muscles turn the cuttlefish's skin into a kind of living display screen.
choices.B: scientists have compared the cuttlefish's skin to a kind of living display screen.
choices.C: the cuttlefish's skin works as a kind of living display screen.
choices.D: the cuttlefish uses its skin as a kind of living display screen.

explanation.why: The modifier "Layered over light-reflecting cells and packed with millions of tiny elastic sacs of pigment" describes a tissue, not the whole animal: it is the skin that lies over reflecting cells and holds the pigment sacs. So the noun right after the comma must be the skin.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject "muscles" comes right after the modifier, so the sentence says the muscles are packed with pigment sacs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Placing "scientists" right after the modifier says the scientists are packed with pigment sacs, so the modifier dangles.
explanation.C: Correct. The subject "the cuttlefish's skin" comes right after the modifier, so it is the skin that is layered over reflecting cells and packed with pigment sacs.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Placing "the cuttlefish" right after the modifier says the whole animal is layered over light-reflecting cells; the modifier describes its skin.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 2005 NASA's Cassini spacecraft detected jets of water vapor and ice grains erupting from four long fractures, nicknamed "tiger stripes," near the south pole of Saturn's moon Enceladus. Later flybys showed that the material comes from a salty ocean hidden beneath the moon's icy crust. Among the substances that Cassini's instruments identified in the plumes, and that have made this small moon a leading target in the search for life beyond Earth, ______ molecular hydrogen, a potential source of chemical energy for microbes, and a variety of organic compounds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: is
choices.B: has been
choices.C: was
choices.D: are

explanation.why: This sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb. "Among the substances ... in the plumes" is a prepositional phrase, not the subject. The subject is the compound "molecular hydrogen ... and a variety of organic compounds," and two subjects joined by "and" are plural, so the verb must be "are."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Is" is singular; it seems to agree with "molecular hydrogen" alone, but the subject is the compound "molecular hydrogen ... and a variety of organic compounds."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Has been" is singular, so it doesn't agree with the compound subject joined by "and."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Was" is singular, so it doesn't agree with the plural compound subject that follows the verb.
explanation.D: Correct. The plural verb "are" agrees with the compound subject "molecular hydrogen ... and a variety of organic compounds," which comes after the verb in this inverted sentence.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For eleven years the Vidal sisters had run the bakery on Calle Ombú together, and for eleven years they had quarreled over their mother's recipe for anise bread: Inés wanted a slower rise, while Paloma swore by an extra spoonful of honey. So when a reporter from the neighborhood paper asked which of them deserved credit for the loaf that had made the shop famous, Inés braced herself for an argument. Paloma only brushed the flour from her apron. "Neither of us," she said. "The credit belongs to our mother, who taught Inés and ______ everything we know about bread."
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: mine
choices.B: I
choices.C: myself
choices.D: me

explanation.why: Inside the quotation, the blank is part of a compound object of the verb "taught": the mother taught "Inés and ______." Test it by dropping "Inés and": the mother taught "me," not "I." An object takes the object pronoun "me."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Mine" is a possessive pronoun meaning "the one belonging to me"; "taught Inés and mine" doesn't name a person who was taught.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "I" is a subject pronoun; you wouldn't say "who taught I everything," so it can't be the object of "taught."
explanation.C: Incorrect. A reflexive pronoun such as "myself" needs an antecedent in the same clause; the subject of "taught" is "who" (the mother), so "myself" has nothing to refer back to.
explanation.D: Correct. The object pronoun "me" is correct as part of the compound object of "taught."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Marie and Pierre Curie handled radium and polonium for years without any protection, unaware of how dangerous the elements they had discovered could be. More than a century later, the ______ laboratory notebooks, which are now kept in lead-lined boxes at the National Library of France in Paris, are still contaminated with radium-226, an isotope with a half-life of about 1,600 years. Researchers who wish to consult them must sign a waiver and wear protective clothing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Curie's
choices.B: Curies's
choices.C: Curies'
choices.D: Curies

explanation.why: The notebooks belonged to both Marie and Pierre, the couple referred to with "the" as a family name. The plural of the surname is "Curies," and a plural ending in s forms its possessive with an apostrophe alone: "the Curies'."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Curie's" is the possessive of one person, but "the" signals the couple, and the notebooks belonged to both scientists.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A plural noun ending in s takes only an apostrophe to show possession; "Curies's" is not standard.
explanation.C: Correct. "Curies'" is the plural possessive, showing that the notebooks belonged to Marie and Pierre together.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Curies" is a plain plural with no apostrophe, so it doesn't show ownership of the notebooks.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: When astronomers predicted that Earth would pass through the tail of Halley's Comet in May 1910, and spectroscopes had already detected cyanogen, a poisonous gas, in comets, some newspapers printed alarming speculation about what might happen to life on Earth. Enterprising sellers in the United States, sensing an opportunity in the public's anxiety and hoping to profit before the predicted date arrived, ______ "comet pills" that supposedly protected buyers from the gas. In reality, the tail was far too thin to cause harm.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: marketing
choices.B: having marketed
choices.C: to market
choices.D: marketed

explanation.why: The subject "Enterprising sellers" is followed by two long participial phrases ("sensing an opportunity ..." and "hoping to profit ..."), but those phrases are only modifiers. The sentence still needs a main verb for "sellers," so the blank must be a finite verb in the past tense: "marketed."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Marketing" is a participle like "sensing" and "hoping"; without a main verb, the sentence would be a fragment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Having marketed" is a participial phrase, not a main verb, so the subject "sellers" would still have no verb.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "To market" is an infinitive, which can't serve as the main verb of a sentence.
explanation.D: Correct. The past-tense verb "marketed" gives the subject "sellers" the main verb the sentence needs and fits the 1910 setting.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1930 Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar left Madras, India, by ship to begin graduate study at the University of Cambridge in England. Only nineteen years old and working through the long voyage with little more than pen and paper, ______ That mass, now known as the Chandrasekhar limit and estimated at about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun, became one of the cornerstones of the modern theory of how stars die.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: the calculation that Chandrasekhar completed showed that a white dwarf star above a certain mass cannot support itself against its own gravity.
choices.B: Chandrasekhar calculated that a white dwarf star above a certain mass cannot support itself against its own gravity.
choices.C: Chandrasekhar's calculation showed that a white dwarf star above a certain mass cannot support itself against its own gravity.
choices.D: a white dwarf star above a certain mass, Chandrasekhar calculated, cannot support itself against its own gravity.

explanation.why: The introductory modifier "Only nineteen years old and working through the long voyage with little more than pen and paper" describes a person, the young scientist. The noun right after the comma must therefore be Chandrasekhar himself, used as the subject, not his calculation and not a star.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject is "the calculation," so the sentence says a calculation was nineteen years old and working with pen and paper.
explanation.B: Correct. "Chandrasekhar" is the subject and comes right after the modifier, so he is clearly the one who was nineteen and working during the voyage.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Although Chandrasekhar's name appears first, it is a possessive; the subject is "calculation," so the modifier still describes the calculation, not the person.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The subject "a white dwarf star" comes right after the modifier, so the sentence says a star was nineteen years old and on a voyage; the interrupting "Chandrasekhar calculated" doesn't fix this.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1291 the government of Venice ordered the city's glassmakers to move their furnaces to the nearby island of Murano, largely to protect the crowded, wooden city from fire. The move also made the craft easier to control. Under later laws, a glassmaker who left the Venetian Republic to practice his trade abroad risked severe consequences: either penalties imposed on the relatives he had left behind or a long prison sentence, should he ever be caught and brought back, ______ prescribed as punishment for taking the secrets of Venetian glass to a rival city.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: was
choices.B: are
choices.C: were
choices.D: have been

explanation.why: When two subjects are joined by "either ... or," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. The plural "penalties" comes first, but the nearer subject is "a long prison sentence," which is singular; the interrupting phrase "should he ever be caught and brought back" doesn't change that. The passage is set in the past, so the singular past-tense "was" is correct.
explanation.A: Correct. The singular past-tense verb "was" agrees with the nearer subject, "a long prison sentence."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Are" is plural and present tense, so it neither agrees with the singular "sentence" nor fits the past setting.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Were" agrees with the farther subject, "penalties," but with "either ... or" the verb must agree with the nearer subject, the singular "sentence."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Have been" is plural, so it doesn't agree with the nearer singular subject "sentence."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Around 1562 the young Mughal emperor Akbar commissioned an illustrated copy of the Hamzanama, a sprawling adventure romance, and the project occupied his imperial workshop for roughly fifteen years. Supervised first by Mir Sayyid Ali and later by Abd al-Samad, two Persian masters whom Akbar's father, Humayun, had brought to India, more than one hundred artists, most of them trained in Indian painting traditions, produced some 1,400 large paintings on cotton cloth for the project. Only about 200 of ______ survive today, scattered among museums and private collections around the world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: them
choices.B: its
choices.C: they
choices.D: it

explanation.why: What survives today is a number of the paintings: "Only about 200 of ______" refers back to "some 1,400 large paintings." That antecedent is plural, and the pronoun is the object of the preposition "of," so it must be the plural object pronoun "them." The singular nouns "project," "workshop" and "Hamzanama" are tempting, but you can't have "200 of" a single project.
explanation.A: Correct. The plural object pronoun "them" refers to the plural "paintings" and correctly follows the preposition "of."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Its" is a singular possessive that must be followed by a noun, so "200 of its" is incomplete and doesn't match the plural "paintings."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "They" is a subject pronoun, so it can't be the object of the preposition "of"; "200 of they" is not standard.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "It" is singular and would point to the project or the Hamzanama, but the 200 surviving items are some of the plural "paintings."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Pangolins are the only mammals covered in large, overlapping scales. Made of keratin, the same protein that forms human fingernails, the scales can account for as much as a fifth of an animal's body weight.
