When a pangolin that has wandered far from its burrow at night is confronted by a predator such as a lion or leopard, ______ first response is usually to curl into a tight ball, presenting the attacker with a hard, sharp-edged shell that even big cats struggle to pry open.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: its'
choices.C: it's
choices.D: their

explanation.why: The pronoun refers to "a pangolin," a singular noun, and it shows possession of "first response." The singular possessive pronoun is "its," with no apostrophe. The plural "Pangolins" at the start of the passage makes "their" tempting, but this clause is about one pangolin.
explanation.A: Correct. "Its" is the singular possessive pronoun, matching "a pangolin" and showing that the first response belongs to it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Its'" is not a word in standard English; the possessive form of "it" is simply "its."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "It's" is a contraction of "it is" or "it has"; "it is first response" makes no sense, and possessive pronouns never take apostrophes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Their" is plural, but the antecedent in this sentence is the singular "a pangolin."

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, then a graduate student at the University of Cambridge, noticed an odd signal in the charts produced by a radio telescope she had helped build: a series of pulses arriving every 1.33 seconds with clocklike regularity. The source turned out to be a pulsar, a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radio waves across space like a lighthouse. In the decades since that discovery, astronomers ______ thousands of additional pulsars, some of which rotate hundreds of times per second.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have found
choices.B: find
choices.C: had found
choices.D: found

explanation.why: The phrase "In the decades since that discovery" describes a period that began in the past and continues up to the present. An action spread over such a period takes the present perfect: "have found." The present-tense "rotate" later in the sentence confirms that the time frame reaches the present.
explanation.A: Correct. The present perfect "have found" fits a period that began in 1967 and continues to the present.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The simple present "find" describes habitual or current actions and can't be paired with "since" to describe a stretch of time leading up to now.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The past perfect "had found" needs a later past moment to look back from; here the period runs to the present, not to a point in the past.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The simple past "found" treats the discoveries as finished at a past time, but "since that discovery" describes a period lasting up to now.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Machu Picchu sits on a narrow ridge high above the Urubamba River in the Andes of Peru. Built around 1450, probably as a royal estate for the Inca ruler Pachacuti, and abandoned roughly a century later, ______ Many of its walls were made of granite blocks cut so precisely that they fit together without mortar.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: historians note that the site was never discovered by the Spanish conquistadors, so many of its buildings remain largely intact.
choices.B: the Spanish conquistadors never discovered the site, so many of its buildings remain largely intact.
choices.C: the Spanish conquistadors' failure to discover the site explains why many of its buildings remain largely intact.
choices.D: the site was never discovered by the Spanish conquistadors, so many of its buildings remain largely intact.

explanation.why: The introductory modifier "Built around 1450 ... and abandoned roughly a century later" describes the place as a whole: Machu Picchu was the royal estate that was built and abandoned. The noun right after the comma must therefore be "the site." Choice C is the near miss: it begins with "the Spanish conquistadors' failure," but the subject is "failure," not the site.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Placing "historians" right after the modifier says the historians were built around 1450 and abandoned, which makes no sense.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Placing "the Spanish conquistadors" right after the modifier says the conquistadors were built as a royal estate, so the modifier dangles.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The subject is "failure" ("conquistadors' " is only a possessive), so the sentence says a failure was built as a royal estate and later abandoned.
explanation.D: Correct. "The site" comes right after the modifier, so it is the site that was built as a royal estate and later abandoned.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Along parts of the Pacific coast of North America, purple sea urchins multiplied rapidly in the mid-2010s, after a wasting disease killed most of the sunflower sea stars that prey on them. Freed from their main predator, the urchins grazed once-dense kelp forests down to bare rock, creating what ecologists call "urchin barrens." At some monitored sites off northern California, the number of urchins on each square meter of seafloor, once only a handful, ______ to several dozen, and the kelp has not returned.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: have risen
choices.B: has risen
choices.C: are rising
choices.D: rise

explanation.why: The subject is "the number," a singular noun; "of urchins on each square meter of seafloor" and "once only a handful" only describe it. "The number of" takes a singular verb (unlike "a number of," which means "several" and takes a plural verb). The present perfect "has risen" also matches the present-tense "has not returned."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Have risen" is plural; it seems to agree with "urchins," but the subject is the singular "number."
explanation.B: Correct. The singular verb "has risen" agrees with the subject "the number."
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Are rising" is plural, so it doesn't agree with the singular subject "the number."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Rise" is plural, so it doesn't agree with the singular subject "the number."

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The quilters of Gee's Bend, a small, isolated community on a bend of the Alabama River, have worked for generations with whatever fabric was at hand: worn work clothes, feed sacks, and scraps of old dresses. Their bold, improvised designs drew national attention after a 2002 museum exhibition. Although many of the quilts share certain features, such as large blocks of color and off-center patterns, each of the hundreds of quilts now held in collections across the country bears ______ maker's distinct sense of rhythm and balance.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: its
choices.B: their
choices.C: it's
choices.D: they're

explanation.why: The subject of the main clause is "each," not "quilts"; "of the hundreds of quilts now held in collections" only tells which items are meant. "Each" is singular (as the singular verb "bears" shows), and the pronoun refers to one quilt, a thing, so the singular possessive "its" is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. The singular possessive "its" agrees with the singular antecedent "each" (each quilt).
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Their" is plural and seems to match "quilts" or "quilters," but the antecedent is the singular "each" quilt.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "It's" is a contraction of "it is" or "it has," not a possessive; "bears it is maker's" makes no sense.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "They're" is a contraction of "they are," not a possessive, and it is plural.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the Hunza Valley of northern Pakistan, the apricot harvest arrives in early summer. Because fresh fruit spoils quickly and the winters at that altitude are long, each household has traditionally preserved much of its crop by drying it in the sun. For several weeks the ______ flat rooftops are covered with trays of halved apricots, so that whole villages glow orange when seen from the slopes above, and the dried fruit and the oil pressed from the kernels are stored for the cold months ahead.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: families
choices.B: family's
choices.C: families'
choices.D: familys'

explanation.why: The rooftops belong to the many households that make whole villages glow orange, so the word in the blank must be plural and possessive. The plural of "family" is "families," and a plural ending in s adds only an apostrophe: "families'." The singular "each household" in the previous sentence makes "family's" tempting, but one family's roof can't turn "whole villages" orange.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Families" is a plain plural; without an apostrophe it doesn't show that the rooftops belong to the families.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Family's" is singular possessive, but the rooftops belong to the many families across whole villages.
explanation.C: Correct. "Families'" is the correctly spelled plural possessive, showing that the rooftops belong to many families.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Familys'" misspells the plural; a noun ending in a consonant plus y changes y to i and adds -es ("families") before the apostrophe.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The varnish, Mr. Okonkwo had warned on her first day, could not be hurried. Yet on the morning the cellist was due to collect her repaired instrument, Adaeze, who had spent three weeks under his patient eye learning to brush the amber liquid on in coats so thin they were nearly invisible and who knew perfectly well what he thought of shortcuts, ______ the final coat with a borrowed hair dryer while he was out buying bread, and listened, the whole time, for his key in the lock.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: to hurry
choices.B: having hurried
choices.C: hurried
choices.D: hurrying

explanation.why: The subject "Adaeze" is separated from its verb by a long "who" clause ("who had spent three weeks ... and who knew perfectly well ..."). The verbs inside that clause belong to it, so the sentence still needs a main verb for "Adaeze." The later "and listened" is a past-tense verb that must be parallel with it, so the blank must be the past-tense "hurried."
explanation.A: Incorrect. "To hurry" is an infinitive, which can't serve as the main verb of a sentence or pair with "and listened."
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Having hurried" is a participial phrase, not a main verb, and "and" can't join a participle to the finite verb "listened" as if they were parallel.
explanation.C: Correct. The past-tense verb "hurried" gives "Adaeze" a main verb and is parallel with "listened."
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Hurrying" is a participle, not a main verb, so the sentence would lack a main verb, and it isn't parallel with "listened."

items.subject: science
items.passage: In the third century BCE, Eratosthenes, the chief librarian at Alexandria, learned that at noon on the summer solstice the Sun shone straight down a well in Syene, a city far to the south, while in Alexandria a vertical stick still cast a short shadow. Comparing the angle of that shadow with the distance between the two cities, ______ Historians still debate how close his figure came to the true value, because the exact length of the stadion that he used is uncertain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

choices.A: Earth's circumference was calculated by Eratosthenes to be about 250,000 stadia.
choices.B: an estimate of about 250,000 stadia for Earth's circumference was the result.
choices.C: Eratosthenes calculated that Earth's circumference was about 250,000 stadia.
choices.D: Eratosthenes' calculation put Earth's circumference at about 250,000 stadia.

explanation.why: The introductory phrase "Comparing the angle of that shadow with the distance between the two cities" describes the person doing the comparing. The noun right after the comma must be that person, Eratosthenes, used as the subject of the main clause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The subject "Earth's circumference" comes right after the modifier, so the sentence says the circumference did the comparing; the phrase "by Eratosthenes" comes too late to fix this.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The subject "an estimate" comes right after the modifier, so the sentence says an estimate did the comparing.
explanation.C: Correct. "Eratosthenes" is the subject and comes right after the modifier, so he is the one who compared the angle with the distance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Eratosthenes'" is a possessive, so the subject is "calculation"; the sentence says a calculation compared the angle and distance.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Plants take in carbon dioxide through tiny pores in their leaves called stomata, but water vapor escapes through the same pores. Most plants open their stomata during the day. Many cacti, however, open their stomata only at night, when the desert air is cooler and more humid. Since less water evaporates into cool, humid air, this habit most likely helps cacti ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: survive without taking in any carbon dioxide at all.
choices.B: grow taller than plants that open their stomata in daylight.
choices.C: lose less water than they would by opening their stomata during the day.
choices.D: lose more water at night than they do during the hot daytime hours.

explanation.why: The text gives two facts: water escapes through open stomata, and less water evaporates into cool, humid air. Cacti open their stomata only at night, when the air is cool and humid, so this timing must reduce how much water they lose.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says plants take in carbon dioxide through their stomata; cacti still open them, just at night.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about how tall cacti grow compared with other plants.
explanation.C: Correct. Opening the stomata only in cool, humid air means less water escapes than would escape in daytime heat.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the logic; the cool, humid night air reduces water loss rather than increasing it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In many earlier European churches, thick walls had to hold back the heavy outward push of stone ceilings, so windows had to stay small; large openings would have weakened the walls. In the late twelfth century, builders began using flying buttresses, stone arches on the outside of a building that carry much of that push down to supports beyond the walls. With less force pressing on the walls, builders could ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: make the walls even thicker than they had been before.
choices.B: cut larger window openings without weakening the walls.
choices.C: build the ceilings out of wood instead of heavy stone.
choices.D: place every window in the ceiling rather than the walls.

explanation.why: The text explains that windows stayed small because large openings would weaken walls that were resisting the push of heavy ceilings. Flying buttresses took much of that force off the walls, so the reason for keeping windows small was removed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Less force on the walls means they need less thickness, not more.
explanation.B: Correct. Once the walls bore less force, larger openings would no longer weaken them dangerously.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions changing the material of the ceilings.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text gives no reason to move windows into the ceiling; it is about openings in the walls.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Archaeologists working at sites of the Indus Valley Civilization, which flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE in what is now Pakistan and northwestern India, have found hundreds of small stone cubes that were used as weights. The cubes follow the same system of sizes whether they come from Harappa, from Mohenjo-daro, or from settlements hundreds of kilometers away. Because the civilization's writing has never been deciphered, no surviving text explains how this system was kept in place. Even so, the uniformity of the weights suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: people in widely separated settlements shared common standards for measuring goods.
choices.B: every one of the weights was produced in a single workshop in Mohenjo-daro.
choices.C: scholars have learned how the weights were used by reading Indus inscriptions.
choices.D: trade between distant Indus settlements was rare and of little importance.

explanation.why: The key fact is that weights from many distant sites follow the same system of sizes. Even without written records, matching weights across far-apart places point to a shared standard that people in those places followed.
explanation.A: Correct. Identical weight systems in settlements hundreds of kilometers apart indicate shared measuring standards.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about where the weights were made; uniform sizes could result from many makers following one standard.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the Indus writing has never been deciphered, so no one can read such inscriptions.
explanation.D: Incorrect. A shared system of weights across distant places suggests that exchange mattered, not that it was rare.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Bloodroot, a woodland wildflower of eastern North America, produces seeds with a small fatty attachment called an elaiosome. Native ants carry the seeds to their nests, eat the elaiosomes, and discard the intact seeds in waste piles, where many later sprout. Ecologist Anneke de Vries compared two forests: one with plenty of native ants and one where those ants had been replaced by an invasive ant species that ignores the seeds. Bloodroot seeds sprouted equally well in both forests, but in the second forest nearly every seedling grew within half a meter of a parent plant. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the invasive ants eat bloodroot seeds, which keeps most of the seeds from sprouting.
choices.B: bloodroot seeds can sprout only after native ants have placed them in waste piles.
choices.C: bloodroot will soon disappear from every forest that the invasive ants have entered.
choices.D: native ants help bloodroot spread to new spots but are not needed for its seeds to sprout.

explanation.why: Two findings must be combined. Seeds sprouted equally well with or without native ants, so ants are not needed for sprouting. But without native ants, seedlings stayed right next to parent plants, so the ants are what move seeds to new places.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the invasive ants ignore the seeds, and seeds sprouted equally well in both forests.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Seeds sprouted just as well in the forest without native ants, so they do not need the waste piles to sprout.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text shows only that seedlings stayed near parent plants, not that the species will disappear.
explanation.D: Correct. It matches both findings: equal sprouting in both forests, but movement away from parent plants only where native ants were present.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Prussian blue, often described as the first modern synthetic pigment, was first made in Berlin in the early 1700s and was unavailable to painters before then. A landscape in a private collection bears an inscription dating it to 1690, yet conservator Hiroshi Tanabe detected Prussian blue in its sky. That detection alone would not settle the matter, since restorers routinely repaint damaged areas with pigments of their own era. Tanabe's cross-sections, however, place the Prussian blue in the lowest layer of paint, beneath layers that show no sign of having been scraped away or disturbed. Taken together, these observations suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the date in the inscription is unlikely to reflect when the landscape was actually painted.
choices.B: a later restorer added the Prussian blue when repairing a damaged area of the sky.
choices.C: the landscape was most likely painted in Berlin, where Prussian blue was first produced.
choices.D: the inscription was added to the landscape by someone other than the artist who painted it.

explanation.why: The pigment did not exist before the early 1700s, so a 1690 date is suspicious. The text then rules out the other explanation, a later restoration, because the blue sits in the very first layer under undisturbed paint. The blue was therefore part of the original painting, which means the painting was probably made after 1690.
explanation.A: Correct. If the original paint contains a pigment not available until the early 1700s, the 1690 date is probably not the true date of the painting.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is the explanation the cross-sections rule out: the blue lies in the lowest layer, beneath undisturbed paint, so it was not added during a repair.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Knowing where the pigment was invented says nothing about where this painting was made; the pigment could have been sold elsewhere.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The evidence shows only that the date is probably wrong; the artist could have written the inaccurate date, so who added the inscription is not established.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The transit method detects a planet by the slight dimming that occurs when it passes in front of its star. Such a passage is visible only if the planet's orbit happens to be tilted so that, from Earth, the planet crosses the face of its star. For a giant planet orbiting very close to a sunlike star, only about one orbit in ten is tilted this way, and the fraction is far smaller for planets on wider orbits. Surveying 50,000 sunlike stars, astronomer Chidi Nwosu's team detected transits by close-orbiting giant planets around 26 of them, roughly one star in 2,000. Assuming these detections are accurate, the results imply that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: about one in ten of the stars the team surveyed has a close-orbiting giant planet.
choices.B: most close-orbiting giant planets went undetected because they were too small to dim their stars.
choices.C: considerably more of the surveyed stars have close-orbiting giant planets than the team directly detected.
choices.D: the transit method is unable to detect any planet that orbits far from its star.

explanation.why: Only about one in ten close-orbiting giant planets has an orbit tilted so that it transits. So for each such planet the team saw, roughly nine others around surveyed stars would have produced no transit at all. The true number of stars with these planets must therefore be well above the 26 detected.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "One in ten" is the share of orbits that are tilted the right way, not the share of stars that have such planets; the data point to roughly one star in 200.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives orbital tilt, not planet size, as the reason planets go undetected, and giant planets are the easiest to see.
explanation.C: Correct. Because most such orbits are not tilted toward Earth, the 26 detections must be only a fraction of the planets actually present.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the fraction of detectable orbits is "far smaller" for wider orbits, not that such planets can never be detected.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians of trade often treat customs ledgers as rough measures of commerce, since officials recorded the cargoes that passed through a port. Akosua Mensah's study of one Mediterranean port complicates that practice. The port's ledgers list pepper and cloves in nearly every year from 1620 to 1649, record almost none from 1650 to 1671, and list them regularly again thereafter. Mensah also located a city charter that, hoping to lure merchants away from a rival port, exempted spice cargoes from customs duties between 1650 and 1671, and she observes that clerks entered a cargo in the ledgers only when duty was owed on it. Mensah's findings therefore suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the port's spice imports fell sharply between 1650 and 1671 before recovering to their earlier level.
choices.B: the exemption succeeded in drawing spice merchants away from the rival port to Mensah's port.
choices.C: customs ledgers cannot serve as reliable evidence for the trade of any port in any period.
choices.D: the ledgers' near silence about spices from 1650 to 1671 may reflect the exemption rather than the trade.

explanation.why: Combine the two facts Mensah found: clerks recorded only cargoes that owed duty, and spice cargoes owed no duty from 1650 to 1671. Spices would then vanish from the ledgers during exactly those years whether or not they kept arriving, so the gap cannot be read as a drop in trade.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This takes the ledgers at face value, which is exactly the reading Mensah's findings call into question.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The charter shows what the city hoped for, but because exempt cargoes went unrecorded, the ledgers cannot show whether more spice merchants actually came.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Mensah's point concerns one gap at one port caused by a specific exemption; it does not show that all ledgers everywhere are unreliable.
explanation.D: Correct. Since untaxed cargoes went unrecorded, the missing spice entries could result from the exemption rather than from fewer spices arriving.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The Indus river dolphin, found mainly in Pakistan, has eyes so reduced that it is nearly blind; it finds prey in the river's muddy water by echolocation, interpreting the echoes of its own rapid clicks. Biologist Saima Qureshi recorded the dolphins along two stretches of the river that held similar numbers of fish. Along the stretch with heavy motorboat traffic, the dolphins clicked far more often than along a quiet stretch. Qureshi points out that animals relying on echolocation tend to repeat their signals when background noise drowns out the returning echoes. If her reasoning is correct, the higher click rate in the busy stretch most likely indicates that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the busy stretch offered the dolphins more prey to locate than the quiet stretch did.
choices.B: the dolphins there needed more clicks to perceive their surroundings, not that they had more to find.
choices.C: motorboat noise has left the dolphins in the busy stretch unable to catch enough food to survive.
choices.D: the dolphins there were clicking to keep in contact with one another over the noise of the boats.

explanation.why: Two pieces of the text must be combined. The stretches held similar numbers of fish, so the extra clicking was not caused by more prey. Qureshi's point about noise drowning out echoes then explains it: in the noisy stretch, the dolphins had to click more to get usable echoes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says both stretches held similar numbers of fish, which rules out more prey as the cause.
explanation.B: Correct. With prey similar in both places and noise masking echoes, extra clicks most likely reflect the extra effort needed to sense the surroundings.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text shows that the dolphins clicked more, not that they were failing to catch food or were in danger of starving.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text describes the clicks as a tool for echolocation; it never says the dolphins use them to communicate.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sea turtle hatchlings usually leave their nests at night and must reach the ocean quickly. On a natural beach, the brightest direction is the open horizon over the water, where moonlight and starlight reflect off the waves, and hatchlings crawl toward that brightness. On beaches lined with hotels and streetlights, however, the brightest light often comes from the land behind the beach. As a result, hatchlings on brightly lit beaches are likely to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: stay in their nests until the lights are turned off.
choices.B: crawl away from the ocean instead of toward it.
choices.C: reach the water faster than hatchlings on natural beaches.
choices.D: use the sound of the waves to find the water.

explanation.why: The text says hatchlings crawl toward the brightest direction. On a lit beach, the brightest light comes from the land, not the sea, so the hatchlings will be drawn toward the land, away from the water.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says hatchlings wait in their nests; it describes them crawling toward light.
explanation.B: Correct. Hatchlings move toward the brightest light, and on lit beaches that light is on land, away from the ocean.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Lights on land pull hatchlings in the wrong direction, so they would reach the water more slowly, not faster.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text discusses only light as a guide; sound is never mentioned.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Jute, a plant fiber used to make rope and sacks, has long been one of Bangladesh's most important crops. After the tall stalks are harvested, they must be soaked in water for several weeks so that the fibers loosen and can be pulled away from the woody stem. Bangladesh lies on a low river delta, where ponds, canals, and slow-moving streams are found almost everywhere. This geography means that many Bangladeshi farmers ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: have water for soaking their jute close to their fields.
choices.B: can harvest their jute only once every several years.
choices.C: grow jute mainly for its woody stems rather than its fibers.
choices.D: rarely need to soak their jute before removing the fibers.

explanation.why: Jute stalks must be soaked in water for weeks, and the text says Bangladesh's delta has ponds, canals, and slow streams almost everywhere. Putting these facts together, farmers there usually have the water they need for soaking nearby.
explanation.A: Correct. Soaking needs standing or slow water, and the delta has such water almost everywhere.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about how often jute can be harvested.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says jute is used for its fiber; the stems are what the fibers are pulled away from.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the stalks must be soaked; the delta's water makes soaking easy, not unnecessary.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: All week, Marisol hurried to her room after school and shut the door. When her mother knocked, Marisol called out that she was busy and slid something under her bed before opening the door. On Saturday morning, her mother's birthday, Marisol came to breakfast holding a small package wrapped in paper she had painted herself. Marisol's behavior during the week most likely suggests that she ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: had been secretly preparing a gift for her mother.
choices.B: was upset with her mother and wanted to be left alone.
choices.C: was studying for an important test at school.
choices.D: had forgotten that her mother's birthday was coming.

explanation.why: Marisol hid something whenever her mother came to the door, and on her mother's birthday she appeared with a package wrapped in paper she painted herself. Her secrecy during the week is best explained by her getting a birthday gift ready.
explanation.A: Correct. The hiding, the timing, and the handmade wrapping all point to a secret birthday gift.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing shows that Marisol was upset; the gift at the end suggests the opposite.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions a test, and studying would not explain hiding something under the bed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The prepared package shows that she remembered the birthday.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In true fresco, a method used by many Italian Renaissance painters, pigment is brushed onto fresh, wet plaster. As the plaster dries, the color becomes locked into the wall, but once the plaster has dried, it no longer absorbs new paint. For this reason, painters spread fresh plaster over only the section of wall they expected to finish in a single day. This practice suggests that a large fresco ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was usually painted on dry plaster prepared weeks earlier.
choices.B: was typically painted in sections on different days.
choices.C: could be completed by one painter in a single day.
choices.D: used fewer colors than paintings made on wood or canvas.

explanation.why: Painters plastered only as much wall as they could paint in one day, because dry plaster no longer takes paint. A large fresco covers more wall than one day's work, so it must have been built up section by section over many days.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says pigment goes onto fresh, wet plaster; dry plaster no longer absorbs paint.
explanation.B: Correct. Since each day's plaster covered only one section, a large work had to be made in many daily sections.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Each day covered only one section, so a large fresco would take more than one day.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares the number of colors in frescoes with other paintings.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Pacific salmon hatch in freshwater streams, then swim out to the ocean, where they spend several years feeding and growing. When they are ready to reproduce, most return to the very stream where they hatched, sometimes traveling hundreds of kilometers. Each stream carries a distinctive mix of chemicals from its soil and plants, and young salmon appear to memorize this scent before leaving. These observations suggest that adult salmon ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: rely mainly on their eyesight to recognize familiar landmarks.
choices.B: probably use smell to help them find their home streams.
choices.C: can reproduce only in the ocean, far from where they hatched.
choices.D: choose a new stream each year based on how much food it holds.

explanation.why: Each stream has its own scent, young salmon seem to memorize it, and adults return to the stream where they hatched. The most logical link is that the remembered scent helps guide them home.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes scent, not sight; eyesight is never mentioned.
explanation.B: Correct. A memorized stream scent is the only guide the text describes, so smell probably helps them return.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says salmon return to freshwater streams to reproduce, not that they reproduce in the ocean.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says most salmon return to the same stream where they hatched, not a new one.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For centuries, merchants carried goods across Asia along the routes now known as the Silk Road, often on camels that could carry only a limited load. A journey could take many months, and traders had to pay for food, animals, and protection along the way. Silk was especially popular with these merchants because a small, light bundle of it could be sold for a very high price. This suggests that merchants on these routes probably preferred goods that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: were worth a great deal compared with their weight.
choices.B: were heavy but cheap to produce, such as stone or timber.
choices.C: could already be bought in every town along the way.
choices.D: would spoil quickly if the journey took too long.

explanation.why: Loads were limited and long journeys were costly, and silk was popular because a light bundle sold for a high price. Merchants would therefore favor goods that packed high value into little weight.
explanation.A: Correct. Silk is the example: light to carry but sold for a high price.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Heavy, cheap goods would use up the limited loads without paying for the costly trip.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Goods available everywhere would be hard to sell at a high price after a long journey.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The long trips would make quickly spoiling goods a poor choice; nothing suggests merchants wanted them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The seawater around Antarctica stays close to −1.9°C, a temperature below the point at which the blood of most fish would freeze. Yet many fish thrive there. One group, the notothenioids, produces special proteins that attach to tiny ice crystals in the fishes' blood and body fluids and stop the crystals from growing larger. Without these proteins, ice would spread through the fishes' tissues. These proteins therefore most likely allow the fish to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: swim north to warmer water whenever ice begins to form.
choices.B: survive water colder than their blood could otherwise stand.
choices.C: warm the surrounding seawater to above its freezing point.
choices.D: grow larger ice crystals that help protect their tissues.

explanation.why: The water is colder than the freezing point of most fish blood, but the proteins stop ice crystals from growing in these fishes' bodies. That is what lets them live in such cold water.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the fish thrive in Antarctic water; nothing mentions moving north.
explanation.B: Correct. By keeping ice crystals small, the proteins let the fish live in water that would otherwise freeze their blood.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The proteins work inside the fish; the text never says they change the temperature of the seawater.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The proteins stop ice crystals from growing; they do not make them larger.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Yoruba, a language spoken by millions of people in Nigeria and neighboring countries, is a tonal language: whether a syllable is spoken at a high, middle, or low pitch can change the meaning of a word. Yoruba drummers play an hourglass-shaped instrument called the dùndún, whose pitch rises or falls as the player squeezes the cords along its sides. Because the drum can copy these rises and falls in pitch, skilled drummers can ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: imitate spoken phrases that listeners can recognize.
choices.B: replace the Yoruba language with a new system of sounds.
choices.C: play only a single note during an entire performance.
choices.D: be heard more clearly than any other instrument in Nigeria.

explanation.why: In Yoruba, pitch helps carry the meaning of words, and the dùndún can copy the rises and falls in pitch of speech. A drum that copies the pitch patterns of words can therefore imitate speech that listeners understand.
explanation.A: Correct. Because Yoruba meaning depends on pitch, a drum that copies those pitches can imitate recognizable phrases.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The drum copies the pitch patterns of Yoruba itself; it does not replace the language.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the drum's pitch rises and falls, so it is not limited to one note.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares how loudly or clearly different instruments can be heard.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Below about 1,000 meters, the deep ocean receives no sunlight at all, and food is scarce. Many female anglerfish living there have a long spine on the head that ends in a glowing tip, lit by bacteria living inside it. The fish holds this lure in front of its mouth and stays almost perfectly still. Small fish and shrimp in the deep sea are often drawn toward points of light. The lure most likely helps the anglerfish ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: avoid being noticed by other animals nearby.
choices.B: attract prey close to its mouth without chasing it.
choices.C: warm the cold water that surrounds its body.
choices.D: spot predators approaching from far away in the dark.

explanation.why: Small fish and shrimp swim toward points of light, and the anglerfish holds a glowing lure in front of its mouth while staying still. The lure therefore brings food to the anglerfish instead of the anglerfish going after its food.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A glowing light in total darkness draws attention; it does not help the fish hide.
explanation.B: Correct. Prey drawn to the light come right up to the mouth of the still anglerfish.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The lure gives off light; the text never suggests it gives off heat.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about using the light to watch for predators.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: When the results of the 800-meter race were announced, Tobias had finished fourth, one place short of a medal. He shook hands with the winner, smiled for his teammates, and told his coach that he felt fine. But on the bus ride home, he sat alone in the back row, staring out the window, and did not answer when his best friend asked if he wanted to play cards. These details suggest that Tobias ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was pleased with his result but too tired to talk.
choices.B: did not care at all how he had done in the race.
choices.C: was more disappointed than he had shown others.
choices.D: was angry at the winner for beating him unfairly.

explanation.why: In public, Tobias shook hands, smiled, and said he felt fine. Later, alone on the bus, he stared out the window and ignored his friend. The contrast suggests that his calm behavior hid real disappointment about missing a medal.
explanation.A: Incorrect. His silence and isolation on the bus suggest unhappiness, not pleasure with his result.
explanation.B: Incorrect. His withdrawn behavior on the bus shows that the result did matter to him.
explanation.C: Correct. His cheerful public behavior contrasts with his silence later, showing hidden disappointment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. He shook hands with the winner, and nothing suggests he thought the race was unfair.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Before 1914, a ship sailing from New York to San Francisco had to travel all the way around the southern tip of South America, a voyage of more than 20,000 kilometers. That year, the Panama Canal opened across a narrow strip of land in Central America, connecting the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. Ships could now pass between the two oceans without going around the continent. As a result, the voyage from New York to San Francisco most likely became ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: longer, because ships now had to wait to enter the canal.
choices.B: possible by sea for the first time in history.
choices.C: much shorter than it had been before the canal opened.
choices.D: unnecessary, because the canal linked the two cities directly.

explanation.why: Before the canal, ships had to sail around South America. The canal let them cross between the oceans through Central America instead, which cut out that long detour and made the trip much shorter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives no information about waiting times, and avoiding a 20,000-kilometer detour would shorten the trip.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says ships already made this voyage before 1914 by going around South America.
explanation.C: Correct. Skipping the trip around South America would greatly shorten the voyage.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The canal crosses Central America; it does not connect New York and San Francisco directly.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Water heats up and cools down much more slowly than land does. In summer, the ocean slowly stores heat, and in winter it slowly releases that heat into the air above it. Lisbon, Portugal, sits on the Atlantic coast, while Madrid, Spain, lies far inland at a similar distance from the equator. Based on these facts, winter temperatures in Lisbon are most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: determined mainly by Lisbon's distance from the equator.
choices.B: colder than Madrid's because the ocean absorbs heat from the air.
choices.C: nearly the same as summer temperatures in Lisbon.
choices.D: generally milder than those in inland Madrid.

explanation.why: In winter, the ocean releases heat it stored during summer, warming the air near the coast. Lisbon is on the coast and Madrid is inland at a similar latitude, so Lisbon should have the milder winters.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The two cities are a similar distance from the equator, so that distance cannot explain a difference; the ocean can.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says that in winter the ocean releases heat into the air, which would make the coast warmer, not colder.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The ocean only softens the change between seasons; nothing suggests winter and summer would feel the same.
explanation.D: Correct. Heat released by the Atlantic in winter would keep coastal Lisbon milder than inland Madrid.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Biologists have long debated why zebras have stripes. One idea is that the stripes discourage biting flies such as horseflies, which spread disease among grazing animals. To test this idea, researchers observed horseflies around horses wearing either plain cloth coats or black-and-white striped ones. Flies approached both groups of horses at similar rates, but they landed far less often on the striped coats, frequently flying past or bumping into them. Because the animals beneath the coats were all horses, these results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: striped coats keep horses cooler than plain coats do.
choices.B: horseflies cannot detect striped animals from a distance.
choices.C: a striped pattern itself can make it harder for flies to land.
choices.D: stripes protect animals from every insect that spreads disease.

explanation.why: The only difference between the two groups was the pattern of the coat; the animals underneath were all horses. Since flies approached both groups equally but landed less on the striped coats, the stripes themselves seem to interfere with landing.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about temperature; the study measured fly behavior.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Flies approached both groups at similar rates, so they did detect the striped horses; the difference came only at landing.
explanation.C: Correct. With the same animal under every coat, the pattern is the factor that reduced landings.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The study observed only horseflies, so it cannot support a claim about every disease-carrying insect.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Under the Mughal Empire, which ruled much of South Asia from the 1500s to the 1700s, official messages were often carried by a relay system. Posts were set up at regular intervals along major roads, and each kept fresh horses or runners ready. A messenger hurried to the next post, where a rested rider or runner took the message and set off at once. Because no single messenger or horse had to cover the whole route, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: each messenger had to know the entire route from one end of the empire to the other.
choices.B: messages were delivered more slowly than if one rider had traveled the whole way.
choices.C: ordinary people across the empire came to depend on the system for their letters.
choices.D: messages could cross long distances faster than one rider could have carried them.

explanation.why: In a relay, each messenger covers only one short stage and hands the message to someone rested. Since nobody has to slow down from exhaustion over the whole route, the message keeps moving quickly, faster than one tiring rider could manage.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Each messenger traveled only to the next post, so no one needed to know the whole route.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the point of the relay; rested messengers at each stage would make delivery faster, not slower.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text describes official messages only; it says nothing about ordinary people's letters.
explanation.D: Correct. Fresh riders and horses at each post let the message move quickly over the full distance.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The vivid blue on much Chinese blue-and-white porcelain of the early Ming dynasty (1368–1644) came from cobalt imported from Persia. This imported cobalt contained very little manganese and fired to a bright, sapphire-like blue. Cobalt mined in China, by contrast, was rich in manganese, which gave the blue a duller, grayish tone. Historical records indicate that supplies of Persian cobalt were interrupted during certain decades. A specialist examining an undated Ming piece with a grayish blue might therefore reasonably conclude that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the piece contains more Persian cobalt than bright blue pieces do.
choices.B: the piece must have been made outside China by Persian potters.
choices.C: the piece was fired at a lower temperature than other Ming wares.
choices.D: the piece may have been made when imported cobalt was scarce.

explanation.why: A grayish blue points to manganese-rich Chinese cobalt rather than imported Persian cobalt. Since Persian supplies were sometimes interrupted, a piece colored with local cobalt may date from one of those periods.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Persian cobalt produced the bright blue, so a grayish piece likely contains less of it, not more.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The grayish tone points to cobalt mined in China, not to Persian potters working elsewhere.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text explains color by the cobalt's manganese content; firing temperature is never discussed.
explanation.D: Correct. Grayish blue suggests local cobalt, which potters would likely have used when Persian imports were cut off.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For a month, Ximena had been teaching her grandfather to send text messages, and for a month he had insisted the phone was a nuisance he would never need. He typed with one finger, sighed at every mistake, and reminded her that a proper letter took real effort. The evening after Ximena moved away to begin her nursing course, her phone buzzed: "Arrived safe? Room cold? I bought you warm socks. Will mail." It had taken him, she guessed, nearly twenty minutes to write. The message most strongly suggests that Ximena's grandfather ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: still believed that a text message could never be sincere.
choices.B: had always enjoyed using the phone and only pretended to dislike it.
choices.C: cared enough about his granddaughter to use a tool he had resisted.
choices.D: wanted Ximena to give up her course and return home.

explanation.why: The grandfather complained about the phone and typed slowly, yet right after Ximena left he spent about twenty minutes writing her a caring text. His concern for her outweighed his dislike of the phone.
explanation.A: Incorrect. He chose a text to express real care, which shows he was willing to use it sincerely.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The slow, effortful message suggests he still found the phone hard; nothing shows he secretly enjoyed it.
explanation.C: Correct. He overcame his resistance to the phone to check on her and tell her about the socks.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The message asks about her room and promises socks; it never asks her to come home.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Monarch butterfly caterpillars feed on milkweed and store the plant's toxic chemicals in their bodies, so adult monarchs taste bitter and often make birds that eat them vomit. Birds that have had this experience tend to avoid orange-and-black butterflies afterward. The viceroy butterfly, which looks very similar to the monarch, was long assumed to be harmless to eat, although later tests showed that viceroys can also taste unpleasant to birds. Whether or not a viceroy itself tastes bad, its resemblance to the monarch likely means that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: birds are more likely to attack viceroys than to attack monarchs.
choices.B: viceroys are the only butterflies that birds have learned to avoid.
choices.C: birds that avoid monarchs are also likely to avoid viceroys.
choices.D: viceroy caterpillars must feed on milkweed in order to survive.

explanation.why: Birds sickened by monarchs learn to avoid orange-and-black butterflies, and viceroys look very much like monarchs. Regardless of their own taste, viceroys therefore probably benefit when birds avoid them by mistaking them for monarchs.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Looking like a monarch would make birds less likely, not more likely, to attack a viceroy.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Birds avoid monarchs too, and the text gives no basis for saying viceroys are the only ones avoided.
explanation.C: Correct. A bird that avoids orange-and-black butterflies would likely avoid the look-alike viceroy as well.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says monarch caterpillars eat milkweed; it never says what viceroy caterpillars eat.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Rome, near the bank of the Tiber River, stands Monte Testaccio, a hill about 35 meters high made almost entirely of broken pottery. Archaeologists estimate that it contains the remains of tens of millions of amphorae, large clay jars that the Romans used to ship olive oil. Stamps and painted labels on the fragments show that most of the jars came from Baetica, a province in what is now southern Spain, and that they were discarded over a period of more than two centuries. Taken together, these findings suggest that Rome ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: valued its amphorae so highly that it rarely threw them away.
choices.B: relied heavily on Baetican olive oil for a long time.
choices.C: imported olive oil from Spain only during a single short period.
choices.D: produced more olive oil than any of its provinces did.

explanation.why: The hill holds tens of millions of oil jars, most labeled as coming from Baetica, and they were thrown away over more than two centuries. Such a huge, long-lasting pile of Baetican jars shows that Rome depended on large shipments of Spanish olive oil for a long time.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A hill of tens of millions of broken jars shows that amphorae were thrown away in enormous numbers.
explanation.B: Correct. The huge number of Baetican jars, dumped over more than two centuries, shows heavy and lasting reliance on that oil.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The jars were discarded over more than two centuries, which is not a single short period.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The jars show oil coming into Rome from a province, which points away from Rome being the main producer.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In much of India, leopards share their forests with tigers, which are larger and sometimes kill leopards. There, leopards tend to hunt at night and often take smaller prey, patterns that may help them avoid tigers. Sri Lanka has no tigers, so the leopard is the island's largest predator. Wildlife biologist Dilini Perera compared camera-trap records from parks in both countries and found that Sri Lankan leopards were more often active during the day and more often hunted large prey such as adult deer. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the presence of tigers may affect when and what leopards hunt.
choices.B: leopards in India hunt by day to avoid competing with tigers.
choices.C: Sri Lankan leopards have grown larger than the tigers of India.
choices.D: leopards everywhere prefer to hunt large prey during the night.

explanation.why: Where tigers are present, leopards hunt mainly at night and take smaller prey; where tigers are absent, leopards are more active by day and take larger prey. The difference suggests that tigers may shape leopards' hunting habits.
explanation.A: Correct. Leopards behave differently where tigers are absent, which points to tigers as a possible influence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says leopards in India tend to hunt at night, not by day.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text compares leopards' behavior, not their size, and never says any leopard is larger than a tiger.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Leopards' habits differ between the two countries, so no single preference holds everywhere.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the early 1600s, plays at the Globe, an open-air playhouse in London, were performed in the afternoon and relied on daylight. There was no way to dim the light or darken the stage, and scenery was minimal. Yet many plays of the period include scenes set at night or during storms. Scholars note that in such scenes, characters often remark on the darkness, carry torches or lanterns, or describe the weather around them. These details suggest that playwrights ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: avoided writing night scenes because the stage could not show them.
choices.B: preferred indoor theaters, where candles let them control the light.
choices.C: used speech and props to suggest what the stage could not show.
choices.D: expected audiences to attend performances only after sunset.

explanation.why: The daylit Globe stage could not look dark or stormy, yet plays included night and storm scenes. Characters' remarks about darkness and weather, along with torches and lanterns, told the audience what the stage itself could not show.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says many plays of the period include night scenes, so playwrights did not avoid them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never mentions indoor theaters or candles, so it does not support a claim about playwrights' preferences.
explanation.C: Correct. Spoken descriptions and props like torches let the audience imagine darkness and storms in daylight.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says plays at the Globe were performed in the afternoon.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mesosaurus was a small reptile that lived about 280 million years ago. Its fossils have been found in southern Africa and in eastern South America but nowhere in between. Studies of its skeleton and of the rocks where it was buried indicate that it lived in fresh or slightly salty coastal waters and was not built for long journeys across the open sea. Today, the two regions where its fossils appear are separated by thousands of kilometers of the South Atlantic Ocean. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the South Atlantic was much saltier when Mesosaurus lived.
choices.B: Mesosaurus regularly swam across the South Atlantic Ocean.
choices.C: Mesosaurus must have lived on every southern continent.
choices.D: southern Africa and South America were probably once joined.

explanation.why: Mesosaurus could not cross an open ocean, yet its fossils are found on both sides of the South Atlantic. The most logical explanation is that the two regions were connected, or much closer together, when it lived.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives no information about how salty the ancient ocean was.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says Mesosaurus was not built for long journeys across the open sea.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Its fossils are found only in southern Africa and South America, so the text does not support every southern continent.
explanation.D: Correct. An animal unable to cross the open sea could live in both places only if the land was once connected.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the late 900s and early 1000s, merchants in Sichuan, a region in southwestern China, used coins made of iron rather than copper. Iron coins were worth little, so a large purchase required a heavy load of them; the coins needed to buy a single bolt of silk could weigh many kilograms. Merchants began leaving their coins with trusted shops in exchange for paper receipts, which they could pass to one another in place of the coins. Given these circumstances, the receipts most likely appealed to merchants because they ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: allowed merchants to buy silk without paying for it.
choices.B: were made of a material more valuable than iron.
choices.C: spared merchants from carrying heavy loads of coins.
choices.D: were accepted in every region of China, unlike coins.

explanation.why: The problem the text describes is weight: iron coins were worth so little that large purchases required many kilograms of them. A paper receipt that stood in for those coins solved that problem, since merchants could trade the receipt instead of hauling the coins.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The receipts represented coins that had been deposited, so merchants were still paying.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The receipts were valuable because they stood for stored coins, not because paper was worth more than iron.
explanation.C: Correct. Passing a light paper receipt in place of the coins avoided the burden of moving heavy iron.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text discusses only Sichuan and never says the receipts were accepted throughout China.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Nusrat had grown up in Dhaka, and she spent the long bus ride to her cousins' village listing everything she would miss: fast internet, her favorite café, the hum of the city at night. On her first evening, the power went out during a heavy monsoon rain. Her cousin Rafiq lit a lantern, and the family gathered on the veranda to tell stories while rain drummed on the tin roof. Nusrat, who had planned to go to bed early, was still listening when the lantern burned low near midnight. The details suggest that Nusrat ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was frightened by the storm and afraid to go to her room alone.
choices.B: had decided to move to her cousins' village permanently.
choices.C: found the evening more enjoyable than she had expected to.
choices.D: still wished she had stayed in Dhaka instead of visiting.

explanation.why: Nusrat expected to miss city life and planned to go to bed early, yet she stayed up until midnight listening to the family's stories. Her change of plans shows that the evening turned out better than she had imagined.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests fear; she stayed to listen to the stories, not to avoid being alone.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Enjoying one evening does not show that she planned to live in the village for good.
explanation.C: Correct. She meant to go to bed early but stayed up until midnight, showing she enjoyed the evening.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Staying up late with the family suggests she was not longing to be back in the city that night.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Psychologist Ingrid Halvorsen taught two groups of adults a list of words from a language none of them spoke. Both groups were tested on the words twelve hours later, when everyone was fully awake. One group learned the words at 9 p.m. and slept through the night before the test; the other learned them at 9 a.m. and stayed awake through the day. Although the time between learning and testing was the same for both groups, the group that had slept remembered noticeably more words. These results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: sleeping soon after learning may help people retain new words.
choices.B: adults remember familiar words better than unfamiliar ones.
choices.C: people can learn new words only while they are asleep.
choices.D: staying awake after learning helps memory more than sleep does.

explanation.why: Both groups had the same twelve-hour gap before the test, but only one group slept during it, and that group remembered more. The sleep after learning is therefore a likely reason for their better memory.
explanation.A: Correct. With the delay held equal, the group that slept after learning retained more of the words.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Everyone learned unfamiliar words, so the study made no comparison with familiar ones.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Both groups learned the words while awake; the study tested memory after sleep, not learning during it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the result; the group that slept remembered more.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Qawwali, a form of devotional music performed across Pakistan and northern India, is traditionally flexible in length. At a live gathering, singers may repeat and extend a single line many times in response to the mood of the listeners, so one song can last half an hour or more. When qawwali was first recorded in the early 1900s, however, each side of a gramophone disc could hold only about three minutes of sound. Because of this limit, early qawwali recordings most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: captured the full length of typical qawwali performances at live gatherings.
choices.B: replaced traditional qawwali songs with entirely new compositions for discs.
choices.C: caused qawwali singers to stop repeating lines in their live performances.
choices.D: offered shortened versions of songs that ran far longer when performed live.

explanation.why: Live qawwali songs can last half an hour or more, but a disc side held only about three minutes. To fit on a disc, recorded songs would have had to be much shorter than live versions.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A three-minute side could not hold a performance lasting half an hour or more.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives no evidence that recordings used new songs; the time limit points to shortening, not replacing.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text describes a limit on recordings; it gives no evidence that live performances changed.
explanation.D: Correct. A three-minute disc side could hold only a small part of a song that might last thirty minutes live.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Until the 1880s, most towns in the United States set their clocks by the Sun, declaring noon to be the moment the Sun stood highest overhead. Because the Sun reaches that point at slightly different moments in places farther east or west, nearby towns often kept times that differed by several minutes. Railroad companies, whose trains passed through many towns in a single day, had to publish timetables that accounted for dozens of local times. In 1883 the railroads adopted a small number of standard time zones, a change that most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: allowed each town to keep its own local time on the timetables.
choices.B: made trains travel faster between distant cities in the country.
choices.C: simplified timetables for trains that passed through many towns.
choices.D: made noon in every town fall exactly when the Sun was highest.

explanation.why: The railroads' problem was that timetables had to deal with dozens of different local times. Replacing them with a few standard zones meant many towns shared one time, which would make timetables far simpler.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Standard zones replaced the many local times rather than keeping them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The change affected how time was recorded, not how fast trains moved.
explanation.C: Correct. A few zones in place of dozens of local times would make railroad timetables much simpler.
explanation.D: Incorrect. With a few shared zones, most towns would no longer set noon by the Sun's exact position.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Lichens absorb water and nutrients directly from the air rather than through roots, so they also take in whatever pollutants the air carries. Many species are badly harmed by sulfur dioxide, a gas released when coal is burned. In the mid-1900s, when coal was widely burned in homes and factories, surveys of a large European city found only a few hardy lichen species near its center. Since then, coal burning in the city has dropped sharply, and recent surveys have found dozens of species, including several sensitive ones, growing in the same areas. This pattern suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: coal burning has little effect on which lichens can grow in cities.
choices.B: the city's center now has more lichen species than nearby rural areas.
choices.C: lichens have become resistant to sulfur dioxide in recent decades.
choices.D: less sulfur dioxide in the air has allowed sensitive lichens to return.

explanation.why: Coal burning releases sulfur dioxide, which harms many lichens. As coal burning fell, the variety of lichens rose, including sensitive species. The most logical link is that cleaner air let those species grow again.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Lichen variety changed sharply as coal burning fell, which suggests a strong effect.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never compares the city with rural areas.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The returning species are described as sensitive, so the text points to cleaner air, not to lichens becoming resistant.
explanation.D: Correct. Less coal burning means less sulfur dioxide, which explains why sensitive lichens have come back.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For thirty years, Mr. Takahashi had locked the greenhouse himself every evening and kept its only key on a cord around his neck. The neighbors' children were allowed to admire his orchids from the doorway but never to touch a watering can. So when Mateus, who had spent the summer quietly sweeping the paths and asking the name of each plant, arrived on Monday, he was surprised to see the old man holding out the cord. "The tall ones need water before noon," Mr. Takahashi said. The passage suggests that Mr. Takahashi ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: had come to trust Mateus with the care of the greenhouse.
choices.B: had always let the neighbors' children water his orchids.
choices.C: wanted Mateus to stop asking questions about the plants.
choices.D: planned to sell the greenhouse and its orchids to a neighbor.

explanation.why: Mr. Takahashi had guarded the greenhouse for thirty years and let no child touch a watering can. Handing his only key to Mateus, along with watering instructions, shows that Mateus's careful summer of work had earned his trust.
explanation.A: Correct. Giving away the only key and explaining when to water show new trust in Mateus.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says children were never allowed to touch a watering can.
explanation.C: Incorrect. He answers Mateus with plant-care instructions, which invites more involvement, not less.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in the text mentions selling the greenhouse.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Hangul, the Korean alphabet, was created in the 1440s under King Sejong. A text published to explain the new script describes how its basic consonant letters were designed to picture the speech organs: the letter for the k sound, for example, shows the back of the tongue raised toward the roof of the mouth, and the letter for the m sound shows the shape of the mouth. Letters for related sounds were then formed by adding strokes to these basic shapes. This design suggests that a learner who knows one basic letter could ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: use its shape to help learn the letters for related sounds.
choices.B: understand Chinese characters more easily than other learners.
choices.C: pronounce Korean words without moving the tongue or lips.
choices.D: read the whole script without learning any other letters.

explanation.why: Related sounds were written by adding strokes to the basic letters. A learner who knows a basic letter can therefore recognize it inside the related letters, which makes those letters easier to learn.
explanation.A: Correct. Because related letters are built from the basic shapes, knowing one basic letter gives a head start on the related ones.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never mentions Chinese characters.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The letters picture how the tongue and mouth move; they do not remove the need to move them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Knowing one letter would help with related letters, but the learner would still need to learn the others.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In Ladakh, a high, dry region in the Indian Himalayas, farmers depend on meltwater from glaciers to irrigate their fields. The glaciers usually do not melt much until early summer, however, while crops need water when they are planted in April and May. To bridge this gap, villagers have built ice stupas: in winter, stream water is piped uphill and sprayed into the freezing air, where it builds up into tall cones of ice. Because a cone exposes little surface to the sun for its size, it melts slowly. Ice stupas are therefore most likely intended to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: release water gradually during the spring planting season.
choices.B: stay frozen until the glaciers begin melting in early summer.
choices.C: replace the glaciers as the region's year-round source of water.
choices.D: cool the air over the fields so that crops grow more slowly.

explanation.why: Farmers need water in April and May, before the glaciers melt in early summer. Ice stupas store winter water as ice that melts slowly, so they are meant to supply water bit by bit during that spring gap.
explanation.A: Correct. Melting slowly through the spring, the stupas supply water when crops are planted but glaciers have not yet melted.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The stupas are meant to bridge the gap before the glaciers melt, so staying frozen until then would defeat their purpose.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The stupas are built to fill a seasonal gap, not to replace glaciers all year.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never suggests the stupas are meant to change the air or slow crop growth.

items.subject: science
items.passage: During the Antarctic winter, male emperor penguins guarding eggs crowd together in huddles of hundreds or even thousands of birds. Inside a dense huddle, the air is far warmer than outside, while birds on the windward edge bear the full force of the cold. Huddles slowly shift, however, as birds on the exposed side move along the edge and rejoin the group elsewhere. Researchers who tracked individual penguins found that, over a whole winter, nearly all of them spent similar amounts of time at the edge and in the center. This finding suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the penguins on the edge of a huddle are mostly those that have lost their eggs.
choices.B: the strongest males manage to keep the warm center of the huddle for themselves.
choices.C: huddling raises the temperature of the air around the whole breeding colony.
choices.D: the warmth inside a huddle is shared fairly evenly among the birds over time.

explanation.why: The text says the center of a huddle is warm and the edge is cold, and that huddles shift so birds keep changing places. Tracking showed that nearly all birds spent "similar amounts of time at the edge and in the center." Together, these facts mean each bird gets a roughly equal share of the warm interior over the winter.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never mentions birds losing their eggs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If a few birds kept the center, they would spend more time there than others, which the tracking did not find.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text describes warmth inside a huddle, not a change in the air around the colony.
explanation.D: Correct. Similar time in the warm center and the cold edge means the warmth is shared fairly evenly.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Radiocarbon dating measures how long ago a living thing stopped taking in carbon. In a tree, each ring stops taking in carbon soon after it forms, so wood from the center of a 400-year-old trunk can give a date centuries earlier than the year the tree was cut. At a coastal settlement, archaeologist Mateus Ribeiro dated charcoal from a hearth to around 1150 CE; the charcoal came from the heartwood of a slow-growing cedar. Seeds of a grass that lives for only one year, found burned together with the charcoal in a single thin layer of ash, dated to around 1400 CE. These results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the settlement was occupied without a break from 1150 CE to 1400 CE.
choices.B: the fire in the hearth probably burned closer to 1400 CE than to 1150 CE.
choices.C: the cedar was burned in the hearth long before the grass seeds were.
choices.D: radiocarbon dates from hearths are unreliable whatever material is tested.

explanation.why: The text explains that heartwood from an old tree can give a date centuries earlier than when the wood was used. The one-year grass seeds have no such problem, and they were burned in the same thin ash layer as the charcoal, so they mark the same fire. Combining these points, the fire most likely happened near the seeds' date, around 1400 CE, and the cedar date is misleadingly early.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing in the text shows people living at the site through the whole period; the earlier date reflects the age of the wood.
explanation.B: Correct. The short-lived seeds date the fire reliably, and the old heartwood explains why the charcoal date is earlier.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The charcoal and seeds were found together in a single thin layer of ash, which points to one fire, not two.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text shows that short-lived material such as one-year seeds can date a hearth well; only old wood is the problem.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In certain lakes, sediment settles in yearly pairs of layers called varves: a pale, coarse layer laid down in summer and a thin, dark one in winter. By counting these pairs downward from the surface, scientists can date events recorded in the mud, much as they count tree rings. The method works only where the layers stay intact.
