In most lakes, worms and other burrowing animals churn the bottom mud and blend the layers together; varves survive mainly where the deep water holds too little oxygen for such animals to live. In a sediment core from a lake in Norway, geologist Ingrid Solheim found a section, about 40 centimeters thick, full of worm burrows. A count of varves through that section would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: reveal how many kinds of worms lived in the lake at that time.
choices.B: provide an especially precise date for the events recorded in that section.
choices.C: record fewer years than actually passed as that sediment built up.
choices.D: show that summers were longer than winters during that period.

explanation.why: Two facts must be combined. Varves can be counted only where layers stay intact, and burrowing animals blend the layers together. The worm burrows show that animals lived in the mud when that section formed, so many yearly layers would have been mixed and could not be counted. A count would therefore miss years.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The burrows show that animals were present; a count of layers would not reveal how many kinds of worms lived there.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Blended layers make the count less precise, not more.
explanation.C: Correct. Layers blended by burrowing animals cannot be told apart, so a count would come up short.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never links the thickness of layers to the length of seasons.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the seventeenth century, Mughal authorities and wealthy patrons built caravanserais, walled inns for travelers and their animals, along the major roads of northern India. On well-traveled routes, these serais were usually spaced about a day's journey apart, roughly 25 to 30 kilometers. Historian Farah Naqvi mapped the surviving serais along one route through Punjab and found a single gap of about 55 kilometers between neighboring serais. A merchant's travel diary from the period, however, records that he spent a night at a walled inn in a town lying almost exactly halfway between them. Together, these findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a serai probably once stood in or near that town but has not survived to the present.
choices.B: caravans on that part of the route usually covered twice the normal distance in a day.
choices.C: Mughal builders placed serais only in towns that had already grown up along the road.
choices.D: the merchant's diary is unreliable and should not be used to map the route's serais.

explanation.why: Serais were usually a day's journey apart, yet the map shows one gap about twice that long. The merchant stayed at a walled inn in a town right in the middle of the gap. Combining the usual spacing with the diary, the most likely explanation is that a serai once stood there and has since disappeared.
explanation.A: Correct. The usual spacing and the diary together point to a missing serai at the halfway town.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The merchant stopped for the night in the middle of the gap, which suggests normal day-long stages, not double ones.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says nothing about whether serais were built only in existing towns.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The diary fits the usual spacing well; nothing in the text casts doubt on it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Young male zebra finches learn their songs by copying an adult male, or tutor, usually their father. Males that hear a tutor between about 20 and 65 days after hatching copy its song closely. Males raised with one tutor and then given a new tutor after they are 100 days old copy almost nothing from the newcomer, which led researchers to describe song learning as limited to an early window of time. Biologist Kenji Morimoto, however, raised a group of young males in isolation, hearing no song at all, until they were 100 days old. When he then introduced them to a tutor, many copied its song well. These results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: female zebra finches prefer males that learned their songs early in their lives.
choices.B: the learning window closes partly because of hearing a tutor, not because of age alone.
choices.C: being raised in isolation permanently prevents zebra finches from learning to sing.
choices.D: male zebra finches can learn a new song from a tutor equally well at any point in their lives.

explanation.why: At 100 days, birds that had already heard a tutor learned almost nothing from a new one, but birds that had heard no song learned well. The two groups were the same age, so age alone cannot explain the difference. What differed was earlier experience of hearing a tutor, which suggests that this experience helps close the window.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never discusses the preferences of female finches.
explanation.B: Correct. Same age, different outcomes: the key difference is whether the bird had already heard a tutor.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The isolated birds learned well once they were given a tutor.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Birds that had already learned from a tutor copied almost nothing at 100 days, so learning is not equally easy at any age.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the era of hand-operated presses, printers often corrected errors in the middle of printing a book: a proofreader would spot a mistake partway through the run, the press would stop, and the type would be fixed. Paper was costly, so sheets printed before the correction were not thrown away but were bound into copies along with corrected ones. Book historian Aiko Tanaka compared two copies of a 1640 edition of a book of sermons, one held in Edinburgh and one in Boston, and found that a single word on one page differs between them. In every other respect, including typeface, layout, and misprints elsewhere in the book, the two copies are identical. Tanaka can reasonably conclude that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: printers of the 1640s rarely corrected their errors once they had started printing a book.
choices.B: the Boston copy must be a later forgery that was made by imitating the Edinburgh copy.
choices.C: the copies probably come from one printing, with one holding a sheet printed before a correction.
choices.D: the Edinburgh copy is the one that preserves the exact wording that the author originally intended.

explanation.why: The text explains that mid-run corrections were common and that uncorrected sheets were bound into copies along with corrected ones. Two copies that match in every detail, even in their misprints, except for one word fit this practice exactly. The single difference does not require a different edition or a forgery.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says printers often made such corrections during printing.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives no evidence of forgery; the identical misprints and layout point to the same printing.
explanation.C: Correct. A single changed word in otherwise identical copies matches the practice of binding uncorrected and corrected sheets together.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text gives no way to tell which of the two words the author intended.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 2021 a European city began charging most vehicles a fee to enter its center between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. The city's cameras, which operate only during those hours, recorded a 30 percent drop in delivery trucks entering the center during the first year. Yet a survey of shops in the center found that the number of deliveries they received was almost unchanged, and the city made no other changes to delivery rules during the period. Comparing the two sources, urban economist Paolo Ferri concluded that the fee had most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: cut daytime truck traffic, with many deliveries moving to hours without the fee.
choices.B: led shops in the center to order smaller deliveries that arrived more often than before.
choices.C: reduced the total number of deliveries that shops in the center received.
choices.D: removed delivery trucks from the city center at every hour of the day.

explanation.why: The cameras show fewer trucks only during charging hours, because that is when they operate. Shops, however, received about as many deliveries as before. If deliveries stayed the same while daytime trucks fell, many deliveries were probably made at night, when the cameras do not record and no fee applies.
explanation.A: Correct. This fits both sources: trucks fell during charging hours, while unchanged deliveries point to a shift to other hours.
explanation.B: Incorrect. More frequent deliveries would mean more trucks, and the text says nothing about delivery size.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The shop survey shows the number of deliveries was almost unchanged.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The cameras show a 30 percent drop during charging hours only, not the disappearance of trucks at all hours.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many moths fly toward artificial lights at night, and in cities this behavior can be costly: moths that circle streetlights are easily eaten by predators and spend less time feeding and mating. Researchers in Switzerland collected young ermine moths from areas with heavy light pollution and from areas with dark night skies and raised all of them from the larval stage in identical laboratory conditions. When the adults were tested, moths from the light-polluted populations were noticeably less likely to fly to a light than moths from the dark-sky populations. Because the moths had been raised under the same conditions, the results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the urban moths' weaker attraction to light is likely inherited, not learned.
choices.B: streetlights have no effect on the survival of moths that live in large cities.
choices.C: moths from dark-sky areas will soon lose their attraction to light as well.
choices.D: moths that avoid lights are less able than others to find food at night.

explanation.why: Since all the moths grew up in identical conditions, a difference between them cannot easily be explained by their surroundings during their lives. The text also says that moths drawn to lights in cities are more likely to be eaten and to mate less. Together, these points suggest that city populations have come to inherit a weaker attraction to light.
explanation.A: Correct. Identical rearing rules out learning from surroundings, so the difference is most likely inherited.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says flying to streetlights is costly for city moths, the opposite of having no effect.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nothing in the text predicts a change in moths from dark areas, where lights are rare.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says moths that circle lights spend less time feeding, not that moths avoiding lights do.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In parts of the Himalayas, herders cross yaks with cattle to produce hybrids known as dzo. Yaks thrive in high pastures but suffer in the heat of lower valleys, while cattle do poorly in the thin, cold air at high elevations; dzo cope reasonably well in both settings and are especially valued in villages at middle elevations. Male dzo, however, are sterile. Female dzo can bear calves when bred to a yak or cattle bull, but these calves are generally less hardy than first-generation hybrids. Herders who want a steady supply of dzo will therefore most likely need to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: breed female dzo with male dzo to produce each new generation.
choices.B: keep both yaks and cattle so that the two can be crossed again.
choices.C: move their herds to the high pastures where yaks are healthiest.
choices.D: stop raising yaks, since dzo do better than yaks at every elevation.

explanation.why: Male dzo cannot father calves, and the calves of female dzo are less hardy than true first-generation hybrids. So dzo herds cannot simply breed themselves. To keep getting first-generation dzo, herders must keep crossing the two parent species, which means keeping both yaks and cattle.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says male dzo are sterile, so this breeding is impossible.
explanation.B: Correct. New first-generation dzo come only from crossing yaks with cattle.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Moving to high pastures would not produce dzo, and the text says dzo are valued at middle elevations.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says yaks thrive in high pastures; it never says dzo outperform them everywhere.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mrs. Okafor had kept the hardware store's ledger for thirty years, entering every sale in blue ink and every refund in red; red, she had once told her son, was for losses. Since her husband's death in March, the neighbors had remarked that she opened on schedule, swept the step each morning, and greeted every customer by name, and several of them concluded that she was coping remarkably well. In October her son looked through the ledger. The entries continued without a break, each figure correct and the blue pen in its usual place beside the register, but from March onward every line, sale and refund alike, was written in red. The son most likely concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: his mother's grief ran deeper than her steady routine had suggested.
choices.B: the store had issued more refunds than it had made sales since March.
choices.C: his mother had begun to confuse the store's sales with its refunds.
choices.D: the neighbors had been right that his mother was coping remarkably well.

explanation.why: Two details must be combined. Mrs. Okafor uses red "for losses," and since her husband's death she has written every entry, even sales, in red, although the figures are correct and the blue pen is at hand. The choice of ink is deliberate, so it signals that she regards everything since March as loss, a grief her calm routine hides.
explanation.A: Correct. The deliberate use of the ink she reserves for losses reveals grief that her outward routine conceals.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says sales were also written in red, so the color does not show more refunds.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Her figures are all correct, so she has not confused sales with refunds; the red ink is a choice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The ledger suggests the opposite of the neighbors' view.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A hoard of coins cannot have been buried before its most recent coin was made, but it could have been buried long afterward, so archaeologists look for further clues. One such clue is wear: coins lose detail steadily as they pass from hand to hand. A hoard of 1,400 Roman silver coins found in a field in what is now France contained coins made over a span of about sixty years, the latest in 268 CE. Numismatist Claire Fontaine found that the latest coins were nearly as crisp as when they left the mint, while older coins in the same hoard were heavily worn. These observations suggest that the hoard was ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: hidden by a soldier who was fleeing from an invading army in the year 268 CE.
choices.B: buried several decades after 268 CE, once even the newest coins had begun to wear.
choices.C: buried some years before 268 CE by a person who had collected coins for decades.
choices.D: most likely buried within a few years after the latest coins were made in 268 CE.

explanation.why: The latest coin sets the earliest possible burial date, 268 CE. Wear shows how long coins circulated: the newest coins were almost unworn, so they had spent little time in use before burial. Together, the clues point to burial soon after 268 CE.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives no information about who buried the hoard or why.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The newest coins were nearly crisp, which suggests a short time in circulation, not decades.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says a hoard cannot be buried before its most recent coin was made.
explanation.D: Correct. The earliest possible date (268 CE) plus the nearly unworn newest coins point to burial soon after that date.

items.subject: science
items.passage: American crows often gather noisily around a dead crow, a behavior some researchers think helps the birds learn about threats. In one experiment, volunteers wearing one of two equally unfamiliar masks stood at feeding sites where crows regularly ate. Volunteers in the first mask stood beside a dead crow; volunteers in the second stood beside a dead pigeon. On later days, the volunteers returned to the sites without any dead birds. Crows refused to approach food near volunteers in the first mask and scolded them loudly, but they approached food near volunteers in the second mask normally. These results suggest that crows ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: learn to treat a person as dangerous after seeing that person near a dead crow.
choices.B: avoid any person wearing an unfamiliar mask, regardless of what they have seen before.
choices.C: avoid any feeding site where they have seen a dead bird of any kind.
choices.D: gather around dead crows mainly to feed on them once other birds leave.

explanation.why: The two groups of volunteers differed only in what they had stood beside: a dead crow or a dead pigeon. Later, crows avoided only the people who had been seen with a dead crow. So the crows linked those particular people with danger because of the dead crow.
explanation.A: Correct. Only people seen with a dead crow were later avoided and scolded.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Crows approached volunteers in the second mask normally, so masks alone did not cause avoidance.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Crows fed normally where a dead pigeon had been, so not every dead bird caused avoidance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never suggests crows feed on dead crows.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Many rhymes in English poetry of the late 1500s no longer work in modern speech: poets paired "love" with "prove," for instance, and Shakespeare rhymed "die" with "memory." Some scholars treat such pairs as direct evidence of how people of the period pronounced these words. But poets also used traditional rhymes inherited from earlier English, which could survive in verse long after the sounds had changed in speech, much as later poets went on rhyming "wind" with "mind." Pronunciation guides and spellings in ordinary people's letters, which often recorded words as they sounded, therefore carry special weight. If such sources show that "love" and "prove" had different vowels at the time, that would suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: poets who paired the two words used a traditional rhyme, not one that matched their speech.
choices.B: letter writers of the period pronounced most words differently than poets and their readers did.
choices.C: poets who paired the two words were making a mistake that their readers would have noticed.
choices.D: none of the rhymes in poetry of the late 1500s can tell scholars how words were pronounced.

explanation.why: The text offers two explanations for rhymes that no longer work: the words once sounded alike, or the poets used traditional rhymes that outlived the pronunciation. If sources that record actual speech show different vowels, the first explanation fails, leaving the second: the pairing was a traditional rhyme.
explanation.A: Correct. Evidence that the words sounded different in speech points to the traditional-rhyme explanation that the text offers.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text treats letters as a record of how people spoke generally; it never says letter writers spoke differently from poets.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text presents traditional rhymes as an accepted practice, not as an error.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Evidence about one pair of words would not show that every rhyme of the period is useless as evidence.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Place-names ending in -by, from an Old Norse word for a farm or village, are common in the parts of eastern and northern England that came under Scandinavian control in the late ninth century, such as Yorkshire and Lincolnshire, and are rare elsewhere. Historians agree that these names reflect Scandinavian settlement but disagree about its character. A study of one Lincolnshire district found that villages with -by names typically lay on poorer, higher ground, while villages with Old English names occupied the most fertile land in the valleys. This pattern suggests that in this district, Scandinavian settlers ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: may often have founded new villages on land that English villagers had not occupied.
choices.B: gave names ending in -by to most of the English villages that they took over.
choices.C: outnumbered the English population in every part of eastern and northern England.
choices.D: chose higher ground for their villages because it was easier to defend against attack.

explanation.why: The -by names mark Scandinavian settlements. In the district studied, those settlements lay on poorer land, while the best land kept villages with English names. If the newcomers had taken over and renamed English villages, -by names would be expected on the fertile valley land too. The pattern instead suggests they often settled on land the English had left unused.
explanation.A: Correct. The -by villages sit on poorer land the English villages had not claimed, which fits new settlement rather than takeover.
explanation.B: Incorrect. If settlers had renamed the villages they took over, -by names would appear on the fertile land, which kept English names.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A study of one district cannot show the size of the Scandinavian population everywhere.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never mentions defense as a reason for choosing land.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries, builders in Bengal raised hundreds of brick temples whose walls are covered with terracotta panels showing epics, hunts, and daily life. Some scholars have read this tradition as a sign that Bengali patrons simply preferred fired clay to stone. Yet the wide river delta that makes up most of Bengal has abundant clay and almost no building stone, which had to be brought in at great cost. Art historian Rupa Sen found that in a western district where stone was quarried locally, temples built in the same period by the same communities were usually made of stone and decorated with carved stone panels. Sen's findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: every temple built in Bengal during this period was made of brick and terracotta panels.
choices.B: terracotta in the delta mainly reflected the local materials, not a preference for clay.
choices.C: terracotta panels have lasted longer than carved stone panels in Bengal's humid climate.
choices.D: the stone temples were built by artisans who had never learned to work in terracotta.

explanation.why: Two facts combine. In the delta, stone was scarce and costly while clay was everywhere. Where stone was available locally, the same communities built in stone. If they had preferred clay, they would have used it even where stone was at hand. The terracotta tradition therefore seems to follow from available materials.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes stone temples in a western district, so not every temple was terracotta.
explanation.B: Correct. The same communities used stone where it was available, so terracotta in the delta most likely reflects the lack of stone.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares how well the two materials have lasted.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the stone temples were built by the same communities that built in terracotta.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In laboratory tests, dark bird eggs placed under a lamp warmed faster and reached higher temperatures than pale eggs did, a possible advantage in cold places, where eggs left uncovered while a parent feeds can chill quickly. A team of ornithologists compared egg color with climate across several hundred bird species and found that darker eggs were more common in colder regions. The pattern held only for species that nest in the open, however. Among species that lay their eggs inside dark tree holes or burrows, egg darkness showed no relationship to climate. The team's results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: egg color likely matters for warmth mainly where sunlight can actually reach the eggs.
choices.B: dark eggs are more likely than pale eggs to become dangerously hot in cold regions.
choices.C: birds that nest in tree holes or burrows lay darker eggs than birds that nest in the open.
choices.D: birds in cold regions tend to lay more eggs in each nest than birds in warm regions do.

explanation.why: Dark eggs gain heat from light, which helps in the cold. The link between egg darkness and cold climate appeared only for open nests, where light reaches the eggs, and vanished for nests in dark holes and burrows. Combining these points, egg color seems to matter for temperature mainly when the eggs are exposed to sunlight.
explanation.A: Correct. The relationship appears only where light can reach the eggs, matching the lamp experiment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text presents faster warming as an advantage in cold places, not a danger.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares how dark the eggs of hole-nesting and open-nesting birds are.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about the number of eggs in a nest.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Many English surnames began as descriptions of a person's work: a Baker baked bread, and a Fletcher made arrows. Over the 1300s and 1400s, however, surnames increasingly became hereditary, passing from parent to child regardless of the child's trade. Historian Helen Ashby examined tax lists from one Norfolk market town that record both each taxpayer's surname and, separately, his or her occupation. In a list from the 1290s, nearly every taxpayer with an occupational surname worked in the trade the name described. In a list from the 1450s, fewer than one in five did. Ashby's findings suggest that, for the town in the 1450s, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: people chose surnames describing the trades they hoped to enter rather than their own trades.
choices.B: occupational surnames had never had any real connection to the work that people did.
choices.C: a person's occupational surname is a poor guide to the work that person actually did.
choices.D: the number of people working as bakers and arrow makers had fallen sharply since the 1290s.

explanation.why: The text explains that surnames became hereditary, passing to children whatever their trade. The tax lists confirm the effect: in the 1290s names matched jobs, but by the 1450s fewer than one in five did. So by the 1450s, a surname alone tells little about a person's work.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text explains the mismatch through inherited surnames, not chosen ones.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The 1290s list shows that names once matched jobs closely.
explanation.C: Correct. With fewer than one in five names matching the recorded occupations, the surname is an unreliable guide.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The lists compare names with jobs; they do not show how many people worked in each trade.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: A restaurant chain asks diners to fill out comment cards voluntarily at the end of their meals. Of the cards collected last year, 70 percent contained complaints, and a manager concluded that most of the chain's customers were unhappy. Survey researchers have long found, however, that people with strong feelings, particularly negative ones, are much more likely than others to volunteer feedback. When the chain later telephoned a randomly selected group of recent diners, 85 percent said they were satisfied with their meals. Taken together, these findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the comment cards likely exaggerate how common dissatisfaction is among diners.
choices.B: the quality of the chain's meals improved after the comment cards were collected.
choices.C: most diners who fill out comment cards are visiting the chain for the first time.
choices.D: the telephone survey mainly reached diners who had already filled out comment cards.

explanation.why: Comment cards are voluntary, and unhappy people are especially likely to volunteer feedback, so complaints will be overrepresented on the cards. The random phone survey avoids that problem and found most diners satisfied. Together, these points suggest the cards overstate dissatisfaction.
explanation.A: Correct. Self-selected cards overrepresent strong negative feelings, and the random survey shows most diners were satisfied.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text offers no evidence that the food changed; the difference comes from who answered.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text gives no information about how often card writers had visited.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the phone survey reached a randomly selected group, not mainly people who had complained.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The great Indian bustard, a heavy grassland bird now found mainly in the Thar Desert of western India, is critically endangered, and collisions with power lines are among the leading causes of its deaths. Many birds avoid such collisions when lines are fitted with bright diverters, devices that make wires easier to see. But a bustard's eyes are set on the sides of its head, giving it a narrow view straight ahead, and in flight it often looks downward. Because it is so heavy, it also cannot change direction quickly once it sees an obstacle. These facts suggest that for the great Indian bustard, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: diverters would prevent all collisions if they were placed closer together on the wires.
choices.B: flying faster would let the birds clear power lines before striking them.
choices.C: making wires more visible may prevent fewer deaths than it does for many other birds.
choices.D: power lines pose less danger than they do for lighter birds that can turn quickly.

explanation.why: Diverters work by helping birds see wires. Bustards, however, see poorly straight ahead and often look down in flight, so they may not notice even marked wires in time, and their weight keeps them from turning quickly once they do. Combining these facts, diverters are likely to help bustards less than they help many other birds.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The problem is the bird's vision and slow turning, so no spacing would guarantee that it avoids every wire.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never suggests that speed would help; a heavy bird moving faster would have even less time to react.
explanation.C: Correct. Poor forward vision and slow turning reduce the benefit of a measure that relies on birds seeing wires and swerving.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says power lines are a leading cause of bustard deaths, and its traits make collisions more likely, not less.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Two nearly identical panels showing a woman reading by a window survive from sixteenth-century Flanders, and scholars have long debated which is the original and which a workshop copy. Infrared imaging can reveal the drawing an artist made on a panel before painting it. A copyist, working from a finished picture, usually transfers its outlines directly, so the underdrawing of a copy tends to match the painted surface closely. When conservator Lotte Vermeulen examined both panels, she found that in the first, the underdrawing shows the woman's head turned toward the window and a second book on the table, details later painted over. In the second panel, the underdrawing matches the visible painting almost exactly. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the second panel was painted first, and its design was later revised in the first.
choices.B: the artist of the first panel was less skilled at drawing than the artist of the second.
choices.C: the first panel is more likely the original, and the second is more likely the copy.
choices.D: both panels were copied from a third version of the scene that has since been lost.

explanation.why: Copyists transfer the outlines of a finished picture, so a copy's underdrawing should match its surface. The second panel matches; the first shows changes made while the composition was still being worked out. Changes of this kind fit an original, so the first panel is the likelier original.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If the second were first, the copyist of the first would have had a finished model, and its underdrawing should match the surface rather than show changes.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The changes show revision of the design, not weaker drawing skill.
explanation.C: Correct. The changes in the first panel fit an artist inventing the design, while the exact match in the second fits a copy.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in the text points to a third, lost version.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A healthy coral reef is a noisy place, crackling with snapping shrimp and the grunts and pops of fish, and many young reef fish, which spend their earliest weeks drifting in open water, are thought to use such sounds to find a reef on which to settle. In field trials, more young fish settled on patches of reef where recordings of a healthy reef were played than on matching silent patches. Degraded reefs, by contrast, are far quieter, since they hold fewer of the animals that produce sound. Because the fish that settle on a reef help keep it healthy, for example by grazing on algae that would otherwise smother corals, these findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: snapping shrimp produce more sound on degraded reefs than they do on healthy reefs.
choices.B: young fish avoid noisy healthy reefs because those reefs hold too many of their predators.
choices.C: a degraded reef's quietness may itself slow its recovery by drawing fewer young fish.
choices.D: playing recordings of healthy reefs would fully restore any degraded reef within a few years.

explanation.why: Three points combine: young fish are drawn to reef sounds, degraded reefs are quiet, and settling fish help keep reefs healthy. A quiet, degraded reef would therefore attract fewer of the fish that could help it recover, so its damage may tend to sustain itself.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says degraded reefs are quieter because they hold fewer sound-producing animals.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The trials show young fish are drawn toward healthy-reef sounds, not that they avoid them.
explanation.C: Correct. Quiet reefs attract fewer settlers, and settlers help reefs stay healthy, so the quiet may slow recovery.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The trials show more fish settling, not that recordings fully restore reefs; "fully" and "any" go far beyond the text.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Large volcanic eruptions can cool the climate for a few years by filling the upper atmosphere with fine droplets that reflect sunlight; such eruptions leave layers of sulfate in polar ice, and the cold summers that follow often appear as unusually narrow tree rings. Historian Brigid Lennon studied the annals of a monastery in northern Europe that record a severe famine lasting two years. Ice cores show a major eruption in the year before the famine began, and tree rings from the region reveal two exceptionally cold summers matching the famine years. The same annals, however, also report a widespread cattle disease during those years. Taken together, this evidence suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the monks exaggerated the famine, since the tree rings show only mild cooling.
choices.B: the eruption may have contributed to the famine, though other causes remain possible.
choices.C: the eruption was the only cause of the two-year famine that the monastery's annals recorded.
choices.D: the cattle disease was caused by the cold summers that followed the eruption.

explanation.why: The timing lines up: an eruption, then two cold summers that match the famine years, a plausible chain from eruption to crop failure. But the annals also report a cattle disease in the same years, which could have caused or worsened the famine on its own. The evidence supports a possible contribution from the eruption without ruling out other causes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the tree rings show "exceptionally cold summers," not mild cooling.
explanation.B: Correct. This claims only what the evidence allows: a likely contribution, with other causes still possible.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The cattle disease is a competing possible cause, so the evidence cannot show the eruption was the only one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never links the cattle disease to the cold summers.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the humid climate of southern India, the palm-leaf manuscripts on which Tamil literature was long preserved seldom last more than a few centuries, so a text survived only if it was copied again and again. As a result, the oldest surviving manuscript of a work is often far younger than the work itself. Consider a Tamil devotional poem whose oldest known manuscript was copied in the 1700s. Literary historian Kavitha Raman has shown that a commentary on Tamil grammar, written by a scholar whose life can be dated to the 1200s by temple inscriptions, quotes several passages from the poem as examples of fine style. Raman's evidence indicates that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: at least the quoted passages of the poem already existed by the 1200s, centuries before 1700.
choices.B: the grammar scholar wrote the poem himself and then claimed that an earlier poet had written it.
choices.C: every Tamil poem quoted by medieval scholars survives in some manuscript older than the 1700s.
choices.D: the poem was most likely composed in the 1700s, when its oldest known manuscript was copied.

explanation.why: Palm-leaf copies rarely last long, so a manuscript from the 1700s says little about when the poem was written. A scholar from the 1200s quoted passages from it, and he could only quote lines that already existed. The quoted passages therefore date to the 1200s or earlier.
explanation.A: Correct. A writer of the 1200s could quote only passages that existed in his time, so the quoted lines are at least that old.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives no reason to think the scholar wrote the poem.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This poem's oldest manuscript is from the 1700s, which contradicts the claim.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text explains that the oldest manuscript is often much younger than the work, and the quotations show the poem is older than 1700.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The brothers Anselm and Teodor Varga had divided their father's orchard with a fence of split rails the year after his funeral, and in the twenty years since, neither had spoken a word to the other; the village regarded their quarrel as a fixed feature of the landscape, like the church or the river. The old pear tree had been left exactly on the line. Each September, the pears from Teodor's side appeared in a basket on Anselm's porch, set down, it was said, before dawn, though no one had seen who brought them. Each December, a jar of pear preserves, unlabeled and sealed with red wax as their mother had sealed hers, appeared on Teodor's step. To the village, the brothers' silence proved that their feud had never ended; the pears and the preserves suggest instead that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the brothers have secretly resolved their quarrel and now speak to each other often.
choices.B: Teodor wants Anselm to sell him the other half of their father's orchard.
choices.C: the brothers keep up a wordless exchange that neither is willing to acknowledge.
choices.D: the pear tree has produced more fruit each year since the fence was put up.

explanation.why: The village sees only silence and concludes the feud continues. But every year pears from Teodor's side reach Anselm, and preserves sealed in their mother's way reach Teodor, all delivered unseen. Combining the silence with these secret gifts, the brothers maintain a connection they will not openly admit.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the brothers have not spoken in twenty years; the gifts are exchanged secretly, not in conversation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests Teodor wants to buy Anselm's land.
explanation.C: Correct. The unseen deliveries show a continuing bond, while the silence shows neither will acknowledge it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares the tree's harvests over time.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Library fines for late returns are often defended as the only thing that makes borrowers bring items back on time. When a city library system abolished late fines in 2019, while making no other changes to its lending rules, researcher Tomás Aguilar compared the two years before the change with the two years after. The share of items returned late rose modestly, from 8 percent to 11 percent. Over the same period, however, the number of borrowers whose accounts were blocked for unpaid fines, many of whom had stopped using the library without returning what they had borrowed, fell sharply, and the number of items never returned dropped by about 40 percent. Aguilar's findings suggest that abolishing fines ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: had no measurable effect on when or whether borrowers returned their items.
choices.B: made returns slightly less prompt but reduced how many items were lost.
choices.C: showed that borrowers with unpaid fines had returned items faster than others.
choices.D: removed the main reason that borrowers had for returning items on time at all.

explanation.why: Two results must be combined. Late returns rose a little (8 to 11 percent), so fines did encourage some promptness. But blocked accounts fell and items never returned dropped by about 40 percent, which suggests fines had been driving some borrowers away with their items. The overall effect was slightly later returns but fewer permanent losses.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Both late returns and lost items changed after the fines ended.
explanation.B: Correct. This captures both results: a small rise in late returns and a large drop in items never returned.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says many blocked borrowers stopped using the library without returning items, the opposite of returning them faster.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Late returns rose only from 8 to 11 percent, so most borrowers still returned items on time without fines.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: To identify the author of an anonymous play, scholars sometimes compare how often it uses common function words such as "the," "and," and "of," on the theory that writers use these words out of unconscious habit. Function-word rates, however, also differ by genre: comedies, with their quick exchanges of dialogue, tend to use them differently from tragedies, whatever the author. One study compared an anonymous comedy from the 1590s with the known plays of two candidate authors. The first candidate wrote mainly comedies; all of the surviving plays by the second are tragedies. The anonymous play's function-word rates closely matched those of the first candidate. Because of how the comparison was set up, this match ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: establishes that the first candidate must be the author of the anonymous play.
choices.B: may reflect a shared genre as much as a shared author.
choices.C: proves that writers choose function words deliberately to suit each genre.
choices.D: shows that the anonymous play is more likely a tragedy than a comedy.

explanation.why: Function-word rates depend partly on genre. The anonymous play is a comedy, the first candidate's plays are mostly comedies, and the second's are all tragedies. A close match with the first candidate is therefore expected from genre alone, whoever wrote the play, so the study cannot separate genre from authorship.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Because genre could explain the match, it cannot establish authorship.
explanation.B: Correct. The comparison pits comedies against tragedies, so the match could come from genre rather than from the author.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text describes function-word use as unconscious habit and says nothing about deliberate choice.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text identifies the anonymous play as a comedy.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Weeks before a powerful hurricane struck two small Caribbean islands, biologist Elena Marsh had measured hundreds of anole lizards there. After the storm, she returned and measured the survivors. On average, they had larger toe pads, which help a lizard cling to branches in high winds, than the lizards measured before the storm. Larger toe pads among survivors alone would not show that the population had changed in a lasting way, since lizards might grow larger pads in response to their surroundings. The following year, however, Marsh collected eggs laid by survivors and raised the hatchlings in a laboratory, where they were never exposed to strong winds. These lizards also had larger toe pads than the pre-storm average. Taken together, these findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: anole lizards grow larger toe pads in direct response to experiencing strong winds.
choices.B: every lizard now living on the two islands has larger toe pads than before the storm.
choices.C: the hurricane appears to have changed the population's inherited traits.
choices.D: hurricanes have become more frequent in the Caribbean during the lizards' lifetimes.

explanation.why: First, survivors had larger toe pads than the population before the storm, so the storm favored lizards with larger pads. Second, the survivors' offspring, raised without strong winds, also had larger pads. Because the lab lizards never felt the winds, the trait was passed on rather than caused by surroundings, suggesting a lasting, inherited change in the population.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The lab-raised lizards had larger pads without ever experiencing strong winds, which argues against this.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The findings concern averages; they do not show that every lizard has larger toe pads.
explanation.C: Correct. Survival favored larger pads, and offspring raised without wind inherited them, indicating an inherited change.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text describes a single hurricane and says nothing about how often hurricanes occur.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Historians have often used the number of known ancient shipwrecks as a rough measure of seaborne trade in the Roman Mediterranean. The count rises to a peak between about 100 BCE and 100 CE and then falls steeply, a pattern long read as evidence of declining commerce. Most known wrecks, however, were found by divers who spotted heaps of amphorae, the clay jars in which wine and oil were shipped; a wreck without such a heap is far harder to find. From the second century CE onward, merchants in parts of the empire increasingly shipped wine in wooden barrels, which rarely survive on the seafloor. Taken together, these facts suggest that the fall in known wrecks after the peak ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: occurred because ships carrying barrels were less likely to sink.
choices.B: proves that Roman trade collapsed in the centuries after 100 CE.
choices.C: shows that seaborne trade in the Mediterranean actually grew after 100 CE.
choices.D: may overstate how much seaborne trade actually declined after that time.

explanation.why: Wrecks are found mainly by their heaps of amphorae, and after the second century some cargo moved in barrels that leave little trace. Ships carrying barrels would be undercounted, so part of the drop in known wrecks may reflect changing containers rather than less trade. The decline in trade may therefore be smaller than the wreck count suggests.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says barrels are hard to find, not that ships carrying them sank less often.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text's point is that the wreck count may be misleading, so it cannot prove a collapse.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text suggests the decline may be overstated, not that trade grew; it gives no evidence of growth.
explanation.D: Correct. Barrels leave few traces, so wrecks after the shift are harder to find, which could exaggerate the apparent decline.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In Mughal India, the right to have coins struck in one's own name was among the clearest public claims to rule, and each coin recorded the name of the ruler and the city whose mint produced it. Numismatist Imran Qadri examined coins from a provincial mint during a period when a rebellious prince challenged the emperor. Coins from that mint dated to one year carry the prince's name; coins from the same mint dated to the years just before and after carry the emperor's name. Because a prince could strike coins at a mint only if he controlled the city where it operated, Qadri's findings suggest that the prince ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was accepted as the rightful ruler throughout Mughal India for that year.
choices.B: probably held that city for a time before the emperor's forces regained it.
choices.C: persuaded the emperor's own officials to strike coins in his name as an honor.
choices.D: never controlled that city, since its mint went on using the emperor's name.

explanation.why: Coins could be struck in a ruler's name only where he controlled the mint's city. Coins from one year carry the prince's name, so he held the city then; coins from the years before and after carry the emperor's name, so the emperor held it before and again afterward. Together, the coins point to a brief period of control by the prince.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Coins from one provincial mint cannot show that the prince was accepted everywhere.
explanation.B: Correct. The switch to the prince's name and back to the emperor's fits a short period of control before the city was lost.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text presents coins as a claim to rule, not as an honor granted by the emperor's officials.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The coins from that one year carry the prince's name, which shows he did control the city then.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Nineteenth-century theaters kept prompt books, working copies of plays in which the stage manager marked cuts, added lines, and recorded cues for performers. For one popular melodrama of the 1840s, two versions survive: the text the playwright published the year the play opened, and the prompt book from the theater that first staged it. The prompt book cuts nearly a third of the second act and adds a song for the heroine that appears nowhere in the published text. Several newspaper reviews of the play's opening week praise that song. These sources suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the playwright wrote the heroine's song after the published text had appeared.
choices.B: the published text may not reflect what audiences at the first performances saw.
choices.C: the playwright disapproved of the changes that the theater made to the second act.
choices.D: prompt books are more reliable guides than published texts for every play of the period.

explanation.why: The prompt book records a version of the play with a shortened second act and an added song. Reviews of the opening week praise the song, which is missing from the published text, so audiences saw the prompt-book version, at least in part. The published text therefore may not match what was performed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The reviews show the song was sung in the opening week, the same year the text was published; nothing indicates who wrote it or when.
explanation.B: Correct. The reviews confirm that a feature found only in the prompt book was performed, so the published text differs from what audiences saw.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text gives no information about the playwright's opinion of the changes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Evidence about one melodrama cannot establish a rule for every play of the period.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Merriam's kangaroo rats live in the deserts of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico, where open water is rare. These small rodents eat mostly dry seeds. When their bodies break down the seeds for energy, the chemical reactions release water as a by-product, and the animals' kidneys are extremely efficient at holding on to that water. These facts suggest that kangaroo rats ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: must find a pond or stream to drink from every few days.
choices.B: can survive for long periods without drinking any water at all.
choices.C: choose seeds because seeds hold more water than other desert foods.
choices.D: lose more water through their kidneys than most other rodents do.

explanation.why: The text says open water is rare where kangaroo rats live, that digesting seeds releases water inside their bodies, and that their kidneys hold on to that water. An animal that makes and keeps its own water does not need to drink, so it can go a long time without drinking.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text stresses that open water is rare and explains how the rats get water without drinking, so it gives no reason to think they need ponds or streams.
explanation.B: Correct. Water released while digesting seeds, kept by very efficient kidneys, lets the rats go without drinking.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text calls the seeds "dry"; the water comes from breaking the seeds down, not from water stored in them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says their kidneys are extremely efficient at holding on to water.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Inca Empire, which stretched along the Andes Mountains of South America in the 1400s and 1500s, had no horses or wheeled vehicles for carrying messages. Instead, it relied on chasquis, runners stationed at posts along its roads. Each runner carried a message only a short distance before handing it to a fresh runner waiting at the next post. Because no single runner had to cover the whole route, messages could ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: be carried on horseback along the empire's flatter stretches of road.
choices.B: travel long distances much faster than one tired runner could carry them.
choices.C: reach distant cities only after long delays caused by exhausted runners.
choices.D: be written down so that runners would not have to remember them.

explanation.why: Each runner covered only a short stretch and then passed the message to a rested runner. Since nobody had to run the whole way and grow tired, the message could keep moving at a fast pace over long distances.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the empire had no horses for carrying messages.
explanation.B: Correct. Handing the message to a fresh runner at each post keeps it moving quickly, which one runner could not do over a long route.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The relay system avoided exhausted runners, so it would reduce delays rather than cause them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about writing messages down or about runners' memory.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The khejri tree grows across the Thar Desert of India and Pakistan, where nearly all the year's rain falls in just a few months. Its main root can grow many meters down to reach water stored deep underground, far below the dry upper layers of soil where most grasses and small shrubs have their roots. As a result, the khejri is likely to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: draw most of its water from the upper layers of the soil.
choices.B: stay green in the dry months, after many shallow-rooted plants have withered.
choices.C: lose its leaves earlier in the dry season than the grasses around it do.
choices.D: grow shorter than the grasses and small shrubs that grow near it.

explanation.why: Rain falls in only a few months, so the upper soil dries out for most of the year. The khejri's deep root reaches water far below that dry layer, so the tree can keep getting water when plants with shallow roots cannot.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the root reaches water "far below the dry upper layers," the opposite of this choice.
explanation.B: Correct. Reaching deep water lets the khejri keep growing when the upper soil, where shallow-rooted plants get water, is dry.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the logic: the khejri's deep root gives it water after the grasses' shallow roots have dried out, so it should keep its leaves longer, not lose them sooner.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says nothing about the tree's height compared with nearby plants.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In Japan during the Edo period (1603–1868), color woodblock prints were made by teams of artists and craftspeople. In the usual method, a carver cut a separate wooden block for each color in a design. A printer then pressed each block onto the same sheet of paper, one color at a time, lining up every block carefully. Under this method, a print that used ten colors would have required ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a carver who had also designed the picture being printed.
choices.B: one carved block holding all ten colors at the same time.
choices.C: more carved blocks than a print that used three colors.
choices.D: fewer carved blocks than a print that used three colors.

explanation.why: The text says each color had its own block. A ten-color print therefore needed ten blocks, which is more than the three blocks a three-color print needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text describes teams of workers but never says carvers designed the pictures.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says a separate block was cut for each color, not one block for all of them.
explanation.C: Correct. One block per color means ten blocks for ten colors, more than a three-color print needed.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses the relationship: more colors means more blocks, not fewer.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Most birds make a whooshing sound when they flap their wings, but many owls fly almost silently. The front edges of an owl's main flight feathers have stiff, comblike fringes, and the back edges are soft and frayed. Together, these features break up the rushing air that would otherwise make noise. Since owls often hunt mice and other small animals with sharp hearing, silent flight probably helps owls ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: catch mice that make no sound at all as they move.
choices.B: get close to their prey before the prey can hear them coming.
choices.C: fly faster than birds whose feathers lack comblike fringes.
choices.D: frighten their prey out of hiding before diving at it.

explanation.why: The text links two facts: owls fly almost silently, and their prey has sharp hearing. An owl that makes no noise can approach without warning the animal it is hunting.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text is about the owl's sound, not the sound the mice make.
explanation.B: Correct. Prey with sharp hearing would notice a noisy bird, so silence lets the owl approach unheard.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text discusses noise, not speed, so it gives no basis for this comparison.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Silent flight would keep prey from noticing the owl; frightening prey would require noise.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Amaka's grandmother had never flown a kite, but she held the spool of string while Amaka ran across the field. On the fourth try, the wind caught the kite and lifted it high above the trees. Amaka turned around, expecting to see her grandmother staring up at the sky. Instead, her grandmother was watching Amaka, smiling widely and clapping with the spool tucked under her arm. The grandmother's behavior suggests that she ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: did not notice that the kite had finally risen into the air.
choices.B: wanted to take a turn running across the field with the kite.
choices.C: took more pleasure in Amaka's success than in the kite itself.
choices.D: was disappointed that the kite had needed four tries to fly.

explanation.why: When the kite finally rises, the grandmother is not looking at the kite; she is looking at Amaka, smiling and clapping. Her attention and joy are focused on her granddaughter's achievement.
explanation.A: Incorrect. She is clapping as the kite flies, which shows she knows it has risen.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests she wanted to run with the kite herself.
explanation.C: Correct. She watches Amaka rather than the kite and claps happily, showing that Amaka's success is what delights her.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Smiling widely and clapping show delight, not disappointment.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Starting in April 1860, riders of the Pony Express carried mail on horseback between Missouri and California, a trip that took about ten days. In October 1861, workers completed a telegraph line across the United States, allowing messages to cross the country in a matter of minutes. The Pony Express shut down just days later. These events suggest that the Pony Express most likely closed because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: the telegraph had made messages between the states slower to arrive.
choices.B: the telegraph could deliver messages far faster than riders could.
choices.C: its riders could no longer find horses that were fast enough.
choices.D: the new telegraph line had been built across the riders' route.

explanation.why: The Pony Express took about ten days, while the telegraph took minutes. The service closed right after the telegraph line was finished, which points to the much faster telegraph as the reason.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the text: the telegraph made messages arrive much faster, not slower.
explanation.B: Correct. A ten-day trip could not compete with minutes, and the timing of the closure fits this cause.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions any shortage of horses.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text does not say where the telegraph line ran or that it blocked anything.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the dry zone of northern and eastern Sri Lanka, most of the year's rain falls within a few months, and the land can be parched for the rest of the year. More than two thousand years ago, communities there began building tanks, large reservoirs enclosed by earthen banks, to catch and hold rainwater. Channels then carried water from the tanks to rice fields. These tanks most likely allowed farmers to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: move their rice fields to the wetter parts of the island.
choices.B: stop depending on rain as a source of water for their crops.
choices.C: grow rice only during the months of heaviest rain.
choices.D: water their crops even during months with little rain.

explanation.why: Rain falls in only a few months, but the tanks stored that rain and channels carried it to the fields. Stored water could therefore reach the crops during the dry part of the year.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about moving fields elsewhere on the island.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This goes too far: the tanks were filled by rainwater, so farmers still depended on rain.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the purpose of the tanks; storing water frees farmers from the rainy months alone.
explanation.D: Correct. Water stored during the rainy months could be sent to fields when little rain was falling.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun, at an average distance of about 58 million kilometers, and Venus is nearly twice as far away. Yet the surface of Venus, at about 465 degrees Celsius, is hotter than even the hottest parts of Mercury. Venus is wrapped in a thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide that traps heat, while Mercury has almost no atmosphere. This comparison suggests that a planet's surface temperature ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: depends only on how far the planet is from the Sun.
choices.B: cannot be measured on planets with thick atmospheres.
choices.C: depends on its atmosphere as well as its distance from the Sun.
choices.D: rises whenever a planet is farther away from the Sun.

explanation.why: If distance were all that mattered, Mercury would be hotter than Venus. Venus is hotter even though it is farther away, and the text explains that its thick atmosphere traps heat, so the atmosphere must also affect temperature.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Venus is farther from the Sun but hotter, which shows distance is not the only factor.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives a temperature for Venus, which has a thick atmosphere, so this cannot be right.
explanation.C: Correct. Venus's heat-trapping atmosphere makes it hotter than Mercury despite its greater distance, so both factors matter.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This overgeneralizes from one comparison; the text explains Venus's heat by its atmosphere, not by its distance.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In medieval Europe, books were often written on parchment, a material made from animal skin that was costly and slow to produce. When a book was no longer wanted, a scribe would sometimes scrape the ink off its pages and write a new text on the same parchment. Faint traces of the older writing often remained, and modern scientists have used special imaging to read them. As a result, some old parchment books ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: show no trace of the writing that was scraped off their pages.
choices.B: contain hidden texts older than the ones that can be seen on their pages.
choices.C: were copied onto paper by scribes before their pages were scraped.
choices.D: were scraped clean because parchment was cheap and easy to replace.

explanation.why: Scribes wrote new texts over scraped-off older ones, and traces of the older writing remained. Scientists can now read those traces, so some books hold an earlier text underneath the one that is visible.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says faint traces of the older writing often remained.
explanation.B: Correct. The scraped-off writing came first and still leaves traces under the newer text, so these books contain older, hidden texts.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never mentions copying old texts onto paper.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says parchment was costly and slow to produce, which is why it was reused.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Changthangi goats are raised by herding families on the Changthang plateau of Ladakh, in northern India, where winter nights are bitterly cold. As winter approaches, each goat grows a thick layer of extremely fine wool, called pashm, beneath its coarse outer hair. When the weather warms in spring, the goats begin to shed this soft layer. It is therefore most likely that herders collect pashm ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: only from goats that live in warmer valleys below the plateau.
choices.B: from the coarse outer hair rather than the layer beneath it.
choices.C: in spring, around the time the goats begin to shed it.
choices.D: in early autumn, before the goats have grown their soft layer.

explanation.why: The pashm grows as winter approaches and is shed when spring comes. The sensible time to collect it is in spring, when the layer is full and starting to come loose.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text gives no information about goats in warmer valleys; it links the soft layer to cold weather.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says pashm is the fine layer beneath the coarse outer hair, not the outer hair itself.
explanation.C: Correct. In spring the layer is fully grown and already loosening, so herders can gather it then.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Before winter the goats have not yet grown the soft layer, so there would be little pashm to collect.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In ancient Mesopotamia, scribes wrote by pressing marks into tablets of soft clay. Many tablets were simply left to dry in the sun, and sun-dried clay can crumble or turn back into mud if it gets wet. Strong heat, however, hardens clay into a material much like pottery. When the city of Nineveh was burned by invading armies in 612 BCE, the fire may have ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: led scribes to stop writing on clay and start writing on stone.
choices.B: softened the tablets so that their marks could no longer be read.
choices.C: destroyed every clay tablet that had been stored in the city.
choices.D: helped preserve some tablets by baking them hard.

explanation.why: Sun-dried tablets are fragile, but strong heat turns clay hard like pottery. A large fire would have supplied that heat, so it could have made some tablets more durable.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about scribes switching to stone.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the text, which says heat hardens clay rather than softening it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says heat hardens clay, so a fire would not necessarily destroy the tablets.
explanation.D: Correct. Strong heat hardens clay, so the fire could have baked some tablets into a lasting form.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Rafael had played his audition piece for the city orchestra that morning, and the results would be posted at six o'clock. By five, he had tuned his violin twice, though he had no plans to play it, and had reread the same page of his book so many times that he could not have said what it was about. Every few minutes, he glanced at the clock on the wall. These details suggest that Rafael ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: was confident that he had already won a place in the orchestra.
choices.B: was too anxious about the results to focus on anything else.
choices.C: was hoping to practice once more before the results appeared.
choices.D: had lost interest in music after a difficult audition.

explanation.why: Rafael keeps doing pointless tasks, cannot take in what he reads, and checks the clock again and again while waiting for the results. These are signs of nervous waiting.
explanation.A: Incorrect. His restless behavior shows worry, not calm confidence.
explanation.B: Correct. Retuning an instrument he will not play, rereading without understanding, and watching the clock all show anxiety.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says he had no plans to play the violin.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing suggests he has lost interest in music; he is eagerly waiting for the results.

items.subject: science
items.passage: On Earth, footprints in soil or sand are soon erased by wind and rain. The Moon, however, has almost no atmosphere, so it has no wind and no weather. Astronauts who walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972 left footprints in its fine, powdery dust. Given these conditions, many of those footprints are most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: deeper now than they were when the astronauts made them.
choices.B: preserved only because the dust froze solid after the astronauts left.
choices.C: still there today, since no wind or rain has worn them away.
choices.D: long gone, swept away by winds blowing across the lunar surface.

explanation.why: Wind and rain erase footprints on Earth, but the Moon has neither. Without those forces, the footprints have nothing to wear them away quickly, so they are probably still there.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests the footprints would grow deeper over time.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text explains the footprints' survival by the lack of wind and weather, not by freezing.
explanation.C: Correct. With no wind or weather to erase them, the footprints should remain.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the Moon has no wind.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Much of the Netherlands consists of polders, areas of low land surrounded by dikes, which are earthen walls that hold back rivers and the sea. Many polders lie below sea level, so rainwater and water seeping through the ground collect in them instead of draining away. Beginning in the 1400s, the Dutch built windmills that lifted this water over the dikes. Without some way to remove water, the polders would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: rise slowly above the level of the sea.
choices.B: need fewer dikes to keep out the sea.
choices.C: dry out and become too dusty to farm.
choices.D: gradually fill with water and flood.

explanation.why: Water collects in the polders because they are low and cannot drain on their own. The windmills removed that water, so without them it would keep building up.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nothing in the text suggests the land would rise.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Nothing in the text links removing water to the number of dikes needed; the dikes hold back rivers and the sea, which would still be there.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the problem: polders collect water rather than lose it.
explanation.D: Correct. Water collects in the polders and cannot drain away, so without pumping it would build up until the land flooded.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, which kill many other small fish. It has often been assumed that clownfish are simply born immune to the stings. To test this idea, marine biologist Lena Okoro raised young clownfish in tanks without anemones and then placed each fish beside one. At first, the fish only brushed briefly against the tentacles, sometimes darting away after being stung. Over several hours, their contact grew longer, and within a day they were nestling among the tentacles unharmed. Okoro's results suggest that a clownfish's protection from anemone stings ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: is permanently lost if the fish spends its early life in a tank without anemones.
choices.B: comes mainly from the fish's ability to dart away before the tentacles can sting it.
choices.C: develops through contact with an anemone rather than being fully present at birth.
choices.D: is present at birth, which is why the young fish settled among the tentacles at once.

explanation.why: The young fish were stung at first but, after hours of gradually longer contact, could nestle among the tentacles unharmed. Protection that appears only after contact must build up through that contact, which challenges the idea that clownfish are born fully immune.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Fish raised without anemones still became protected within a day, so the protection was not lost.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Darting away happened only at first; later the fish stayed among the tentacles unharmed, so escape cannot explain their protection.
explanation.C: Correct. The fish were stung at first and became unharmed only after repeated contact, so their protection developed over time.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The fish did not settle in at once; they were stung and darted away at first.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: At Vindolanda, a Roman fort in northern England, archaeologists have recovered hundreds of thin wooden tablets on which soldiers and their families wrote letters, supply lists, and even party invitations nearly two thousand years ago. Wood normally rots quickly in the ground, but these tablets lay in waterlogged soil containing almost no oxygen, which slowed their decay. At most other Roman forts, the soil is dry and well drained, and no such tablets have been found there. The absence of tablets at those other forts therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: indicates that soldiers at those forts wrote on stone instead of on wood.
choices.B: proves that writing was rare among the soldiers stationed at them.
choices.C: shows that the Vindolanda tablets were carried there from other forts.
choices.D: may reflect conditions in the soil rather than how much people there wrote.

explanation.why: The tablets at Vindolanda survived only because unusual soil slowed the decay of the wood. In the dry soil of other forts, any tablets would probably have rotted away, so finding none there does not tell us whether people at those forts wrote less.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never mentions writing on stone; it gives soil conditions, not a different writing material, as the likely explanation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This goes too far: tablets at the other forts may simply have rotted in dry soil, so their absence proves nothing about how often people wrote.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says nothing about tablets being moved from one fort to another.
explanation.D: Correct. Because wood rots quickly in dry soil, the missing tablets could be explained by poor preservation rather than by a lack of writing.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In the Mithila region of Bihar, India, women have long painted bright scenes of gods, animals, and plants on the mud walls of their homes, often to mark a wedding or a festival. Mud walls must be replastered regularly, however, and each fresh coat covered the paintings beneath it. In the 1960s, artists from the region began painting the same kinds of images on paper, which could be sold and carried far away. Because of this history, scholars studying Mithila painting most likely ______
