Titan's surface has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.
Titan is surrounded by a thick atmosphere, whereas Europa has only an extremely thin one.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the surfaces of Europa and Titan. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Titan is surrounded by a thick atmosphere, whereas Europa has only an extremely thin one.
choices.B: Although Europa orbits Jupiter and Titan orbits Saturn, both moons are thought to hide liquid water beneath their surfaces.
choices.C: Europa's surface is a cracked shell of water ice, while Titan's surface holds lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.
choices.D: Titan, a moon of Saturn, has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane on its surface.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: it must show a difference, and the difference must be about the surfaces. The notes describe Europa's icy, cracked surface and Titan's surface of methane and ethane lakes; only one choice sets these against each other.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is a real difference, but it concerns the moons' atmospheres, not their surfaces. It is tempting because it uses a contrast word.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It mentions the surfaces, but it stresses something the moons share (hidden water), so it shows a similarity.
explanation.C: Correct. It contrasts Europa's cracked ice surface with Titan's lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes only Titan's surface, so no difference from Europa is shown.

items.subject: history_social
notes: In 2023, a city library system in the Netherlands began keeping three of its branches open until 10 p.m. instead of 6 p.m.
Sociologist Femke de Vries wanted to know whether the longer hours would affect how many teenagers used the libraries.
She compared visitor counts at those three branches with counts at three branches that kept the usual hours.
After one year, visits by teenagers had risen by 35 percent at the branches with longer hours but stayed about the same at the others.
Most of the extra teenage visits took place after 7 p.m.
items.stem: The student wants to present the aim and the finding of de Vries's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: De Vries compared teenage visits at three branches open until 10 p.m. with visits at three that kept the usual hours.
choices.B: After a Dutch library system kept three branches open later, teenage visits there rose by 35 percent, mostly after 7 p.m.
choices.C: Asking whether longer hours would affect teenage library use, de Vries found that teenage visits rose 35 percent at branches open late.
choices.D: De Vries wanted to find out whether keeping library branches open until 10 p.m. would affect how many teenagers used them.

explanation.why: The goal names two parts: the aim (what de Vries wanted to learn) and the finding (what she learned). One choice states the question about longer hours and teenage use and then reports the 35 percent rise.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This describes the study's method, the comparison of branches, rather than its aim or its finding.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It reports the finding but never says what de Vries set out to learn, so it, too, covers only half the goal.
explanation.C: Correct. "Asking whether longer hours would affect teenage library use" is the aim, and the 35 percent rise is the finding.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It states the aim but leaves out the finding, so it accomplishes only half the goal.

items.subject: humanities
notes: Theater flourished in ancient Athens in the 400s BCE, with plays performed in large open-air theaters.
Greek actors wore masks, and all the roles, including women's roles, were played by men.
Noh, a form of Japanese musical drama, developed in the 1300s.
In Noh, the lead actor often wears a carved wooden mask, and the roles have traditionally been performed by men.
Noh plays are performed on a square stage covered by its own roof.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between ancient Greek theater and Noh. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Noh developed in Japan in the 1300s, more than 1,500 years after theater flourished in ancient Athens.
choices.B: In both ancient Greek theater and Japanese Noh, actors wore masks and the roles were traditionally played by men.
choices.C: Ancient Greek plays were performed in large open-air theaters, while Noh plays are performed on a square stage with its own roof.
choices.D: In Noh, the lead actor often wears a carved wooden mask, and men have traditionally performed the roles.

explanation.why: A similarity must name both traditions and state what they share. The notes show that both used masks and that men traditionally played the roles in both. Only one choice joins the two traditions on these shared features.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It compares the traditions' dates, which emphasizes how far apart they are rather than what they share.
explanation.B: Correct. It names both traditions and points to what they share: masks and male performers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It discusses both traditions, which makes it tempting, but it contrasts their stages, so it shows a difference.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes the very features the traditions share, but only for Noh, so the reader never sees the similarity to Greek theater.

items.subject: science
notes: Tarbela Dam, completed in 1976 on the Indus River in Pakistan, is one of the largest earth-filled dams in the world.
Its reservoir stores water for farm irrigation and supplies a hydroelectric power plant.
The Indus carries large amounts of sand and silt washed down from the Himalaya and Karakoram mountains.
When the river's flow slows in the reservoir, much of this sediment sinks to the bottom and stays there.
Since the dam opened, the reservoir has lost a large share of its original storage capacity.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why Tarbela's reservoir can hold less water than it once could. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Tarbela Dam, completed in 1976 on the Indus River in Pakistan, is one of the largest earth-filled dams in the world.
choices.B: Sand and silt carried by the Indus settle to the bottom of Tarbela's reservoir and stay there, reducing the space for water.
choices.C: The Indus River carries large amounts of sand and silt that wash down from the Himalaya and Karakoram mountains.
choices.D: Since Tarbela Dam opened, its reservoir, which stores water for irrigation and power, has lost a large share of its capacity.

explanation.why: The goal asks for a cause, so the sentence must explain how the reservoir lost capacity, not just state that it did. The notes connect the river's sediment to the reservoir: the sand and silt sink and stay there, taking up room that water once filled.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It introduces the dam but gives no reason for the lost capacity.
explanation.B: Correct. It explains that sediment settling in the reservoir reduces the space available for water.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It gives the source of the sediment but does not say that the sediment builds up in the reservoir, so the explanation is incomplete.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It states the result, the lost capacity, without explaining what caused it. It is tempting because it describes exactly what the goal asks about.

items.subject: science
notes: Bioluminescence is the production of light by living things through a chemical reaction.
Fireflies flash light signals to attract mates.
A female deep-sea anglerfish has a glowing lure on its head that draws prey close to its mouth.
Some glowing mushrooms appear to attract insects that then carry the mushrooms' spores to new places.
Most bioluminescent species live in the ocean.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about how living things use bioluminescence. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Fireflies, which produce light through a chemical reaction, flash light signals to attract mates.
choices.B: Most bioluminescent species live in the ocean, where the deep-sea anglerfish, for example, has a glowing lure.
choices.C: Living things that produce their own light use it for a variety of purposes, from attracting mates to luring prey.
choices.D: Bioluminescence is the production of light by living things through a chemical reaction.

explanation.why: The generalization must be broad (about living things in general) and must concern how they use their light. The firefly, anglerfish, and mushroom examples each use light for a different job, so the generalization is that light serves many purposes.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes how one animal uses light, which is a single example rather than a generalization.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It is a generalization, which makes it tempting, but it is about where bioluminescent species live, not how they use their light.
explanation.C: Correct. It makes a broad statement about the uses of bioluminescence and supports it with two examples from the notes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It defines bioluminescence but says nothing about how living things use it.

items.subject: history_social
notes: The Hanseatic League was a network of merchant groups and trading towns in northern Europe.
It was most powerful from the 1200s to the 1400s.
Its member towns, led by Lübeck in what is now Germany, lay mostly along the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.
League merchants traded goods such as fish, timber, grain, and furs.
The league held its last general meeting in 1669.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce the Hanseatic League to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Hanseatic League was a network of northern European merchant groups and trading towns, most powerful from the 1200s to the 1400s.
choices.B: Merchants of the Hanseatic League, whose towns lay mostly along the North Sea and the Baltic Sea, traded fish, timber, grain, and furs.
choices.C: The Hanseatic League, which held its last general meeting in 1669, had been most powerful from the 1200s to the 1400s.
choices.D: Led by Lübeck, in what is now Germany, the league's member towns lay mostly along the North Sea and the Baltic Sea.

explanation.why: An audience that has never heard of the Hanseatic League first needs to know what it was. Only one choice explains that it was a network of merchant groups and trading towns and places it in northern Europe at a particular time.
explanation.A: Correct. It defines the league, says where it operated, and tells when it was most powerful.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It tells where the league's towns were and what its merchants traded, but it never explains what the league itself was.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It gives dates for the league but never says what kind of organization it was, so an unfamiliar reader would be lost.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It refers to "the league" as though readers already know what it is, and it never explains what the league was.

items.subject: science
notes: In western Kenya, many farmers grow maize and beans together in the same field, a practice called intercropping.
Beans, like other legumes, can add nitrogen to the soil with the help of bacteria in their roots.
Agronomist Wanjiru Kamau planted 30 small plots: half with maize alone and half with maize and beans in alternating rows.
She used no fertilizer on any plot.
At harvest, the intercropped plots produced slightly less maize than the maize-only plots but more food in total once the beans were counted.
items.stem: The student wants to present the method and the finding of Kamau's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Kamau planted 30 small plots without fertilizer, half with maize alone and half with maize and beans in alternating rows.
choices.B: Kamau's study showed that intercropped plots produced slightly less maize than maize-only plots but more food in total.
choices.C: Comparing unfertilized maize-only plots with maize-and-bean plots, Kamau found that the mixed plots produced more food overall.
choices.D: Intercropping, a common practice in western Kenya, combines maize with beans, which can add nitrogen to the soil.

explanation.why: The goal needs both the method (how Kamau set up her test) and the finding (what she learned). One choice describes the comparison of unfertilized maize-only and maize-and-bean plots and then reports that the mixed plots produced more food.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes the method in detail but never says what Kamau found.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It reports the finding but leaves out how the study was carried out.
explanation.C: Correct. The opening phrase gives the method, and the main clause gives the finding.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It gives background about intercropping and beans but nothing about Kamau's study.

items.subject: humanities
notes: In true fresco, an artist paints with pigments mixed in water onto a layer of wet lime plaster.
As the plaster dries, the pigment becomes bound into the wall, so each section must be finished within about a day.
Oil paint is made by mixing pigment with an oil, such as linseed oil.
Oil paint dries slowly, often over several days, which allows artists to blend colors and make changes.
Fresco was widely used for wall paintings in Renaissance Italy.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in how much time the two methods give an artist to work. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Because oil paint dries slowly, often over several days, artists who use it can blend colors and make changes.
choices.B: In fresco, pigment is mixed with water, while in oil painting it is mixed with an oil such as linseed oil.
choices.C: A fresco painter must finish each section within about a day, whereas an oil painter can keep making changes for several days.
choices.D: Fresco, which was widely used for wall paintings in Renaissance Italy, binds pigment into the plaster as it dries.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: a difference between the two methods, and specifically a difference in working time. The notes give about a day for each fresco section and several days for oil paint.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes the working time for oil paint only, so it does not show how fresco differs.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It contrasts the two methods, which makes it tempting, but the difference is in materials, not working time.
explanation.C: Correct. It contrasts the single day a fresco painter has with the several days an oil painter has.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes fresco alone and focuses on how the pigment bonds, not on working time compared with oil.

items.subject: history_social
notes: Nalanda was a Buddhist center of learning in what is now the Indian state of Bihar.
It flourished from about the 400s CE until the late 1100s.
Its teachers taught subjects such as philosophy, logic, grammar, and medicine.
It drew students from places as distant as China, Korea, and Central Asia.
The Chinese monk Xuanzang studied there in the 600s and later wrote about it.
Its ruins were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how far beyond India Nalanda's reputation reached. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2016, the ruins of Nalanda, a center of learning in what is now Bihar, were named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
choices.B: Nalanda, a Buddhist center of learning in what is now Bihar, flourished for more than seven centuries.
choices.C: Nalanda's teachers covered a wide range of subjects, including philosophy, logic, grammar, and medicine.
choices.D: Nalanda drew students from as far away as China, Korea, and Central Asia, among them the Chinese monk Xuanzang.

explanation.why: To show how far Nalanda's reputation reached, the sentence needs evidence that people from distant lands knew of it and came to it. The notes give that evidence: students came from China, Korea, and Central Asia, including Xuanzang.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It tells when the ruins were honored in modern times; it says nothing about how far Nalanda's reputation spread while it was active.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It stresses how long Nalanda lasted, which is reach in time, not in distance.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It shows the wide range of subjects taught, not how far away Nalanda was known.
explanation.D: Correct. Students traveling from China, Korea, and Central Asia show that Nalanda's reputation reached far beyond India.

items.subject: science
notes: Sharks are fish that breathe through gills.
Dolphins are mammals that breathe air through a blowhole on top of their heads.
Both sharks and dolphins have smooth, streamlined bodies and a fin on their backs.
A shark swims by sweeping its tail from side to side, while a dolphin moves its tail up and down.
Scientists think the two animals developed their similar shapes independently.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity in the two animals' appearance while acknowledging that they belong to different groups of animals. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Although sharks are fish and dolphins are mammals, both have smooth, streamlined bodies with a fin on their backs.
choices.B: Sharks are fish that breathe through gills, whereas dolphins are mammals that breathe air through a blowhole.
choices.C: A shark swims by sweeping its tail from side to side, but a dolphin swims by moving its tail up and down.
choices.D: Sharks and dolphins both have smooth, streamlined bodies with a fin on their backs.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: a similarity in appearance and an acknowledgment that sharks and dolphins belong to different groups. Only one choice both notes that one is a fish and the other a mammal and points to their shared body shape.
explanation.A: Correct. "Although sharks are fish and dolphins are mammals" acknowledges the different groups, and the rest of the sentence stresses their similar shape.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It shows that the animals belong to different groups but never mentions a similarity in appearance.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It describes a difference in how the animals swim, not a similarity in how they look.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It gives the similarity in appearance but leaves out that the animals belong to different groups, so it meets only half the goal.

items.subject: history_social
notes: The bell tower of the cathedral in Pisa, Italy, is known worldwide as the Leaning Tower of Pisa.
Construction began in 1173 and continued, with long pauses, until 1372.
The tower was built on a shallow foundation, only about three meters deep.
The ground beneath it is soft clay and sand and is softer on the south side than on the north side.
As the heavy stone walls rose, the softer ground on the south side sank more, and the tower began to tilt.
From 1990 to 2001, engineers reduced the tilt by removing soil from beneath the tower's north side.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why the tower began to lean. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The ground beneath the Leaning Tower of Pisa is soft clay and sand, and it is softer on the south side than on the north side.
choices.B: Construction of the Leaning Tower of Pisa began in 1173 and continued, with long pauses, until 1372.
choices.C: Resting on a shallow foundation over soft ground, the tower tilted as its softer south side sank under the heavy walls.
choices.D: From 1990 to 2001, engineers reduced the tower's tilt by removing soil from beneath its north side.

explanation.why: An explanation of why the tower leans must connect the ground conditions to the tilt. The notes say the shallow foundation sat on soft ground and that the softer south side sank more under the weight of the walls. Only one choice makes that connection.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes the uneven ground but never connects it to the tower's tilt, so it gives only part of the explanation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It gives the dates of construction, which do not explain the lean.
explanation.C: Correct. It links the shallow foundation, the soft ground, and the heavy walls to the tower's tilt.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes how engineers reduced the lean, not what caused it.

items.subject: humanities
notes: In ancient Egypt, scribes wrote on papyrus, a material made from the stems of a reed that grew along the Nile River.
In ancient China, before paper came into wide use, many texts were written on thin strips of bamboo tied together.
In South Asia, many texts were written for centuries on dried and treated palm leaves.
In medieval Europe, many books were written on parchment, a material made from animal skin.
items.stem: The student wants to make a generalization about the materials that early societies used for writing. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Parchment, a material made from animal skin, was used for many of the books produced in medieval Europe.
choices.B: Many early societies wrote on materials made from plants, such as papyrus, bamboo, and palm leaves.
choices.C: Whereas ancient Chinese texts were often written on bamboo strips, medieval European books were often written on parchment.
choices.D: Ancient Egyptian scribes wrote on papyrus, which was made from the stems of a reed that grew along the Nile River.

explanation.why: A generalization makes a broad statement that covers several cases. Three of the four societies in the notes wrote on plant materials, so the fair generalization is that many early societies did so. The word "many" keeps the claim accurate, since medieval Europe used parchment.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes only medieval Europe, and parchment is the one example that does not fit the broader pattern.
explanation.B: Correct. It draws a general pattern from three of the examples and is worded carefully enough to remain accurate.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It contrasts two societies' materials instead of making a broad statement that covers several of them.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes the material of a single society, which is one example rather than a generalization.

items.subject: science
notes: Most of the world's coffee comes from two species: arabica and robusta.
Arabica beans contain about 1.2 to 1.5 percent caffeine by weight.
Robusta beans contain about 2.2 to 2.7 percent caffeine by weight.
Arabica plants grow best at higher elevations, while robusta plants tolerate hotter, lower-lying areas.
Caffeine tastes bitter and helps protect coffee plants from insects.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in caffeine content between the two species. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Caffeine, which tastes bitter, helps protect coffee plants such as arabica and robusta from insects.
choices.B: Robusta beans, one of the two main types of coffee, contain about 2.2 to 2.7 percent caffeine by weight.
choices.C: Arabica plants grow best at higher elevations, while robusta plants tolerate hotter, lower-lying areas.
choices.D: With about 2.2 to 2.7 percent caffeine, robusta beans have nearly twice as much as arabica beans do.

explanation.why: The goal is a difference in caffeine, so the sentence must compare the caffeine in both species. Robusta's 2.2 to 2.7 percent is nearly twice arabica's 1.2 to 1.5 percent, and only one choice makes that comparison.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It explains what caffeine does for coffee plants in general; it does not compare the species.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It gives robusta's caffeine content but no figure for arabica, so the reader cannot see a difference.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It contrasts the two species, which makes it tempting, but the difference is in where they grow, not in caffeine.
explanation.D: Correct. It compares the two species directly, showing that robusta has nearly twice as much caffeine.

items.subject: history_social
notes: A karez is an underground channel that carries groundwater by gravity from the foot of a hill to fields and villages.
Karezes have been used for centuries in Balochistan, Pakistan, and in recent decades many of them have dried up.
Hydrologist Saima Kakar wanted to know whether the spread of electric tube wells was linked to the drying up of karezes.
She mapped 60 karezes and recorded how many tube wells had been drilled within two kilometers of each one.
Karezes with more tube wells nearby were far more likely to have dried up.
items.stem: The student wants to present the aim and the method of Kakar's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Kakar wanted to know whether the spread of electric tube wells in Balochistan was linked to the drying up of karezes.
choices.B: To learn whether tube wells were linked to karezes drying up, Kakar mapped 60 karezes and counted the tube wells near each.
choices.C: Kakar mapped 60 karezes, underground channels that carry groundwater by gravity from the foot of a hill to fields.
choices.D: Kakar found that karezes with more tube wells nearby were far more likely to have dried up than other karezes.

explanation.why: The goal needs the aim (what Kakar wanted to learn) and the method (what she did to learn it). One choice opens with her question about tube wells and then describes the mapping and counting.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It states the aim but leaves out the method, so it meets only half the goal.
explanation.B: Correct. "To learn whether tube wells were linked to karezes drying up" is the aim, and mapping 60 karezes and counting nearby tube wells is the method.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It gives part of the method and explains what a karez is, but it never states what Kakar wanted to learn.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It presents the study's finding, which the goal does not ask for.

items.subject: history_social
notes: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz was a poet and scholar born in the mid-1600s in New Spain, in what is now Mexico.
Women were not allowed to attend university in New Spain, so she educated herself largely through reading.
In 1669 she entered a convent, where she continued to study, write, and collect books.
Her writings include poems, plays, and essays.
In a 1691 letter, now known as the Reply to Sister Philothea, she argued that women have the right to study and learn.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize Sor Juana's role as a defender of women's education. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, a poet and scholar from New Spain, wrote poems, plays, and essays.
choices.B: In her 1691 Reply to Sister Philothea, Sor Juana argued that women have the right to study and learn.
choices.C: In 1669, Sor Juana entered a convent, where she continued to study, write, and collect books.
choices.D: Barred as a woman from attending university in New Spain, Sor Juana educated herself largely through reading.

explanation.why: To show Sor Juana as a defender of women's education, the sentence must show her arguing for it, not simply pursuing her own studies. The notes say that in her 1691 letter she argued that women have the right to study and learn.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It lists the kinds of works she wrote without saying anything about women's education.
explanation.B: Correct. It presents her argument, in a named letter, that women have the right to study and learn.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It shows that Sor Juana herself kept studying, not that she defended other women's right to do so.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This is the most tempting choice because it involves women and education, but it describes her own learning, not a defense of women's education.

items.subject: science
notes: Pando is a stand of quaking aspen trees in south-central Utah.
It covers about 43 hectares and contains roughly 47,000 trunks.
Genetic tests show that all of the trunks share the same DNA.
The trunks are connected by a single underground root system.
New trunks sprout from the roots rather than growing from seeds.
Pando is often described as one of the heaviest known living organisms.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize Pando's size while explaining why it is considered a single organism. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Pando is considered a single organism because genetic tests show that all of its trunks share the same DNA and a single root system.
choices.B: In Pando, a stand of quaking aspen in Utah that is often described as one of the heaviest organisms, new trunks sprout from the roots.
choices.C: Spread over some 43 hectares, Pando's 47,000 or so trunks count as one organism because they share the same DNA and one root system.
choices.D: Pando, a stand of quaking aspen trees in south-central Utah, covers about 43 hectares and contains roughly 47,000 separate trunks.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: show how big Pando is and explain why it counts as one organism. The size comes from the area and trunk count; the reason comes from the shared DNA and single root system. Only one choice combines both.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It explains why Pando is one organism but says nothing about its size. This is the closest near miss because it meets the harder half of the goal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It mentions how new trunks grow and repeats a description of Pando's weight, but it does not explain why the trunks form one organism.
explanation.C: Correct. It gives Pando's size (43 hectares, about 47,000 trunks) and the reason it is one organism (shared DNA and one root system).
explanation.D: Incorrect. It conveys Pando's size but never explains why it is considered a single organism.

items.subject: history_social
notes: Before 1840, British letters were usually paid for by the person receiving them, not the sender.
Charges depended on the distance a letter traveled and the number of sheets it contained.
Reformer Rowland Hill proposed a cheap, uniform rate paid in advance by the sender.
In May 1840, Britain issued the Penny Black, the world's first adhesive postage stamp.
With it, a letter weighing up to half an ounce could be sent anywhere in Britain for one penny.
The stamp showed a profile portrait of Queen Victoria.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast how postage was paid in Britain before and after the Penny Black was introduced. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Before 1840, the cost of a British letter depended on how far it traveled and how many sheets it contained, and the receiver usually paid.
choices.B: Rowland Hill proposed a cheap, uniform rate paid in advance, and in 1840 Britain issued the Penny Black, the world's first adhesive stamp.
choices.C: Before 1840, British letters were usually paid for by their receivers; with the Penny Black, senders prepaid one penny for any destination.
choices.D: Issued in May 1840 and bearing a profile of Queen Victoria, the Penny Black was the first adhesive postage stamp in the world.

explanation.why: A contrast between "before" and "after" needs both sides: how postage was paid before 1840 and how it was paid once the Penny Black arrived. The notes give the before (receivers paid, by distance and sheets) and the after (senders prepaid a single penny).
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes only the old system and leaves out what changed with the Penny Black.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It explains where the new system came from but never describes the old system, so there is no contrast.
explanation.C: Correct. It sets the old system (receivers paid) against the new one (senders prepaid one penny for any destination).
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes the stamp itself but says nothing about how postage was paid before or after it.

items.subject: science
notes: In some coastal deserts, fog is common even though rain almost never falls.
Fog collectors are large panels of fine mesh set up on hillsides facing the wind.
As fog drifts through the mesh, tiny droplets cling to the fibers and merge into larger drops.
The drops run down into a gutter and are piped to storage tanks.
In the 1990s, fog collectors supplied drinking water to Chungungo, a fishing village in Chile's Atacama Desert.
items.stem: The student wants to describe what fog collectors are and explain how they gather water. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In some coastal deserts, rain almost never falls, but fog is common enough that it can be turned into drinking water for nearby towns.
choices.B: In the 1990s, fog collectors supplied drinking water to Chungungo, a fishing village in the Atacama Desert of Chile, where rain is rare.
choices.C: Fog collectors, mesh panels set on windy hillsides, gather water as fog droplets cling to the mesh, merge, and drain into a gutter.
choices.D: Fog collectors are large panels of fine mesh that are set up on hillsides facing the wind in coastal deserts where fog is common.

explanation.why: The goal asks for two things: what fog collectors are and how they gather water. The notes supply both: they are mesh panels on windy hillsides, and they work because droplets cling to the mesh, merge, and drain away.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes the conditions that make fog collection useful but never mentions the collectors themselves.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It gives an example of fog collectors in use but does not describe them or explain how they work.
explanation.C: Correct. It identifies fog collectors as mesh panels on windy hillsides and explains the process by which they collect water.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes what fog collectors are but not how they gather water. It meets only half the goal, which makes it the closest near miss.

items.subject: science
notes: Browning of foods during cooking can result from two different chemical processes.
Caramelization is the breakdown of sugars alone when they are strongly heated.
The Maillard reaction takes place between sugars and amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.
The Maillard reaction produces the browned crust of bread and the seared surface of meat.
Caramelization produces the color and flavor of caramel made from heated table sugar.
Both processes speed up greatly at the high temperatures used in baking, roasting, and frying.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference in the substances involved in caramelization and the Maillard reaction. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Whereas caramelization involves sugars alone, the Maillard reaction takes place between sugars and amino acids.
choices.B: The Maillard reaction gives bread its browned crust and meat its seared surface, while caramelization gives caramel its color and flavor.
choices.C: Food can brown during cooking through either of two chemical processes: caramelization or the Maillard reaction.
choices.D: Caramelization and the Maillard reaction, the two processes that brown food, both speed up greatly at high cooking temperatures.

explanation.why: The goal is narrow: a difference in the substances each process involves. The notes say caramelization involves "sugars alone," while the Maillard reaction involves sugars and amino acids. Only one choice contrasts the ingredients of the two reactions.
explanation.A: Correct. It contrasts the substances: sugars alone versus sugars and amino acids.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It does contrast the two processes, but by the foods they produce, not by the substances that react. This is the most tempting choice because it is a real difference, just not the one the goal names.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It names the two processes but does not say how they differ.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It points out a similarity, not a difference.

items.subject: history_social
notes: Mehrgarh is an archaeological site in Balochistan, Pakistan.
People lived there from about 7000 BCE, making it one of the earliest farming settlements in South Asia.
Its inhabitants grew barley and wheat and raised cattle, sheep, and goats.
Molars from burials dated to roughly 9,000 to 7,500 years ago contain small, neatly drilled holes.
Researchers concluded that the holes were made with flint-tipped drills in living people, an early form of dentistry.
items.stem: The student wants to present the dental finding from Mehrgarh and explain its significance. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Mehrgarh, in Balochistan, Pakistan, was settled around 7000 BCE and is one of the earliest farming settlements in South Asia.
choices.B: The early farmers of Mehrgarh grew barley and wheat and raised cattle, sheep, and goats from around 7000 BCE onward.
choices.C: At Mehrgarh, an early farming settlement in Balochistan, molars from burials dated to roughly 9,000 to 7,500 years ago contain small, neatly drilled holes.
choices.D: Small holes drilled into molars from Mehrgarh, roughly 7,500 to 9,000 years old, appear to be an early form of dentistry on living people.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: state the finding (drilled holes in ancient molars) and explain why it matters (it is evidence of early dentistry on living people). Only one choice does both.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes the site's age and importance for farming but says nothing about the dental finding.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It describes the inhabitants' farming, which is unrelated to the dental finding.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It reports the finding accurately but does not say what the holes mean. It is the closest near miss because it covers half the goal.
explanation.D: Correct. It presents the drilled molars and explains their significance as an early form of dentistry.

items.subject: humanities
notes: In the early 1800s, French army officer Charles Barbier developed "night writing," a code of raised dots meant to let soldiers read messages without light.
Barbier's code represented sounds rather than letters and used cells of up to twelve dots.
Louis Braille, a blind student in Paris, encountered the code at about age twelve.
He found that a twelve-dot cell was too large to feel with a single fingertip.
By 1824, Braille had devised a system based on cells of only six dots, each cell representing a letter.
A six-dot cell can be read with one touch of the fingertip.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how Braille's system improved on Barbier's code. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: By 1824, Louis Braille had devised a reading system for blind people based on cells containing only six raised dots.
choices.B: Louis Braille was a blind student in Paris, about twelve years old, when he first encountered Barbier's code of raised dots.
choices.C: Braille cut Barbier's twelve-dot cells to six dots, small enough to read with one fingertip, and had each cell stand for a letter.
choices.D: In the early 1800s, Barbier, a French army officer, created "night writing" so that soldiers could read raised-dot messages without any light.

explanation.why: To explain an improvement, a sentence must show what Braille changed relative to Barbier's code and why the change helped. The notes give the change (twelve dots to six, sounds to letters) and the benefit (a six-dot cell fits under one fingertip).
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes Braille's system but never compares it to Barbier's or says why six dots were better. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It gives background about Braille but does not describe his system at all.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows how Braille changed Barbier's code and why the change made reading easier.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It explains the purpose of Barbier's code but says nothing about Braille's system.

items.subject: humanities
notes: The Ndebele people of South Africa have a long tradition of painting the outside walls of their homes.
The paintings are made by women and feature bold geometric patterns outlined in black.
Early paintings used natural pigments such as clay, ochre, and soot in earthy colors.
From the mid-twentieth century, many painters adopted bright commercial paints in blues, reds, greens, and yellows.
Artist Esther Mahlangu brought the style to international attention, painting murals and, in 1991, a BMW car.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce the Ndebele wall-painting tradition and describe a change in the materials it uses. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Ndebele artist Esther Mahlangu brought her people's painting style to international attention, even painting a BMW car in 1991.
choices.B: The Ndebele of South Africa paint their homes' outer walls, a tradition that has moved from clay, ochre, and soot to commercial paints.
choices.C: Many Ndebele wall painters adopted bright commercial paints in blues, reds, greens, and yellows from the mid-twentieth century on.
choices.D: Ndebele wall paintings, which are made by women, feature bold geometric patterns that are outlined in black.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: introduce the tradition to a reader who does not know it and describe how its materials changed. The key must say who paints what, and must show the shift from natural pigments to commercial paints.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes one artist's fame, not the tradition's materials.
explanation.B: Correct. It introduces the tradition (the Ndebele paint their outer walls) and describes the shift from natural pigments to commercial paints.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It mentions the newer paints but does not introduce the tradition or say what the paints replaced. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes the paintings' look but says nothing about a change in materials.

items.subject: literature
notes: Arthur Conan Doyle studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh in the late 1870s.
One of his teachers there, the surgeon Joseph Bell, was known for deducing details of patients' lives from small observations.
Doyle later said that Bell was an important model for Sherlock Holmes.
Holmes first appeared in the novel A Study in Scarlet, published in 1887.
In that novel, Holmes deduces on first meeting that Dr. Watson has recently been in Afghanistan.
items.stem: The student wants to explain the connection between Doyle's medical training and the character of Sherlock Holmes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Sherlock Holmes first appeared in A Study in Scarlet (1887), in which he deduces on first meeting that Watson has been in Afghanistan.
choices.B: Before he created Holmes, Arthur Conan Doyle studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh in the late 1870s.
choices.C: Joseph Bell, a surgeon at Edinburgh, was known among his students for deducing details of patients' lives from small observations.
choices.D: Doyle modeled Holmes partly on Joseph Bell, his Edinburgh teacher, who deduced details of patients' lives from small observations.

explanation.why: To connect Doyle's medical training to Holmes, the sentence must link three things: Doyle's teacher at medical school, the teacher's deductive habit, and the character modeled on him. Only one choice draws that line.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes Holmes's first appearance and a famous deduction but never mentions Doyle's training.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It mentions Doyle's medical training but does not connect it to Holmes.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It describes Bell's skill but does not connect Bell to Doyle or to Holmes. This is the most tempting near miss.
explanation.D: Correct. It links Doyle's Edinburgh teacher, Bell, and his observational skill to the creation of Holmes.

items.subject: humanities
notes: In Hindustani classical music, a raga is a melodic framework that sets out the notes and characteristic phrases a musician uses to improvise.
Many ragas are traditionally linked with particular times of day.
Raga Bhairav is associated with early morning.
Raga Yaman is associated with the evening hours.
Some musicians hold that a raga's mood is strongest when it is performed at its proper time.
Modern concerts and recordings often present ragas without regard to their traditional times.
items.stem: The student wants to present the tradition of linking ragas to times of day and note how modern practice departs from it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: A raga, in Hindustani classical music, is a melodic framework that sets out the notes and phrases a musician uses to improvise.
choices.B: In Hindustani classical music, Raga Bhairav is associated with early morning, while Raga Yaman is associated with the evening hours.
choices.C: Ragas such as Bhairav and Yaman are traditionally tied to morning and evening, but modern concerts and recordings often ignore such times.
choices.D: Some musicians hold that a raga's mood is strongest when it is performed at the time of day with which it is traditionally linked.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: present the time-of-day tradition and show how modern practice departs from it. The notes give examples of the tradition (Bhairav, Yaman) and the departure (modern concerts and recordings ignore the times).
explanation.A: Incorrect. It defines a raga but never mentions times of day.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It illustrates the tradition but says nothing about modern practice. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.C: Correct. It presents the tradition with two examples and then states how modern practice departs from it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It explains why some musicians value the tradition but does not mention any departure from it.

items.subject: science
notes: Each year, winds carry millions of tons of dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic Ocean.
Much of the dust comes from the Bodélé Depression, a dry lakebed in Chad.
Some of the dust settles on the Amazon rainforest in South America.
The dust contains phosphorus, a nutrient that plants need to grow.
Heavy rains continually wash phosphorus out of the Amazon's soils.
Scientists estimate that the phosphorus delivered in Saharan dust roughly makes up for the amount lost.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why the Amazon rainforest needs phosphorus from elsewhere and how Saharan dust supplies it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Saharan dust that settles on the Amazon contains phosphorus, a nutrient plants need, in roughly the amount the rainforest loses.
choices.B: Because heavy rains wash phosphorus from Amazon soils, the rainforest relies on wind-borne Saharan dust to bring in the nutrient.
choices.C: Each year, winds carry millions of tons of dust from the Sahara, much of it from a dry lakebed in Chad, across the Atlantic Ocean.
choices.D: Heavy rains in the Amazon continually wash phosphorus, a nutrient that plants need in order to grow, out of the rainforest's soils.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: why the Amazon needs outside phosphorus (rain washes it from the soil) and how the Sahara supplies it (wind-borne dust carries it). Only one choice links the cause of the shortage to the source of the supply.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It explains how the dust supplies phosphorus but not why the Amazon needs it from elsewhere; "the amount the rainforest loses" is mentioned without saying how it is lost. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.B: Correct. It explains the shortage (rain washes phosphorus away) and the remedy (Saharan dust brings it in).
explanation.C: Incorrect. It describes the dust's journey but does not mention phosphorus or why the Amazon needs it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It explains why phosphorus is lost but never mentions Saharan dust.

items.subject: science
notes: Bare-nosed wombats, burrowing marsupials of Australia, produce droppings shaped like cubes.
A wombat can deposit 80 to 100 of these cubes each night.
Wombats often leave their droppings on rocks and logs, possibly as signals to other wombats.
Researchers found that the cubes take shape in the last part of the intestine.
There, the intestinal wall has regions of differing stiffness that mold the droppings into flat sides and corners.
items.stem: The student wants to describe what is unusual about wombat droppings and explain how they get that way. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The intestinal wall of the bare-nosed wombat has regions of differing stiffness that mold its droppings into flat sides and corners.
choices.B: Bare-nosed wombats often leave their droppings on rocks and logs, possibly as a way of sending signals to other wombats.
choices.C: Wombat droppings are cube-shaped, a form molded in the last part of the intestine by walls whose regions differ in stiffness.
choices.D: Bare-nosed wombats, burrowing marsupials of Australia, produce droppings shaped like cubes, depositing 80 to 100 each night.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: what is unusual (the droppings are cubes) and how that shape forms (regions of differing stiffness in the last part of the intestine). Only one choice gives both.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It explains the mechanism, and "flat sides and corners" hints at a cube, but it never says plainly that the droppings are cube-shaped. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It explains a possible use for the droppings but does not say what is unusual about them or how they form.
explanation.C: Correct. It states the unusual shape and explains how the intestine produces it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes the unusual shape but not how it forms.

items.subject: humanities
notes: Sashiko is a style of hand stitching that developed in rural Japan during the Edo period (1603–1868).
Farming and fishing families used rows of small running stitches to layer and reinforce worn cloth.
The stitching made garments warmer and helped them last longer.
Sashiko was usually done in white cotton thread on cloth dyed with indigo.
Over time, stitchers developed many decorative geometric patterns, such as overlapping circles and waves.
Today, sashiko is popular worldwide as a way of mending clothes visibly.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize that sashiko began as a practical technique but also became decorative. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Sashiko, which developed in rural Japan during the Edo period, is popular worldwide today as a way of mending clothes visibly.
choices.B: In rural Japan, families used sashiko's rows of small running stitches to layer and reinforce worn cloth, making garments warmer.
choices.C: Developed to reinforce worn cloth in rural Japan, sashiko stitching came to feature decorative patterns such as circles and waves.
choices.D: Sashiko, a style of stitching from Edo-period Japan, was usually done in white cotton thread on cloth that had been dyed with indigo.

explanation.why: The goal sets up a contrast between the technique's practical origin and its later decorative role. The notes give the origin (reinforcing worn cloth) and the later development (decorative geometric patterns).
explanation.A: Incorrect. It notes sashiko's origin and modern popularity but says nothing about its practical purpose becoming decorative.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It describes only the practical side of sashiko and leaves out its decorative patterns. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.C: Correct. It names the practical origin (reinforcing worn cloth) and the decorative development (patterns such as circles and waves).
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes the colors of thread and cloth but not the technique's purpose or its patterns.

items.subject: history_social
notes: The cog was the main type of cargo ship used by merchants of the Hanseatic League, a network of trading towns in northern Europe.
Cogs had flat bottoms, high sides, and a single square sail.
Historians knew about cogs mainly from images on town seals and from written records.
In 1962, workers dredging the Weser River in Bremen, Germany, uncovered the remains of a cog.
Tree-ring dating showed that the ship was built around 1380.
The Bremen cog is among the best-preserved cogs ever found.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why the 1962 discovery was valuable to historians. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Cogs, the main cargo ships of the Hanseatic League's network of trading towns in northern Europe, had flat bottoms, high sides, and a single square sail.
choices.B: Historians, who had known cogs mainly from town seals and written records, gained a well-preserved example in the Bremen cog of 1962.
choices.C: In 1962, workers dredging the Weser River in Bremen uncovered the remains of a cog that was built around 1380.
choices.D: The Hanseatic League, a network of trading towns in northern Europe, relied on cogs as the main type of cargo ship.

explanation.why: To show why the find was valuable, a sentence must contrast what historians had before (images on seals and written records) with what the discovery gave them (a well-preserved actual ship). Only one choice makes that comparison.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes what cogs looked like but says nothing about the discovery.
explanation.B: Correct. It shows that the find gave historians an actual, well-preserved ship where before they had only seals and records.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It reports the discovery accurately but does not explain why it mattered. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It explains what cogs were used for but does not mention the discovery.

items.subject: literature
notes: In June 1816, Mary Godwin (later Mary Shelley) was staying near Lake Geneva in Switzerland with Percy Shelley, Lord Byron, and others.
Cold, stormy weather kept the group indoors for days.
Byron proposed that each of them write a ghost story.
Mary's contribution grew into the novel Frankenstein.
Frankenstein was first published, anonymously, in January 1818.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how Frankenstein began and when it was first published. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In June 1816, cold and stormy weather kept Mary Godwin, Percy Shelley, Lord Byron, and others indoors near Lake Geneva for days.
choices.B: While staying near Lake Geneva in 1816, Lord Byron proposed that each member of his group write a ghost story.
choices.C: Frankenstein was first published in January 1818, without the name of its author, Mary Shelley, appearing on it.
choices.D: Frankenstein, first published in January 1818, grew out of a ghost-story challenge Byron set near Lake Geneva in 1816.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: how the novel began (as Mary's entry in Byron's ghost-story challenge) and when it was first published (January 1818). Only one choice gives both.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It sets the scene for the novel's origin but never mentions the ghost-story challenge, the novel, or its publication.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It describes the challenge but does not connect it to Frankenstein or give a publication date. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It gives the publication date but does not explain how the novel began.
explanation.D: Correct. It explains the novel's origin in Byron's challenge and gives its first publication date.

items.subject: humanities
notes: The Lahore Fort, in Pakistan, contains a wall known as the Picture Wall.
The wall stretches for about 450 meters along the fort's northern and western sides.
It was begun under the Mughal emperor Jahangir and completed in 1632, during the reign of Shah Jahan.
It is decorated with tile mosaics showing elephant fights, polo matches, angels, and other scenes.
It is considered one of the largest murals in the world.
Conservation work begun in the 2010s has restored parts of the wall.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize both the size of the Picture Wall and the variety of its subjects. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Stretching about 450 meters, the Picture Wall depicts subjects ranging from elephant fights and polo matches to angels.
choices.B: Considered one of the largest murals in the world, the Picture Wall of the Lahore Fort stretches for about 450 meters.
choices.C: The Picture Wall in Pakistan's Lahore Fort is decorated with tile mosaics showing elephant fights, polo matches, and angels.
choices.D: Begun under Jahangir and completed in 1632 under Shah Jahan, the Picture Wall of the Lahore Fort has recently been partly restored.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: the wall's size and the variety of what it shows. The notes give the size (about 450 meters) and a range of subjects (elephant fights, polo matches, angels). Only one choice includes both.
explanation.A: Correct. It gives the wall's length and a range of very different subjects.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It stresses the wall's size twice over but says nothing about its subjects. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It shows the variety of subjects but leaves out the wall's size.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It gives the wall's history and conservation, not its size or subjects.

items.subject: science
notes: Sprites are brief flashes of red light that occur high above large thunderstorms.
They appear about 50 to 90 kilometers above the ground, far above the clouds that produce lightning.
Each sprite lasts only a few thousandths of a second.
For decades, airline pilots occasionally reported seeing flashes above storms, but scientists had no images to confirm the reports.
In 1989, researchers from the University of Minnesota were testing a low-light camera and accidentally recorded a sprite.
Since then, sprites have been photographed thousands of times, including from the International Space Station.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why sprites long went unconfirmed and how they were finally documented. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Sprites, red flashes that last only thousandths of a second, appear 50 to 90 kilometers up, far above the clouds that produce lightning.
choices.B: Pilots' reports of the brief flashes long went unconfirmed because no one had images of them, until a 1989 camera test happened to record a sprite.
choices.C: Pilots reported flashes above storms for decades, but without images to support those reports, scientists could not confirm that sprites existed.
choices.D: Since a camera test by University of Minnesota researchers first captured one in 1989, sprites have been photographed thousands of times, even from space.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: the reason sprites went unconfirmed (they are extremely brief and occur far above the clouds) and how they were finally documented (a 1989 camera test captured one by accident). Only one choice joins the reason to the resolution.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It gives the facts that explain why sprites are hard to see, but it does not connect them to the lack of confirmation or say how sprites were documented.
explanation.B: Correct. It gives both parts of the goal from the notes: why sprites went unconfirmed (reports but no images) and how they were finally documented (a 1989 camera test that accidentally recorded one).
explanation.C: Incorrect. It shows that sprites went unconfirmed but not why, and it never says how they were finally documented. This is tempting because it describes the long gap in evidence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It explains how sprites came to be documented and photographed but gives no reason they had gone unconfirmed for so long.

items.subject: history_social
notes: The Sogdians, from a region around Samarkand in Central Asia, were among the most active merchants on the Silk Road.
In 1907, the archaeologist Aurel Stein found a bundle of letters in a ruined watchtower west of Dunhuang, in China.
The letters, written in the Sogdian language, date to the early fourth century CE.
They were never delivered; they may have been lost or seized on their way.
The letters mention trade in goods such as silk, musk, and silver and refer to Sogdian merchants based in several Chinese cities.
One letter, from a woman named Miwnay, complains that her husband left her stranded in Dunhuang.
items.stem: The student wants to describe how the letters were found and indicate what they reveal about Sogdian trade. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Written in the Sogdian language in the early fourth century CE, the letters were never delivered and were found by Aurel Stein in 1907 in a ruined watchtower west of Dunhuang.
choices.B: Found by Aurel Stein in a watchtower near Dunhuang in 1907, the undelivered letters refer to Sogdian merchants in several Chinese cities trading silk, musk, and silver.
choices.C: The letters, which mention trade in silk, musk, and silver, show that Sogdian merchants were based in several Chinese cities in the early fourth century CE.
choices.D: Among the letters that Aurel Stein found near Dunhuang in 1907 is one from a woman named Miwnay, who complains that her husband left her stranded there.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: how the letters were found (by Stein, in a watchtower near Dunhuang, in 1907) and what they reveal about trade (goods such as silk, musk, and silver, and merchants based in Chinese cities). Only one choice covers both.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It describes the discovery in detail but says nothing about trade. This is a strong near miss because it is the most complete account of how the letters were found.
explanation.B: Correct. It explains the discovery and shows what the letters reveal about Sogdian trade.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It shows what the letters reveal about trade but not how they were found.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes the discovery but highlights a personal complaint rather than anything about trade.

items.subject: history_social
notes: Babylonian scribes used a symbol to mark an empty place in numbers but did not treat it as a number in its own right.
The Maya also developed a symbol for zero, which they used in their calendars.
In 628 CE, the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta completed the Brahmasphutasiddhanta.
In it, he treated zero as a number in its own right, giving rules such as that a number minus itself equals zero.
He also set out rules for working with negative numbers, which he called "debts."
Some of his rules, such as those for dividing by zero, differ from those that mathematicians accept today.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize how Brahmagupta's treatment of zero differed from an earlier use of a zero symbol. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Both the Babylonians and the Maya developed symbols for zero, the Babylonians to mark empty places in numbers and the Maya for their calendars.
choices.B: In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE), Brahmagupta gave rules for calculating with zero, such as that a number minus itself equals zero.
choices.C: Brahmagupta's work set out rules for zero and for negative numbers, though some, such as those for dividing by zero, differ from today's.
choices.D: Where Babylonian scribes used a zero symbol only to mark an empty place, Brahmagupta treated zero as a number with its own rules.

explanation.why: To show a difference, the sentence must set Brahmagupta's approach against an earlier one. The Babylonians used a zero symbol only as a placeholder, while Brahmagupta treated zero as a number and gave rules for calculating with it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It compares two earlier uses of a zero symbol but never mentions Brahmagupta.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It describes Brahmagupta's treatment of zero accurately but does not compare it with any earlier use. This is the most attractive near miss because it includes the key detail about calculating with zero.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It notes how some of Brahmagupta's rules differ from modern ones, which is a different comparison from the one the goal asks for.
explanation.D: Correct. It contrasts the Babylonians' placeholder symbol with Brahmagupta's treatment of zero as a number.

items.subject: literature
notes: The Tale of Genji was written in the early eleventh century by Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese imperial court.
It follows the life and romances of Hikaru Genji, the son of an emperor, across more than fifty chapters.
It is often called the world's first novel.
Scholars who question that label point out that long works of prose fiction existed earlier, such as the ancient Greek romances.
Other scholars defend the label, citing the work's psychological depth and its attention to characters' inner lives.
items.stem: The student wants to present the claim that the Tale of Genji is the first novel while acknowledging a reason to doubt it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Written by Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Japanese court, the Tale of Genji follows Hikaru Genji across more than fifty chapters.
choices.B: The Tale of Genji is often called the first novel, though some scholars note that earlier prose fictions, such as the Greek romances, existed.
choices.C: Often called the world's first novel, the Tale of Genji is valued by many scholars for its psychological depth and its attention to inner lives.
choices.D: Long works of prose fiction, such as the ancient Greek romances, were written centuries before Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: state the "first novel" claim and acknowledge a reason to doubt it. The notes supply the doubt: long prose fictions such as the Greek romances came earlier.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It summarizes the work and its author but does not mention the "first novel" claim.
explanation.B: Correct. It states the claim and then acknowledges the earlier prose fictions that cast doubt on it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It presents the claim but follows it with a reason to accept it, not a reason to doubt it. This is the most attractive near miss because it also cites scholars.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It gives the reason for doubt but never states the claim it casts doubt on.

items.subject: literature
notes: Premchand (1880–1936) is one of the most celebrated writers of modern Hindi and Urdu fiction.
He was born Dhanpat Rai and first published his stories in Urdu under the name Nawab Rai.
In 1908, he published Soz-e-Watan, a collection of patriotic Urdu stories.
British colonial authorities banned the collection, and copies of it were burned.
Afterward, he began publishing under the new pen name Premchand.
His later works, such as the novel Godaan (1936), portray the hardships of village life.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how the writer came to use the name Premchand, including the name he had published under before. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Born Dhanpat Rai, the writer now celebrated as Premchand first published his stories in Urdu under the name Nawab Rai.
choices.B: Premchand, born Dhanpat Rai, became one of the most celebrated writers of Hindi and Urdu fiction, known for works such as Godaan.
choices.C: After British authorities banned and burned Soz-e-Watan, a 1908 collection of patriotic Urdu stories, its author's works were published under a new name.
choices.D: Once British authorities banned Soz-e-Watan, the patriotic stories he had published as Nawab Rai, the writer adopted the pen name Premchand.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: the name he used before and the reason he came to use "Premchand." The notes connect them: the stories he had published as Nawab Rai were banned, and afterward he adopted the new pen name.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It gives his earlier pen name but does not explain why he changed it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It gives his birth name and later fame, not how he came to use the name Premchand.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It explains the cause of the change but never says what the old or the new name was. This is the most attractive near miss because it tells the key event in detail.
explanation.D: Correct. It names the earlier pen name (Nawab Rai), the event that led to the change (the ban on Soz-e-Watan), and the new name.

items.subject: humanities
notes: In 1887, L. L. Zamenhof published the first book describing Esperanto, a language he had constructed.
Zamenhof hoped that Esperanto would become a universal second language, easing communication between peoples.
Esperanto's grammar is highly regular; for example, every verb follows the same pattern of endings.
No country has adopted Esperanto as an official language.
Estimates of the number of people who speak it today range from tens of thousands to about two million.
A small number of people have learned Esperanto from birth as the children of Esperanto-speaking parents.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast Zamenhof's hopes for Esperanto with the language's actual reach. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Since Zamenhof first described it in 1887, Esperanto has gained speakers whose number is estimated at anywhere from tens of thousands to about two million.
choices.B: Zamenhof hoped Esperanto would become a universal second language, and he gave it a highly regular grammar in which every verb follows the same endings.
choices.C: Although no country has adopted Esperanto as an official language, a small number of people have learned it from birth from Esperanto-speaking parents.
choices.D: Zamenhof hoped Esperanto would be a universal second language, but no country has made it official, and estimates of its speakers top out near two million.

explanation.why: A contrast needs both sides: Zamenhof's hope (a universal second language) and the language's limited reality (no official status and, at most, about two million speakers). Only one choice sets the two against each other.
explanation.A: Incorrect. It gives the number of speakers but not Zamenhof's hope, so the reader cannot see how far short of it the language fell. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It states the hope but follows it with a feature of the grammar rather than the language's actual reach.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It describes the language's reach in two ways but never mentions Zamenhof's hopes, so there is nothing to contrast with.
explanation.D: Correct. It sets Zamenhof's hope for a universal language against Esperanto's limited official status and number of speakers.

items.subject: history_social
notes: The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed in May 1869 at Promontory Summit, Utah.
The Central Pacific Railroad built the line eastward from Sacramento, California, through the Sierra Nevada.
At the peak of construction, Chinese immigrants made up as much as 90 percent of the Central Pacific's workforce.
They blasted tunnels through granite and worked through severe mountain winters.
In the best-known photograph of the completion ceremony, no Chinese workers can be identified.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the contrast between Chinese workers' contribution to the railroad and their absence from the way its completion was recorded. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Chinese immigrants, as much as 90 percent of the Central Pacific's workforce at its peak, blasted tunnels through granite and worked through harsh winters.
choices.B: Building eastward from Sacramento through the Sierra Nevada, the Central Pacific met its partner line at Promontory Summit, Utah, in May 1869.
choices.C: The best-known photograph of the 1869 ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah, which marked the railroad's completion, shows no identifiable Chinese workers.
choices.D: Although Chinese immigrants made up as much as 90 percent of the Central Pacific's workforce, none can be identified in the best-known photo of its completion.

explanation.why: The goal requires both sides of a contrast: how much Chinese workers contributed (as much as 90 percent of the workforce) and how they were left out of the record (absent from the best-known photograph). Only one choice joins the two with "Although."
explanation.A: Incorrect. It emphasizes the workers' contribution but says nothing about their absence from the record.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It describes the railroad's route and completion without mentioning the Chinese workers at all.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It describes the absence from the photograph but not the scale of the workers' contribution, so the contrast is lost.
explanation.D: Correct. It sets the workers' large share of the workforce against their absence from the best-known photograph.

items.subject: literature
notes: Miguel de Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote in 1605.
The novel follows an aging gentleman who reads so many tales of chivalry that he sets out to become a knight himself.
In 1614, before Cervantes had finished his own sequel, a writer calling himself Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda published an unauthorized second part.
The true identity of "Avellaneda" remains unknown.
In his own second part, published in 1615, Cervantes has characters mock the false sequel.
He also has Don Quixote change his travel plans in order to avoid the events the false sequel describes.
items.stem: The student wants to describe the unauthorized sequel and explain how Cervantes responded to it in his own second part. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Cervantes answered Avellaneda's unauthorized 1614 sequel in his own 1615 second part, in which characters mock it and Quixote changes plans to avoid its events.
choices.B: In 1614, before Cervantes finished his own sequel, a writer calling himself Avellaneda, whose true identity is still unknown, published an unauthorized second part.
choices.C: Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote, about a gentleman who reads so many tales of chivalry that he sets out to become a knight, in 1605.
choices.D: In Cervantes's own second part of Don Quixote (1615), characters mock a false sequel, and Don Quixote changes his plans to avoid the events it describes.

explanation.why: The goal has two parts: identify the unauthorized sequel (Avellaneda's 1614 second part) and explain Cervantes's response within his own 1615 second part (mockery and a change in Quixote's route). Only one choice does both.
explanation.A: Correct. It identifies the unauthorized sequel and explains both ways Cervantes answered it in his 1615 second part.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It describes the unauthorized sequel but says nothing about how Cervantes responded.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It describes the first part of the novel, which has nothing to do with the sequel.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It describes Cervantes's response but refers only vaguely to "a false sequel" without saying who wrote it, when, or that it was unauthorized. This is the most attractive near miss.

items.subject: science
notes: Fast radio bursts are flashes of radio waves that last only a few thousandths of a second.
The first was identified in 2007, in data that a radio telescope had recorded in 2001.
Most bursts come from galaxies far beyond our own, which has made their sources hard to identify.
Astronomers proposed many possible sources, including magnetars, the dense, highly magnetic remains of dead stars.
In April 2020, telescopes detected a fast radio burst coming from a known magnetar in our own galaxy.
It was the first time a fast radio burst had been traced to a known object.
items.stem: The student wants to present the 2020 detection as evidence for one proposed explanation of fast radio bursts. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Magnetars had been proposed as one possible source of fast radio bursts, and in 2020 a burst was detected coming from a known magnetar in our galaxy.
choices.B: In April 2020, for the first time, telescopes traced a fast radio burst to a known object, a finding that came thirteen years after the first burst was identified.
choices.C: The first fast radio burst was identified in 2007, in data that a radio telescope had recorded six years earlier, in 2001.
choices.D: Because most fast radio bursts come from galaxies far beyond our own, astronomers have found it hard to identify their sources and have proposed many possibilities.

explanation.why: To present the detection as evidence for an explanation, the sentence must name the explanation (magnetars as a proposed source) and show that the 2020 burst came from a magnetar. Only one choice links the observation to the hypothesis it supports.
explanation.A: Correct. It names magnetars as a proposed source and reports a burst traced to a known magnetar, so the detection reads as evidence for that idea.
explanation.B: Incorrect. It reports the 2020 detection but never says what kind of object produced the burst or which explanation it supports. This is the most attractive near miss because it stresses that the detection was a first.
explanation.C: Incorrect. It gives the history of the first detection, not the 2020 evidence.
explanation.D: Incorrect. It explains why the sources were hard to identify but does not mention the 2020 detection.

items.subject: science
notes: When a drop of water lands on a pan only slightly hotter than water's boiling point, it spreads out and boils away within seconds.
On a much hotter pan, above roughly 200 °C, a drop can instead skitter across the surface and last for a minute or more.
This is called the Leidenfrost effect, after the German doctor Johann Gottlob Leidenfrost, who described it in 1756.
