items.passage: For thousands of years, Aboriginal peoples of Australia's Western Desert created designs in sand, on rock, and on their bodies, often for ceremonies. In 1971, at the settlement of Papunya, a group of senior men began painting such designs with acrylic paint on boards and, later, on canvas. <u>Because these works could be moved, sold, and exhibited, they carried Western Desert imagery far beyond the communities where it had been made.</u> Within two decades, paintings in this style hung in major museums, though some artists took care to alter or hide designs considered too sacred for outsiders to see.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It explains a consequence of the change in materials described just before it.
choices.B: It describes the ceremonies for which the earliest desert designs were originally made.
choices.C: It explains why some artists hid certain designs from outside viewers.
choices.D: It argues that the new paintings were less meaningful than the older designs.

explanation.why: The sentence before the underlined one describes a change: designs once made in sand, on rock, and on bodies were now painted on boards and canvas. The underlined sentence begins "Because these works could be moved, sold, and exhibited," and tells what followed from that change: the imagery spread far beyond its home communities.
explanation.A: Correct. Portable paintings could travel, so the sentence explains how the new materials carried the imagery to distant audiences.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the older designs were often made for ceremonies but never describes those ceremonies.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Hiding sacred designs is mentioned only in the last sentence; the underlined sentence is about how the paintings spread, not about concealment.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never judges the new paintings as less meaningful; this claims far more than it says.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sea otters along the Pacific coast of North America eat large amounts of hard-shelled prey such as clams, mussels, and snails. Many otters crack these shells by floating on their backs, placing a flat rock on their chests, and pounding the prey against it. Not every otter uses tools equally, however. Researchers in California have found that females are more likely than males to use rocks, and that tool users can eat harder prey while suffering less damage to their teeth. Tool use, it appears, helps otters make the most of foods that would otherwise be difficult to eat.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe a sea otter behavior and explain how it benefits the otters that use it
choices.B: To explain why sea otters prefer hard-shelled prey to all other kinds of food
choices.C: To argue that tool use is the main reason sea otters survive along the Pacific coast
choices.D: To report that female sea otters use rocks as tools more often than males do

explanation.why: The text first describes how otters use rocks to open shells, then reports what researchers found about which otters use tools and how it helps them. The last sentence sums up the point: tool use "helps otters make the most of foods that would otherwise be difficult to eat." The text describes a behavior and explains its benefit.
explanation.A: Correct. The text describes otters cracking shells with rocks and explains that tool users can eat harder prey with less damage to their teeth.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says otters eat hard-shelled prey but never says they prefer it to other foods or explains such a preference.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says tool use helps otters eat difficult foods; it never claims tool use explains the species' survival.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This finding is mentioned, but it is only one detail in a text about how and why otters use tools.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Aristotelian cosmology held that the heavens beyond the Moon were perfect and unchanging, so any novelty in the sky, such as a comet, was assumed to occur in the air below the Moon. When a brilliant new star appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia in November 1572, the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe set out to determine where it was. <u>Measuring its position night after night, he found that it showed no parallax, the slight shift against the background stars that an object as near as the Moon displays over the course of a night.</u> The star, he concluded, lay far beyond the Moon, in the very region that was supposed never to change.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It reports the observation behind a conclusion that defied a traditional view.
choices.B: It describes a difficulty that kept Tycho from determining the new star's location.
choices.C: It explains why comets had been placed in the region of the air below the Moon.
choices.D: It states the assumption that Tycho's measurements were intended to confirm.

explanation.why: The first sentence gives the traditional view that the heavens beyond the Moon never change. The underlined sentence reports Tycho's measurement that the new star showed no parallax, and the final sentence draws the conclusion: the star lay "far beyond the Moon," in the region that was "supposed never to change." The underlined sentence supplies the observation behind a conclusion that contradicts the traditional view.
explanation.A: Correct. The lack of parallax showed the star was beyond the Moon, where, according to Aristotelian cosmology, nothing new should appear.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Finding no parallax is what allowed Tycho to locate the star far beyond the Moon; it was not an obstacle.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The reason comets were placed below the Moon is given in the first sentence; the underlined sentence concerns the new star of 1572.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The underlined sentence reports a measurement, not an assumption; and the measurement led Tycho to contradict the traditional view, not confirm it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Beginning in the late nineteenth century, an expanding network of canals turned large parts of the Punjab plain, in what is now Pakistan, into productive farmland. The canals, however, lost much of their water through seepage into the ground, and over the following decades the water table beneath many irrigated districts rose steadily. Where it came within a few feet of the surface, fields became waterlogged, and as the water evaporated it left behind crusts of salt that made the soil unfit for crops. In the 1960s, Pakistan launched the Salinity Control and Reclamation Projects, which installed thousands of tubewells to pump out groundwater and lower the water table in affected areas.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes a problem, evaluates several solutions that failed, and concludes that the problem remains unsolved today.
choices.B: It presents two competing explanations for a problem in a farming region and then argues in favor of one of them.
choices.C: It describes a beneficial development, a problem it caused, and a measure taken in response.
choices.D: It traces the history of a farming region from its earliest settlement up to the present day.

explanation.why: The text begins with a benefit (canals created "productive farmland"), turns with "however" to a problem the canals caused (seepage, a rising water table, waterlogging, and salt), and ends with the response (tubewells to "lower the water table"). The structure is benefit, resulting problem, remedy.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Only one response is described, and the text does not say whether it failed or whether the problem continues.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text gives only one cause for the waterlogging, seepage from canals, and does not weigh rival explanations.
explanation.C: Correct. The canals brought farmland, their seepage caused waterlogging and salt, and the tubewell projects were the response.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text covers one development and its consequences from the late 1800s to the 1960s, not the whole history of the region.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In 1925, Herbert Bayer, a young teacher at the Bauhaus school of design in Germany, proposed an alphabet with no capital letters at all. His reasoning was practical as much as aesthetic. German, which capitalizes every noun, required writers, typesetters, and typewriter makers to manage two complete sets of letters, and Bayer argued that a single set of simple, geometric forms would save time and effort while reading just as clearly. The Bauhaus adopted lowercase-only printing for its own publications, but the idea never spread far beyond such circles; the habit of capitals proved far more durable than Bayer had hoped.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that German writers should give up the practice of capitalizing every noun
choices.B: To explain the reasoning behind a design proposal and note its limited influence
choices.C: To show how the Bauhaus persuaded printers across Germany to stop using capital letters
choices.D: To describe the geometric shapes that Bayer chose for each letter of his alphabet

explanation.why: Most of the text explains Bayer's proposal and the practical reasons behind it, such as the burden of "two complete sets of letters." The last sentence notes that the idea "never spread far beyond" the Bauhaus. The text explains the reasoning behind a proposal and notes its limited influence.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text reports Bayer's argument but does not itself argue for the change; it notes that the idea failed to spread.
explanation.B: Correct. The text sets out why Bayer wanted a lowercase-only alphabet and then says the idea did not spread widely.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says the idea "never spread far beyond such circles," so the Bauhaus did not persuade printers generally.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text mentions "simple, geometric forms" only in passing and never describes the individual letters.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: All through June, Maren fought the oars. She pulled too hard with her right arm, and the little boat swung in lazy circles while her uncle watched from the dock, saying nothing. She slapped the water, splashed herself, and twice lost an oar entirely. <u>Then one still evening in July, without quite knowing when it had happened, she noticed that the dock had grown small behind her and the boat was gliding straight across the bay.</u> She let the oars rest, listened to the water dripping from their blades, and found that she did not want to turn back.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It shows that Maren's uncle has finally decided to give her instructions on how to row.
choices.B: It marks the moment Maren's struggles give way to a skill she had gained unnoticed.
choices.C: It explains why Maren had been pulling much harder with one arm than with the other.
choices.D: It reveals that Maren has grown tired of rowing and wants to return to the dock.

explanation.why: Before the underlined sentence, Maren struggles: the boat "swung in lazy circles," and she lost an oar twice. The underlined sentence, introduced by "Then," shows the boat "gliding straight," and she realizes this "without quite knowing when it had happened." It marks the turn from struggle to a skill she gained without noticing.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The uncle is never shown giving instructions; the underlined sentence does not mention him at all.
explanation.B: Correct. The sentence shifts from her clumsy June to a moment when she finds the boat moving straight, a change she had not noticed happening.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The underlined sentence describes her success in July; it gives no reason for her earlier uneven rowing.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The final sentence says she "did not want to turn back," the opposite of wanting to return.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Since it was first observed in 1996, devil facial tumor disease has spread across most of Tasmania, killing the great majority of infected Tasmanian devils. The disease is unusual in that the cancer cells themselves are contagious, passing from one devil to another through bites. For years, many researchers expected the species to disappear from the wild. More recent genetic studies, however, have found that in several affected populations, gene variants associated with immune function became more common within only a few generations, suggesting that devils may be evolving some resistance. The researchers caution that such changes are no guarantee of recovery, since the tumors themselves continue to evolve as well.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain how the cancer cells that cause the disease pass from one Tasmanian devil to another
choices.B: To report evidence that a species may be adapting to a disease and note a caution
choices.C: To criticize earlier researchers for wrongly predicting that the species would soon become extinct
choices.D: To argue that devil facial tumor disease no longer poses a serious threat to Tasmanian devils

explanation.why: After describing the disease and the fear of extinction, the text turns with "however" to genetic evidence that devils "may be evolving some resistance." The final sentence adds a limit: these changes are "no guarantee of recovery." The text presents a hopeful finding and qualifies it.
explanation.A: Incorrect. How the disease spreads is a single detail; the text's focus is on evidence that devils may be adapting.
explanation.B: Correct. The text presents genetic evidence of possible resistance and then cautions that recovery is not guaranteed.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text mentions the earlier expectation but does not criticize anyone, and it does not say the prediction has been proved wrong.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the changes are "no guarantee of recovery," so it does not claim the threat has passed.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1580s, the Mughal emperor Akbar commissioned a Persian translation of the Mahabharata, the vast Sanskrit epic, which became known as the Razmnama, or "Book of War." Sanskrit scholars explained the text aloud, Persian writers rendered it into polished prose, and court painters produced lavishly illustrated copies. The project is often cited as evidence of Akbar's curiosity about the religious traditions of his subjects. <u>Some historians add that it also served a political purpose, presenting an Indian epic of kingship to the Persian-speaking nobility in the language of the court.</u> The two explanations are not exclusive: a single manuscript could satisfy an emperor's curiosity and advance his authority at once.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It rejects the common view that the project reflected Akbar's curiosity about his subjects.
choices.B: It describes the method that scholars and writers used to produce the translation.
choices.C: It explains why the Persian version of the epic was given the title "Book of War."
choices.D: It introduces an additional motive for a project beyond the one that is commonly cited.

explanation.why: The sentence before the underlined one gives the usual explanation for the project, Akbar's curiosity. The underlined sentence says some historians "add" a political purpose, and the final sentence says the two explanations "are not exclusive." The underlined sentence supplies a second motive alongside the common one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The historians "add" a purpose rather than replacing the first one, and the next sentence says the explanations "are not exclusive."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The method is described in the second sentence; the underlined sentence concerns why the project was undertaken.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never explains the choice of title; the underlined sentence is about the project's purpose.
explanation.D: Correct. The word "add" and the following sentence ("not exclusive") show that the political purpose is offered alongside, not instead of, Akbar's curiosity.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Plants are usually thought of as silent. Yet when researchers placed microphones near tomato and tobacco plants, they recorded brief ultrasonic clicks, far too high-pitched for human ears, that became much more frequent when the plants were deprived of water or had their stems cut. Unstressed plants produced only occasional sounds. A computer program trained on the recordings could even distinguish a thirsty plant from a cut one. The clicks may result from air bubbles forming and bursting in the plant's water-conducting tissue, a purely physical process. Whether any insect or animal actually listens to them, and responds, has yet to be shown.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It reports a finding about stressed plants and then argues that insects use the sounds to locate weakened plants.
choices.B: It counters a common assumption with a finding, suggests a cause, and notes an open question.
choices.C: It describes a hypothesis about plants, explains how it was tested, and reports that the test failed to support it.
choices.D: It compares two plant species and then explains why one of them produces many more sounds than the other.

explanation.why: The text opens with a common belief ("Plants are usually thought of as silent"), counters it with the recordings, offers a possible cause ("The clicks may result from air bubbles"), and ends with an unanswered question about whether any animal "listens." The structure is assumption, contrary finding, possible explanation, open question.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says it "has yet to be shown" whether any animal listens, so it makes no such argument.
explanation.B: Correct. The text moves from "usually thought of as silent" to the recorded clicks, to the bubble explanation, to the unresolved question of listeners.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The recordings support the idea that plants make sounds; nothing in the text describes a failed test.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Tomato and tobacco are both studied, but the text compares stressed and unstressed plants, not the two species.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Bible that Johannes Gutenberg printed in Mainz in the 1450s is often treated as the moment when mechanical reproduction replaced the handmade book. Yet a buyer who acquired one received something unfinished. The printed pages left blank spaces where large initial letters belonged, and headings and chapter markers were generally added in red ink by hand. Purchasers then hired local artists to supply decoration in whatever style and quantity they could afford, so that the surviving copies differ noticeably from one another. In its own time, the most famous printed book in Europe was, in a real sense, still partly a manuscript.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain why surviving copies of the Gutenberg Bible are now so rare and so valuable
choices.B: To complicate a common view of an early printed book by showing the handwork it required
choices.C: To argue that Gutenberg's printing press was far less important than historians have claimed
choices.D: To describe the decorative styles that artists in fifteenth-century Mainz preferred

explanation.why: The text begins with a common view, that Gutenberg's Bible marks the replacement of the handmade book, and then says "Yet" each copy was "unfinished," needing handwritten headings and hand-painted decoration. The last sentence concludes that the book was "still partly a manuscript." The text complicates the common view.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says the copies differ from one another but says nothing about their rarity or value.
explanation.B: Correct. The text sets up the view that printing replaced handmade books and then shows that each copy still needed handwork.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text qualifies how complete the change was in the 1450s; it does not dismiss the press's importance.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says buyers chose decoration they "could afford" but never describes particular styles.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For three weeks Suman had tried to center clay on the wheel in his uncle's workshop in Bhaktapur, and for three weeks the lump had wobbled, leaned, and finally collapsed. His uncle, Krishna Prajapati, offered little instruction. He would only say, "You are fighting it," and return to his own wheel. One morning, as yet another lump began to lurch, the old man came over, set his wet hands lightly over Suman's, and held them still. The wheel kept turning. Beneath their four hands the clay rose, steadied, and became smooth. "There," his uncle said, and walked away. Suman understood that he had been gripping far too hard.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To show that the apprentice resents his uncle's refusal to explain the craft to him
choices.B: To describe the series of steps that a potter follows to shape a clay vessel on the wheel
choices.C: To depict an apprentice learning through touch a lesson that words had not taught him
choices.D: To suggest that the uncle doubts the apprentice will ever master the potter's wheel

explanation.why: The uncle's words ("You are fighting it") do not help Suman, but when the uncle places his hands over Suman's and holds them still, the clay steadies, and Suman finally understands he had been "gripping far too hard." The passage shows a lesson learned through touch after words had failed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Suman is never shown feeling resentment; the passage focuses on his frustration with the clay and his final understanding.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The passage concerns only centering the clay and one moment of learning, not the full process of making a vessel.
explanation.C: Correct. Suman understands only after his uncle physically steadies his hands, even though the spoken advice had come weeks earlier.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The uncle helps Suman succeed and says "There" with apparent satisfaction; nothing suggests doubt.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: European accounts of West Africa written in the colonial era often described the region as lacking a tradition of written scholarship, its history preserved only in oral form. The manuscripts of Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, tell a different story. Hundreds of thousands of them, many centuries old, survive on subjects ranging from law and theology to astronomy, medicine, and grammar. Most have been preserved not in public institutions but in the private libraries of local families, who copied, repaired, and handed them down for generations, a fact that helps explain why outsiders long overlooked them.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes a mistaken belief, presents evidence against it, and explains why it was missed.
choices.B: It lists the subjects covered by a collection and then describes how the collection was moved to safety.
choices.C: It compares oral and written traditions and then argues that written records are the more reliable of the two.
choices.D: It presents a theory about a region's history and then explains how later scholars confirmed that theory.

explanation.why: The text opens with a colonial-era belief that West Africa lacked written scholarship, then says the Timbuktu manuscripts "tell a different story" and describes their number and range. The final sentence explains that they were kept in family libraries, which "helps explain why outsiders long overlooked them." The structure is belief, counterevidence, reason the evidence was missed.
explanation.A: Correct. The colonial view is contradicted by the manuscripts, and their private keeping explains why outsiders missed them.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text lists the subjects but says nothing about moving the manuscripts anywhere.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never compares the reliability of oral and written traditions.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The manuscripts contradict the colonial-era view rather than confirming it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Great tits living in noisy parts of cities tend to sing songs with higher minimum pitches than great tits in quieter areas. A widely cited explanation is that traffic noise is concentrated at low frequencies, so birds that shift their songs upward are more easily heard by rivals and potential mates. <u>Some researchers, however, point out that when birds sing more loudly, their songs often rise in pitch as a side effect, much as human voices do when people shout.</u> If that is the case, higher urban songs may reflect birds simply singing louder over the din rather than adjusting their pitch to escape it, and experiments are now trying to separate the two possibilities.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It shows that the widely cited explanation has already been disproved by controlled experiments.
choices.B: It introduces an alternative account of the pattern described at the beginning of the text.
choices.C: It explains why birds with higher-pitched songs are more easily heard by their rivals and mates.
choices.D: It provides evidence that traffic noise in cities is concentrated mainly at low frequencies.

explanation.why: The first two sentences describe a pattern (higher songs in noisy areas) and the usual explanation (birds move above low-frequency noise). The underlined sentence, introduced by "however," raises another possibility: the higher pitch may be a side effect of singing louder. The last sentence calls these "the two possibilities."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says experiments "are now trying to separate the two possibilities," so neither has been disproved.
explanation.B: Correct. It suggests higher pitch may be a by-product of louder singing, which the final sentence treats as one of "two possibilities."
explanation.C: Incorrect. That is the reasoning of the first explanation; the underlined sentence offers a different one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. That claim belongs to the widely cited explanation in the second sentence; the underlined sentence is about loudness and pitch.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Between 1980 and 1994, conservators removed centuries of candle soot, grime, and layers of glue applied in earlier restorations from Michelangelo's frescoes on the Sistine Chapel ceiling. The cleaned surfaces revealed brilliant pinks, greens, and oranges that startled viewers accustomed to a somber, brownish ceiling. Critics charged that the conservators had also stripped away a final layer of shading that Michelangelo himself had added after the plaster dried. Defenders replied that he had worked almost entirely in true fresco, painting into wet plaster, so that the bright colors were his own. The dispute turned less on taste than on a technical question: what had the artist actually put on the wall?
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe a dispute over a restoration and identify the factual question on which it turned
choices.B: To argue that the conservators damaged Michelangelo's frescoes by removing his final shading
choices.C: To explain the technique Michelangelo used to prepare the plaster for the ceiling frescoes
choices.D: To show that most viewers eventually came to prefer the brighter colors of the cleaned ceiling

explanation.why: The text describes the cleaning, the critics' charge, and the defenders' reply without taking a side. The final sentence states what the argument depended on: "a technical question" about what Michelangelo "actually put on the wall." The purpose is to describe the dispute and identify its central factual issue.
explanation.A: Correct. The text presents both sides and then names the technical question at the heart of the disagreement.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is only the critics' charge; the text also gives the defenders' reply and does not take a side.
explanation.C: Incorrect. True fresco is mentioned only as part of the defenders' argument; the text's focus is the dispute.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says viewers were "startled" but never says they came to prefer the new colors.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the 1860s, the fastest sailing ships in the world competed to carry each year's first tea harvest from China to London, where the earliest cargoes fetched the highest prices. The Cutty Sark, launched in Scotland in November 1869, was built to win that race. <u>That very month, however, the Suez Canal opened, giving steamships a far shorter route between Asia and Europe, one that sailing ships, dependent on favorable winds, could not easily use.</u> Within a few years, steamers had taken over most of the tea trade, and the Cutty Sark earned her lasting reputation carrying wool from Australia instead.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It describes a feature of the Cutty Sark's design that made her faster than her rivals.
choices.B: It introduces a development that undermined the purpose for which a ship had been built.
choices.C: It explains why the earliest tea cargoes of each year fetched the highest prices in London.
choices.D: It presents the event that first made the tea trade profitable for fast sailing ships.

explanation.why: The sentence before the underlined one says the Cutty Sark "was built to win" the tea race. The underlined sentence, beginning with "however," reports the Suez Canal's opening, which favored steamships. The final sentence shows the result: steamers took the tea trade, and the ship turned to wool. The underlined sentence introduces the development that undercut the ship's purpose.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The underlined sentence says nothing about the ship's design; it describes the opening of the canal.
explanation.B: Correct. The canal gave steamships a shorter route, so they took over the tea trade the Cutty Sark had been built to win.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The high prices of early cargoes are stated in the first sentence; the underlined sentence concerns the canal.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The canal helped steamships, and the final sentence says steamers then took over the tea trade from sailing ships.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The mangrove forests of the Sundarbans, which stretch across the delta of the Ganges and Brahmaputra Rivers in India and Bangladesh, grow in mud so waterlogged that it holds almost no oxygen. Roots buried in such mud cannot draw in the air they need. Many of the region's trees solve this problem with pneumatophores: pencil-like roots that grow upward out of the mud and are dotted with tiny pores through which air enters at low tide. The same adaptation, however, is a point of weakness. When heavy deposits of sediment bury the pneumatophores, or when spilled oil coats their pores, the roots beneath can be starved of oxygen.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes a forest, explains why its trees are declining, and proposes a way to protect them.
choices.B: It presents a hypothesis about how mangroves obtain air and then reports evidence against it.
choices.C: It compares two kinds of mangrove roots and argues that one is better suited to the delta.
choices.D: It names an environmental challenge, explains how some trees meet it, and notes a weakness.

explanation.why: The first two sentences describe a problem: the mud "holds almost no oxygen." The third explains how trees "solve this problem" with pneumatophores. The last two sentences, beginning with "however," describe how that same feature makes the trees vulnerable. The structure is challenge, adaptation, resulting weakness.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says the trees are declining and proposes no protective measures.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The explanation of pneumatophores is presented as established, not as a hypothesis that is then challenged.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only one root type, the pneumatophore, is described; nothing is compared.
explanation.D: Correct. Oxygen-poor mud is the challenge, pneumatophores are the solution, and their exposure to burial or oil is the weakness.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The brothers had not spoken in four years when their father's will left them his old sailboat jointly, on the condition that it be made seaworthy before it was sold. They met at the boatyard in silence and worked from opposite ends of the hull, Anders scraping paint at the bow and Lars at the stern. By the third Saturday they had reached the middle. <u>Lars held out the sanding block without a word, and Anders, after a moment, took it.</u> They worked side by side until dark, and when they stopped, Anders asked whether Lars still took his coffee black.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It depicts a small gesture that signals the start of the brothers' reconciliation.
choices.B: It reveals the reason the brothers stopped speaking to each other four years earlier.
choices.C: It shows that Lars has decided to leave the rest of the work on the boat to Anders.
choices.D: It suggests that the brothers' long quarrel has become more bitter than before.

explanation.why: Before the underlined sentence, the brothers work "in silence" from "opposite ends." In the underlined sentence, one offers a tool and the other accepts it. Afterward they work "side by side," and Anders asks a friendly question. The small exchange marks the start of their reconciliation.
explanation.A: Correct. The silent offer and acceptance of the sanding block leads directly to the brothers working together and talking.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never explains the cause of the brothers' silence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. After the exchange the brothers work "side by side," so Lars does not stop working.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The brothers begin cooperating and talking after the exchange, the opposite of growing more bitter.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Among the clay tablets excavated at Nippur and Ur, cities of ancient Mesopotamia, are thousands that no scribe ever meant to preserve: the exercises of students learning to write in the early second millennium BCE. Some are small round tablets bearing a teacher's model on one side and a student's attempt to copy it on the other, complete with misshapen signs and smoothed-over mistakes. Studied together, such tablets allow scholars to reconstruct the order in which pupils learned, from simple signs to lists of words and finally to proverbs and literary works. Discarded schoolwork, in other words, has become one of the best records of how ancient scribes were trained.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe the shape and size of the clay tablets used in Mesopotamian schools
choices.B: To argue that Mesopotamian students made more errors than students in later periods
choices.C: To explain how routine student exercises became a key source on ancient education
choices.D: To show that scholars once mistook students' exercises for important literary works

explanation.why: The text describes student exercise tablets and explains that, "studied together," they let scholars reconstruct the stages of a scribe's training. The final sentence states the point: "Discarded schoolwork" is now "one of the best records" of scribal education.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The round shape of some tablets is a detail; the text's focus is what the exercises reveal.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text mentions mistakes on the tablets but never compares students across periods.
explanation.C: Correct. The text shows what the exercise tablets contain and what scholars learn from them about scribal training.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never says scholars confused exercises with literary works.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A flock of thousands of starlings can wheel and fold across the evening sky without breaking apart, even as it stretches thin one moment and packs tightly the next. Many early models of flocking assumed that each bird responds to all neighbors within a fixed distance. When researchers in Rome reconstructed the positions of individual birds in three dimensions from photographs, however, they found that each starling appeared to track a roughly constant number of nearest neighbors, about six or seven, no matter how far away those neighbors were. Such a rule, the researchers argued, would keep the flock together as its density changed, since a bird would never find itself without neighbors to follow.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It reports a finding about how starlings flock and then explains why other researchers have since rejected that finding.
choices.B: It describes how researchers photographed flocks of starlings and then lists the difficulties of that method.
choices.C: It compares the flocking behavior of starlings with that of other bird species and identifies a common rule.
choices.D: It describes a behavior, contrasts an old assumption with a new finding, and shows how the finding explains it.

explanation.why: The text opens with a behavior that needs explaining (a flock that stays together while changing density), contrasts an earlier assumption (a fixed distance) with the Rome finding (a fixed number of neighbors), and ends by explaining how that rule keeps the flock together. The structure is puzzle, old assumption versus new finding, explanation.
explanation.A: Incorrect. No one is said to reject the Rome finding; the text presents it as accounting for the flock's behavior.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The photographs are mentioned briefly, and the text describes no difficulties with the method.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only starlings are discussed; no other species is mentioned.
explanation.D: Correct. The flock's cohesion is the behavior, fixed distance versus fixed number is the contrast, and the last sentence links the rule to cohesion.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For decades, archaeologists catalogued small clay objects, cones, spheres, and disks, found at sites across the ancient Near East without knowing what they were. The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-Besserat proposed that they were counters used to keep track of goods. She noted that, by the late fourth millennium BCE, such tokens were sometimes sealed inside hollow clay balls whose outer surfaces bore impressions of the tokens within, and she argued that accountants eventually realized the impressions alone were enough, a step toward writing on flat tablets. Other scholars accept that tokens served for accounting but doubt that they explain the full range of early written signs.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes a puzzle, presents a proposed solution and its evidence, and notes a reservation.
choices.B: It describes the invention of writing in one region and then traces how writing spread across the Near East.
choices.C: It presents two rival theories about some ancient objects and then explains why scholars abandoned both of them.
choices.D: It reports a proposal about some ancient objects and then explains how later excavations confirmed every part of it.

explanation.why: The text begins with a puzzle (clay objects of unknown purpose), presents Schmandt-Besserat's proposal and the evidence she cited (sealed clay balls marked with impressions), and ends with other scholars' reservation that tokens do not explain "the full range of early written signs." The structure is puzzle, proposed solution with evidence, reservation.
explanation.A: Correct. The unknown objects are the puzzle, the accounting-to-writing theory is the solution, and the doubts of other scholars are the reservation.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about how writing spread from one place to another.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only one theory is presented, and other scholars accept part of it rather than abandoning it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The last sentence expresses doubt about part of the proposal; no excavation confirms all of it.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Visitors to museums often look at a Mughal painting from the court of Akbar and ask who painted it. The question is reasonable but frequently has more than one answer. Many pages produced in the imperial workshop in the late sixteenth century carry small notes in the margins naming two or more artists: one credited with the tarh, the design or outline of the composition, and another with the amal, the coloring and finishing. On some pages a third artist, a specialist in portraiture, painted the faces. Such inscriptions suggest that, for these works at least, the modern idea of the solitary artist can obscure how the images were actually made.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To define two terms that modern art historians use when they classify Mughal paintings
choices.B: To show that many paintings from a royal workshop were the work of several artists
choices.C: To argue that the artists of Akbar's workshop deserve far more fame than they receive today
choices.D: To describe how museum visitors usually react when they first encounter Mughal paintings

explanation.why: The text says the question of who painted a Mughal page "frequently has more than one answer" and supports this with margin notes crediting different artists with design, coloring, and faces. The last sentence states the point: the idea of "the solitary artist" can hide how these works were really made.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Tarh" and "amal" are defined, but they come from the original margin notes, and defining them is not the text's main aim.
explanation.B: Correct. The margin notes name different artists for design, coloring, and faces, so many pages had more than one painter.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text is about how the paintings were made, not about how famous the artists should be.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The visitors' question only introduces the topic; the text is about how the paintings were produced.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Miss Lavinia Croft had inherited, along with her father's fortune, his conviction that money ought never to be mentioned, and she held to it with a consistency that cost her nothing, since she had never once been obliged to think about money at all. She subscribed to every charity that applied to her, chiefly because a refusal would have required an explanation, and she was much praised in the neighborhood for a generosity she would have been astonished to hear described as a virtue. When her steward ventured to suggest that her accounts would not bear another such year, she looked at him with mild surprise, as at a man who had remarked upon the weather in a foreign language.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To criticize a wealthy woman for knowingly wasting the fortune she inherited from her father
choices.B: To show how a loyal steward gradually persuades his employer to manage her money more carefully
choices.C: To describe the local charities that depended on the support of a generous heiress
choices.D: To portray a woman whose admired traits owe more to her situation than to virtue

explanation.why: Each detail shows that Miss Croft's admired traits come from her situation, not from effort or choice: her principle "cost her nothing," she gives "chiefly because a refusal would have required an explanation," and she would be "astonished" to hear her generosity called a virtue. Even the steward's warning makes no sense to her. The passage portrays a character whose apparent virtues are products of her circumstances.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The passage stresses that she has never thought about money, so her spending is not knowing; and its tone is ironic rather than openly critical.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The steward makes one suggestion, which she meets with "mild surprise"; he persuades her of nothing.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The charities are mentioned only in passing and are never described; the focus is on Miss Croft herself.
explanation.D: Correct. Her principle costs her nothing, her giving avoids explanations, and she does not see it as virtue; her wealth explains all three.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The claim that hot water can freeze faster than cold water has a long history; Aristotle mentions it, and it became widely known as the Mpemba effect after a Tanzanian student, Erasto Mpemba, reported the phenomenon in the 1960s. Since then, researchers have proposed many mechanisms, from faster evaporation reducing the volume of hot water to differences in dissolved gases. <u>Yet experiments have produced strikingly inconsistent results, and some carefully controlled studies have found no effect at all.</u> Part of the difficulty lies in definition: whether "freezing" means the first appearance of ice or complete solidification, and where in the container temperature is measured, can change which sample appears to win.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It explains why researchers proposed so many different mechanisms for the effect.
choices.B: It establishes that the effect was disproved soon after Mpemba first reported it.
choices.C: It offers support for one of the mechanisms mentioned in the previous sentence.
choices.D: It raises a doubt about the evidence that the next sentence partly accounts for.

explanation.why: After the text describes the effect's history and proposed mechanisms, the underlined sentence, starting with "Yet," raises a problem: the evidence is inconsistent, and some studies found no effect. The next sentence begins "Part of the difficulty lies in definition," partly explaining why results disagree. The underlined sentence introduces a doubt that the following sentence helps account for.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The mechanisms were proposed to explain the effect; the underlined sentence questions whether the effect is reliable.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Only "some" studies found no effect, and the text treats the question as unsettled, not disproved.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sentence reports inconsistent results and no effect in some studies, which supports no particular mechanism.
explanation.D: Correct. The inconsistent results are then traced in part to how "freezing" is defined and where temperature is measured.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The notion that the centuries after the fall of Rome were a "dark" age owes much to the fourteenth-century Italian poet Petrarch, who contrasted the brilliance of classical Latin literature with what he saw as the obscurity of the writing that followed it. His judgment was, in origin, a literary one, made by a scholar who prized the eloquence of Cicero and Virgil. Later writers stretched it far beyond its original scope, until "Dark Ages" came to suggest a general collapse of learning, invention, and order across Europe. Modern historians have largely abandoned the phrase, pointing out that it ignores, among much else, the monasteries in which many of the very classical texts Petrarch revered had been copied and preserved.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes a historical period and then explains how scholars recovered the literature it had lost.
choices.B: It contrasts two kinds of medieval writing and then argues that one did more to preserve classical learning.
choices.C: It presents a poet's view of history and then argues that his taste in Latin literature was mistaken.
choices.D: It traces a label to its origin, shows how it was later broadened, and explains its rejection.

explanation.why: The text first traces the idea of a "dark" age to Petrarch's literary judgment, then shows how later writers "stretched it far beyond its original scope," and finally explains why modern historians have "largely abandoned the phrase." The structure follows a label from origin to expansion to rejection.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text is about a label for the period, and it says monasteries preserved classical texts, not that the texts were lost and recovered.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Petrarch contrasts classical and later writing, but the text does not weigh two kinds of medieval writing against each other.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never criticizes Petrarch's literary taste; it says his judgment was later stretched by others.
explanation.D: Correct. Petrarch's literary judgment, its later stretching into "Dark Ages," and modern historians' objections follow in that order.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Spelling in early seventeenth-century England was far from standardized, and the workmen who set type for printed books often followed their own habits rather than those of the manuscripts in front of them. Bibliographers studying the 1623 First Folio of Shakespeare's plays have turned this inconsistency into evidence. One compositor, for instance, tended to set "doe," "goe," and "here," while another preferred "do," "go," and "heere." <u>By tracking such preferences page by page, scholars have been able to assign much of the volume to individual workmen and to estimate how carefully each one worked.</u> The results bear on editing: a reading that looks like Shakespeare's own peculiar choice may instead be the signature of the man who set it.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It offers an example of the contrasting spelling habits of two compositors who worked on the volume.
choices.B: It establishes that most of the apparent errors in the First Folio were introduced by its typesetters.
choices.C: It explains why English spelling had not yet become standardized when the First Folio was printed.
choices.D: It shows how a pattern described earlier was used as evidence, preparing for the point about editing.

explanation.why: The earlier sentences explain that typesetters had their own spelling habits and give an example. The underlined sentence shows how scholars used those habits as evidence to identify who set each page and how carefully. The final sentence then draws the consequence for editing. The underlined sentence links the pattern to the point about editing.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The example of "doe" and "do" appears in the previous sentence; the underlined sentence describes how such habits were used.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The sentence says scholars can estimate each workman's care, not that most errors came from typesetters.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text states that spelling was not standardized but never explains why; the underlined sentence is about scholars' methods.
explanation.D: Correct. It explains what scholars did with the compositors' spelling habits, which leads to the final sentence's warning to editors.

items.subject: science
items.passage: For decades after the Apollo missions, the Moon's surface was widely regarded as bone-dry; the rock samples astronauts brought back contained so little water that traces were often attributed to contamination on Earth. In 2009, scientists analyzing data from the Moon Mineralogy Mapper, a NASA instrument carried aboard India's Chandrayaan-1 orbiter, reported a faint signature of absorbed light indicating hydroxyl or water molecules bound to the lunar soil, stronger toward the poles. Data from two other spacecraft soon corroborated the finding. The quantities involved are minute, far less than in the driest desert sand on Earth, but the discovery overturned a long-standing assumption and reopened questions about how water reaches and moves across the Moon.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that the Moon holds enough water to support future crewed bases near its poles
choices.B: To compare the instruments aboard Chandrayaan-1 with those aboard two other spacecraft
choices.C: To present a discovery that changed a long-held view of the Moon and note its limits
choices.D: To explain why scientists dismissed traces of water in Apollo samples as contamination

explanation.why: The text sets up the old view (the Moon was "bone-dry"), reports the 2009 finding of water or hydroxyl in lunar soil and its confirmation, and then notes both its limit ("The quantities involved are minute") and its importance (it "overturned a long-standing assumption"). The purpose is to present a discovery that changed a long-held view while noting its limits.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text calls the amounts "minute" and says nothing about supporting crewed bases.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The other spacecraft are mentioned only as confirming the finding; no instruments are compared.
explanation.C: Correct. The text reports that water or hydroxyl was detected on a Moon thought "bone-dry" and stresses that the amounts are "minute."
explanation.D: Incorrect. This detail sets up the old view; the text's focus is the 2009 discovery that revised it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: From the late seventh century, the Byzantine navy defended Constantinople with a weapon its enemies called Greek fire: a burning liquid, projected through tubes, that continued to burn on the surface of the sea. The Byzantines guarded its composition as a state secret, and in the tenth century the emperor Constantine VII advised his son never to share it with foreigners. Knowledge of the recipe appears to have been confined to a small circle of specialists. <u>The very secrecy that protected the weapon may have doomed it, for when that circle dwindled, there was no wider body of knowledge from which the recipe could be recovered.</u> Today historians can only speculate about its ingredients, though most suspect it was based on crude petroleum.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It suggests that a practice described earlier as protecting the weapon may also explain its loss.
choices.B: It offers evidence that the weapon was based on crude petroleum rather than on other materials.
choices.C: It explains the methods Byzantine specialists used to keep the recipe hidden from foreign enemies.
choices.D: It argues that the Byzantines were foolish to refuse to share the recipe with their allies.

explanation.why: The earlier sentences show secrecy protecting the weapon: it was a "state secret" known only to "a small circle." The underlined sentence turns this around, suggesting that "the very secrecy that protected the weapon may have doomed it," because no one else knew the recipe. The final sentence confirms the loss: historians "can only speculate." The underlined sentence presents secrecy as both protection and cause of loss.
explanation.A: Correct. Secrecy kept the recipe from enemies but also kept it from surviving once the few specialists were gone.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The petroleum suggestion comes in the final sentence and is described as speculation; the underlined sentence concerns the recipe's loss.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sentence describes a consequence of the secrecy, not how the secret was kept.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The sentence offers a possible explanation ("may have doomed it"), not a judgment of the Byzantines, and allies are never mentioned.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: On the morning of his last day, Rahmat Ali climbed the rope ladder up the freighter's side as he had done some nine thousand times before, nodded to the captain on the bridge, and took his place beside the helmsman. The Karnaphuli ran brown and quick with the tide. He called the turns without looking at a chart: the shoal off the old jetty, the bend where the current set hard toward the eastern bank. Forty years earlier, on his first passage, his hands had shaken so badly that the senior pilot had made him hold them behind his back. Now, as the berths of Chittagong came into view, he turned to the young pilot who had been shadowing him all week and, without a word, stepped aside to let him call the final turn.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It follows a man through a familiar task, recalls his beginnings, and ends as he hands it to a successor.
choices.B: It introduces a young pilot, traces the stages of his training, and ends with his first passage without supervision.
choices.C: It contrasts two rivers on which a pilot has worked and explains why he has come to prefer one of them.
choices.D: It describes a dangerous passage up a river, explains what went wrong, and shows the pilot accepting the blame.

explanation.why: The passage follows Rahmat Ali through a routine he has repeated "some nine thousand times," pauses to recall his nervous first passage "forty years earlier," and ends with him stepping aside so "the young pilot" can call the final turn. The structure is familiar task, memory of beginnings, handing on of the task.
explanation.A: Correct. The routine passage, the memory of his first voyage, and his stepping aside for the young pilot occur in that order.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The young pilot appears only at the end; the passage centers on Rahmat Ali and never traces anyone's training.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Only one river, the Karnaphuli, is described.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing goes wrong in the passage; Rahmat Ali calls the turns with ease.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Astronomers can estimate how fast the universe is expanding, a quantity known as the Hubble constant, in two broadly different ways. One works outward from nearby galaxies, using stars of known brightness to measure distances and comparing those distances with how fast the galaxies are receding. The other works forward from the cosmic microwave background, the faint radiation left from the early universe, using a standard model of cosmic history to predict the rate today. As measurements have grown more precise, the two approaches have not converged; they continue to disagree by roughly 8 percent. If the gap is not the product of some unrecognized error, it may signal that the standard model itself is missing something.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It explains how the expansion of the universe was discovered and traces early attempts to measure its rate.
choices.B: It describes two methods of measuring a quantity, reports a lasting disagreement between them, and considers its meaning.
choices.C: It presents a standard model of cosmic history and then reports new observations that have confirmed it.
choices.D: It describes two methods of measuring a quantity, explains which one is more reliable, and recommends dropping the other.

explanation.why: The text describes two methods of estimating the Hubble constant, reports that they "continue to disagree by roughly 8 percent" even as precision improves, and ends by considering what the gap could mean: an error or a flaw in "the standard model itself." The structure is two methods, persistent disagreement, possible significance.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about the discovery of expansion or the history of early measurements.
explanation.B: Correct. The two approaches, their failure to converge, and the two possible explanations for the gap appear in that order.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The disagreement may mean the model "is missing something," so the observations do not simply confirm it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never judges either method more reliable; it treats the gap as unexplained.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Giorgio Vasari's Lives of the Artists, first published in 1550 and expanded in 1568, remains the starting point for much of what is known about Italian Renaissance art. It is also, by modern standards, an unreliable book. Vasari favored artists from his native Tuscany, repeated anecdotes that cannot be verified, such as the story that the young Giotto was discovered drawing sheep on a rock, and sometimes misattributed works or confused dates. Historians nonetheless cannot do without it. Where documents survive, they test Vasari against them; where none survive, his account is often the only one. And even his embellishments are revealing, for they show what a sixteenth-century writer believed an artist's life ought to look like.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe how sixteenth-century writers imagined the ideal life of an artist
choices.B: To explain why historians continue to rely on a source even though they recognize its flaws
choices.C: To argue that historians should replace Vasari's account with evidence drawn from documents
choices.D: To catalog the kinds of errors that make Vasari's book unreliable as a historical source

explanation.why: The text admits that Vasari's book is "unreliable" and lists its faults, but then says historians "nonetheless cannot do without it," explaining how they use it and why even its embellishments are useful. The purpose is to explain why historians keep relying on a flawed source.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This idea appears only in the last sentence, as one reason the book is useful.
explanation.B: Correct. The text lists the book's faults and then gives reasons historians "cannot do without it."
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text says that where no documents survive, Vasari's account "is often the only one," so it does not call for replacing him.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The errors are listed in one sentence, but the text goes on to explain why the book remains essential.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1896, two young Oxford scholars, Bernard Grenfell and Arthur Hunt, began digging into the ancient rubbish mounds outside Oxyrhynchus, a town in Egypt's Nile Valley. Over the following years they recovered papyrus fragments in enormous numbers: tax receipts, contracts, private letters, school exercises, and, scattered among them, pieces of literary works lost for centuries, including poems by Sappho and scenes from the comedies of Menander. <u>The townspeople who threw these papers away had no thought of posterity; it was the desert's dryness, not any act of preservation, that kept them intact.</u> As a result, the collection offers something deliberate archives rarely do: a record of what ordinary people wrote and read, unfiltered by anyone's judgment of what deserved to survive.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It explains why Grenfell and Hunt chose to dig in rubbish mounds rather than in the town's buildings.
choices.B: It stresses that the papyri survived by chance, setting up the claim about their value.
choices.C: It contrasts the everyday documents in the collection with the literary works found among them.
choices.D: It suggests that the people of Oxyrhynchus placed little value on the literary works they owned.

explanation.why: The underlined sentence stresses that the papyri survived by accident: they were thrown away, and only "the desert's dryness" preserved them. The next sentence, beginning "As a result," draws on that point: because no one chose what to keep, the collection is "unfiltered by anyone's judgment." The underlined sentence sets up the claim about the collection's special value.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text never says why the scholars chose the rubbish mounds.
explanation.B: Correct. Because no one selected what to keep, the collection is "unfiltered," the point made in the final sentence.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The sentence treats all the discarded papers alike; it does not set the two kinds of documents against each other.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The sentence says the papers were discarded with "no thought of posterity," not that their owners disliked or undervalued the works when they had them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Geckos can run up glass windows and even hang upside down from ceilings, yet their feet are not sticky. Instead, each toe is covered with ridges that hold millions of tiny hairs called setae. The tip of each hair splits into hundreds of even smaller branches. Because these branches touch a surface so closely, weak attractive forces between molecules hold the gecko in place. Added together, these forces easily support the animal's weight.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain how the structure of a gecko's feet lets it cling to smooth surfaces
choices.B: To argue that geckos are better climbers than any other animal
choices.C: To point out that the tips of gecko hairs split into smaller branches
choices.D: To describe the different places where geckos usually live

explanation.why: The text opens with a puzzle: geckos cling to glass and ceilings even though "their feet are not sticky." Every later sentence explains part of the answer, from the ridges and hairs to the "weak attractive forces between molecules." So the text's purpose is to explain how the feet work.
explanation.A: Correct. The whole text explains how the toes' ridges, hairs, and tiny branches let a gecko hold onto surfaces like glass.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never compares geckos with other animals, so it does not argue that they are the best climbers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The splitting hair tips are one step in the explanation, not the purpose of the whole text.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Windows and ceilings are mentioned only as surfaces geckos can climb; the text does not discuss where geckos live.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Mei stood at the edge of the pool, her toes curled over the wet tiles. Her stomach felt tight, and the water looked colder and deeper than it had during practice. She glanced up at the crowded bleachers. There, in the second row, her older brother Jun was waving a sign he had painted the night before: "Go, Mei!" She laughed out loud. When the whistle blew, she dove in without a second thought.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It shows Mei growing more nervous as she notices the large crowd.
choices.B: It describes a swimming race from start to finish and then reports the result.
choices.C: It explains why Mei joined a swim team and how she trained for races.
choices.D: It presents Mei's nervousness before a race and then shows what eases it.

explanation.why: At first Mei is anxious: "Her stomach felt tight," and the water looks "colder and deeper." Then she sees her brother's sign, laughs, and dives in "without a second thought." The text moves from nervousness to relief, and the sign is what causes the change.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Looking at the crowd is what calms Mei, because she finds her brother there. Her nervousness decreases rather than grows.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text ends as the race begins; it never describes the race itself or tells who won.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Practice is mentioned once, but the text never explains why Mei joined a team or how she trained.
explanation.D: Correct. The text first shows Mei's tight stomach and fear, then shows her brother's sign making her laugh and dive in confidently.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Kallanai, a dam across the Kaveri River in Tamil Nadu, India, is often described as one of the oldest water-control structures still in use. Tradition credits it to the Chola king Karikalan, who ruled nearly two thousand years ago. <u>Built of unshaped stones piled across the riverbed, the dam slowed the river and sent part of its flow into channels that watered nearby fields.</u> Repaired many times since, it still serves farmers today.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It explains how the dam was built and how it helped farmers.
choices.B: It identifies the ruler who is traditionally credited with the dam.
choices.C: It suggests that the dam no longer serves any practical purpose.
choices.D: It argues that the dam should be replaced with a modern structure.

explanation.why: The underlined sentence describes the dam's construction ("unshaped stones piled across the riverbed") and what it did: it sent water "into channels that watered nearby fields." It explains how the dam was made and how it supported farming.
explanation.A: Correct. The sentence tells what the dam was made of and how it moved river water to the fields.
explanation.B: Incorrect. King Karikalan is named in the previous sentence, not in the underlined one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The last sentence says the dam "still serves farmers today," and the underlined sentence describes its usefulness.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never suggests replacing the dam; it notes that the dam still serves farmers.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The Bayeux Tapestry, a cloth nearly 70 meters long, tells the story of the Norman conquest of England in 1066. Despite its famous name, it is not actually a tapestry. In a true tapestry, the picture is woven into the cloth as the cloth itself is being made. The images of the Bayeux work, however, were stitched with colored wool onto a finished piece of linen, which makes it an embroidery.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain why the Bayeux Tapestry's name does not accurately describe it
choices.B: To explain how tapestries were woven in England in the 1000s
choices.C: To argue that the Bayeux Tapestry should be given a new name
choices.D: To describe the battle scenes pictured on the Bayeux Tapestry

explanation.why: The key sentence is "Despite its famous name, it is not actually a tapestry." The rest of the text explains the difference between weaving a picture into cloth and stitching it onto finished cloth. The purpose is to show why the name is inaccurate.
explanation.A: Correct. The text explains that the work was stitched onto finished linen, so it is an embroidery, not a tapestry.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text defines a tapestry in general terms; it says nothing about weaving methods in England in the 1000s.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text points out that the name is inaccurate but never says the work should be renamed. This claims more than the text does.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says the work tells the story of the Norman conquest but never describes any of its scenes.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Old church windowpanes in Europe are often thicker at the bottom than at the top. A popular explanation holds that glass is a very slow liquid that has sagged over time. <u>Calculations show, however, that glass at room temperature is far too stiff to flow measurably even over millions of years.</u> The real cause is how the panes were made: older methods produced sheets of uneven thickness, and workers often set the heavier edge at the bottom.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It supports the popular explanation given in the previous sentence.
choices.B: It presents evidence against the explanation offered in the previous sentence.
choices.C: It explains how church windows were installed in the Middle Ages.
choices.D: It states the true cause of the panes' uneven thickness.

explanation.why: The sentence before the underlined one gives a popular explanation: the glass has slowly flowed downward. The underlined sentence, signaled by "however," says glass is "far too stiff to flow measurably." It rules out the popular explanation, and the final sentence then gives the real cause.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If glass cannot flow measurably, it cannot have sagged, so the sentence argues against the popular explanation.
explanation.B: Correct. The calculations show that glass cannot flow enough to explain the thicker bottoms, which undercuts the popular idea.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text does not describe how windows were installed in any period, and the underlined sentence is about the stiffness of glass.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The real cause, uneven sheets with the heavier edge placed at the bottom, is given in the final sentence, not the underlined one.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Rain had soaked the forest, and Nkechi's matches kept dying against the wet sticks. She sat back, ready to give up on a hot dinner. Her friend Rosa walked over to a fallen log, pulled off a strip of bark, and scraped out a handful of dry wood from inside. <u>Within minutes, small flames were curling around the twigs.</u> Nkechi stared at the fire, then at Rosa. "How did you know to look there?" she asked.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It explains why Nkechi was ready to give up on a hot dinner.
choices.B: It shows the success of Rosa's idea, which leads to Nkechi's reaction.
choices.C: It describes how Rosa first learned to find dry wood.
choices.D: It reveals that Nkechi finally lit the fire without any help.

explanation.why: Rosa finds dry wood inside a log, and the underlined sentence tells the outcome: "small flames were curling around the twigs." The next sentences show Nkechi staring and asking how Rosa knew where to look. The sentence gives the result that causes her reaction.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Nkechi's reason for giving up, matches dying against wet sticks, appears in the first sentence.
explanation.B: Correct. The sentence reports that Rosa's dry wood worked, which is why Nkechi stares at her and asks her question.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nkechi asks how Rosa knew, but the text never answers.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The fire starts because of the dry wood Rosa found, and Nkechi's question shows she did not know the trick herself.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the first century CE, Roman engineers built an aqueduct to carry water about 50 kilometers to the city of Nîmes, in what is now southern France. The aqueduct had no pumps. Instead, its channel sloped downward very gently, dropping only about 12 meters over the whole route, so that gravity alone kept the water moving. To cross a deep river valley, the channel ran along the top of a tall stone bridge, the Pont du Gard.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe the kinds of stone used to build the Pont du Gard
choices.B: To argue that Roman aqueducts were better built than modern water systems
choices.C: To describe daily life in the city of Nîmes in the first century CE
choices.D: To explain how a Roman aqueduct carried water a long distance without pumps

explanation.why: The text says the aqueduct "had no pumps" and then explains what it used instead: a channel that sloped gently so that "gravity alone kept the water moving," plus a bridge to cross a valley. Its purpose is to explain how the aqueduct worked.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The Pont du Gard is called a "tall stone bridge," but the text does not describe the stone; the bridge is one detail of the route.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never compares the aqueduct with modern water systems.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Nîmes is named only as the aqueduct's destination; the text says nothing about life there.
explanation.D: Correct. The text explains that a gentle downward slope let gravity move water about 50 kilometers without any pumps.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Lonar Lake, in the Indian state of Maharashtra, fills a round hollow nearly two kilometers wide. Because the surrounding land is made of volcanic rock, early observers assumed that the hollow was the mouth of an ancient volcano. Later studies found something different: rock and glass in the area showed signs of a sudden, enormous shock. Scientists now agree that the hollow was made by a meteorite striking Earth.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes a meteorite strike and then explains how the strike created volcanic rock.
choices.B: It describes a lake and then explains how its water became salty.
choices.C: It presents an early explanation for a landform and then describes evidence that led to a different one.
choices.D: It compares two lakes in Maharashtra that formed in different ways.

explanation.why: After describing the hollow, the text gives the early view that it was "the mouth of an ancient volcano." Then "Later studies found something different": signs of a sudden shock, which led scientists to conclude a meteorite made it. The text moves from an old explanation to the evidence for a new one.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The volcanic rock was already there; the text never says the meteorite created it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says nothing about the lake's water being salty.
explanation.C: Correct. The volcano idea is presented first, and then shock evidence leads to the meteorite explanation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Only one lake is discussed.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Kente cloth, made by Asante and Ewe weavers in Ghana, is known for its bright, bold patterns. The cloth is woven on narrow looms that produce long strips only about ten centimeters wide. To make a larger piece, a weaver cuts the strips to equal lengths and sews them together side by side. Because each strip is carefully planned, the patterns line up across the finished cloth to form a single design.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To compare the weaving methods used by Asante and Ewe weavers
choices.B: To explain how narrow woven strips are made into a large piece of Kente cloth
choices.C: To argue that Kente cloth is more beautiful than other woven fabrics
choices.D: To describe the meanings of the colors used in Kente cloth

explanation.why: After introducing Kente cloth, the text explains a process step by step: weaving narrow strips, cutting them to equal lengths, sewing them side by side, and lining up the patterns. Its purpose is to explain how the large cloth is assembled.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Both groups are named, but the text describes one process and never compares their methods.
explanation.B: Correct. Most of the text describes how narrow strips are cut, sewn together, and planned so their patterns match.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text calls the patterns "bright, bold" but never compares Kente with other fabrics.
