It then says ecological evidence "complicates the story without wholly overturning it" and describes rats eating palm nuts. The conclusion keeps a human role ("People still cleared land") but says "human choices alone" cannot explain the loss.
explanation.A: Correct. The rat evidence adds a second cause, and the conclusion says the human-only explanation is incomplete rather than wrong.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the evidence does not "wholly" overturn the story and states that "People still cleared land."
explanation.C: Incorrect. No archaeological methods are compared; the text discusses causes of the deforestation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The settlers' arrival is mentioned only to explain where the rats came from; the text does not trace stages of clearing.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: It was past midnight when the coach set me down at the inn of St. Aurel, and the landlord, a stooped man who carried his candle as though it were heavier than it looked, led me without a word to the only chamber that remained. Above the hearth hung the portrait of a lady in the dress of a former age, whose painted eyes, by some trick of the artist, appeared to follow the light as it moved about the room. <u>I confess I laughed at myself for remarking it, and I took some pains to turn my back upon her while I undressed.</u> Of the night that followed I shall say only this: I did not sleep, and when the gray light came through the shutters, I found that I had, at some hour I cannot recollect, turned the portrait to face the wall.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It exposes a gap between the narrator's professed amusement and his conduct, anticipating his unease.
choices.B: It establishes that the narrator dismisses the portrait as harmless and is untroubled by it all night.
choices.C: It suggests that the landlord deliberately placed the narrator in a room meant to frighten him.
choices.D: It explains the method by which the artist made the eyes of the portrait appear to move.

explanation.why: In the underlined sentence the narrator says he "laughed at" himself for noticing the portrait, yet he also "took some pains" not to face it. That mismatch between words and behavior hints at hidden unease, which the final sentence confirms: he did not sleep and turned the portrait to the wall.
explanation.A: Correct. He laughs off the portrait yet avoids facing it, a tension that prepares for his sleepless night.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The final sentence shows the narrator sleepless and turning the portrait around, so he was clearly troubled.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The landlord gives him "the only chamber that remained," and nothing suggests any intent to frighten him.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The previous sentence mentions "some trick of the artist," but no method is explained anywhere.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Today the word "Luddite" is applied to anyone who distrusts new technology, a usage implying that the original Luddites, English textile workers who smashed machinery between 1811 and 1816, were simply hostile to machines. The record of their actions suggests a narrower grievance. Many of the stocking frames they broke were not new inventions at all, having been in use for more than two centuries, and raiders often wrecked the frames of employers who paid below customary rates or produced cheap, poorly made goods while sparing those of employers who did not. What the Luddites opposed, in other words, was less machinery as such than the uses to which particular employers put it, a distinction their modern namesake has largely erased.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To show that the Luddites opposed only machines that had recently been invented
choices.B: To argue that the Luddites' resistance succeeded in raising textile workers' wages
choices.C: To contend that a familiar term misrepresents the motives of the group it is named for
choices.D: To explain how the Luddites organized and carried out their raids on textile employers

explanation.why: The text opens with the modern meaning of "Luddite," which implies the original Luddites "were simply hostile to machines." It then gives evidence (old machines, selective raids) of "a narrower grievance" and concludes that the modern usage has "largely erased" that distinction. The purpose is to correct what the term suggests about the group.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text stresses that many frames they broke had been in use for more than two centuries.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never says whether the raids changed wages; it discusses only what the Luddites objected to.
explanation.C: Correct. The author argues that the modern word wrongly implies a general hostility to machines that the Luddites' actions do not show.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Details about which frames were broken serve as evidence about motives; the text does not explain how raids were organized.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In 1921, returning to India by ship from a scientific meeting in England, the physicist C. V. Raman spent hours studying the deep blue of the Mediterranean. The prevailing explanation, associated with the British physicist Lord Rayleigh, held that the sea's color was largely a reflection of the blue sky. Raman doubted it. Viewing the water through a polarizing prism, which suppressed the light reflected from its surface, he found that the blue remained, and he argued that the color arose instead from light scattered by the water's own molecules. Pursuing that question, Raman and his colleagues in Calcutta spent the next several years studying how liquids scatter light, research that culminated in 1928 in the discovery of the effect that now bears his name and that earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe the instrument Raman used to observe the sea during his voyage
choices.B: To argue that the Raman effect could have been found only by studying the sea
choices.C: To trace how a challenge to an accepted explanation led to a major discovery
choices.D: To argue that Rayleigh's explanation of the blue color of the sky was mistaken

explanation.why: Raman questions the accepted view that the sea is blue because it reflects the sky, tests it with a polarizing prism, and proposes molecular scattering instead. "Pursuing that question" links this doubt to years of research that led to the 1928 discovery and a Nobel Prize. The text follows the path from one challenge to a major result.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The polarizing prism is one detail in Raman's test, not the focus of the whole text.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the sea question started Raman's research, not that it was the only possible route to the discovery.
explanation.C: Correct. Raman's doubt about the reflection explanation started the line of research that produced the Raman effect.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Rayleigh's explanation that Raman doubted concerned the color of the sea, not the sky.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: The story is often told that in 1890 a thirteen-year-old Pablo Casals, browsing in a secondhand music shop in Barcelona, rediscovered Johann Sebastian Bach's six suites for unaccompanied cello, forgotten since the composer's death. The suites had not, in fact, been lost: printed editions had circulated since the 1820s, and cello students had long worked through them. What they lacked was standing. Regarded chiefly as exercises for building technique, they were rarely performed whole before an audience. Casals studied them for more than a decade before playing them publicly, and his recordings of the complete set in the late 1930s helped establish them as concert works. His achievement, then, was not to recover the music but to change what listeners believed it was for.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes how Bach composed the suites and then traces their influence on later music for the cello.
choices.B: It recounts a popular story and then dismisses Casals's role in the suites' later fame as exaggerated.
choices.C: It recounts a popular story, confirms it with new evidence, and then explains why the suites were forgotten.
choices.D: It recounts a popular story, corrects an assumption in it, and then redefines the central figure's achievement.

explanation.why: The text opens with the story that Casals "rediscovered" forgotten suites. It corrects this ("had not, in fact, been lost"), explains that they lacked "standing," and concludes that Casals's real achievement was "to change what listeners believed it was for." The structure is story, correction, and a redefined achievement.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says nothing about how Bach composed the suites or about later music they influenced.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The author still credits Casals with helping establish the suites as concert works; only the idea of rediscovery is rejected.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text contradicts the popular story; it says the suites were never lost or forgotten.
explanation.D: Correct. The assumption that the suites were lost is corrected, and Casals's achievement is redefined as changing how the suites were seen.

items.subject: science
items.passage: In large stretches of the open ocean, the water holds plenty of nitrate and phosphate yet supports surprisingly little phytoplankton, a puzzle that oceanographers in the late 1980s traced to a scarcity of iron. Experiments since the 1990s have confirmed the diagnosis: when ships have spread dissolved iron across patches of such water, phytoplankton have bloomed within days. <u>From this result, some have drawn a proposal: fertilize the oceans with iron on a vast scale, and the resulting blooms will draw carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere.</u> The step from bloom to lasting carbon storage, however, is longer than the proposal implies. Carbon is kept out of the atmosphere for centuries only if the plankton sink into the deep ocean before being consumed, and in most experiments only a small fraction appears to have done so.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It provides evidence that adding iron to the ocean would remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere for centuries.
choices.B: It presents a proposal drawn from an experimental result, which the text then says overlooks a necessary condition.
choices.C: It states the hypothesis that the iron experiments described in the previous sentence were designed to test.
choices.D: It explains why waters rich in nitrate and phosphate nonetheless support little phytoplankton.

explanation.why: The underlined sentence turns the experimental finding (iron causes blooms) into a proposal to fight climate change. The next sentence says the step to "lasting carbon storage" is "longer than the proposal implies": the plankton must sink to the deep ocean, and in most experiments few did. So the text presents the proposal and then identifies the condition it overlooks.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The underlined sentence states a proposal, not evidence, and the text goes on to doubt that the carbon would stay out of the atmosphere.
explanation.B: Correct. The proposal assumes blooms will remove carbon, but the text explains that lasting removal also requires the plankton to sink, which rarely happened.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The experiments tested whether iron scarcity limits phytoplankton; the proposal was drawn from their results afterward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The first sentence explains the puzzle by pointing to iron scarcity; the underlined sentence describes a proposal.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Crossing the square at four o'clock, with the pigeons lifting and settling and the clock on the post office striking a quarter late, as it always had, Agnes was thinking of nothing in particular (of the price of lemons, of whether the cleaner's would have her blue coat ready) when the smell of roasting chestnuts from a cart by the fountain brought back, entire and without warning, the winter she was nine: her father's hand closed over hers inside his coat pocket, the steam of their breath, the paper cone too hot to hold. She stopped so abruptly that a man behind her stepped around her, muttering. And then the clock finished striking, and she went on, a little more slowly, toward the cleaner's.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It traces a character's idle thoughts, a memory revived by a smell, and her slightly altered return to her errand.
choices.B: It contrasts a character's errands with her father's habits and concludes that she has grown to resemble him.
choices.C: It shows a character straining to recall a memory and then succeeding only after she has left the square.
choices.D: It describes a character's memory of her father and then explains why she has avoided the square ever since.

explanation.why: Agnes begins "thinking of nothing in particular" when the chestnut smell brings back a childhood memory "entire and without warning." She stops, then continues "a little more slowly" toward the cleaner's. The text moves from ordinary thoughts, to a sudden memory, to her return to the errand with a small change in her pace.
explanation.A: Correct. Idle thoughts give way to a vivid memory, and she goes on with her errand, "a little more slowly."
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text never compares her habits to her father's or says she resembles him; it presents one memory of him.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The memory arrives suddenly and "without warning" while she is in the square; she makes no effort to recall it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Agnes crosses the square as part of an ordinary errand; nothing suggests she has avoided it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: After vast natural gas reserves were found in the northern Netherlands in 1959, gas exports brought the country a flood of foreign revenue. Yet by the 1970s, observers noticed that Dutch manufacturing was struggling, and in 1977 a British magazine coined a term for the paradox: "Dutch disease." The mechanism is now well understood. As foreign buyers acquire a country's currency to pay for its resource exports, the currency's value rises, making the country's other exports more expensive abroad; at the same time, workers and investment are drawn toward the booming sector. A resource windfall can thus weaken the very industries that might have sustained an economy after the resource runs out.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To explain how an apparent benefit can cause economic harm, using the case that named it
choices.B: To describe the discovery of natural gas reserves in the northern Netherlands in 1959
choices.C: To show that the struggles of Dutch manufacturing had causes unrelated to natural gas
choices.D: To argue that countries should avoid selling their natural resources to foreign buyers

explanation.why: The text calls the Dutch experience a "paradox": gas revenue arrived, yet manufacturing struggled. It explains the mechanism (a stronger currency and resources shifting to the booming sector) and concludes that a windfall "can thus weaken" other industries. The Netherlands is the example that gave the problem its name.
explanation.A: Correct. The text explains how a resource windfall can harm other industries, using the Dutch case that the term is named after.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The 1959 discovery is background in the first sentence; most of the text explains the mechanism.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text links the manufacturing problems directly to the effects of gas exports.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text explains a risk of resource exports; it never recommends that countries stop them.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Every winter afternoon, when the sun came low and thin through the arches of the Qissa Khwani Bazaar in Peshawar, Gul Rahim set out his books on a faded carpet and waited. He did not call to the passersby as the fruit sellers did; he held that a book which must be shouted for is not worth the reading. Students stopped, turned a page or two, and went on. A soldier once bought a volume of verse for its red binding and was gently advised to take a cheaper one with better poems. By evening Gul Rahim had generally sold nothing, and he would wrap the books again in their cloth, one by one, with the air of a man who has spent his day exactly as he wished.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To suggest that a bookseller's gentle manner hides a growing bitterness
choices.B: To portray a bookseller whose principles matter more to him than making sales
choices.C: To describe the ordinary trade of a bazaar's fruit sellers and its booksellers
choices.D: To show how a bookseller's refusal to advertise eventually brings him success

explanation.why: Gul Rahim refuses to shout for customers on principle, and he even talks a buyer into a cheaper book with "better poems." Though he "generally sold nothing," he packs up like "a man who has spent his day exactly as he wished." The passage portrays someone who values his ideas about books over making money.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The last sentence shows contentment, not hidden bitterness.
explanation.B: Correct. His refusal to advertise, his advice to the soldier, and his contentment despite poor sales all show principles valued above profit.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The fruit sellers appear only once, as a contrast that shows Gul Rahim's character.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text says he "generally sold nothing," so his methods do not bring success.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Until about 2010, the colors of extinct feathered dinosaurs were left to the imagination of illustrators. Then paleontologists, examining fossil feathers under powerful microscopes, identified melanosomes, tiny structures that hold the pigment melanin, and noticed that in living birds their shapes correspond closely to color: long, narrow melanosomes tend to produce black or gray, round ones reddish brown. By measuring fossil melanosomes, researchers reconstructed the plumage of several species. <u>The method, however, captures only part of the story of a feather's color.</u> Yellows and reds in many birds come from carotenoid pigments, which are not stored in melanosomes, and experiments simulating fossilization have shown that heat and pressure can alter melanosome shapes. Reconstructions are therefore best read as partial outlines of an animal's appearance, not finished portraits.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?

choices.A: It supports the claim that melanosome shape reliably predicts color in living birds.
choices.B: It explains how researchers worked out which melanosome shapes produce which colors.
choices.C: It introduces a limit that the text then develops to temper confidence in the results.
choices.D: It suggests that reconstructions produced by the method are almost entirely inaccurate.

explanation.why: Before the underlined sentence, the text describes the melanosome method and its successes. The underlined sentence, signaled by "however," says the method captures "only part" of the story. The next sentence gives reasons (carotenoids, changes during fossilization), and the last calls reconstructions "partial outlines," not "finished portraits."
explanation.A: Incorrect. The underlined sentence starts a discussion of the method's shortcomings rather than adding support for it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The link between shape and color is described in the second sentence; the underlined sentence turns to the method's limits.
explanation.C: Correct. The limit is explained in the following sentence, and the conclusion urges reading reconstructions as partial.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text calls the reconstructions "partial outlines," which means incomplete, not almost entirely wrong.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: In April 1855, during the Crimean War, the British photographer Roger Fenton made two exposures of the same desolate stretch of road from the same position. In one, cannonballs lie scattered across the road; in the other, the road is nearly clear and the balls lie in the ditch beside it. Which came first matters a great deal: if the empty road was photographed first, someone apparently moved the balls onto it to heighten the scene's drama. Because the pictures carry no dates, investigators have compared minute details, such as small rocks that seem to have shifted between exposures, and many now conclude that the empty road came first. Even so, that conclusion rests on inference, and the photographs themselves cannot reveal who moved the balls, or why.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It describes two images, explains why their order matters, reports a likely order, and notes what is unknown.
choices.B: It explains a photographer's wartime methods and then compares his work with that of later photographers.
choices.C: It describes two images, argues that Fenton staged both, and then explains how he arranged each scene.
choices.D: It describes two images and then argues that the order in which they were made cannot be determined.

explanation.why: The text describes the two photographs, explains that their order matters because it would show whether the scene was arranged, and reports that "many now conclude" the empty road came first. It ends by noting that the conclusion "rests on inference" and that the photos cannot show "who moved the balls, or why."
explanation.A: Correct. The text moves from the two images, to why their order matters, to the likely order, to the questions that remain.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text discusses only these two photographs and makes no comparison with later photographers.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text never says both images were staged, and it does not explain how any scene was arranged.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text reports that many investigators have reached a conclusion about the order; what remains unknown is who moved the balls and why.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Early telescopes produced images ringed with false color because glass lenses bend different colors of light by different amounts. Isaac Newton's solution was to replace the main lens with a curved mirror, which reflects all colors at the same angle. ______ his reflecting telescope produced sharper images than refracting telescopes of the same length.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: As a result,
choices.B: However,
choices.C: For example,
choices.D: Similarly,

explanation.why: The mirror reflects all colors at the same angle, so it avoids the false color that lenses cause. The last sentence states the effect of that design choice: sharper images. A cause-and-effect transition is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "As a result" shows that the sharper images were caused by using the mirror.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "However" signals a contrast, but the sharper images follow from the solution rather than contrasting with it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The last sentence is a consequence, not an example of the previous idea.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Similarly" signals a parallel idea, but the sentence describes a result.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The letter from her grandmother had been sitting on Ines's desk for three days. Every morning she picked it up, turned it over, and set it back down, telling herself she would answer it after school. ______ when she finally sat down to write, the words came so easily that she filled two pages before dinner.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For example,
choices.B: However,
choices.C: Similarly,
choices.D: In addition,

explanation.why: Ines puts off answering the letter for three days, which suggests she expects writing it to be hard. The last sentence says the opposite happened: "the words came so easily." A contrast transition is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The last sentence is not an example of Ines putting the letter aside; it describes what happened when she stopped putting it aside.
explanation.B: Correct. "However" signals the contrast between her days of delay and how easily the letter was written once she began.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Similarly" signals that the next idea is like the previous one, but writing easily is unlike avoiding the letter.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "In addition" adds another point of the same kind, but the last sentence reverses the expectation set up earlier.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sea otters eat large numbers of sea urchins, spiny animals that graze on the stalks of giant kelp. Along the coast of central California, otters keep urchin populations small enough that kelp can grow faster than it is eaten. ______ kelp forests where otters live tend to be dense and tall, while nearby areas without otters are often bare rock covered with urchins.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: However,
choices.B: Likewise,
choices.C: Nevertheless,
choices.D: As a result,

explanation.why: The second sentence explains a cause: otters keep urchins few, so kelp "can grow faster than it is eaten." The last sentence describes the effect that follows: dense kelp where otters live and bare rock where they do not. A cause-and-effect transition is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The last sentence contains a contrast between two areas, but it does not contrast with the sentence before it; it follows from it. This is the most tempting trap.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Likewise" introduces a similar, separate point, but the last sentence is the outcome of the otters' feeding, not a parallel to it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Nevertheless" means "in spite of that," but dense kelp is exactly what you would expect when urchins are kept in check.
explanation.D: Correct. "As a result" shows that the dense kelp forests are the effect of otters keeping urchin numbers low.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In the dry regions of western India, communities once built stepwells: deep stone structures in which long flights of stairs lead down to the water. Some of these wells were far more than practical sources of water; they were elaborately decorated works of art. ______ Rani ki Vav in Patan, Gujarat, built in the eleventh century, has walls lined with hundreds of carved stone figures arranged along its descending levels.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For example,
choices.B: In contrast,
choices.C: As a result,
choices.D: Even so,

explanation.why: The second sentence makes a general claim: some stepwells "were elaborately decorated works of art." The last sentence describes one particular stepwell with hundreds of carved figures, which illustrates that claim. A transition that introduces an example is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "For example" introduces Rani ki Vav as a specific case of a decorated stepwell.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Rani ki Vav agrees with the claim about decorated wells; it does not contrast with it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The carvings at Rani ki Vav are not caused by the fact that some stepwells were decorated; they are an instance of it. This is a tempting trap because the two ideas are closely connected.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Even so" signals something true despite the previous point, but the last sentence supports the previous point.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Climate models that simulate the circulation of the Atlantic Ocean have grown steadily more sophisticated over recent decades, and most now reproduce, with reasonable fidelity, the broad pattern of the Gulf Stream carrying warm surface water northward along the coast of North America. ______ many of these models still place the point at which the current turns away from the coast too far north, an error that leaves simulated waters off New England several degrees warmer than measurements from ships and satellites indicate.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Instead,
choices.B: For instance,
choices.C: However,
choices.D: As a result,

explanation.why: The first sentence credits the models with reproducing the Gulf Stream's broad pattern. The second sentence introduces a limitation that exists alongside that success: the models still misplace where the current leaves the coast. The transition must signal a contrast without suggesting that the success was rejected or replaced.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the models do the misplacing in place of reproducing the broad pattern, but the text says they do reproduce it. The error is an exception within that success, not a replacement for it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Placing the current too far north is an error, so it cannot be an example of the models' fidelity.
explanation.C: Correct. "However" signals that, despite the models' overall success, a specific error remains.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The error is not caused by the models' growing sophistication or by their reproducing the broad pattern.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Earthen architecture poses obvious practical difficulties for those who build and maintain it. Walls of sun-dried mud brick erode under heavy rain and must be replastered at regular intervals, a labor-intensive task that in some towns of the West African Sahel is carried out communally every year. ______ many builders across the region have continued to choose earth over concrete, valuing walls whose thickness and mass slow the passage of heat and keep interiors noticeably cooler during the hottest hours of the day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Accordingly,
choices.B: Nevertheless,
choices.C: Instead,
choices.D: For example,

explanation.why: The first two sentences describe the drawbacks of mud brick: it erodes and needs regular, labor-intensive repair. The last sentence says builders keep choosing it anyway because of a benefit. The transition must signal that something remains true in spite of the drawbacks just described.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Accordingly" means "for that reason," but the drawbacks are not the reason builders choose mud brick; they choose it despite them.
explanation.B: Correct. "Nevertheless" shows that builders keep using earth in spite of the erosion and repair work described earlier.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Instead" signals that one thing replaces another, but the text names nothing the builders rejected in favor of earth before this sentence. It is contrast-like, but it does not fit the concession here.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Choosing earth over concrete is not an example of the practical difficulties; it is a response to them.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Although the script of the Indus civilization remains undeciphered, leaving historians without written records of how its cities were organized, the physical remains of sites such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, in present-day Pakistan, attest to a remarkable degree of standardization. Among the most telling evidence are the bricks themselves, which, whether fired in kilns or dried in the sun, were molded in a single, fixed proportion across settlements hundreds of kilometers apart. ______ a brick's thickness, width, and length stand in a ratio of 1:2:4 regardless of its overall size.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Moreover,
choices.B: Nevertheless,
choices.C: Consequently,
choices.D: Specifically,

explanation.why: The second sentence says the bricks were molded in "a single, fixed proportion" but does not say what that proportion is. The last sentence supplies exactly that detail: 1:2:4. A transition that introduces a precise statement of something just mentioned in general terms is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Moreover" adds a further point, but the last sentence does not add new evidence of standardization; it states exactly what the "single, fixed proportion" was. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The ratio does not contrast with the claim about a fixed proportion; it confirms and spells it out.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The ratio is not a result of the bricks being molded in a fixed proportion; it is the proportion.
explanation.D: Correct. "Specifically" signals that the last sentence states precisely what the "single, fixed proportion" was.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Linguists have long described the relationship between most words and the things they name as arbitrary. Apart from a small class of imitative words, such as "buzz" and "hiss," whose sounds echo what they denote, nothing about a word's sound follows from any property of the thing it refers to: the plant that English speakers call a "tree" is an "arbre" to speakers of French and a "Baum" to speakers of German, and none of these names fits the plant better than the others. ______ for the great majority of words, the pairing of sound and meaning rests on no natural connection, only on the agreement of a language's speakers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For instance,
choices.B: Specifically,
choices.C: In other words,
choices.D: Similarly,

explanation.why: The text opens with a technical claim, that the link between words and meanings is "arbitrary," and then illustrates it with "tree," "arbre," and "Baum." The last sentence returns to the general claim and states it again in plainer terms: the pairing rests on agreement, not on any natural connection. A restatement transition is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The last sentence is a general statement about "the great majority of words," not a particular example; the examples came in the sentence before.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Specifically" would introduce a narrower, more detailed point, but the last sentence moves from the detailed tree example back to a broad summary. This is the closest near miss.
explanation.C: Correct. "In other words" signals that the last sentence restates what "arbitrary" means for most words.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Similarly" introduces a separate case that resembles the previous one, but the last sentence describes the same case, not a parallel one.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Maple syrup begins as sap, a thin, slightly sweet liquid that flows inside sugar maple trees in early spring. Producers first collect the sap through small taps drilled into the trunks. ______ they boil the sap for hours until most of its water evaporates and a thick, sweet syrup remains. About 40 liters of sap are needed to make a single liter of syrup.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For example,
choices.B: In contrast,
choices.C: Similarly,
choices.D: Afterward,

explanation.why: The text describes the steps in making maple syrup. Producers "first collect the sap," and the next sentence describes what they do with it once it has been collected: boil it. A transition that shows the next step in a sequence is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Boiling the sap is not an example of collecting it; it is a separate, later step.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "In contrast" signals a difference, but boiling does not contrast with collecting; it follows it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Similarly" signals a step like the one before, but boiling is a different kind of step that comes next.
explanation.D: Correct. "Afterward" shows that boiling the sap is the step that comes after collecting it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Almost every national flag in the world is a rectangle, although the proportions of width to height vary from one country to another. ______ the flag of Nepal is shaped like two triangles stacked one on top of the other. The upper triangle holds a white moon, and the lower triangle holds a white sun.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For example,
choices.B: In addition,
choices.C: However,
choices.D: As a result,

explanation.why: The first sentence says that almost every national flag is a rectangle. The next sentence describes a flag that is not a rectangle at all: Nepal's flag is made of two triangles. A transition that introduces a contrast, here an exception to the general pattern, is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A flag made of triangles is not an example of a rectangular flag; it is an exception to that pattern.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "In addition" adds a similar point, but Nepal's flag goes against the pattern rather than adding to it.
explanation.C: Correct. "However" signals that Nepal's triangular flag differs from the rectangular flags described first.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Most flags being rectangles does not cause Nepal's flag to be triangular.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Many desert animals avoid the fierce heat of the day by staying out of the sun until evening. ______ the fennec fox, a small fox of the Sahara, spends hot days resting in a cool underground den and comes out to hunt insects and rodents after dark.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For example,
choices.B: However,
choices.C: Instead,
choices.D: As a result,

explanation.why: The first sentence makes a general statement: many desert animals stay out of the sun until evening. The second sentence describes one particular animal, the fennec fox, that does exactly this. A transition that introduces an example is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "For example" introduces the fennec fox as one desert animal that avoids the daytime heat.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The fennec fox's behavior agrees with the general statement; it does not contrast with it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the fox does something in place of what was just described, but the fox does the same thing.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The fox's habits are not caused by other animals avoiding the heat; they are one case of that behavior.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Roman engineers laid their main roads in several layers of stone and gravel, which gave each road a firm base that did not sink in wet weather. ______ they built the surface of the road slightly higher in the middle than at the edges, so that rainwater ran off into ditches at the sides instead of collecting in puddles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Instead,
choices.B: For example,
choices.C: In addition,
choices.D: However,

explanation.why: The first sentence describes one feature of Roman roads: their layered base. The second sentence describes another, separate feature: a surface raised in the middle to shed rain. A transition that adds a further point is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the engineers raised the middle of the road in place of laying layers, but they did both.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A raised surface is not an example of a layered base; it is a different feature.
explanation.C: Correct. "In addition" adds a second feature of Roman road building to the first one.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The second feature does not contrast with the first; both help the roads stand up to wet weather.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: The water of the mountain lake was so cold that Matteo's toes ached the moment he stepped in. All he wanted was to run back to the warm towel he had left on the shore. ______ he had promised his older sister that he would swim out to the wooden raft before the summer ended, so he took a deep breath and waded in up to his waist.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For example,
choices.B: Similarly,
choices.C: Even so,
choices.D: As a result,

explanation.why: The first two sentences say the water was painfully cold and Matteo wanted to leave. The last sentence says he went into the water anyway because of a promise. A transition that shows he acted in spite of what was just described is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. His promise is not an example of wanting to run back to the shore; it works against that wish.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Similarly" signals a matching idea, but wading in is the opposite of running back to the towel.
explanation.C: Correct. "Even so" shows that Matteo waded in despite the cold and his wish to return to his towel.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The cold water and Matteo's wish to leave did not cause him to wade in; he waded in despite them.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Koalas, which live in the eucalyptus forests of eastern Australia, are folivores. ______ they feed almost entirely on leaves, mainly those of eucalyptus trees. Because these leaves provide little energy and are hard to digest, koalas spend most of the day, often 18 hours or more, sleeping or resting.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Finally,
choices.B: However,
choices.C: For example,
choices.D: In other words,

explanation.why: The first sentence uses a technical term: koalas are "folivores." The next sentence explains in plain words what that means: they eat almost nothing but leaves. A transition that restates an idea more simply is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Finally" signals the last step or point in a series, but the sentence explains the term just used.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Eating leaves does not contrast with being a folivore; it is what being a folivore means.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Feeding on leaves is not one example of being a folivore; it is the definition of the term. This is the most tempting trap.
explanation.D: Correct. "In other words" signals that the sentence restates "folivores" in plainer language.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Much of Bangladesh lies on low, flat land crossed by large rivers, and during the monsoon season these rivers often overflow their banks. ______ many families in rural areas build their homes on raised platforms of packed earth, which help keep floors and stored grain dry when the water rises.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Therefore,
choices.B: In contrast,
choices.C: For example,
choices.D: Similarly,

explanation.why: The first sentence explains a problem: rivers in low-lying Bangladesh often flood. The second sentence describes what families do because of that problem: they raise their homes on earth platforms. A cause-and-effect transition is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "Therefore" shows that families build raised homes because the rivers often flood.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Building raised homes does not contrast with the flooding; it is a response to it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A raised home is not an example of a river overflowing; it is a way of dealing with floods.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Similarly" signals a parallel fact, but the second sentence describes a result of the first.

items.subject: science
items.passage: African elephants have enormous ears, which they flap to release body heat in the hot savanna. ______ Asian elephants have much smaller, rounder ears. The two species also differ in their trunks: an African elephant's trunk ends in two fingerlike tips, while an Asian elephant's trunk ends in only one.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: In addition,
choices.B: As a result,
choices.C: In contrast,
choices.D: For example,

explanation.why: The first sentence says African elephants have enormous ears. The second says Asian elephants have much smaller ears, and the third sentence notes that the two species "also differ." A transition that signals a difference is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "In addition" adds a similar point, but the sentence points out a difference between the species.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The size of African elephants' ears does not cause Asian elephants to have smaller ones.
explanation.C: Correct. "In contrast" signals the difference between the large ears of African elephants and the smaller ears of Asian elephants.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Asian elephants' small ears are not an example of African elephants' large ears.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Most painters work with a brush on a canvas that stands upright on an easel, but some artists have found very different ways to apply paint. ______ the American painter Jackson Pollock often spread his canvas flat on the floor of his studio and dripped or poured paint onto it from sticks and cans.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: As a result,
choices.B: For instance,
choices.C: Similarly,
choices.D: However,

explanation.why: The first sentence ends by saying that some artists have found "very different ways to apply paint." The second sentence describes one artist who did so: Pollock dripped and poured paint onto a canvas on the floor. A transition that introduces an example is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Other artists' methods did not cause Pollock's method; his method is one case of them.
explanation.B: Correct. "For instance" introduces Pollock as one artist who found a very different way to apply paint.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Similarly" would compare Pollock to an artist already described, but no particular artist has been described yet.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Pollock's method agrees with the idea that some artists work differently, so there is no contrast.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A frog begins life as an egg laid in water. The egg hatches into a tadpole, which breathes through gills and swims by moving its long tail. ______ the tadpole grows legs, its tail shrinks, and it develops lungs. Once these changes are complete, the young frog can leave the water and breathe air.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Over time,
choices.B: In contrast,
choices.C: Instead,
choices.D: For example,

explanation.why: The text traces the stages of a frog's life in order: egg, tadpole, and then a young frog. The blank sentence describes changes that happen gradually after the tadpole stage begins. A transition that shows the passing of time in a sequence is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "Over time" shows that the tadpole's legs, shrinking tail, and lungs develop gradually after it hatches.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Growing legs and lungs is the next stage of the tadpole's development, not a contrast with it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the tadpole changes in place of hatching, but the changes come after hatching.
explanation.D: Incorrect. These changes are not an example of the tadpole breathing through gills or swimming with its tail.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Darjeeling, a district in the hills of eastern India, has tea gardens at heights of up to about 2,000 meters, where the air stays cool and is often misty. In these conditions, tea bushes grow slowly. ______ their leaves develop a light, delicate flavor that has made Darjeeling tea famous around the world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For example,
choices.B: Similarly,
choices.C: However,
choices.D: Consequently,

explanation.why: The text says the cool, misty hills make tea bushes "grow slowly." The last sentence describes what this slow growth produces: leaves with a light, delicate flavor. A cause-and-effect transition is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The flavor of the leaves is not an example of slow growth; it is a result of it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Similarly" signals a parallel point, but the sentence describes an outcome of the conditions just described.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The delicate flavor does not contrast with the slow growth; it comes from it.
explanation.D: Correct. "Consequently" shows that the delicate flavor is an effect of the bushes growing slowly.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Thandiwe held her breath as she stared at the pieces of her grandfather's favorite clay pot scattered across the kitchen floor. She was sure he would scold her for being so careless. ______ he knelt beside her, gathered up the pieces, and laughed as he told her about the time he had broken his own mother's best bowl.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Instead,
choices.B: In addition,
choices.C: As a result,
choices.D: For example,

explanation.why: Thandiwe expects her grandfather to scold her. The last sentence shows him doing something else entirely: he kindly helps her and laughs. A transition that shows something happening in place of what was expected is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "Instead" shows that the grandfather comforts Thandiwe rather than scolding her as she expected.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "In addition" would mean he did these things along with scolding her, but he does not scold her at all.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Thandiwe's fear did not cause her grandfather to laugh and help her.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Kneeling and laughing are not an example of scolding; they are the opposite of it.

items.subject: science
items.passage: A familiar saying claims that someone who cannot see well is "as blind as a bat." ______ no species of bat is actually blind. All bats can see, and many fruit bats have large eyes and find their food mainly by sight and smell rather than by echolocation.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: As a result,
choices.B: For example,
choices.C: In addition,
choices.D: However,

explanation.why: The first sentence repeats a popular saying that suggests bats are blind. The next sentence says that the saying is wrong: no bat species is blind. A transition that signals a contrast is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The saying does not cause bats to be able to see.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The fact that no bat is blind is not an example of the saying; it shows the saying is wrong.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "In addition" adds a point that agrees, but the sentence contradicts the saying.
explanation.D: Correct. "However" signals that the facts about bats contrast with the familiar saying.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Early lighthouses used oil lamps placed in front of curved mirrors, but much of the light escaped in useless directions. In 1822, the French physicist Augustin Fresnel designed a lens made of rings of glass prisms that gathered the light and bent it into a single strong beam. ______ lighthouses fitted with his lens could be seen by sailors many kilometers farther out at sea.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: As a result,
choices.B: For example,
choices.C: However,
choices.D: Similarly,

explanation.why: The second sentence explains what Fresnel's lens did: it gathered the light into "a single strong beam." The last sentence describes the effect of that stronger beam: lighthouses could be seen from much farther away. A cause-and-effect transition is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "As a result" shows that the greater visibility was caused by the lens's strong beam.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Being visible farther out at sea is not an example of the lens design; it is what the design achieved.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The greater visibility does not contrast with the lens's strong beam; it follows from it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Similarly" signals a parallel idea, but the sentence states a consequence of the invention.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Some words and phrases are palindromes. ______ they read exactly the same from right to left as they do from left to right. The words "level" and "radar" are simple palindromes, and some palindromes are whole sentences, such as "Never odd or even." Writers have long enjoyed creating them as word puzzles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: However,
choices.B: For example,
choices.C: In other words,
choices.D: As a result,

explanation.why: The first sentence names a term, "palindromes," without explaining it. The next sentence explains what the term means: they read the same in both directions. A transition that restates or explains an idea is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Reading the same in both directions does not contrast with being a palindrome; it is what a palindrome is.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The sentence explains what a palindrome is; the examples ("level" and "radar") come in the sentence after it. This is the most tempting trap.
explanation.C: Correct. "In other words" signals that the sentence explains the meaning of "palindromes."
explanation.D: Incorrect. Reading the same in both directions is not a result of being a palindrome; it is the definition.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: In 1951, Abdul Sattar Edhi opened a small free medical dispensary in Karachi, Pakistan, to care for poor families in his neighborhood. ______ he and his wife, Bilquis Edhi, built the Edhi Foundation into a nationwide network of ambulances, shelters, and homes for orphans. Its ambulance service eventually became one of the largest volunteer-run ambulance networks in the world.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: In contrast,
choices.B: Later,
choices.C: Instead,
choices.D: For example,

explanation.why: The first sentence describes how Edhi's work began in 1951 with a small dispensary. The next sentence describes how that work grew into a nationwide network in the years that followed. A transition that shows a later point in time is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The network does not contrast with the dispensary; it continued and expanded the same work.
explanation.B: Correct. "Later" shows that the Edhi Foundation grew into a nationwide network after the dispensary opened in 1951.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the Edhis built the network in place of opening the dispensary, but the dispensary came first.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The nationwide network is not an example of the small dispensary; it is what the work grew into afterward.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Sound travels as a vibration passed from one particle to the next, so it needs air, water, or some other material to move through. The space between planets and stars is almost completely empty of such particles. ______ an explosion in outer space would make no sound that a distant observer could hear, no matter how bright its flash.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Similarly,
choices.B: For example,
choices.C: Therefore,
choices.D: However,

explanation.why: The text explains that sound needs particles to travel through and that space has almost none. The last sentence states what follows from these two facts: a distant observer would hear nothing from an explosion in space. A cause-and-effect transition is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Similarly" signals a parallel fact, but the sentence states a consequence.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A silent explosion is not an example of empty space; it is a conclusion drawn from the facts given.
explanation.C: Correct. "Therefore" shows that the silence of an explosion in space follows from the lack of particles there.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The silence agrees with the facts about sound and space; it does not contrast with them.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Instead of tearing down old industrial buildings, some cities have turned them into places for art. ______ the Tate Modern, one of the most visited art museums in London, occupies a former power station on the bank of the River Thames that stopped producing electricity in 1981.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: However,
choices.B: Instead,
choices.C: Similarly,
choices.D: For example,

explanation.why: The first sentence makes a general claim: some cities turn old industrial buildings into places for art. The second sentence names one specific case: a London art museum in a former power station. A transition that introduces an example is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The Tate Modern supports the general claim rather than contrasting with it.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the museum is an alternative to the practice just described, but it is a case of that practice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Similarly" would compare the Tate Modern to an earlier example, but no example has been given yet.
explanation.D: Correct. "For example" introduces the Tate Modern as one industrial building that has been turned into a place for art.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Although water covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface, very little of the planet's water is fresh water that people can readily use. ______ about 97 percent of Earth's water is salty ocean water, and roughly two-thirds of the remaining fresh water is locked away in glaciers and ice sheets. Most of what is left lies underground, so the water in lakes and rivers makes up only a tiny fraction of the total.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Nevertheless,
choices.B: Specifically,
choices.C: Moreover,
choices.D: Instead,

explanation.why: The first sentence makes a general claim: "very little" of Earth's water is usable fresh water. The next sentence gives the exact figures behind that claim: 97 percent is ocean water, and most of the rest is frozen. A transition that introduces precise details of a point just made is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Nevertheless" signals that something is true despite the previous point, but the figures confirm that point. The word "Although" earlier may make a contrast seem likely, but that contrast is already complete in the first sentence.
explanation.B: Correct. "Specifically" signals that the sentence states precisely why so little of Earth's water is usable fresh water.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Moreover" would add a new, separate point, but the figures do not add a new idea; they spell out exactly how little water is usable. This is a tempting trap.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the figures replace the earlier claim, but they support it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The penny-farthing, a bicycle popular in the 1870s and 1880s, had a front wheel that could be about 1.5 meters tall, with the rider perched high above it. A stone or bump in the road could throw the rider headfirst over the handlebars, an accident so common that it earned its own nickname: "taking a header." ______ thousands of young riders in Britain and the United States eagerly bought penny-farthings, drawn by their speed and by the thrill of riding so high above the road.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Instead,
choices.B: Still,
choices.C: For example,
choices.D: Therefore,

explanation.why: The first two sentences stress how dangerous the penny-farthing was. The last sentence says many young riders bought one anyway. A transition that shows something happened in spite of what was just described is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean riders bought penny-farthings in place of something mentioned earlier, but buying them does not replace the accidents. This is a tempting trap because the sentence does go against the danger.
explanation.B: Correct. "Still" shows that riders bought penny-farthings despite the danger of "taking a header."
explanation.C: Incorrect. Eager buyers are not an example of the bicycle's dangers.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The danger of falling would not cause people to buy the bicycle. This is tempting because the last sentence gives reasons, but those reasons are speed and thrill, not the danger.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: For much of the twentieth century, Sialkot, a city in northeastern Pakistan, was famous for its hand-stitched soccer balls, each sewn together panel by panel by skilled workers. In the 2000s, however, major tournaments began using balls whose panels were joined with heat and glue instead of thread, producing a smoother surface that hand stitching could not reproduce. ______ several Sialkot manufacturers began buying heat-bonding machines and training workers to use them; one of these firms, Forward Sports, went on to produce the official ball for the 2014 World Cup.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Nevertheless,
choices.B: Similarly,
choices.C: Consequently,
choices.D: For example,

explanation.why: The second sentence describes a change: tournaments switched to heat-bonded balls that hand stitching "could not reproduce." The last sentence describes how Sialkot manufacturers responded to that change by adopting the new method. A cause-and-effect transition is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Nevertheless" would mean the manufacturers adopted the new method in spite of the shift to bonded balls, but the shift is the reason they adopted it. This is tempting because the change threatened the city's old craft.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Similarly" would mean the manufacturers did something parallel to what tournaments did, but their action is a response to the tournaments' choice. This is tempting because both involve the new method.
explanation.C: Correct. "Consequently" shows that the manufacturers bought heat-bonding machines because tournaments had switched to bonded balls.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Buying machines is not an example of tournaments using bonded balls; it is a reaction to that change.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Scientists describe how much sunlight a surface reflects with a measure called albedo. Fresh snow has a very high albedo, reflecting up to 90 percent of the sunlight that strikes it, while open ocean water reflects less than 10 percent. ______ snow sends most of the Sun's energy back toward space, whereas dark water absorbs most of it and warms up. This difference helps explain why the loss of snow-covered Arctic sea ice can speed up warming in the region.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: For example,
choices.B: Similarly,
choices.C: In other words,
choices.D: In contrast,

explanation.why: The second sentence gives figures: snow reflects up to 90 percent of sunlight, and ocean water reflects less than 10 percent. The blank sentence says the same thing in plainer terms: snow sends most of the energy back, and water absorbs most of it. A transition that restates the previous point is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The sentence does not give an example of high or low albedo; it restates the figures just given.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Similarly" would introduce a new case like the one just described, but the sentence describes the same snow and water again.
explanation.C: Correct. "In other words" signals that the sentence explains the albedo figures in plainer language.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The sentence contains a contrast between snow and water, but the previous sentence already makes that same contrast, so the two sentences agree. This is the most tempting trap.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: Uncle Tavita had insisted on cooking the whole birthday feast himself, and all afternoon he stood over the smoking grill behind the house, turning fish and taro and refusing every offer of help. ______ inside the house, his nieces and nephews were stringing paper flowers across the ceiling as fast as they could, determined to finish before he came in to find out why everyone had grown so quiet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Meanwhile,
choices.B: For example,
choices.C: Afterward,
choices.D: As a result,

explanation.why: The first sentence shows Uncle Tavita cooking "all afternoon" outside. The second shows the children decorating inside, hurrying to finish "before he came in." Both activities happen at the same time, so a transition that shows events happening simultaneously is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "Meanwhile" shows that the children decorate inside while Tavita is still cooking outside.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The children's decorating is not an example of Tavita's cooking or of his refusing help.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Afterward" would place the decorating after the cooking, but the children are racing to finish before Tavita comes in. This is a tempting trap.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The children do not decorate because Tavita refused help; they are preparing a surprise. This is tempting because his staying outside gives them the chance, but the sentence does not present the decorating as an effect.

items.subject: science
items.passage: The thorny devil, a small, spiky lizard of the Australian desert, rarely finds standing water to drink. Its skin, however, is covered with tiny grooves that run between its scales and lead to the corners of its mouth. When the lizard stands on damp sand or is caught in the rain, water seeps into these grooves and is pulled along them, much as a paper towel draws up a spill. ______ the lizard can gather water through its skin and gulp it down without ever lowering its head to a puddle.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Thus,
choices.B: Similarly,
choices.C: For instance,
choices.D: Nevertheless,

explanation.why: The third sentence explains how water moves through the grooves in the lizard's skin toward its mouth. The last sentence states what this makes possible: the lizard can collect water without drinking from a puddle. A cause-and-effect transition is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "Thus" shows that the lizard's ability to collect water through its skin results from the grooves described before.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The paper towel comparison is already made in the previous sentence; the last sentence states a result, not another similar case. This is a tempting trap.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Gathering water is not an example of water moving through the grooves; it is the result.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Nevertheless" would mean the lizard gathers water in spite of the grooves pulling water along, but the grooves are what let it do so. The lack of standing water in the first sentence may make a contrast seem likely, but "however" in the second sentence has already answered that problem.

items.subject: humanities
items.passage: Many people think of snakes and ladders as a simple race to the finish decided entirely by the roll of a die. The game, however, descends from gyan chaupar, a board game played in India for centuries, whose boards were designed to teach moral lessons. ______ each ladder rose from a square standing for a virtue, such as generosity, while each snake slid down from a square standing for a vice, such as anger.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: However,
choices.B: For instance,
choices.C: Likewise,
choices.D: Instead,

explanation.why: The second sentence makes a general claim: gyan chaupar boards were "designed to teach moral lessons." The last sentence shows how this worked on the board: ladders started on virtues and snakes on vices. A transition that introduces an illustration of the claim is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The virtue and vice squares support the claim about moral lessons rather than contrasting with it. This is tempting because "however" appears in the sentence before.
explanation.B: Correct. "For instance" introduces the virtue and vice squares as an illustration of how the boards taught moral lessons.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Likewise" would introduce a separate, similar point, but the squares are part of the boards' design, not a parallel case.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the ladders and snakes replaced the moral lessons, but they are how the lessons were taught. This is tempting because the text already contrasts the game with a "simple race."

items.subject: science
items.passage: Dragline silk, the thread a spider uses as a safety line when it drops from a height, is remarkably strong: weight for weight, it can bear more pulling force before snapping than steel can. ______ dragline silk is highly elastic, stretching by about a quarter of its length or more before it breaks. Together, this strength and stretchiness let a web absorb the impact of a flying insect without tearing, and they have led engineers to spend decades trying to make artificial versions of the silk.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Furthermore,
choices.B: As a result,
choices.C: Specifically,
choices.D: However,

explanation.why: The first sentence describes one impressive property of dragline silk: its strength. The blank sentence describes a second, different property: its elasticity. The final sentence treats the two as qualities that work "together," so a transition that adds another point is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "Furthermore" adds the silk's elasticity as a second remarkable property alongside its strength.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The silk's strength does not cause it to stretch; the two are separate properties.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Specifically" would give precise details about the silk's strength, but elasticity is a different property. This is a tempting trap because the sentence does contain precise figures.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Elasticity is presented as another advantage that works together with strength, not as a drawback or a contrast. This is tempting if a reader assumes strong materials must be stiff, but the text does not say so.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Some public libraries in Canada and the United States now lend out tools such as drills, ladders, and sewing machines along with books. Critics argue that this stretches the idea of a library too far. Supporters reply that libraries have always existed to share resources that many people could not easily afford on their own. ______ a power drill is not a book, but for a family that needs one for a single afternoon, borrowing it serves the same purpose as borrowing an expensive reference volume.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Admittedly,
choices.B: Similarly,
choices.C: Consequently,
choices.D: Instead,

explanation.why: The last sentence continues the supporters' argument. It first grants a point that critics might make ("a power drill is not a book") and then, after "but," explains why lending drills still fits a library's purpose. A transition that concedes a point before answering it is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "Admittedly" signals that the supporters grant that a drill is not a book before arguing that lending one serves a library's purpose.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Similarly" would introduce a parallel point, but the statement "a power drill is not a book" grants a difference. This is tempting because the sentence later compares a drill to a reference volume.
explanation.C: Incorrect. A drill not being a book is not a result of libraries sharing resources. This is tempting because the sentence supports the supporters' reasoning, but its first part is a concession, not a conclusion.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the sentence replaces the supporters' view, but it continues that view.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: Botanists classify the tomato as a fruit, since it develops from the flower of the plant and contains the plant's seeds. ______ in 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled that tomatoes should be taxed as vegetables when they were brought into the country. The court reasoned that in everyday life, people serve tomatoes as part of the main meal, as they do carrots or beans, rather than as dessert, as they do most fruits.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Therefore,
choices.B: Nevertheless,
choices.C: In other words,
choices.D: For example,

explanation.why: The first sentence says that, scientifically, a tomato is a fruit. The second sentence says the Supreme Court treated it as a vegetable anyway, for everyday rather than scientific reasons. A transition that shows something is true in spite of what came before is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Botanists calling the tomato a fruit would not lead a court to rule that it is a vegetable. This is a tempting trap because the court's ruling is a decision that follows in time.
explanation.B: Correct. "Nevertheless" shows that the court classified tomatoes as vegetables despite their botanical status as fruits.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "In other words" would restate the first sentence, but calling the tomato a vegetable says the opposite of calling it a fruit. This is tempting because both sentences are about how tomatoes are classified.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The ruling is not an example of the botanical classification; it goes against it.

items.subject: history_social
items.passage: The Great Pyramid of Giza, built more than 4,500 years ago, is aligned with remarkable precision to the four cardinal directions. ______ its sides are turned away from true north-south and east-west by less than a tenth of a degree. Researchers still debate how its builders achieved such accuracy without magnetic compasses; some propose that they tracked the positions of stars, while others suggest that they used the shadow cast by the Sun on the day of an equinox.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Similarly,
choices.B: Nevertheless,
choices.C: Specifically,
choices.D: In addition,

explanation.why: The first sentence says the pyramid is aligned "with remarkable precision." The next sentence states exactly how precise the alignment is: off by less than a tenth of a degree. A transition that introduces a precise statement of a point just made is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Similarly" would introduce a different but comparable case, but the sentence is about the same pyramid's alignment.
explanation.B: Incorrect. A tiny error of alignment confirms the claim of precision rather than going against it. This is tempting because the sentence mentions how far the sides are "turned away" from true directions.
explanation.C: Correct. "Specifically" signals that the sentence states exactly how precisely the pyramid is aligned.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "In addition" would add a new, separate fact, but the sentence measures the same precision just described. This is the most tempting trap.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Ecologist Lucía Ferreyra expected that the largest parks in Buenos Aires would hold the most bird species, since bigger spaces usually offer more food and shelter. When her team surveyed 40 of the city's parks, however, a park's size turned out to matter much less than she had predicted. ______ the strongest predictor of how many species a park supported was the amount of low, dense shrubbery it contained, which gives small birds places to nest and to hide from predators.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Instead,
choices.B: Still,
choices.C: Similarly,
choices.D: For example,

explanation.why: Ferreyra predicted that park size would matter most, but size "turned out to matter much less" than expected. The last sentence names what mattered most in place of size: shrubbery. A transition that introduces an alternative to the expected explanation is needed.
explanation.A: Correct. "Instead" shows that shrubbery, rather than size, turned out to be the strongest predictor of bird species.
explanation.B: Incorrect. "Still" would mean the finding holds in spite of size mattering less, but the finding about shrubbery fits with, and explains, that result. This is tempting because the text contains a contrast with Ferreyra's expectation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Similarly" would introduce a parallel finding, but shrubbery replaces size as the main factor.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The importance of shrubbery is not an example of size mattering less; it is the factor that mattered in size's place. This is a tempting trap.

items.subject: science
items.passage: Flamingos are not born pink; their chicks hatch covered in gray or white down. The birds' famous color comes from their food. The algae and tiny brine shrimp that flamingos filter from shallow, salty lakes contain carotenoids, orange and red pigments that the birds absorb during digestion and deposit in their growing feathers, skin, and legs. ______ flamingos kept in zoos gradually turn pale unless their keepers add carotenoids to the birds' diet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: Nevertheless,
choices.B: As a result,
choices.C: Instead,
choices.D: Similarly,

explanation.why: The text explains that a flamingo's pink color comes from carotenoids in its natural food. The last sentence describes what follows when that food is missing: zoo flamingos turn pale unless carotenoids are added. A cause-and-effect transition is needed.
explanation.A: Incorrect. "Nevertheless" means "in spite of that," but fading without carotenoids is exactly what the explanation predicts, not something that happens despite it.
explanation.B: Correct. "As a result" shows that zoo flamingos fade because their color depends on pigments in their diet.
explanation.C: Incorrect. "Instead" would mean the zoo birds replace something just mentioned, but the last sentence describes a consequence of the diet explanation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. "Similarly" introduces a parallel point, but the last sentence is an outcome of the earlier explanation, not a separate, similar fact.

items.subject: literature
items.passage: For weeks, Mateo had practiced the opening of the sonata until he could play it without looking at the music. On the morning of his audition, he walked into the hall feeling calm and certain, even humming the melody under his breath. ______ the moment he sat down at the unfamiliar piano and saw the three judges watching him, his hands began to tremble, and the first notes came out stiff and uneven.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

choices.A: However,
choices.B: For instance,
choices.C: Therefore,
choices.D: In addition,

explanation.why: The first two sentences show Mateo well prepared and "calm and certain." The last sentence describes the opposite: trembling hands and stiff, uneven notes. A contrast transition is needed.
